The second: it is narrated from 'Ata' that he said: "Allah the Exalted permitted marriage to the women of the Scripture at that time only because there was a scarcity of Muslim women. As for now, there is a great abundance of them, so the need has ceased, and therefore the concession has ceased."

The third: the verses that indicate the obligation of keeping away from the disbelievers, such as His saying: ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:1], and His saying: ﴿Do not take as intimates others besides yourselves﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:118]. Also, when marriage takes place, love may grow strong and this becomes a means of the husband inclining towards her religion, and when a child is born, the child may incline towards her religion. All of this is throwing oneself into harm without need.

The fourth: His saying at the end of this verse: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deeds have become worthless, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter﴾. This is among the strongest deterrents from marrying a disbelieving woman. So if the intended meaning of His saying ﴿and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ were permission to marry a woman of the Scripture, then mentioning this verse right after it would be like a contradiction, and that is not permissible.

The second issue: if we say the intended meaning of "chaste women" is free women, then a female slave from the People of the Book is not included under the verse. If we say the intended meaning of "chaste women" is chaste women in general, then she is included. On this matter there was a disagreement between al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa. According to al-Shafi'i, it is not permissible to marry a female slave from the People of the Book. He said: "Because two kinds of deficiency are combined in her: disbelief and slavery." According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, it is permissible, and he relied on this verse on the basis that the intended meaning of "chaste women" is chaste women in general, and this matter has already been discussed.

[Page 117]

The third issue: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Hasan said: "His saying ﴿and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ includes dhimmi women and harbi (enemy, non-protected) women, so it is permissible to marry all of them." Most jurists hold that this is restricted to dhimmi women only. This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, for he said: "Among the women of the People of the Book, some are lawful for us, and some are not lawful for us." And he recited: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:29], up to His saying: ﴿until they give the jizya willingly/from their hand in humility﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:29]. So whoever gives the jizya is lawful, and whoever does not give it is not lawful.

The fourth issue: they agreed that the Magians have been given the practice of the People of the Book in taking the jizya from them, but not in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women. It is reported from Ibn al-Musayyib that he said: "If a Muslim is sick and he orders a Magian to mention Allah and slaughter, then there is no harm." Abu Thawr said: "And even if he orders him to do so while he is healthy, there is no harm."

The fifth issue: many jurists said: "Marriage to a woman of the Scripture is permitted only if she adhered to the Torah and the Gospel before the revelation of the Qur'an." They said: "The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾. So His saying 'before you' indicates that whoever adhered to the Scripture after the revelation of the Furqan (the Qur'an) has departed from the ruling of the Scripture."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿when you have given them their wages﴾. Restricting the permission to giving their wages indicates the emphasis on the obligation of paying them, and that whoever marries a woman and intends not to give her her dowry is in the position of a fornicator. And calling the mahr a "wage" indicates that the dowry is not fixed in amount, just as the minimum wage is not fixed in hiring contracts.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Chaste, not fornicating, nor taking secret lovers﴾. Al-Sha'bi said: "Zina (illicit sexual intercourse) is of two kinds: sifah (open fornication), which is zina done openly, and ittikhadh al-khidn (taking a secret lover), which is zina done in secret. Allah the Exalted prohibited both of them in this verse, and permitted enjoyment of a woman in the manner of ihsan, which is marriage."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deeds have become worthless﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, there are two views:

The first: its purpose is to encourage adherence to the obligations and rulings mentioned earlier. That is, whoever disbelieves in the laws of Allah and His obligations has failed and lost in this world and the Hereafter.

The second: al-Qaffal said: "The meaning is that although the People of the Book have obtained in this world the merit of marriage and the permission of slaughtered animals, this does not distinguish them from the polytheists in the matters of the Hereafter, or in reward and punishment. Rather, everyone who disbelieves in Allah, his deeds have become worthless in this world, and he does not reach any of the happiness of the Hereafter at all."

The second issue: His saying ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deeds have become worthless﴾ contains a difficulty, which is that disbelief is only conceivable with respect to Allah and His Messenger. As for disbelief in faith (al-iman), it is impossible. For this reason the exegetes differed in several views:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in the faith﴾ means whoever disbelieves in Allah." This metaphor is acceptable because He is the Lord of faith, and the lord of a thing may be named by that thing's name in a metaphorical sense.

The second: al-Kalbi said: "﴿Whoever disbelieves in the faith﴾ means: in the testimony that there is no god but Allah." So he made the word of monotheism faith, since belief in it is obligatory, and faith is among its necessary consequences according to the command of the Law, and attributing the name of a thing to its necessary consequence is a well-known metaphor.

The third: Qatada said: "Some Muslims said: 'How can we marry their women when they are not upon our religion?' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse, meaning: whoever disbelieves in what has been revealed in the Qur'an, then he is such-and-such." So He called the Qur'an "faith," because it is what contains the explanation of everything necessary for faith.

The third issue: those who affirm the nullification of deeds (al-ihbat) said: The meaning of His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deeds have become worthless﴾ is that the punishment for his disbelief removes whatever reward he had obtained for his faith. Those who deny the view of nullification of deeds said: Its meaning is that the deeds he performed after that faith have perished and been lost. For he only performs those deeds after faith because he believes they are better than faith. When the matter is not so, but rather they are wasted and void, then those deeds are void in themselves. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿his deeds have become worthless﴾.

* *

The fourth issue: His saying the Exalted: ﴿and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter﴾ is conditioned on a condition not mentioned in the verse, which is that he dies upon that disbelief. For if he repents from disbelief, he will not be among the losers in the Hereafter. The evidence that this condition is necessary is His saying: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:217], and so on.

﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe over your heads and your feet up to the ankles﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, began the surah with His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts﴾. This is because a covenant of lordship (al-ruboobiyya) and a covenant of servanthood (al-ubudiyya) took place between the Lord and the servant. So His saying ﴿fulfil the contracts﴾ is a demand from Him, exalted is He, that His servants fulfil the covenant of servanthood. It is as if it were said: "Our God, the covenant is of two kinds: the covenant of lordship from You and the covenant of servanthood from us. You are more worthy to take the lead in fulfilling the covenant of lordship and of kindness." Then He, exalted is He, said: "Yes, I first fulfil the covenant of lordship and generosity." It is well known that the benefits of this world are confined to two kinds: the pleasures of food and the pleasures of marriage. So He, glory be to Him, was thorough in explaining what is lawful and unlawful of foods and of marriage. Since the need for food is greater than the need for a spouse, He therefore gave precedence to explaining food over marriage. At the completion of this explanation, it is as if He were saying: "I have fulfilled the covenant of lordship concerning what is sought in this world of benefits and pleasures, so you occupy yourself in this world with fulfilling the covenant of servanthood." Since the greatest acts of obedience after faith is the prayer (al-salah), and the prayer cannot be established except with purity (al-tahara), He, exalted is He, therefore began by mentioning the conditions of ablution (al-wudu'), and He said: ﴿O you who believe, when you stand up for prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows﴾. On the verse there are the following issues:

**Issue 1:** The intention is not the act of standing itself. Two arguments support this:

The first: if standing were meant, it would follow that ablution comes after prayer, and that is invalid by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus).

The second: they agreed that if someone washed the limbs before prayer while sitting or lying down, he would have discharged the obligation. Rather, what is meant is: *when you prepare yourselves* for standing up to pray and intend to do so. This is a metaphor, but a well-known and customary one, and two arguments support it:

The first: the firm intention is the cause of the act, and using the name of the cause for the effect is a well-known metaphor (*majaz*).

The second: the words of God Most High, ﴿Men are the protectors (*qawwamun*) of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 34]. The meaning here is not standing upright. One says, "So-and-so is *qa'im* (standing/responsible) for that matter," and God says, ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. Here "standing" absolutely does not mean being upright, but rather being determined on that act, prepared for it, and ready to bring it into existence. Likewise here, the words ﴿When you stand up for prayer﴾ mean: when you intend to perform the prayer and engage in establishing it.

* * *

**Issue 2:** Some people said: the command to perform ablution follows the command to pray and is not an independent obligation in itself. They argued that the words ﴿When you stand up for prayer, wash﴾ form a conditional sentence, in which the condition is standing up for prayer and the consequence is the command to wash. What is conditional on a thing by a conditional particle is absent when the condition is absent. Therefore this implies that the command to ablution is subordinate to the command to pray.

Others said: the purpose of ablution is purity (*taharah*), and purity is intended in itself, as shown by the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an, it is God's words at the end of the verse: ﴿But He wants to purify you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. As for the hadith, it is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Religion is built upon cleanliness," and he said: "My community will come on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of ablution." Also, many reports state that ablution is a cause for the forgiveness of sins. And God knows best.

* * *

**Issue 3:** Dawud (al-Zahiri) said: ablution is obligatory for every prayer. Most jurists said it is not obligatory. Dawud argued from this verse in two ways:

The first: the apparent wording of the verse indicates this. The words ﴿When you stand up for prayer﴾ either mean one particular standing and one particular prayer, in which case the meaning is specific, or they mean generality. The first is invalid for several reasons:

First: under this interpretation the verse becomes *mujmal* (ambiguous), because the specific occasion is not mentioned in the verse. Taking the verse as ambiguous removes it from its benefit, and that contradicts the default principle.

Second: it is valid to add an exception (*istithna'*) to it, and the function of an exception is to exclude what would otherwise be included, which requires generality.

Third: the community agrees that the command to ablution is not restricted in this verse to a single occasion or a single person. Since this is invalid, it must be understood in its generality, at every standing up for prayer. For if this verse were not understood in this sense, its indication of what God intends would depend on other proofs, and this verse alone would become ambiguous. We have shown that ambiguity contradicts the default principle. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the apparent meaning of this verse indicates the obligation of ablution at every standing up for prayer.

The second way: we derive this generality from the implication of the wording. Prayer is an act of service to the Worshipped, and engagement in service must be accompanied by the greatest degree of honour the servant can give. Among the forms of honour is that he comes to the service in the state of utmost cleanliness. There is no doubt that renewing ablution at every standing up for prayer is an intensification of cleanliness. It is known that mentioning a ruling immediately after a descriptive attribute indicates that the ruling is caused by that suitable attribute, and this implies that the ruling is general with the generality of the attribute. Thus ablution becomes obligatory at every standing up for prayer.

Then Dawud said: it is not permissible to say that an irregular reading (*qira'ah shadhdhah*) has come: "When you stand up for prayer while you are in a state of minor impurity (*muhdithun*)," nor to say that we abandon the apparent meaning of this verse because a solitary report (*khabar al-wahid*) contradicts it.

He said: As for the irregular reading, it is rejected with certainty. For if we allowed the existence of a Qur'an not transmitted by *tawatur* (mass, continuous transmission), it would follow that the whole Qur'an could be doubted, that is, one could say that the Qur'an was much more than it is now but was not transmitted. Also, the knowledge of the rules of ablution is one of the matters most widely needed, and one of the most pressing matters every person needs to know. Therefore, if that were Qur'an, it could not have remained in the category of an anomalous reading.

As for relying on a solitary report, he said: this would imply the abrogation (*naskh*) of the Qur'an by a report, and that is not permissible.

**Issue 4:** The jurists said: the word *idha* ("when") does not indicate generality. The evidence is that if a man says to his wife, "If you enter the house, you are divorced," and she enters once, she is divorced; but if she enters a second time, she is not divorced again. This shows that the word *idha* does not indicate generality. Likewise, if a master says to his slave, "When you enter the market, go to so-and-so and tell him such-and-such," this only commands the act once.

Know that Dawud's position in the question of divorce is not known; perhaps he holds that it indicates generality. He could also say: we have shown that the word *idha* in this verse indicates generality, because the obligations stated in the Qur'an are founded on repetition, and the situation in the cases you mentioned is not like that. The clear indications show that the command in those cases is not founded on repetition.

As for the jurists, they supported their view with what is related: that the Prophet, peace be upon him, "used to perform ablution for every prayer, except on the day of the Conquest (*Fath*) of Mecca, when he prayed all the prayers with one ablution." 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "So I asked him about that, and he said: 'I did it deliberately, O 'Umar.'"

Dawud answered: we have mentioned that a solitary report does not abrogate the Qur'an. Also, this report indicates that he, peace be upon him, was constant in renewing ablution for every prayer, and this implies that it is obligatory for us, based on God's words: ﴿follow him﴾. It remains to be said that this report also states that he left that practice on the day of the Conquest. We say: since there is a conflict, the preference lies with us for several reasons:

First: suppose that renewing ablution for each prayer is not obligatory but is recommended (*mandub*). It is apparent that the Messenger, peace be upon him, used to increase acts of worship on the day of the Conquest and did not reduce them, because that day was the day of the completion of God's favour upon him, and an increase of divine favour corresponds to an increase of acts of worship, not a decrease.

Second: caution (*ihtiyat*) undoubtedly lies on our side, so it is preferable, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt."

Third: the apparent meaning of the Qur'an takes precedence over a solitary report.

Fourth: the Qur'an's indication for our position is verbal (*lafziyyah*), while the indication of the report you transmitted for your position is practical (*fi'liyyah*). A verbal indication is stronger than a practical indication, because a verbal indication does not need a practical one, but not vice versa.

This is what there is in this question, and God knows best.

The strongest argument for establishing the well-known school (of the majority) is to say: if ablution were obligatory for every prayer, the cause of ablution would be standing up for prayer, and nothing else would have any effect in making ablution obligatory. But this is invalid, because God said at the end of this verse: ﴿Or if any of you comes from the toilet, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾. He made tayammum obligatory on the one who has relieved himself and on the one who has had intercourse when he finds no water. This indicates that each of these two is a cause for the obligation of purification when water is available. This implies that the obligation of ablution may arise from a cause other than standing up for prayer, and this supports what we have said.

* * *

**Issue 5:** Scholars discussed whether this verse indicates that ablution is a condition (*shart*) for the validity of prayer. The more correct view is that it does, for two reasons:

The first: God linked the act of prayer to purification with water. Then He explained that when water is unavailable, prayer is valid only with tayammum. If ablution were not a condition, this would not be valid.

The second: God only commanded prayer together with ablution. So one who performs prayer without ablution has abandoned what was commanded, and one who abandons what was commanded deserves punishment. Remaining under the burden of obligation has no meaning except this. Once this is established, it becomes clear that ablution is a condition for the validity of prayer according to the implication of this verse.

* * *

**Issue 6:** Al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) said: intention (*niyyah*) is a condition for the validity of ablution and bathing (*ghusl*). Abu Hanifah (may God have mercy on him) said: it is not so.

Each of them argues for his position from the apparent meaning of this verse.

As for al-Shafi'i, he said: ablution is something commanded, and everything commanded must be done with intention. Therefore ablution must be done with intention. Once this is established, it must be a condition, because no one distinguishes between them. We say that ablution is commanded because of God's words: ﴿wash your faces and your hands to the elbows, and wipe your heads and your feet to the ankles﴾. There is no doubt that the words "wash" and "wipe" are commands. And we say that everything commanded must be done with intention because of God's words: ﴿They were only commanded to worship God, sincerely devoting religion to Him﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. The *lam* in His words "*li-ya'budu*" (in order that they may worship) is apparently a *lam* of causation (*ta'lil*). But ascribing causes to God's rulings is impossible, so it must be understood as the *ba'* (meaning "by/with"), as is known from the permissibility of one preposition standing in place of another. The meaning becomes: they were commanded only *to* worship God sincerely devoting religion to Him. Sincerity (*ikhlas*) is an expression for pure intention, and when pure intention is required, the basic intention is also required. We have thoroughly examined this argument in the commentary on God's words: ﴿They were only commanded to worship God sincerely devoting religion to Him﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5], so refer to it for further precision. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that every ablution is something commanded, and that everything commanded must be done with intention. It follows with certainty that every ablution must be done with intention. At most, our statement "everything commanded must be done with intention" is restricted in some cases, but we established this premise by the general text, and the general text is a valid proof in whatever is not the object of specification.

As for Abu Hanifah, he argued from this verse that intention is not a condition for the validity of ablution. He said: God obligated washing the four limbs in this verse and did not obligate intention in it. Therefore imposing intention is an addition to the text, and an addition to the text is abrogation (*naskh*). Abrogating the Qur'an by a solitary report or by analogy (*qiyas*) is not permissible.

Our answer: we have shown that we imposed intention in ablution by the indication of the Qur'an.

* * *

**Issue 7:** Al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) said: sequence (*tartib*) is a condition for the validity of ablution. Malik and Abu Hanifah (may God have mercy on them both) said: it is not so. Al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) argued from this verse for his view in several ways:

The first: God's words ﴿When you stand up for prayer, wash your faces﴾ require beginning with washing the face, because the *fa'* (the particle of sequence, meaning "then") indicates succession. And if sequence is obligatory for this limb, it is obligatory for the others, because no one distinguishes between them.

If they say: the *fa'* of succession has entered only into the whole of these actions, so the sentence is like saying: "When you stand up for prayer, then perform this whole set of actions together."

"Qultu" ... The fa' of sequence entered upon "the face" because this fa' is attached to the mention of the face. Then, through its entry upon the face, this fa' entered upon the other acts, and on this basis the entry of the fa' upon washing the face is the basic one, while its entry upon the totality of these acts is subordinate to its entry upon washing the face. There is no contradiction between requiring the priority of washing the face and requiring the totality of these acts. We have considered the indication of this fa' in both the basic and the subordinate sense, whereas you have disregarded it in the basic sense and considered it in the subordinate sense; so our position is preferable.

The second argument: We say that the mention began with the face, so the beginning in action must also be with it, based on His saying: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112], and based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Begin with what Allah began with." Although this report was transmitted in the context of as-Safa and al-Marwa, the lesson lies in the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. At most, it is specified in some instances, but a general text is binding in every case outside the scope of the specification.

The third: He, exalted is He, mentioned these members neither in the order required by common sense nor in the order required by the Shariah, and this indicates that the order is obligatory. The proof of the first premise: the order required by common sense is to begin from the head descending to the foot, or from the foot ascending to the head, and the order mentioned in the verse is not like that. As for the order required by the Shariah, it is to combine the members that are washed and to separate the member that is wiped from them, and the verse is not like that, for He has inserted the wiped member among the washed ones.

Having established this, we say: this indicates that the order is obligatory. The evidence is that neglecting order in speech is disapproved, so it is necessary to exempt the speech of Allah, exalted is He, from it. The application of this is abandoned in cases where it is possible that it is a signal that the order is obligatory; thus it remains, in other cases, in accordance with the original rule.

The fourth: The obligation of ablution is not rationally intelligible in its meaning, and this requires that it be performed in the manner stated in the text.

The explanation of the first point is in several aspects:
One: the impurity (hadath) issues from one place, while washing is obligatory on another place, and this is contrary to reason.
Two: the members of one who is in a state of minor impurity are pure, by His saying: ﴿The polytheists are only impure﴾ [at-Tawbah: 28], and "innama" signifies restriction, and by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The believer does not become impure, alive or dead." And purifying the pure is impossible.
Three: the Shariah established tayammum in place of ablution, and there is no doubt that it is the opposite of cleanliness and freshness.
Four: the Shariah established wiping over the leather socks in place of washing, and it is known that this does not at all produce cleanliness in the limb itself.
Five: turbid, stagnant water produces purification, while rose-water does not; thus it is established by this that ablution is not rationally intelligible in its meaning. And when this is established, it is necessary to rely upon the locus of the text, for it is possible that the order mentioned is observed either purely as an act of devotion or for hidden wisdoms that we do not know. For this reason we obligated observing the prescribed order in the pillars of prayer. Rather, here it is more fitting, because when He, exalted is He, mentioned the pillars of prayer in His Book in order, and mentioned the members of ablution in this verse in order, then since order is obligatory there, it is more so here.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, argued by this verse for his position, and said: "The waw does not necessitate order, so the verse is free of an obligation of order; if we say that order is obligatory, that would be an addition to the text, which is abrogation, and that is impermissible."

Our answer: We have shown the indication of the verse to the obligation of order from aspects other than the argument that waw necessitates order. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Issue Seventh: Continuity (muwalah) in the acts of ablution is not a condition for its validity according to the new opinion of ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said that it is a condition.

Our proof: He, exalted is He, obligated these acts, and there is no doubt that the obligation of them is a common element between obligating them in continuity and obligating them in separation. Then He, exalted is He, ruled at the end of this verse that this common element produces the attainment of purity, by His saying: ﴿But He desires to purify you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. Thus it is established that ablution without continuity produces the attainment of purity, and it is therefore necessary that we say prayer with it is permissible, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The key to prayer is purity."

* * *

Issue Eighth: Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What exits from other than the two passages nullifies ablution. Ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It does not nullify it.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, argued by this verse, saying: its apparent meaning requires performing ablution for every prayer, as we explained earlier. This was set aside when no impure exit comes out of the body, so it remains in force when an impure exit comes out. Ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, relied on what is reported: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) had cupping done, prayed, and did no more than wash the traces of his cupping sites."

* * *

Issue Ninth: Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no ablution due to what exits from the two passages if it is not habitual and is clean, in the case of istihadah blood. Rabi'ah said: There is also no ablution due to istihadah blood. Our proof is holding to the generality of the verse.

* * *

Issue Tenth: Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Laughter during prayer that includes bowing and prostration nullifies ablution. The others said: It does not nullify it. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, has the argument of holding to the generality of the verse, as we have established.

* * *

Issue Eleventh: Ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Touching a woman nullifies ablution. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It does not nullify it. Ash-Shafi'i may hold to the generality of the verse. He said: This generality is reinforced by the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or you have touched women﴾. The opponent's proof is a single report (khabar wahid) or analogy (qiyas), and so it does not become a counter-evidence against it.

* * *

Issue Twelfth: Touching the private part nullifies ablution according to ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said it does not nullify it. Ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, may hold to the generality of the verse, and this generality is reinforced by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever touches his penis, let him perform ablution." The report on which the opponent relies is against the generality of the verse, so the preference lies with us.

* * *

Issue Thirteenth: If there is impurity on his body or face and he washes it and intends purification from the minor impurity by that washing, is his ablution valid? I have not seen this issue addressed in the books of our companions. What I say is: it suffices, because He commanded washing in His saying: ﴿Wash﴾, and he has done it, so he is discharged of the obligation. Because when he needs to cool down and cleanse, if he intends it, his ablution is valid; likewise here. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Actions are judged by intentions, and every person gets what he intended." This person intended, so what he intended must be attained for him. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Issue Fourteenth: If he stands under a spout until water flows over him and he intends lifting the minor impurity, is his ablution valid or not? It may be said: It is not valid, because He commanded washing, and washing is an act, and he has not performed an act. And it may be said: It is valid, because washing is an expression for the action that results in being washed, and standing under the spout results in being washed, so that standing is washing.

* * *

Issue Fifteenth: If he washes these members and afterward the skin peels off from them, there is no doubt that what appears beneath the skin is not washed; what was washed is that skin, and it has contracted and fallen off.

* * *

Issue Sixteenth: Washing is an expression for passing water over the limb. So if he moistens these members but the water does not flow over them, it does not suffice, because Allah, exalted is He, commanded passing water over the limb. In the case of major ritual impurity (janabah) there is a possibility that this suffices, and the difference is that what is commanded in ablution is washing, and that is not achieved except by passing water; whereas in janabah what is commanded is purity, which is His saying: ﴿But He desires to purify you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and that is achieved by mere moistening.

* * *

Issue Seventeenth: If he takes snow and passes it over his face, then if the air is hot so that it melts the snow and makes it flow, it is permissible; if the opposite, it is not permissible, contrary to Malik and al-Awza'i. Our proof: His saying: ﴿Wash﴾ requires that he be commanded to wash, and this is not called washing, so it must not suffice.

* * *

Issue Eighteenth: Tripling the acts of ablution is a sunnah, not an obligation; the obligation is only a single time. The proof: He, exalted is He, commanded washing, saying: ﴿Wash your faces and your hands﴾, and the reality of washing comes into existence with a single time. Then He, exalted is He, made the attainment of purity result from this amount, saying: ﴿But He desires to purify you﴾. Thus it is established that a single time suffices for the validity of ablution. This is then reinforced by what is reported: that he (ﷺ) performed ablution once and then said: "This is an ablution without which Allah does not accept prayer."

* * *

Issue Nineteenth: Using the siwak is a sunnah. Dawud said: It is obligatory, but leaving it does not impair the prayer. Our proof: the siwak is not mentioned in the verse; then He ruled that purity is attained by His saying: ﴿But He desires to purify you﴾, and when purity is attained, the permissibility of prayer is attained, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The key to prayer is purity."

* * *

Issue Twentieth: Saying the basmalah at the beginning of ablution is a sunnah. Ahmad and Ishaq said: It is obligatory, and if one deliberately omits it, the purification is nullified. Our proof: the basmalah is not mentioned in the verse; then He ruled that purity is attained, and this inference has been explained already. This is reinforced by what is reported: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever performs ablution and mentions the name of Allah over it, it is a purifier for his whole body, and whoever performs ablution without mentioning the name of Allah over it, it is a purifier for the limbs of his ablution."

* * *

Issue Twenty-first: Some jurists said: Beginning with washing the two hands before ablution is obligatory. According to us, it is a sunnah and not obligatory, and the argument from the verse is as we established regarding the siwak and the basmalah.

* * *

Issue Twenty-second: The limit of the face is from the beginning of the surface of the forehead to the end of the chin in length, and from ear to ear in breadth. The word "face" (wajh) is derived from "confrontation" (mujahah), so all of that must be washed.

* * *

Issue Twenty-third: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: It is obligatory to make water reach the inside of the eye. The others said: It is not obligatory. Ibn 'Abbas's argument is that the washing of the whole face is obligatory by His saying: ﴿Wash your faces﴾, and the eye is part of the face, so washing it must be obligatory. The jurists' argument is that He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿Allah does not desire to place on you any hardship﴾, and there is no doubt that introducing water into the eye involves hardship. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Issue Twenty-fourth: Rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose are not obligatory in ablution or in washing (ghusl) according to ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him; according to Ahmad and Ishaq, may Allah have mercy on them both, they are obligatory in both; according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, they are obligatory in washing but not obligatory in ablution. Our proof: He, exalted is He, obligated washing the face, and the face is that which faces outward, and the inside of the nose is part of it, whereas the mouth does not face outward, so it is not part of the face.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 6 (part 3 of 7):

Once this is established, we say: bringing water to the four limbs produces purity, due to His words: ﴿But He desires to purify you﴾, and purity produces the permissibility of prayer, as we have explained.
* * *
The twenty-fifth issue: Washing the white area between the sideburn (ʿidhar) and the ear is obligatory according to Abu Hanifa, Muhammad and al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on them. Abu Yusuf, may God have mercy on him, said it is not obligatory. Our argument is that it is part of the face, and the face must be washed by the verse,
