Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of God upon you when a people determined to extend their hands toward you, but He withheld their hands from you﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: Concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, there are two views.

The first: At the beginning of the matter, the polytheists were dominant, and the Muslims were subdued and defeated. The polytheists were always wanting to inflict affliction, killing and plunder upon the Muslims, and God, exalted is He, was preventing them from their aim until Islam grew strong and the might of the Muslims became great. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Remember the favor of God upon you when a people﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿determined to extend their hands toward you﴾ with killing, plunder and expulsion, ﴿but God withheld their hands from you, O Muslims, by His subtle kindness and mercy. And such a great blessing obliges you to be mindful of His disobedience and opposition to Him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fear God, and upon God let the believers rely﴾, i.e., be constant in obedience to God, exalted is He, and do not fear anyone in upholding the obligations of God, exalted is He.

The second view: This verse was revealed concerning a particular incident, and there are several opinions on it:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: "The Prophet ﷺ sent a detachment to the Banu 'Amir, and they were all killed at Bi'r Ma'unah except three men: one of them was 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri, and he and another with him returned to the Prophet ﷺ to inform him of the news of the people. They met two men from the Banu Sulaym who had a safe-conduct from the Prophet ﷺ, and they killed them, not knowing that they had a safe-conduct. Their people came seeking blood-money. The Prophet ﷺ went out, and with him were Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, until they entered upon the Banu al-Nadir, and they had made a covenant with the Prophet ﷺ to abstain from fighting and to help him with the blood-money. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A man from among my companions struck two men who had a safe-conduct from me, so their blood-money has become binding upon me, and I want you to help me.' They said: 'Sit until we feed you and give you what you want.' Then they resolved to treacherously kill the Messenger of God and his companions. Gabriel descended and informed him of that, so the Messenger of God ﷺ immediately rose with his companions and they went out. The Jews said: 'Our pots are boiling.' The Messenger informed them that revelation had come to him concerning what they had resolved upon." 'Ata' said: They conspired to drop a millstone or a rock upon him. It was said: rather, they threw [it], but Gabriel, peace be upon him, took it away.

The second: Others said: "The Messenger alighted at a place and the people dispersed from him, and the Messenger of God ﷺ hung his weapon on a tree. A bedouin came, drew the sword of the Messenger of God, then approached him and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'No one.' Then the Messenger of God ﷺ called his companions and informed them, but he refused to punish him." According to these two views, the meaning of His saying: ﴿Remember the favor of God upon you﴾ is reminding them of God's favor upon them by averting evil and harm from their Prophet, for if that had occurred it would have been among the greatest of calamities.

The third: It is narrated that the Muslims stood up to perform the noon prayer in congregation, and that was at 'Usfan. When they prayed, the polytheists regretted and said: "Would that we had attacked them during their prayer." It was said to them: "The Muslims have, after it, a prayer which is dearer to them than their sons and their fathers," meaning the afternoon prayer. So they resolved to attack them when they stood up for it. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended with the prayer of fear.

The second issue: It is said: "He extended his tongue toward him" when he insulted him, and "He extended his hand toward him" when he assaulted him. The meaning of extending the hand is stretching it toward the one being assaulted. Do you not see that the saying "So-and-so is broad-armed (basit al-ba')" and "long-armed (madid al-ba')" have the same meaning? ﴿But He withheld their hands from you﴾, i.e., He prevented them from reaching you.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised up from them twelve chiefs.﴾ And in it are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that there are several views on how this verse connects to what precedes it:

The first: He, exalted is He, addressed the believers earlier, saying: ﴿Remember God's favor upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey."﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 7). Then He now mentions that He took a covenant from the Children of Israel, but they broke it and abandoned fulfilling it. So, O believers, do not be like those Jews in this blameworthy trait, lest you become like them in what befell them of curse, humiliation and wretchedness.

The second: When He mentioned His saying, ﴿Remember God's favor upon you when a people intended to stretch out their hands against you﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 11), and we have mentioned in some reports that this verse was revealed concerning the Jews, and that they intended to inflict harm upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then when God, exalted is He, mentioned that, He followed it with mention of their disgraceful deeds and an explanation that they had always been persistent in breaking agreements and covenants.

The third: The purpose of the preceding verses is to encourage the accountable to accept the obligations and to abandon rebellion and disobedience. So He mentioned that He imposed obligations upon those who were before the Muslims just as He imposed them upon them, so that they would know that God's custom in obligation and binding is not specific to them, but is a custom He follows with all His servants.

**The second issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: *al-naqib* (نَقِيب, "chief/leader") is a form of *fa'il*, its root being from *al-naqb* (النَّقْب), which is a wide hole. One says: "So-and-so is the *naqib* of the people," because he probes into their conditions just as one probes into secrets. From it comes *al-manaqib* (الْمَنَاقِب), which means virtues, because they do not appear except through probing into them. One says *naqabtu al-ha'it* (نَقَبْتُ الْحَائِط), meaning I reached the end of boring through the wall. From it comes *al-nuqbah* (النُّقْبَة), trousers without two legs, because the opening and the boring are exaggerated in it. And one says *kalbun naqib* (كَلْبٌ نَقِيبٌ), a dog whose throat has been pierced so that the sound of its barking does not rise. The stingy among the Arabs used to do this so that a guest would not visit them.

Having understood this, we say: *al-naqib* is a *fa'il* form, and *fa'il* may carry the meaning of the active or the passive. If it carries the meaning of the active, then it is the one who probes into the conditions of the people and searches them out. Abu Muslim said: *al-naqib* here is a *fa'il* in the sense of a *maf'ul* (passive), meaning that He chose them with knowledge of them. A parallel is that the one struck is called *darib* (ضَرِيب), and the one killed is called *qatil* (قَتِيل). Al-Asamm said: They are the ones looked to, and the affairs of the people and the management of their interests are entrusted to them.

**The third issue:** The Children of Israel were twelve tribes, and God, exalted is He, chose from each tribe a man to be their chief and ruler over them. Mujahid, al-Kalbi and al-Suddi said: The chiefs were sent to the city of the giants, whom Moses, peace be upon him, had been commanded to fight alongside, so that they could learn their conditions and return with that information to their prophet Moses, peace be upon him. When they went to them, they saw huge bodies, strength and might, so they were afraid and returned, and their people questioned them. Moses, peace be upon him, had forbidden them to report to the people, but they broke the covenant, except for Caleb son of Jephunneh from the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Nun from the tribe of Ephraim son of Joseph. These are the two about whom God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Two men from among those who feared said﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 23), and so on.

* His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And God said, "Indeed I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend God a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your bad deeds and surely admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow."﴾

And in it are several issues:

**The first issue:** There is an ellipsis in the verse. The estimated meaning is: "God said to them, 'Indeed I am with you,'" but He omitted that because the speech is connected to mention of them.

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾ is addressed to whom? There are two views:

The first: It is addressed to the chiefs, meaning: God said to the chiefs, "Indeed I am with you."

The second: It is addressed to all the Children of Israel. Both are possible, but the first is preferable, because the pronoun refers to the nearest previously mentioned referent, and the nearest mentioned here is the chiefs. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** The speech is complete at His saying ﴿And God said, "Indeed I am with you"﴾, and the meaning is: "I am with you by knowledge and power. So I hear your speech, I see your actions, I know your inner thoughts, and I am able to deliver the recompense to you." So His saying ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾ is a very significant general premise for encouragement and warning. Then, after God set down this general premise, He mentioned after it a conditional sentence, whose condition is composed of five matters, which are His saying: ﴿If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend God a goodly loan﴾. The consequent is His saying ﴿I will surely remove from you your bad deeds﴾, which is an indication of the removal of punishment, and His saying ﴿and surely admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, which is an indication of the bestowal of reward. There are questions regarding the verse:

**The first question:** Why did He delay belief in the messengers after establishing prayer and giving zakah, although belief precedes them?

The answer: The Jews acknowledged that salvation requires establishing prayer and giving zakah, but they were insistent on denying some of the messengers. So He mentioned, after establishing prayer and giving zakah, that belief in all the messengers is necessary for the goal to be achieved. Otherwise, establishing prayer and giving zakah would have no effect in attaining salvation without belief in all the messengers.

**The second question:** What is the meaning of *al-ta'zir* (التَّعْزِير, "supporting/honoring")? The answer: Al-Zajjaj said: *al-'azr* (الْعَزْر) in the language means repelling. The interpretation of "I *'azzartu* so-and-so" is that I did to him what repels him from wrongdoing and restrains him from it. For this reason most scholars said the meaning of His saying ﴿and support them﴾ is "help them," because whoever helps a person has repelled his enemies from him. He said: If *al-ta'zir* meant *al-tawqir* (honoring), then His saying ﴿and honor him and revere him﴾ (al-Fath: 9) would be a repetition.

**The third question:** His saying ﴿and lend God a goodly loan﴾ falls under giving zakah, so what is the benefit of repeating it?

The answer: What is meant by giving zakah is the obligatory duties, and what is meant by this lending is the recommended charities. He singled it out for mention to draw attention to its nobility and the elevation of its rank. Al-Farra' said: If He had said "and lend God a goodly lending," it would also have been correct, except that the noun may stand in place of the verbal noun. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 14:

The indefiniteness of "a portion" (ḥazz) in the verse indicates that the intended portion is one, namely the one we have mentioned, which is belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). He specifically mentioned this one portion, even though they abandoned much of what Allah, Exalted is He, had commanded them, because this is the most magnified and most important of it.

In His saying "among them" (baynahum) there are two possibilities:

The first: among the Jews and the Christians.

And His saying: ﴿And Allah will inform them of what they used to do﴾ is a warning to them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verses 15–16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much﴾

Page 150

Know that when Exalted is He had related about the Jews and the Christians their breaking of the covenant and their abandoning of what they had been commanded, He summoned them, following that, to belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾. By "the People of the Scripture" is meant the Jews and the Christians. He used the singular "Scripture" because it is used in the sense of a genus (jins). Then He described the Messenger with two attributes:

The first: that he makes clear to them much of what they used to conceal. Ibn 'Abbas said: they concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and they concealed the matter of stoning (al-rajm). Then the Messenger (ﷺ) made that clear to them. This is a miracle, because he, upon him be prayers and peace, had not read any book nor learned knowledge from anyone; so when he informed them of the secrets of what was in their Book, that was information about the unseen, and so it constitutes a miracle.

The second attribute of the Messenger: His saying ﴿and pardoning much﴾, meaning he does not disclose much of what you conceal. He did not disclose it because there is no need to disclose it in religion. The benefit in mentioning this is that they know the Messenger is aware of everything they conceal, and so this becomes a motive for them to abandon concealment, lest they be exposed.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾, and concerning it there are sayings:
The first: that by the "light" is meant Muhammad, and by the "Book" the Qur'an.

The second: that by the "light" is meant Islam, and by the "Book" the Qur'an.

The third: that "the light and the Book" is the Qur'an itself, and this is weak, because conjunction (al-'atf) requires difference between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. Calling Muhammad, Islam and the Qur'an "light" is clear, because the apparent light is that by which the sight is strengthened to perceive apparent things, and the inner light is also that by which insight is strengthened to perceive realities and intelligibles.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By it Allah guides﴾, i.e., by the clear Book, ﴿whoever follows His good pleasure﴾, whoever in seeking religion seeks to follow the religion with which Allah, exalted is He, is pleased. As for one whose aim in his religion is to confirm what he became accustomed to, grew up upon, and took from his forefathers, while abandoning reflection and reasoning, such a person is not one who follows the good pleasure of Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿the paths of peace﴾, i.e., the ways of safety. It is permissible that this be by omission of a modifier, i.e., the paths of the House of Peace. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And those who are killed in the way of Allah — He will never waste their deeds. He will guide them﴾ (Muhammad: 4–5). The intended meaning is not the guidance of Islam, but guidance to the path of Paradise.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and brings them out of darknesses into light by His permission﴾, i.e., from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith. That is because in disbelief its possessor is bewildered, as one is bewildered in darkness, and by faith he is guided to the paths of Paradise as one is guided by light. His saying "by His permission", i.e., by His enabling (tawfiq), and the preposition "bi" is connected to "following": i.e., he follows His good pleasure by His permission. It is not permissible for it to be connected to "guidance" or to "bringing out", because that would have no meaning. This indicates that no one follows the good pleasure of Allah except those whom Allah wills it for.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and guides them to a straight path﴾, which is the true religion, because the truth is one in itself and consistent from all its aspects, whereas falsehood is manifold, and all of it is crooked.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 17:

Page 151

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ There is a question regarding this verse: none of the Christians says, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." So how does Allah relate this of them when they do not say it?

Its answer: many of the Hululiyyah (those who hold the doctrine of indwelling, hulul) say that Allah, exalted is He, may indwell the body of a specific person, or his soul. Since this is so, it is not far-fetched to say that a group of Christians adopted this view. Indeed, this is closer to what the Christians hold, for they say that the Hypostasis of the Word (uqnum al-kalimah) was united with ʿIsa, peace be upon him. The Hypostasis of the Word is either an essence (dhat) or an attribute (sifah). If it is an essence, then the essence of Allah, exalted is He, has indwelt ʿIsa and become united with ʿIsa, so ʿIsa would be the God according to this view. And if we say that the hypostasis is an expression for an attribute, then the transfer of an attribute from one essence to another essence is not rationally conceivable. Then, even granting the transfer of the hypostasis of knowledge from the essence of Allah, exalted is He, to ʿIsa, it would follow that the essence of Allah would be devoid of knowledge, and whoever is not knowing is not a god. Thus, the god would then be ʿIsa according to their view. It is established that the Christians, although they do not explicitly state this view, the outcome of their doctrine is nothing but that.

Then, glorified is He, argued against the corruption of this doctrine by His saying: ﴿Say, "Who then can prevent Allah in the least if He wished to destroy the Messiah, the son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely?"﴾ This is a conditional sentence in which the consequent was placed before the condition. The implied meaning: if He wished to destroy the Messiah, the son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely, then who is able to repel Him from His will and what He has power over? His saying, ﴿Who then can prevent Allah in the least﴾ means: who then can possess anything of the acts of Allah? Al-mulk is power (al-qudrah); meaning, who is able to repel any of the acts of Allah, exalted is He, or to prevent any of His will? His saying, ﴿and everyone on earth entirely﴾ means that ʿIsa resembles everyone on earth in form, creation, physicality, composition, and the change of attributes and states. So since you concede that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of all and the Governor of all, it is necessary that He is also the Creator of ʿIsa.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them.﴾ He said ﴿whatever is between them﴾ after mentioning the heavens and the earth, and did not say "between them" (baynahunna), because He treated them in the manner of the two categories and the two kinds.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿He creates what He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾ On this there are two interpretations:

The first: He creates what He wills, so at times He creates a human from a male and a female as is customary, and at times not from a father and mother as in the case of Adam, peace be upon him, and at times from a mother without a father as in the case of ʿIsa, peace be upon him.

The second: He creates what He wills, meaning that when ʿIsa shapes the form of a bird from clay, Allah, exalted is He, creates in it flesh, life, and power as a miracle for ʿIsa; and at times He gives life to the dead and heals the blind and the leper as a miracle for him. There is no objection to Allah, exalted is He, regarding any of His acts.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 18:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved."﴾ There is a question here: the Jews never say this at all, so how is it permissible to attribute this statement to them? As for the Christians, they say it about Jesus, not about themselves, so how is this attribution to them permissible?

The exegetes answered this in several ways.

The first: this is an instance of ellipsis (*hadhf al-mudaf*), and the intended meaning is "We are the children of Allah's messengers." The term that is in fact attached to the messengers was attributed to Allah. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ (al-Fath 48:10).

The second: the word "son" (*ibn*) is applied to a biological son, but it is also applied to one who adopts a son. Adopting someone as a son means singling him out for special compassion and love. When the people claimed that Allah's care for them was greater and more complete than His care for everything else, Allah, exalted is He, expressed their claim of Allah's complete care for them by saying that they claimed to be "the children of Allah."

The third: the Jews claimed that Ezra (*'Uzayr*) is the son of Allah, and the Christians claimed that the Messiah is the son of Allah. Then they claimed that Ezra and the Messiah were from among them. This became as though they had said, "We are the children of Allah." Do you not see that when the relatives of a king boast before a person, they may say, "We are the kings of the world and the sultans of the universe," and they mean by this that they are specially connected to that person who is the king and sultan? So it is the same here.

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas said: The Prophet ﷺ invited a group of Jews to the religion of Islam and warned them of Allah's punishment. They said, "How can you frighten us with the punishment of Allah when we are the children of Allah and His beloved?" This report refers only to that group. As for the Christians, they recite in their Injil (Gospel), which they possess, that the Messiah said to them: "I am going to my Father and your Father."

The overall point is that the Jews and the Christians considered themselves superior to all other creatures because of their noble forefathers among the prophets, until they went so far in exalting themselves that they said, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved."

Then Allah refuted their claim and said: ﴿Say, "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ There is a question here. The gist of this statement is that if they were the children of Allah and His beloved, He would not have punished them; but He did punish them. Therefore, they are not the children of Allah nor His beloved. The objection to this argument is that one may say: Either you claim that Allah punished them in this world, or you claim that He will punish them in the Hereafter. If the point of the argument is punishment in this world, then this does not refute their claim to being the beloved of Allah, because Muhammad ﷺ claimed that he and his community were the beloved of Allah, and yet they were not free from the trials of this world. Look at the battle of Uhud, and at the killing of al-Hasan and al-Husayn. If the point of the argument is that He will punish them in the Hereafter, then the people deny this. The mere report of Muhammad ﷺ is not sufficient in this matter, for if it were sufficient, then his mere report that they lied in claiming to be the beloved of Allah would be sufficient, and then this argument would be futile.

The answer is in several ways.

The first: the point of the argument is punishment in this world, and the objection based on the day of Uhud is not valid. This is because the verse says: If they were the children of Allah and His beloved, Allah would not have punished them in this world. Muhammad ﷺ, peace and blessings be upon him, claimed to be among the beloved of Allah but did not claim to be among the children of Allah, so the question is resolved.

The second: the point of the argument is punishment in the Hereafter, and the Jews and the Christians acknowledged the punishment of the Hereafter, as Allah, exalted is He, related about them that they said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:80).

The third: what is meant by His saying ﴿Why then does He punish you for your sins?﴾ is "Why then did He transform you?" The one actually punished is the Jews who were before the Jews addressed by this address in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. However, since these were of the same kind as those earlier ones, this attribution is acceptable. This answer is better, because Allah, exalted is He, would not have commanded His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to argue against them with something that had not yet come into existence, for they would say: "We do not concede that He punishes us." Rather, it is better to argue against them with something that has already occurred and taken place, so that the argument is strong and firm.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, you are human beings among those He has created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾. This means that no one has a right over Him that obliges Him to forgive him, and no one has a right over Him that prevents Him from punishing him. Rather, the dominion belongs to Him; He does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

Know that we have explained that the intent of their saying "We are the children of Allah and His beloved" is the completeness of His mercy upon them and the completeness of His care for them.

Having understood this, the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school) is that whoever obeys Allah and avoids the major sins, it is obligatory upon Allah by reason that He continue to bestow mercy and blessing upon him forever and ever. If, after thousands of years in the Hereafter, He withheld those blessings from him for a single moment, His divinity would be invalidated and He would depart from the attribute of wisdom. This is greater than the statement of the Jews and the Christians, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved." Just as His saying ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ refutes the statement of the Jews, it is more fitting that it refute the statement of the Mu'tazilah, and more complete.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾. The meaning is: whoever has such dominion and such power, how can a weak human being have a binding right over Him? And how can an ignorant human being, with his deficient worship and meager knowledge, possess a debt over Him? How monstrous is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Him is the final return﴾, that is, to Him the affair of creation returns in the Hereafter, for none possesses harm or benefit on that Day except Him, as He said: ﴿And the Command on that Day belongs to Allah﴾.

**Verse 19**

**Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 19:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O People of the Scripture, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you after a gap (fatra) in the messengers, lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good news and no warner." So there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ And in it are issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿yubayyinu lakum﴾ (making clear to you), there are two aspects.

The first: the object of "making clear" is supplied. On this supposition there are two possibilities:

One: that the thing made clear is the religion and the laws (shara'i'). The object was omitted because everyone knows that the Messenger was sent only to make the laws clear.

The second: the intended meaning is "making clear to you what you used to conceal." The object was omitted because it had already been mentioned.

The second aspect: the object is not supplied, and the meaning is "making clear to you the clarification." Omitting the object is more complete, because on this reading the benefit is more general.

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿yubayyinu lakum﴾ is in the accusative position as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning "making clear to you."

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿ʿalā fatratin mina al-rusul﴾ (after a gap in the messengers). Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means after a cessation of prophets. It is said: "fatara al-shay'" means it slackens, "futūr," when its intensity subsides and it becomes less than it was. The period between the prophets was called a fatra because the motives to act upon those laws had weakened.

Know that His saying ﴿ʿalā fatra﴾ is connected to His saying "jā'akum" (has come to you), meaning: it has come to you at a time of slackness in the sending of messengers. It is said that between ʿIsa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, there were six hundred years, or fewer, or more. And from al-Kalbi: between Musa and ʿIsa, peace be upon them both, there were one thousand seven hundred years and two thousand prophets; and between ʿIsa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, there were four prophets: three from the Children of Israel and one from the Arabs, who was Khalid ibn Sinan al-ʿAbsi.

**The fourth issue:** The benefit of sending Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, at a time of gap in the messengers is that alteration and distortion had crept into the earlier laws because of the long passage of their time and the length of their age. Because of this, truth became mixed with falsehood and truthfulness with lying. This became a clear excuse for people's turning away from worship, for they could say: "O our God, we know that worship of You is necessary, but we do not know how to worship." So Allah, may He be exalted, sent Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, at this time to remove this excuse. This is what is meant by ﴿lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good news and no warner"﴾: that is, We sent Our Messenger to you at a time of gap, lest you say: "No bringer of good news and no warner came to us at this time."

* * *

Then He said, may He be exalted: ﴿So there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner﴾, so this cause was removed and this excuse was lifted.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ The meaning is that the occurrence of a gap necessitates that creation needs the sending of messengers, and Allah, may He be exalted, is competent over all things, so He is competent to send them. Since creation needed the sending, and the Merciful, the Generous, was competent to send, it was necessary, by His generosity and mercy, that He send messengers to them. Thus the intended meaning of His saying ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ is a reference to the proof we have established.

**The Quranic verse:** ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember God's blessing upon you when He appointed prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given to anyone else in the worlds."﴾

Know that the connection (*wajh al-ittisal*, the link between this verse and what precedes it) is as follows. The *waw* in His saying ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ is a *waw* of conjunction, and it is connected to His saying ﴿God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. It is as if it were said: He took the covenant from them, Moses reminded them of God's blessings, and commanded them to fight the tyrants, but they went against the covenant in what they said, and they opposed him in fighting the tyrants. There are several issues regarding the verse:

**The first issue:** God bestowed three favours upon them.

The first is His saying ﴿when He appointed prophets among you﴾, because He did not send among any nation as many prophets as He sent among the Children of Israel. Among them were the seventy whom Moses chose from his people, who went with him to the mountain. Also, they were from the descendants of Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham, and these three were, by consensus, among the greatest prophets. The descendants of Jacob were also, according to the majority, prophets. God informed Moses that He would send prophets only from the descendants of Jacob and the descendants of Ishmael. This honour was therefore obtained through those prophets who had passed, through those who were present with Moses, and through those whom God informed Moses He would send from the descendants of Jacob and Ishmael after that. There is no doubt that this is a great honour.

The second is His saying ﴿and made you kings﴾, and concerning it there are several interpretations:

First, al-Suddi said: it means that He made you free, owning yourselves after you had been in the hands of the Copts, in the position of a *dhimmi* (protected non-Muslim subject, *ahl al-jizyah*) among us, and no one would overpower you over yourselves.

Second, every person who was a messenger and prophet was a king, because he governs the affairs of his community and has authority over them, and his judgement was binding upon them; thus he was a king. For this reason God said: ﴿We had given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We had given them a great kingdom﴾ (al-Nisa: 54).

Third, there were kings and great men among their ancestors and their descendants, and it is said of those among whom there were kings: "You are kings," by way of metaphor.

Fourth, every person who was independent in the affairs of his own self and his livelihood, and was not in need of anyone for his interests, is a king. Al-Zajjaj said: the king is one whom no one may enter upon except with his permission. Al-Dahhak said: their dwellings were spacious, with flowing waters in them, they had many possessions and servants who attended to their affairs, and whoever is like this is a king.

The third kind of blessing mentioned by God in this verse is His saying ﴿and gave you what He had not given to anyone else in the worlds﴾. This is because God singled them out with great kinds of honour:

First, God split the sea for them.

Second, He destroyed their enemy and made them inherit their possessions.

Third, He sent down upon them the manna and the quails.

Fourth, He brought forth for them sweet water from the rock.

Fifth, God shaded them with the clouds.

Sixth, kingship and prophethood were not combined for any people as they were combined for them.

Seventh, in those days they were the people who knew God the most, they were the beloved of God, and the helpers of His religion.

[Page 155]

Know that when Musa (peace be upon him) had reminded them of this blessing and explained it to them, he then commanded them to strive against the enemy, saying:

﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will turn about as losers.﴾

Concerning this there are several issues:

**The First Issue:** It is related that when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) ascended Mount Lebanon, God Most High said to him: "Look. Whatever your sight reaches is holy, and it is an inheritance for your descendants." It was also said: when the people of Musa (peace be upon him) left Egypt, God Most High promised them settlement in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). The Children of Israel used to call the land of al-Sham "the land of promises." Then Musa (peace be upon him) sent twelve chieftains (naqib), from among the trustworthy, to spy out for them the conditions of those lands. When they entered those lands, they saw enormous, terrifying bodies. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When Musa (peace be upon him) sent the chieftains to spy, one of those giants saw them. He seized them, placed them in his sleeve along with some fruit he had brought from his orchard, and brought them to the king. He scattered them before him and said to the king in amazement: "These people want to fight us." The king said: "Return to your companion and inform him of what you have witnessed." Then those chieftains went back to Musa (peace be upon him) and informed him of the event. He commanded them to conceal what they had pledged, but they did not accept his word, except for two men among them: Yushua ibn Nun and Caleb ibn Yufuna. The two of them made the matter easy and said: "It is a good land, abundant in blessings, and though these peoples' bodies are enormous, their hearts are weak." As for the remaining ten, they had instilled cowardice into the hearts of the people, until they openly refused to fight them. They said to Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here.﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 24). Musa (peace be upon him) then invoked [God] against them, and God Most High punished them by keeping them in the wilderness (tih) for forty years. They said: The period of the chieftains' absence for the spying was forty days, so they were punished with forty years of wandering. Those rebellious ones died in the wilderness, and the ten chieftains were destroyed in the wilderness with severe punishments. Some people said that Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both) also died in the wilderness. Others said that Musa (peace be upon him) remained, and Yushua and Caleb went out with him; they fought the giants and overcame them, and entered those lands. This is the story, and God knows best the manner of these matters.

**The Second Issue:** The Holy Land is the purified land, purified from afflictions. The exegetes said: it was purified from polytheism, and made a dwelling and resting place for the prophets. This is open to question, because when Musa (peace be upon him and his blessings) said ﴿Enter the Holy Land﴾, that land was not free from polytheism, nor was it a dwelling place of the prophets. It may be answered that it had been so previously.

**The Third Issue:** They differed concerning that land. Ikrimah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: it is Jericho (Ariha). Al-Kalbi said: Damascus, Palestine, and part of Jordan. It was also said: Mount Sinai (al-Tur).

**The Fourth Issue:** Concerning His saying ﴿God has prescribed for you﴾ there are several interpretations:

First: He wrote in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) that it belongs to you.

Second: God granted it to you.

Third: He commanded you to enter it.

If it is asked: Why did He say ﴿God has prescribed for you﴾, and then say ﴿it is forbidden to them﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 26)?

The answer: Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was a gift, then He forbade it to them because of the evil consequence of their rebellion and disobedience. It was also said: Although the wording is general, the intended meaning is particular, so it becomes as if it were written for some of them and forbidden to others. It was also said: The promise in His saying ﴿God has prescribed for you﴾ is conditional upon obedience. Since the condition was not fulfilled, the conditioned matter was not realized. It was also said: It was forbidden to them for forty years, and when the forty years passed, what He had prescribed came to pass.

**The Fifth Issue:** In His saying ﴿God has prescribed for you﴾ there is a great benefit: although the people were giants, God Most High, when He promised these weak ones that the land would be theirs, if they were believers who affirmed the truthfulness of Musa (peace be upon him), they would know with certainty that God would give them victory over the enemy and empower them against them. They would then necessarily advance to fight them without cowardice, fear or dread. This is the benefit of this phrase.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not turn back on your heels﴾, and concerning this there are two interpretations:

The first: Do not turn away from the true religion into doubt about the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him). For when he (peace be upon him) informed them that God Most High had made that land theirs, this was a promise that God Most High would grant them victory over the enemy. If they did not firmly believe in this victory, they would become doubters concerning the truthfulness of Musa (peace be upon him), and thus become disbelievers in divinity and prophethood.

The second interpretation: The intended meaning is: Do not return from the land you were commanded to enter to the land you left. It is related that the people had resolved to return to Egypt. His saying ﴿so you will turn about as losers﴾ has several interpretations:

First: Losers in the Hereafter, for you will miss the reward and incur punishment.

Second: You will return to humiliation.

Third: You will die in the wilderness and not attain any of the aims of this world or the benefits of the Hereafter.

[p. 156]

Then Allah informed about them that they ﴿said, "O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants (jabbarin)."﴾ Regarding the interpretation of "jabbarin," there are two views:

The first: "al-jabbar" is an intensive form (fa''al) derived from "jabarahu 'ala al-amr," meaning "ajbarahu 'alayh" (compelled him to it), and it is the tyrant who compels people to do what he wants. This is the choice of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: "I have not heard a fa''al form derived from af'ala except in two words: jabbar from ajbara, and darrak from adraka."

The second: that it is derived from the saying of people, "a jabbarah date-palm," when it is tall and elevated, such that hands cannot reach it. It is also said, "a man is jabbar" when he is tall, great, and strong, by way of comparison with the jabbar palm. The people were at the peak of strength and largeness of bodies, such that the hands of the people of Moses could not reach them, so they were called jabbarin for this meaning.

Then the people said: ﴿"Indeed, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So if they leave it, then indeed we will enter."﴾ They said this by way of considering it improbable, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle."﴾ (al-A'raf: 40).

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿"Two men from among those who feared [Allah] upon whom Allah had bestowed favor said, 'Enter upon them through the gate, and when you have entered it, you will be victorious. And upon Allah rely, if you are believers.'"﴾

In this there are issues:

The first issue: these two men are Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yufuna, and they were among those who feared Allah, and Allah had bestowed favor upon them with guidance, trust in the help of Allah, and reliance on the support of Allah.

Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that the meaning is: "Two men from among those whom the Children of Israel feared, namely the tyrants, and they were two men from among them upon whom Allah bestowed favor with faith, so they believed, and they said this statement to the people of Moses to encourage them to fight them." And the reading of the one who read (yukhafuna) with a ḍammah supports this view.

The second issue: regarding His saying, ﴿"upon whom Allah had bestowed favor"﴾, there are two views:

The first: that it is an attribute of His saying ﴿"two men."﴾

The second: that it is a parenthetical clause inserted between, which emphasizes what is the intended meaning of the speech.

The third issue: His saying, ﴿"Enter upon them through the gate"﴾ is an exaggeration in promising victory and triumph, as if he said: whenever you enter the gate of their city, they will be routed, and there will not remain among them one who blows a fire or one who dwells in a house, so do not fear them. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Why these two men were certain in their statement, ﴿"and when you have entered it, you will be victorious"﴾, is that they were certain of the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him. When Moses, peace be upon him, informed them that Allah said, ﴿"Enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you"﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 21), they were, without doubt, certain that victory and triumph were on their side. For this reason they concluded their speech with their saying ﴿"And upon Allah rely, if you are believers,"﴾ meaning: since Allah, exalted is He, has promised you victory, it is not appropriate that you become fearful because of their great strength and the largeness of their bodies; rather, rely upon Allah for the attainment of this victory for you, if you are believers, affirming the existence of the All-Powerful God and believing in the validity of the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They said, "O Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here."﴾ Regarding His words ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾ there are several interpretations:

The first: Perhaps these people were anthropomorphists (mujassimah), who permitted going and coming upon Allah, exalted is He.

The second: It is possible that the intended meaning is not the literal act of going. Rather, it is like the saying, "I spoke to him, and he went to answer me," meaning he intended to answer me. So it is as if they said, "Be you and your Lord intending to fight them."

The third: The implied meaning is, "Go, you and your Lord, while one who helps you, in your claim." So the predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtada', the predicate of the nominal sentence) was omitted.

If it is asked: when we consider the predicate omitted, how can His words ﴿fa-qatila﴾ (so fight) be taken as a predicate as well?

We say: there is no impediment to one predicate following another.

The fourth: By His words "your Lord" is meant his brother Harun, and they called him "lord" because he was older than Musa. The exegetes said: their words ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾, if they said them with the meaning of going from one place to another, then this is disbelief (kufr), and if they said them in the manner of rebelling against obedience, then this is defiant sin (fisq). They indeed committed sin with this statement, as evidenced by His words, exalted is He, in this story: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 26). The purpose of this story is to explain the opposition of these Jews, the intensity of their hatred, and their extremism in disputing with the prophets of Allah, exalted is He, since they existed.

Then, Allah, exalted is He, related of Musa, peace be upon him, that when he heard this statement from them, ﴿he said, "My Lord, I possess none but myself and my brother."﴾

Al-Zajjaj mentioned, regarding the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His words "wa-akhi" (and my brother), two possibilities: the nominative (raf') and the accusative (nasb).

As for the nominative, it is in two ways:

One: that it is coordinated (nasaq) with the position of "inni" (indeed I), and the meaning is: I possess none but myself, and my brother likewise. A similar example is His words: ﴿that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾ (At-Tawbah: 3).

The second: that it is a conjunction (atf) on the pronoun in "amliku" (I possess), which is "ana" (I). The meaning is: neither I nor my brother possess anything but ourselves.

As for the accusative, it is in two ways:

One: that it is coordinated on the ya' (the pronoun "my"), and the implied meaning is: "Indeed I and my brother possess nothing but ourselves."

The second: that "akhi" is conjoined to "nafsi" (myself), so the meaning becomes: I possess none but myself, and I possess none but my brother, because if his brother is obedient to him, then he possesses his obedience.

If it is asked: why did he say, "I possess none but myself and my brother," when the two men mentioned were with him?

We say: it seems he did not fully trust them, because of what he saw of the majority's unanimous rebellion. Also, perhaps he only said that to minimize the number of those who agreed with him. Also, it is permissible that by "brother" is meant one who is a brother to him in religion, and in this case both of them would be included in His words "wa-akhi."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So part between us and the defiantly disobedient people﴾, meaning: separate between us and them by judging for us what we deserve and judging against them what they deserve. This is in the sense of a supplication against them. It is possible that the intended meaning is: deliver us from their company, like His words: ﴿and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ (Al-Qasas: 21).

Then, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "It is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander bewildered in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people."﴾

Regarding this there are issues:

The first issue: His words "fa-innaha" (indeed it), meaning the holy land, are forbidden to them. Regarding His words ﴿forty years﴾ there are two opinions:

One: it is in the accusative by the prohibition, meaning the holy land is forbidden to them for forty years. Then Allah, exalted is He, opened that land to them without fighting. This is what al-Rabi' ibn Anas mentioned.

* * *

[Page 159]

The second opinion: it is in the accusative by His words ﴿they will wander bewildered in the land﴾, meaning they remained in that state for forty years. As for the prohibition, it remained upon them and they died, and then their children entered that town.

The second issue: It is possible that when Musa, peace be upon him, said in his supplication against the people, ﴿So part between us and the defiantly disobedient people﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 25), he did not intend by his supplication this kind of punishment, but something lighter than it. So when Allah, exalted is He, informed him of the wandering, he knew that he would grieve because of that, so He consoled him and made their matter easier for him, saying: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ Muqatil said: When Musa supplicated against them, Allah, exalted is He, informed him of the conditions of the wandering. Then Musa, peace be upon him, informed his people of that, and they said to him, "Why did you supplicate against us?" Musa regretted what he had done, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: ﴿Do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ It is also permissible that this is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: do not grieve over a people whose affair has always been sins and opposition to the messengers. The second issue: It is possible that when Musa, peace be upon him, said in his supplication against the people, ﴿So part between us and the defiantly disobedient people﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 25), he did not intend by his supplication this kind of punishment, but something lighter than it. So when Allah, exalted is He, informed him of the wandering, he knew that he would grieve because of that, so He consoled him and made their matter easier for him, saying: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ Muqatil said: When Musa supplicated against them, Allah, exalted is He, informed him of the conditions of the wandering. Then Musa, peace be upon him, informed his people of that, and they said to him, "Why did you supplicate against us?" Musa regretted what he had done, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: ﴿Do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ It is also permissible that this is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: do not grieve over a people whose affair has always been sins and opposition to the messengers. And Allah knows best.

The Fifth Issue: Whether Musa and Harun remained in the wilderness of Tih or not? People differed. One group said: they were not in the Tih at all, and they cited several points as evidence:

The first: he (peace be upon him) prayed to Allah to separate him from the people who were defiant transgressors, and the supplications of the prophets (peace be upon them) are answered. This indicates that he (peace be upon him) was not with them in that place.

The second: that the Tih was a punishment, and the prophets are not punished.

The third: that the people were punished because they rebelled, while Musa and Harun were not like that, so how could they be with those transgressors in that punishment?

Others said: they were with the people in that Tih, but Allah, exalted is He, made that punishment easy for them, just as He made the fire easy for Ibrahim, turning it into coolness and safety. Then, those who held this view differed as to whether they died in the Tih or left it. One group said: Harun died in the Tih, then Musa died a year after him, and Yusha' ibn Nun remained. He was the son of Musa's sister and his successor after his death, and he is the one who conquered the Holy Land.

It was said: he ruled al-Sham after that. Others said: rather, Musa remained after that, left the Tih, fought the tyrants, subdued them, and took the Holy Land. And Allah knows best.

The Fourth Issue: His saying, ﴿So it is forbidden for them﴾. Most scholars hold that this is a prohibition of prevention, not a prohibition of worship (ta'abbud). It was said that it may also be a prohibition of ta'abbud, so He commanded them to remain in that desert in hardship and affliction as a punishment for them because of their evil conduct.

The Fifth Issue: They differed about the Tih. Al-Rabi' said: it measures six farsakh (parasangs). It was said: nine farsakh by thirty farsakh. It was said: six by twelve farsakh. It was said: they were six hundred thousand horsemen.

If it is asked: how is it conceivable that this great host remained for forty years in this small portion of the desert, such that none of them happened to find a way out of it? And if they had fixed their eyes on the movement of the sun or the stars, they would have come out of it even if they were in the great sea, so how about a small desert?

We say: there are two aspects to this:

The first: that breaking of customary patterns in the time of the prophets is not improbable, for if we open the door of improbability, it would necessitate challenging all miracles, and that is false.

The second: if we interpret that prohibition as a prohibition of ta'abbud, then the question is resolved, since it is possible that Allah, exalted is He, forbade them to return to their homelands, but rather commanded them to remain in that desert for forty years with hardship and trial, as a recompense for their evil conduct. On this interpretation the difficulty is removed.

The Sixth Issue: It is said: taha yatihu taihan, tihan, and tawhan (to wander lost). Al-tih is the most general of these, and al-taihaa' is land in which one cannot find the way.

Al-Hasan said: they would wake up where they had spent the evening, and spend the evening where they had woken up, and their movement in that desert was in a circular path. This is problematic, for if they had fixed their eyes on the course of the sun and had not turned or come back, they would inevitably have come out of the desert. Rather, it is better to read the statement as a prohibition of ta'abbud, as we have established, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 27:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And recite to them the news of the two sons of Adam, in truth﴾. There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: concerning the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are several aspects.

The first: He, the Exalted, said earlier: ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 11). He mentioned that the enemies wish to inflict calamity and trial upon them, but He, the Exalted, protects them by His bounty and prevents their enemies from reaching them with harm. Then, for the sake of consolation and to lighten these states upon the heart, He mentioned many stories showing that everyone whom Allah, the Exalted, favours with great blessings in religion and in the world, people contend with him out of envy and transgression. He first mentioned the story of the twelve nuqaba' (chiefs) and Allah's taking of the covenant from them. Then the Jews broke that covenant until they fell into curse and hardness of heart. After this He mentioned the intensity of the Christians' persistence in their disbelief and their saying of the Trinity after the decisive proofs of the corruption of what they held had appeared, and that this was nothing but their envy of Muhammad (ﷺ) for what Allah gave him of the true religion. Then He mentioned after this the story of Moses in fighting the Jabbarin (tyrants) and his people's persistence in rebellion and disobedience. Then He mentioned after this the story of the two sons of Adam, that one of them killed the other out of envy because Allah, the Exalted, accepted his offering. All these stories indicate that every possessor of blessing is envied. Since Allah's blessings upon Muhammad (ﷺ) were the greatest of blessings, it was not unlikely that the enemies would unite to devise all kinds of deceit and scheming against him. So the mention of these stories was a consolation from Allah, the Exalted, to His Messenger (ﷺ) when a people among the Jews determined to deceive him and to bring upon him a calamity and trial.

The second: that this is connected to His saying: ﴿O People of the Book, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 15). This story and the manner of the prescribing of retaliation (qisas) in it are among the secrets of the Torah.

The third: that this story is connected with what precedes it, namely the story of the fighting of the Jabbarin, meaning: relate to the Jews the account of the two sons of Adam so that they may know that the way of their forefathers in regret and grief resulting from their advancing into disobedience was like the way of the two sons of Adam in the advance of one of them upon killing the other.

The fourth: it has been said that this is connected to His saying, relating the words of the Jews and Christians: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 18), meaning that their being descendants of the prophets does not benefit them along with their disbelief, just as the son of Adam did not benefit, at his disobedience, from his father being a prophet greatly honoured by Allah, the Exalted.

The fifth: when the People of the Book disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) out of envy, Allah, the Exalted, informed them of the account of the son of Adam and that envy led him to an evil end, and the purpose of it is warning against envy.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿And recite to them﴾. Concerning it there are two views:

One of them: recite to the people.

The second: recite to the People of the Book.

Concerning His saying: ﴿the two sons of Adam﴾ there are two views:

The first: that they are the two sons of Adam from his loins, namely Habil and Qabil. Concerning the cause of the dispute between them there are two views:

One of them: that Habil was a keeper of sheep and Qabil was a farmer. Each of them offered a sacrifice. Habil chose the best sheep in his flock and offered it, and Qabil chose the worst wheat in his crop and offered it. Then each drew near to Allah with his offering, and a fire came down from heaven and consumed the offering of Habil but did not consume the offering of Qabil. Qabil knew that Allah, the Exalted, had accepted his brother's offering and had not accepted his, so he envied him and intended to kill him.

The second: what is related, that Adam, peace be upon him, had a child born to him in every birth, a boy and a girl, and he would marry the girl of one birth to the boy of another birth. Qabil was born to him with a twin sister, and after them Habil with his twin sister. Qabil's twin was the most beautiful of people in appearance, so Adam wished to marry her to Habil. Qabil refused this and said: "I am more entitled to her, and he is more entitled to his sister; this is not from Allah, the Exalted, but is your opinion." Adam, peace be upon him, said to them: "Offer an offering, and whichever of you has his offering accepted, I will marry her to him." Allah, the Exalted, accepted Habil's offering by sending down a fire upon his offering, and Qabil killed him out of envy for him.

The second view, which is the view of al-Hasan and al-Dahhak: that the two sons of Adam who offered an offering were not sons of Adam by his loins, but were two men from the Children of Israel. They said: the evidence for this is His saying, the Exalted, at the end of the story: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 32). For it is evident that the commission of this sin by one of the two sons of Adam cannot be a cause for the prescribing of retaliation upon the Children of Israel; whereas when a man of the Children of Israel committed a like disobedience, it was possible to make that a cause for prescribing retaliation upon them, as a deterrent from returning to a like sin. And among what indicates this is also that the purpose of this story is to show the persistence of the Jews, always from ancient times, in rebellion and envy, to the point that the intensity of their envy reached such a degree that when Allah accepted the offering of one of them, the other envied him and proceeded to kill him. There is no doubt that this is a great rank in envy, for when he witnessed that his companion's offering was accepted by Allah, the Exalted, that would prompt him to think well of him and to exaggerate in honouring him. Then when he proceeded to kill him, and killed him in this state, that shows he had reached the furthest extremes of envy. And since the purpose of mentioning this story is to show that envy is an ancient custom among the Children of Israel, it must be said: these two men were from the Children of Israel.

Know that the first view is the one chosen by most of the scholars of reports, and the verse also contains an indication of it: for the verse indicates that the killer did not know what to do with the slain until he learned that from the work of the crow; had he been from the Children of Israel, this matter would not have been hidden from him. And this is the truth, and Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying: (in truth). Concerning it there are several aspects:

The first: in truth, that is, a recitation accompanied by truth and correctness from Allah, the Exalted.

The second: that is, a recitation accompanied by sincerity and truth, agreeing with what is in the Torah and the Gospel.

The third: in truth, that is, with the correct purpose, which is condemning envy, for the polytheists and the People of the Book used to envy the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and act with transgression against him.

The fourth: in truth, that is, so that they may take a lesson from it, not so that they may treat it as play and falsehood like many tales that have no benefit in them, and which are merely idle talk. This indicates that the purpose of mentioning tales and stories in the Qur'an is the lesson, not mere narration. Its parallel is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Certainly there was in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ (Yusuf: 111).

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿when they both offered an offering﴾, and concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: idh (when): what is it governed by? There are two views:

The first: that it is governed by al-naba' (the news), meaning their story at that time.

The second: it is permissible that it be a substitute (badal) for al-naba', meaning: recite to them from the news the news of that time, with the omission of an annexed noun (mudaf) being understood.

The second issue: al-qurban: a name for what one draws near to Allah by, whether a slaughter or charity; the discussion of al-qurban has passed in Surat Al 'Imran.

The third issue: the construction of the sentence, which is His saying: ﴿when they both offered an offering﴾. Each of the two offered an offering, but He combined them in the verb and made the noun singular, because their act indicates that each of them had an offering. It has been said that al-qurban is a noun of genus, so it suits the singular and the plural; and also, al-qurban is a verbal noun like al-ruhjan, al-'udwan and al-kufran, and a verbal noun is neither dualised nor pluralised.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 28–30:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So it was accepted from one of them, but it was not accepted from the other.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: It has been said that the sign of acceptance was that fire would consume it, and this is the view of most of the exegetes (mufassirun). Mujahid said: the sign of rejection is that fire consumes it, but the first view is preferable because most of the exegetes agree upon it. It has also been said: at that time there was no poor person to whom one could give what one offers to draw near to God Almighty, so fire would descend from the sky and consume it.

The second issue: The reason one of the two offerings was accepted and the other rejected is that the attainment of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) is a condition for the acceptance of deeds. God Almighty said here, relating the words of the righteous one: ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous (muttaqun)﴾, and He said regarding what He commanded us concerning sacrifice with camels: ﴿Their flesh does not reach God, nor their blood, but taqwa from you reaches Him﴾ (al-Hajj: 37). Thus He informed that what reaches the presence of God is nothing but taqwa, and taqwa is a quality of the hearts. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Taqwa is here," and he pointed to the heart. The reality of taqwa consists of several matters:

One of them: that one be in fear and trepidation lest one fall short in one's obedience, so that one guards oneself with the utmost of one's ability against the aspects of shortcoming.

The second: that one be in the utmost of guarding oneself from performing that obedience for any purpose other than seeking the good pleasure of God Almighty.

The third: that one guard against there being any partnership (shirk) for other than God in it. How difficult it is to observe these conditions! It has been said regarding this story: one of them made his offering the best of what he had, and the other made his offering the worst of what he had. It has also been said: he concealed in himself that he did not care whether it was accepted or not, and that he would not marry his sister to Habil. It has also been said: Qabil was not among the people of taqwa and obedience, and therefore God did not accept his offering.

Then God Almighty related of Qabil that he said to Habil: ﴿I will surely kill you﴾, and Habil said: ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: as if Habil said, "Why do you kill me?" He said, "Because your offering has been accepted." Habil said, "And what is my sin? Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous." It has also been said: this is a statement of God Almighty to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) as an interjection within the story, as if God Almighty was explaining to Muhammad (ﷺ) that He did not accept his offering only because he was not righteous.

Then God Almighty related of the oppressed brother that he said:

﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, the Lord of the worlds.﴾

The first question: Why did he not repel the killer from himself, although repelling for the sake of the self is obligatory? Grant that it is not obligatory, then at least it is not forbidden. So why did he say, ﴿Indeed, I fear God, the Lord of the worlds﴾?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: It is possible to say that signs appeared to the one who was to be killed which strongly suggested to him that the other intended to kill him, so he spoke these words by way of admonition and advice. That is: "I do not permit myself to initiate against you the unjust, aggressive killing; rather, I will not do it out of fear of God Almighty." He said these words before the killer proceeded to kill him, and his purpose in them was to make the intentional killing abhorrent in the heart of the other. For this reason it is narrated that Qabil waited until Habil slept, then struck his head with a large stone and killed him.

The second aspect of the answer: What is mentioned in the verse is his saying: ﴿I shall not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾, meaning: I will not extend my hand toward you with the aim of killing you; rather I extend my hand toward you only with the aim of repelling. The people of knowledge said: one who repels for the sake of his self must repel by the easiest means and then the next easiest; it is not permissible for him to intend killing, but rather he must intend repelling. Then, if he cannot be repelled except by killing, that is permissible for him.

The third aspect: Some said: if the intended killer wishes to surrender, it is permissible for the one to be killed to do so, and this is what Uthman, may God be pleased with him, did. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Muhammad ibn Maslamah: "Put your cloak over your face, and be the servant of God who is killed, and do not be the servant of God who kills."

The fourth aspect: The obligation of repelling for the sake of the self is a matter that may differ according to the differences of the sacred laws (shara'i'). Mujahid said: repelling for the sake of the self was permissible at that time.

The second question: Why did the condition come with a verb form, while the consequent came with the form of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), namely his saying: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not be one who extends...﴾?

The answer: It is to convey that he does not do what would earn him this dreadful attribute, and therefore he emphasized it with the bā' of emphasis for negation.

* Then God Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and so be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾

On this there are two questions:

The first: How is it conceivable that the killer should bear the sin of the one killed, when He, Exalted, said: ﴿and no bearer of burdens will bear another's burden﴾ (Fatir: 18)?

The answer is in two aspects:

The first: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah, may God be pleased with them, said: its meaning is "you bear the sin of my killing and your sin which was from you before my killing," and this is by omission of the modified noun (idafa).

The second: al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "you return to God," so why did he say, "I want you to bear my sin and your sin"?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: We have mentioned that this speech passed between them when the one to be killed became convinced that the other intended to kill him, and that was before the killer proceeded to carry out the killing. It seems that when he admonished and advised him, he said: "Even if you do not desist from this grave sin because of this advice, you will surely lie in wait for my killing at a time when I am heedless of you and unable to repel you. Then I will not be able to repel you from killing me except by killing you first, on mere suspicion and assumption. This from me would be a grave sin and disobedience. And since it is a matter between my being the doer of this disobedience and your being the doer, I love that this grave sin should be yours and not mine." It is known that wishing for the commission of a sin by another in this situation and on this condition is not forbidden; rather, it is the very essence of obedience and pure sincerity.

The second aspect of the answer: The meaning is: "I want you to bear the punishment of my killing," and there is no doubt that it is permissible for the oppressed to want God to punish his oppressor.

The third: It is narrated that when the oppressor does not find on the Day of Resurrection anything to satisfy his opponent, some of the oppressor's evil deeds are taken from the oppressed and placed upon the oppressor. According to this, it is permissible to say: "I want you to bear my sin," in that it will be laid upon you on the Day of Resurrection if you do not find anything to satisfy me, and "your sin" in your killing of me. This is suitable as an answer to the first question. And God knows best.

* * *

Then God Almighty said: ﴿So his self made the killing of his brother seem easy to him, and he killed him, and so he became among the losers.﴾

Then the exegetes said: his self facilitated for him the killing of his brother. Some of them said: it encouraged him. The reality of the matter is that when a person conceives of intentional, aggressive killing as among the greatest of the grave sins, this belief becomes a deterrent from doing it, so that act becomes like a disobedient, rebellious thing which does not obey him in any way at all. When the self brings forth its various whisperings, that act becomes easy for him; it is as if the self, by its wondrous whisperings, made this act like one obedient to him after it had been like one disobedient and rebellious against him. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So his self made the killing of his brother seem easy to him﴾.

The Mu'tazilites said: if the Creator of all is God Almighty, then that adornment and facilitation would be attributed to God Almighty and not to the self.

Its answer: since actions are attributed to the motives, and the one who creates those motives is God Almighty, the doer of all actions is God Almighty.

Then God Almighty said: (so he killed him). It has been said: Qabil did not know how to kill Habil, so Iblis appeared to him, took a bird and struck its head with a stone, and Qabil learned that from him. Then he found Habil sleeping one day, and struck his head with a stone, and he died. It is narrated from Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing."

* * *

Then God Almighty said: ﴿So he became among the losers.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: he lost his world and his hereafter. As for the world, he angered his parents and remained blameworthy until the Day of Resurrection; as for the hereafter, it is the great punishment. It has been said: when Qabil killed his brother, he fled to Aden in the land of Yemen. Iblis came to him and said: "The fire consumed Habil's offering only because he used to serve the fire and worship it. If you also worship the fire, your aim will be achieved." So he built a fire-temple, and he was the first to worship fire. It is narrated that Habil was killed at the age of twenty, and his killing was at the Uqbat Hira', and it has been said at Basra, at the site of the Great Mosque. It is narrated that when he killed him, his body turned black, though he had been white. Adam asked him about his brother, and he said: "I was not a guardian over him." He said: "Rather, you killed him, and that is why your body has turned black." Adam remained after him for one hundred years without ever laughing. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is narrated that he composed a poem lamenting him. He said: this is a pure lie, and poetry is only fabricated and corrupted, and the prophets are protected from poetry. The author of al-Kashshaf spoke truly in what he said, for that poem is in extreme feebleness, not befitting even foolish teachers; how then can it be attributed to one whom God made his knowledge a proof over the angels?
