The second: al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "you return to God," so why did he say, "I want you to bear my sin and your sin"?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: We have mentioned that this speech passed between them when the one to be killed became convinced that the other intended to kill him, and that was before the killer proceeded to carry out the killing. It seems that when he admonished and advised him, he said: "Even if you do not desist from this grave sin because of this advice, you will surely lie in wait for my killing at a time when I am heedless of you and unable to repel you. Then I will not be able to repel you from killing me except by killing you first, on mere suspicion and assumption. This from me would be a grave sin and disobedience. And since it is a matter between my being the doer of this disobedience and your being the doer, I love that this grave sin should be yours and not mine." It is known that wishing for the commission of a sin by another in this situation and on this condition is not forbidden; rather, it is the very essence of obedience and pure sincerity.

The second aspect of the answer: The meaning is: "I want you to bear the punishment of my killing," and there is no doubt that it is permissible for the oppressed to want God to punish his oppressor.

The third: It is narrated that when the oppressor does not find on the Day of Resurrection anything to satisfy his opponent, some of the oppressor's evil deeds are taken from the oppressed and placed upon the oppressor. According to this, it is permissible to say: "I want you to bear my sin," in that it will be laid upon you on the Day of Resurrection if you do not find anything to satisfy me, and "your sin" in your killing of me. This is suitable as an answer to the first question. And God knows best.

* * *

Then God Almighty said: ﴿So his self made the killing of his brother seem easy to him, and he killed him, and so he became among the losers.﴾

Then the exegetes said: his self facilitated for him the killing of his brother. Some of them said: it encouraged him. The reality of the matter is that when a person conceives of intentional, aggressive killing as among the greatest of the grave sins, this belief becomes a deterrent from doing it, so that act becomes like a disobedient, rebellious thing which does not obey him in any way at all. When the self brings forth its various whisperings, that act becomes easy for him; it is as if the self, by its wondrous whisperings, made this act like one obedient to him after it had been like one disobedient and rebellious against him. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So his self made the killing of his brother seem easy to him﴾.

The Mu'tazilites said: if the Creator of all is God Almighty, then that adornment and facilitation would be attributed to God Almighty and not to the self.

Its answer: since actions are attributed to the motives, and the one who creates those motives is God Almighty, the doer of all actions is God Almighty.

Then God Almighty said: (so he killed him). It has been said: Qabil did not know how to kill Habil, so Iblis appeared to him, took a bird and struck its head with a stone, and Qabil learned that from him. Then he found Habil sleeping one day, and struck his head with a stone, and he died. It is narrated from Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing."

* * *

Then God Almighty said: ﴿So he became among the losers.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: he lost his world and his hereafter. As for the world, he angered his parents and remained blameworthy until the Day of Resurrection; as for the hereafter, it is the great punishment. It has been said: when Qabil killed his brother, he fled to Aden in the land of Yemen. Iblis came to him and said: "The fire consumed Habil's offering only because he used to serve the fire and worship it. If you also worship the fire, your aim will be achieved." So he built a fire-temple, and he was the first to worship fire. It is narrated that Habil was killed at the age of twenty, and his killing was at the Uqbat Hira', and it has been said at Basra, at the site of the Great Mosque. It is narrated that when he killed him, his body turned black, though he had been white. Adam asked him about his brother, and he said: "I was not a guardian over him." He said: "Rather, you killed him, and that is why your body has turned black." Adam remained after him for one hundred years without ever laughing. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is narrated that he composed a poem lamenting him. He said: this is a pure lie, and poetry is only fabricated and corrupted, and the prophets are protected from poetry. The author of al-Kashshaf spoke truly in what he said, for that poem is in extreme feebleness, not befitting even foolish teachers; how then can it be attributed to one whom God made his knowledge a proof over the angels?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 28–30:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So it was accepted from one of them, but it was not accepted from the other.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: It has been said that the sign of acceptance was that fire would consume it, and this is the view of most of the exegetes (mufassirun). Mujahid said: the sign of rejection is that fire consumes it, but the first view is preferable because most of the exegetes agree upon it. It has also been said: at that time there was no poor person to whom one could give what one offers to draw near to God Almighty, so fire would descend from the sky and consume it.

The second issue: The reason one of the two offerings was accepted and the other rejected is that the attainment of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) is a condition for the acceptance of deeds. God Almighty said here, relating the words of the righteous one: ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous (muttaqun)﴾, and He said regarding what He commanded us concerning sacrifice with camels: ﴿Their flesh does not reach God, nor their blood, but taqwa from you reaches Him﴾ (al-Hajj: 37). Thus He informed that what reaches the presence of God is nothing but taqwa, and taqwa is a quality of the hearts. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Taqwa is here," and he pointed to the heart. The reality of taqwa consists of several matters:

One of them: that one be in fear and trepidation lest one fall short in one's obedience, so that one guards oneself with the utmost of one's ability against the aspects of shortcoming.

The second: that one be in the utmost of guarding oneself from performing that obedience for any purpose other than seeking the good pleasure of God Almighty.

The third: that one guard against there being any partnership (shirk) for other than God in it. How difficult it is to observe these conditions! It has been said regarding this story: one of them made his offering the best of what he had, and the other made his offering the worst of what he had. It has also been said: he concealed in himself that he did not care whether it was accepted or not, and that he would not marry his sister to Habil. It has also been said: Qabil was not among the people of taqwa and obedience, and therefore God did not accept his offering.

Then God Almighty related of Qabil that he said to Habil: ﴿I will surely kill you﴾, and Habil said: ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: as if Habil said, "Why do you kill me?" He said, "Because your offering has been accepted." Habil said, "And what is my sin? Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous." It has also been said: this is a statement of God Almighty to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) as an interjection within the story, as if God Almighty was explaining to Muhammad (ﷺ) that He did not accept his offering only because he was not righteous.

Then God Almighty related of the oppressed brother that he said:

﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, the Lord of the worlds.﴾

The first question: Why did he not repel the killer from himself, although repelling for the sake of the self is obligatory? Grant that it is not obligatory, then at least it is not forbidden. So why did he say, ﴿Indeed, I fear God, the Lord of the worlds﴾?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: It is possible to say that signs appeared to the one who was to be killed which strongly suggested to him that the other intended to kill him, so he spoke these words by way of admonition and advice. That is: "I do not permit myself to initiate against you the unjust, aggressive killing; rather, I will not do it out of fear of God Almighty." He said these words before the killer proceeded to kill him, and his purpose in them was to make the intentional killing abhorrent in the heart of the other. For this reason it is narrated that Qabil waited until Habil slept, then struck his head with a large stone and killed him.

The second aspect of the answer: What is mentioned in the verse is his saying: ﴿I shall not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾, meaning: I will not extend my hand toward you with the aim of killing you; rather I extend my hand toward you only with the aim of repelling. The people of knowledge said: one who repels for the sake of his self must repel by the easiest means and then the next easiest; it is not permissible for him to intend killing, but rather he must intend repelling. Then, if he cannot be repelled except by killing, that is permissible for him.

The third aspect: Some said: if the intended killer wishes to surrender, it is permissible for the one to be killed to do so, and this is what Uthman, may God be pleased with him, did. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Muhammad ibn Maslamah: "Put your cloak over your face, and be the servant of God who is killed, and do not be the servant of God who kills."

The fourth aspect: The obligation of repelling for the sake of the self is a matter that may differ according to the differences of the sacred laws (shara'i'). Mujahid said: repelling for the sake of the self was permissible at that time.

The second question: Why did the condition come with a verb form, while the consequent came with the form of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), namely his saying: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not be one who extends...﴾?

The answer: It is to convey that he does not do what would earn him this dreadful attribute, and therefore he emphasized it with the bā' of emphasis for negation.

* Then God Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and so be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 31:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then God sent a raven, digging in the earth, to show him how to conceal the corpse of his brother.﴾ On this there are several issues:

First issue: It is said that when he killed him, he left him, not knowing what to do with him. Then he feared that wild animals would get to him, so he carried him on his back in a bag (jirab) for a year, until the body decayed. Then God sent a raven. On this there are several views:

The first: God sent two ravens, which fought, and one of them killed the other. Then it dug a hole for it with its beak and feet and threw it into the pit. Qabil learned this from the raven.

The second: al-Asamm said: When he killed him and left him, God sent a raven that scattered dirt over the dead one. When the killer saw that God honours the raven's dead companion, [even] after his death, he regretted and said: "Woe is me!"

The third: Abu Muslim said: It is the habit of the raven to bury things. A raven came and buried something, and he learned this from it.

Second issue: The phrase ﴿to show him﴾ has two meanings:

The first: "so that God would show him" or "so that the raven would show him," that is, so that it would teach him. Since it was the cause of his learning, it is as if [the raven] intended to teach him, by way of metaphor (majaz, figurative usage).

Third issue: ﴿how to conceal his brother's nakedness (sawat)﴾ means the private part (awrah) of his brother, which is what must not be exposed of the body. Sawah means disgrace, because of its ugliness. It is also said that "sawat akhihi" means the carcass of his brother.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this raven and conceal my brother's nakedness?" So he became among the regretful.﴾ On this there are several issues:

First issue: There is no doubt that his saying ﴿Woe is me!﴾ is an expression of grief and anguish. The verse allows two possibilities:

The first: He did not know how a slain person is buried. When he learned this from the raven, he knew that the raven had more knowledge than he did, and he knew that he had committed the killing of his brother only because of his ignorance and lack of understanding. So he regretted, lamented and grieved over his act.

The second: He knew how to bury him, for it is unlikely that a human would not be guided to this degree of knowledge. However, when he killed him, he left him in the open, treating him with contempt. When he saw the raven bury the other raven, his heart softened, and he said: The raven came, and it was scattering dirt over the dead one. When he saw that God had honoured him during his life by accepting his offering, and honoured him after his death by sending this raven to bury him under the earth, he knew that [the dead one] was of great rank with God, so he lamented his act. He knew that he had no ability to draw near to his brother except by burying him in the earth. Therefore he said: "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this raven?"

Second issue: His saying ﴿Woe is me!﴾ is a confession against himself of deserving punishment. It is a phrase used when a great calamity befalls someone. Its wording is that of a vocative, as if "woe" (wayl) were not present to him, so he called it to be present, meaning: "O woe, come! This is the time of your coming." The mention of "ya" (O) is for emphasis, as in His saying ﴿Woe is me! Shall I give birth...﴾ (Hud: 72). And God knows best.

Third issue: The word nadam (regret) is used to mean constancy, and from it the boon companion is called nadim, because he is constant in the gathering. On this there is a question:

[Page 166]

It is that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Regret is repentance." Since he was among the regretful, he was among the repentant, so why was his repentance not accepted?

They answered this in several ways:

One of them: Since he did not know how to bury except from the raven, he became among those who regretted carrying him on his back for a year.

The second: He became among those who regretted killing his brother, because he gained nothing from killing him, and his father and brothers were angry with him because of it. So his regret was on account of these causes, not because it was an act of disobedience.

The third: His regret was because he had left him in the open, treating him with contempt after killing him. When he saw that the raven, after killing the raven, buried it, he regretted the hardness of his heart and said: "This is my brother and my full brother, his flesh is mixed with my flesh and his blood is mixed with my blood. If compassion appears from the raven toward the raven, and it does not appear from me toward my brother, I am less than the raven in mercy and in good character." So his regret was for these reasons, not out of fear of God, the Exalted. Therefore that regret did not benefit him.

[Quranic citation] Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind﴾. And concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿Because of that﴾ means "because of his deed."

If it is asked about this, there are two questions:

**The first:** About His saying ﴿Because of that﴾, meaning: because of what has passed of the story of Qabil and Habil, We prescribed retaliation (*qisas*) for the Children of Israel. This is problematic, for there is no connection between the incident of Qabil and Habil and the obligation of retaliation upon the Children of Israel.

**The second:** The obligation of retaliation is a ruling established in all nations, so what is the benefit of specifying it for the Children of Israel?

The answer to the first question has two aspects:

The first: Al-Hasan said: this killing occurred among the Children of Israel, not between the two sons of Adam from his loins. We have already mentioned this issue earlier.

The second: We grant that this killing occurred between the two sons of Adam from his loins, but His saying ﴿Because of that﴾ is not a reference to the story of Qabil and Habil. Rather, it refers to what has been mentioned in this story of the kinds of corruption resulting from unlawful killing. Among them is His saying ﴿so he became one of the losers﴾, and among them is His saying ﴿so he became one of the regretful﴾. His saying ﴿so he became one of the losers﴾ indicates that he suffered the loss of both religion and worldly life. His saying ﴿so he became one of the regretful﴾ indicates that all kinds of remorse, grief and sorrow arose in his heart, even though there was absolutely no way to repel it. Thus His saying ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾ means: because of that which We mentioned in the course of the story of the kinds of corruption arising from deliberate, aggressive killing, We legislated retaliation against the killer. This is a good answer, and Allah knows best.

As for the second question, its answer is that although the obligation of retaliation against the killer is general across all religions and communities, the severity mentioned here regarding the Children of Israel is not established in all religions. This is because He, may He be exalted, has ruled here that the killing of a single soul is equivalent to the killing of all people. There is no doubt that the purpose of this is to emphasize the punishment for deliberate, aggressive killing. The purpose of explaining this emphasis is that the Jews, despite their knowledge of this great emphasis, nevertheless went ahead to kill the prophets and messengers. This indicates the extreme hardness of their hearts and the utmost distance from obedience to Allah the Exalted. Since the purpose of mentioning these stories is to console the Messenger (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, regarding the incident in which, as we mentioned, they resolved to assassinate the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the leading companions, the specification of the Children of Israel in this story with this great emphasis was fitting to the discourse and confirmed the intended meaning.

**The second issue:** The reading of ﴿مِن أجْلِ ذَلِكَ﴾ (*min ajli dhalika*) has been recited with the hamza omitted and the nun vowelled with a fatha, transferring its vowel onto it. Abu Ja'far recited ﴿مِن أجْلِ ذَلِكَ﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, which is a dialectal form. When it is lightened, the nun is given a kasra, transferring the kasra of the hamza onto it.

**The third issue:** Those who uphold analogy (*qiyas*) said: this verse indicates that the rulings of Allah the Exalted may be grounded in causes (*'ilal*, sing. *'illah*). This is because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾ such-and-such, and this is an explicit statement that the prescribing of those rulings is grounded in those meanings indicated by His saying ﴿Because of that﴾. The Mu'tazilah also said: this verse indicates that the rulings of Allah the Exalted are grounded in the welfare (*maslahah*) of the servants. And once this is established, it is impossible for Him to be the creator of disbelief and abominations in them and to will their occurrence from them. This is because the creation of abominations and willing them prevents Him, the Exalted, from taking welfare into account, and that would nullify the causal explanation mentioned in this verse.

Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: the claim that Allah's rulings are grounded in causes is impossible, for several reasons:

**First:** If the cause is eternal, the effect would necessarily be eternal. If the cause is originated, it must itself be caused by another cause, and this leads to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*).

**Second:** If He were acting for a cause, then the existence and non-existence of that cause in relation to Allah the Exalted—if they were equal, it would be impossible for it to be a cause; and if they were not equal, then one of the two would be preferable for Him because of that act. This requires that He derives that preference from that act, and therefore He would be deficient in His essence, perfecting Himself through another, and that is impossible.

**Third:** It has been established that the act depends on motives (*dawa'i*, sing. *da'iyah*), and an infinite regress among the motives is impossible. Rather, they must terminate in the first motive which arose in the servant, not from the servant but from Allah. It has also been established that when the motive arises, the act becomes necessary. On this basis, everything is from Allah, and this prevents the causal explanation of the acts and rulings of Allah the Exalted. Therefore it is established that the apparent meaning of this verse is among the *mutashabihat* (ambiguous verses), not the *muhkamat* (clear verses). What confirms this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Who has any power against Allah if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth together?﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 17). This is an explicit text that everything is permissible from Allah, and that His creation and His ruling do not depend on observing welfare.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿or corruption in the land﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is conjoined to His saying "a soul", and the meaning is: whoever kills a soul other than for a soul or other than for corruption in the land. Allah the Exalted said this because killing is permitted for many reasons. Among them is retaliation, which is what is meant by His saying ﴿whoever kills a soul other than for a soul or for corruption in the land﴾. Among them is disbelief together with armed hostility; among them is apostasy after belief; and among them is highway robbery, which is what is meant by His saying, after this verse, ﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 33). Thus Allah the Exalted gathered all these aspects in His saying ﴿or corruption in the land﴾.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿it is as if he had killed all of mankind﴾, and there is a difficulty in it. It is this: how can the killing of one soul be equal to the killing of all people, for it is impossible that a part should equal the whole? The commentators mentioned, in response to this question, several answers, all of which are based on one premise: that likening one of two things to the other does not require the judgment that they resemble each other in every respect, because our saying "this resembles that" is more general than saying "it resembles it in every respect" or "in some respects." Once the validity of this premise is clear, we say the answer has several aspects:

**The first:** The purpose of likening the killing of one soul to the killing of souls is to emphasize the magnitude of deliberate, aggressive killing and to magnify its gravity. That is, just as the killing of all creation is a matter regarded as grave by everyone, so too the killing of a single human being must be regarded as grave and awesome. The intended point is that the two share in being grave, not that they share in the degree of gravity. And how could it not be grave, when Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment﴾ (al-Nisa': 93).

**The second answer:** If all people knew from one person that he intended to kill all of them, there is no doubt that they would repel him with a force that would prevent him from achieving his aim. Likewise, if they knew from him that he intended to kill one specific person, their zeal and effort in preventing him from killing that person should be like their zeal and effort in the first case.

**The third answer:** When he proceeded to deliberate, aggressive killing, he preferred the motive of desire and anger over the motive of obedience. When this is the case, this preference is present with respect to every person, so that in his heart there is the thought that whoever disputed with him over anything he desired, he would kill him if he were able. The intention of a believer in good deeds is better than his action; likewise, the intention of a believer in evil deeds is worse than his action. Thus the meaning becomes: whoever kills a person intentionally and aggressively, it is as if he had killed all of mankind. These three answers are good.

**The sixth issue:** His saying ﴿And whoever gives it life, it is as if he had given life to all of mankind﴾. The meaning of giving life to a soul is rescuing it from destructive dangers, such as burning, drowning, extreme hunger, and extreme cold or heat. The discussion of whether giving life to one soul is like giving life to souls follows the same analogy as what we established regarding whether killing one soul is like killing souls.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them, after that, are transgressors in the land﴾.

The meaning is that many of the Jews, after that, that is, after the coming of the messengers, and after We had prescribed for them the prohibition of killing, are transgressors, meaning in killing; they do not care about its gravity.

[Page 169]

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to cause corruption on earth is only that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be exiled from the land﴾. Know that when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in the first verse the gravity of the sin of killing a soul without a soul having been killed or corruption having been spread in the land, He followed it by explaining what corruption in the land is that necessitates killing, since some kinds of corruption in the land do not necessitate killing. So He said: ﴿The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger is only...﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

[Page 169]

**The first issue:** There is an objection at the beginning of the verse. Waging war against Allah, the Exalted, is not possible, so it must be taken to mean waging war against the friends of Allah. Waging war against the Messengers is possible. Thus, when the word "waging war" (al-muharabah) is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, it is metaphorical, because what is meant is waging war against the friends of Allah; and when it is attributed to the Messenger, it is literal. So the word "yuharibun" in His words ﴿those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ would have to be understood both metaphorically and literally at once, and that is impossible. This is the statement of the objection.

Its answer has two aspects:

The first: We take "waging war" to mean opposing the command and the obligations. The sense is: "The penalty for those who oppose the rulings of Allah and the rulings of His Messenger and strive to cause corruption on earth is such-and-such."

The second: The sense of the speech is: "The penalty for those who wage war against the friends of Allah, the Exalted, and the friends of His Messenger is such-and-such." In a report it is stated that Allah, the Exalted, said: "Whoever humiliates a friend of Mine has declared war against Me."

**The second issue:** Some people said: this threat is specific to unbelievers; others said: it concerns the sinful among the believers. As for the first group, they mentioned several views:

The first: It was revealed concerning "a group from 'Urayna who came to Medina, showing Islam. Their bodies fell ill and their complexions turned yellow, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent them to the camels of the charity, that they might drink from their urine and milk and recover. When they reached that place and drank and recovered, they killed the herders, drove off the camels, and apostatized. The Prophet ﷺ sent after them, and commanded concerning them; their hands and feet were cut off, their eyes were branded with hot iron, and they were left there until they died." Then this verse was revealed as an abrogation (naskh, the cancelling of an earlier ruling by a later revelation) of what the Messenger had done, so that practice (sunnah, the Prophet's established example) was abrogated by this Qur'an. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, since it is not permissible for the Sunnah to be abrogated by the Qur'an, the abrogating element must have been another Sunnah, and this Qur'an was revealed in agreement with the abrogating Sunnah.

The second: The verse was revealed concerning the people of Abu Barzah al-Aslami, who had made a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. A group from Kinanah passed by, wishing to embrace Islam, while Abu Barzah was absent; they killed them and took their property.

The third: This verse concerns those among the Children of Israel whom Allah, the Exalted, mentioned, who, after Allah had made the punishment for deliberate, transgressive killing severe for them, were excessive in killing and corrupt on earth. So whoever among them committed killing and corruption on earth, his penalty is such-and-such.

The fourth view: This verse was revealed concerning highway robbers among the Muslims, and this is the view of most jurists. They said: What shows that the verse cannot be taken to refer to apostates are several points:

One: The cutting off of an apostate's limbs does not depend on waging war or on displaying corruption in the abode of Islam, whereas the verse requires that.

Second: It is not permissible to limit the punishment for an apostate to cutting off the hand or to banishment, whereas the verse requires that.

Third: The verse requires that the prescribed punishment (hadd) falls away through repentance before one is captured, as His words state: ﴿except those who repent before you have power over them﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:34). An apostate's prescribed punishment falls away through repentance both before and after capture, so this shows that the verse has no connection to apostates.

Fourth: Crucifixion is not prescribed for an apostate, whereas it is prescribed here, so the verse cannot be specific to apostates.

Fifth: His words ﴿those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to cause corruption on earth﴾ encompass everyone who is described by this attribute, whether he is an unbeliever or a Muslim. At most it may be said that the verse was revealed concerning unbelievers, but you know that the criterion is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

**The third issue:** The ones who wage war mentioned in this verse are the people who gather and have a force that protects them against whoever intends them, because they defend one another, and they target Muslims in their lives and their blood. We have considered force and strength because the highway robber is distinguished from the thief only by this condition. They agreed that if this situation occurs in the desert, they are highway robbers. But if it occurs within the town itself, al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: they are also those who strive to cause corruption on earth, and this punishment is applied to them. He said: "And I consider them in a city, if they are not greater in sin, then at least equal." Abu Hanifah and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: if this happens within a city, the prescribed punishment is not applied to them. The basis of al-Shafi'i's view, may Allah have mercy on him, is the text and analogy (qiyas, reasoning from an established ruling to a similar case). As for the text: the generality of His words ﴿The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to cause corruption on earth is only...﴾ applies, and it is known that when this meaning occurs in a town, it is inevitably included under the generality of this text. As for analogy: this is a prescribed punishment (hadd), so it does not differ between a city and outside a city, like all other prescribed punishments. The basis of the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, is that one who enters a city is usually reached by help, so he cannot carry out fighting, and thus he takes the status of a thief.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** His words ﴿that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off or be exiled from the land﴾. The scholars have two views on the word "aw" (or) in this verse:

The first: It is for choice (takhyir). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah, and the view of al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Mujahid. The meaning is that the ruler, if he wishes, may kill, if he wishes, may crucify, if he wishes, may cut off hands and feet, and if he wishes, may exile; he does whichever of these categories he wishes. But Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of 'Ata', said: the word "aw" here is not for choice; rather it is to show that the rulings differ according to the crimes. Whoever is limited to killing is killed; whoever kills and takes property is killed and crucified; whoever is limited to taking property has his hand and foot cut off on opposite sides; and whoever terrorizes the roads without taking property is exiled from the land. This is the view of the majority of scholars and is the school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. What shows the weakness of the first view are two points:

The first: If the verse meant choice, then the ruler would have to be permitted to limit himself to exile. Since they agreed that he is not permitted to do that, we know that the verse does not mean choice.

The second: When this waging-war person has neither killed nor taken property, he has intended a sin but has not committed it, and that does not necessitate killing, like the intention to commit any other sin. Thus it is established that the verse cannot be taken to mean choice. Therefore one must assume a separate action for each separate case, so the sense becomes: "they shall be killed if they killed; or crucified if they combined taking property with killing; or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides if they were limited to taking property; or be exiled if they terrorized the roads." Clear analogy (qiyas jali) also supports what we have said, because deliberate, transgressive killing necessitates killing, so for a highway robber this is made more severe, and killing becomes an obligation from which pardon is not permitted. Taking property entails amputation for other than a highway robber, so for a highway robber this is made more severe by cutting off both sides. If they combined killing with taking property, then for them killing is combined with crucifixion, because leaving him crucified along the road becomes a means of publicizing the carrying out of this punishment, and thus it becomes a deterrent to others from undertaking such disobedience. As for one who is limited to mere terrorizing, the Law limits the punishment for him to a light penalty, which is exile from the land.

**The fifth issue:** Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If he killed and took property, the ruler has a choice among three things: to kill them alone; or to kill them and cut off their hands and feet before killing; or to kill them and crucify them. But according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, crucifixion is necessary, and this is also the view of Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on him.

The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that He, the Exalted, stated crucifixion explicitly just as He stated killing, so it is not permissible to drop crucifixion, just as it is not permissible to drop killing.

Then they differed about the manner of crucifixion. It was said: he is crucified alive, then his belly is pierced with a spear until he dies. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: he is killed first, then prayed over, then crucified.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** They differed about the interpretation of exile from the land. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: its meaning is that if he finds these waging-war people, he kills them, crucifies them, and cuts off their hands and feet on opposite sides; and if he does not find them, he pursues them forever, until when he gains power over them he does to them what we have mentioned. This is also the view of Ahmad and Ishaq, may Allah have mercy on them both. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: exile from the land is imprisonment, and this is the preference of most linguists. They said: What shows this is that His words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾ either mean exile from the entire land, which is impossible while life remains; or mean removing him from that town to another town, which is also impermissible, because the purpose of this exile is to repel his evil from the Muslims, so if we removed him to another town, the Muslims there would be harmed by him; or mean removing him to the abode of unbelief, which is also impermissible, because removing a Muslim to the abode of unbelief exposes him to apostasy, which is impermissible. Since all of these are invalid, nothing remains except that the exile means banishing him from the entire land except the place of confinement. They said: The imprisoned person may be called exiled from the land, because he does not benefit from any of the good things of this world and its pleasures, and does not see any of his loved ones, so he becomes banished from all pleasures, desires and good things, and so he is in reality like one who is exiled.

When they imprisoned Salih ibn 'Abd al-Quddus on the accusation of heresy (zandaqah) in a narrow prison, and his stay there was prolonged, he recited poetry, among which is his saying:

We have gone out from the world and from union with its people, so we are neither among the living nor among the dead.
When the jailer comes to us one day on some errand, we are amazed and say: "This one has come from the world."

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This exile mentioned in the verse is to be understood in two ways:

The first: If these waging-war people kill and take property, then if the ruler captures them, he applies the prescribed punishment to them; and if he does not capture them, he pursues them forever. So their being fearful of the ruler and fleeing from town to town is what is meant by exile.

The second: The people who attend the incident, increase the numbers of these waging-war people, and frighten the Muslims, but who neither killed nor took property: if the ruler captures them, he applies the prescribed punishment to them; and if he does not capture them, he pursues them forever. Al-Shafi'i says here: the ruler captures them, disciplines them (ta'zir, discretionary punishment), and imprisons them, so what is meant by their exile from the land is only this imprisonment, and Allah knows best.

* Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾, that is, disgrace and humiliation, ﴿and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾.

The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates the certainty of the threat against sinners among the people of prayer, and it indicates that their killing has nullified their reward. This is because God, exalted is He, ruled that this is for them a disgrace (*khizy*) in this world and the Hereafter. That indicates that they deserve blame (*dhamm*). Their deserving blame at present prevents their continued deserving of praise and honor, because combining the two is a combination of contraries. If this is the case, then the certainty of the threat against sinners is established, and so is the doctrine of nullification (*ihbat*).

The answer: There is no dispute between us and you that this legal penalty (*hadd*) is carried out as a disgrace and humiliation only when repentance has not occurred. But when repentance has occurred, this penalty is not carried out as a disgrace and humiliation; rather, it is carried out as a trial (*imtihan*). If you are permitted to make this ruling conditional on the absence of repentance, on the basis of a proof that indicates the consideration of this condition, then we likewise make this ruling conditional on the absence of pardon (*'afw*). At that point, the discussion remains only as to whether this proof indicates that God pardons sinners or not. We have already treated this question thoroughly in Surah al-Baqarah, in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin surrounds him, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:81).

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Except for those who repent before you have power over them. So know that God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾

Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: When He explained what is obligatory upon these fighters against God and His messenger (*muharibun*) of the legal penalties and punishments, He excepted from them those who repent before they come under one's power. The summary of this discourse is that those rulings which relate to the rights of God, exalted is He, fall away after this repentance, while those which relate to the rights of human beings do not fall away. So if these fighters killed a person and then repented before they came under one's power, the guardian of the blood (*wali al-dam*) retains his right to retaliation (*qisas*) or pardon, except that the obligation of execution is removed by this repentance. If they took property, it is obligatory for them to return it, and they are not subject to the amputation of the hand or foot. As for when they repent after they have come under one's power, the apparent meaning of the verse is that repentance does not benefit them, and the penalties are enforced upon them.

Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: It is possible that every penalty of God falls away through repentance, because when Ma'iz was stoned, he manifested his repentance. When they completed his stoning, they mentioned that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "Why did you not leave him?" or a wording with this meaning. This indicates that repentance removes from the accountable person everything that relates to the right of God, exalted is He.

When they completed his stoning, they mentioned that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "Why did you not leave him?" or a wording with this meaning. This indicates that repentance removes from the accountable person everything that relates to the right of God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him, and strive in His cause that you may be successful.﴾ And in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: concerning the arrangement (nazm) there are two aspects:

The first: Know that we have already explained that when He, exalted is He, informed His Messenger that a group of the Jews had intended to stretch out their hands against the Messenger and his brethren among the believers and companions with treachery and deceit, and Allah, exalted is He, prevented them from their aim, then at that point He explained to the Messenger the severity of their defiance against the prophets and the completeness of their persistence in harming them, and the speech extended to this point. Thereupon the speech returned to the primary subject and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means to Him﴾. It is as if it were said: You have known the completeness of the Jews' audacity in sins and transgressions and their distance from acts of obedience, which are the means for the servant to the Lord. So be, O believers, the opposite of that: be mindful of the disobedience of Allah, seeking means to Allah through the obedience of Allah.

The second aspect concerning the arrangement: He, exalted is He, related about them that they said: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 18), meaning: we are the sons of the prophets of Allah. Their pride was in the deeds of their forefathers. So He, exalted is He, said: O you who have believed, let your boasting be in your own deeds, not in the nobility of your fathers and ancestors. So fear Allah and seek the means to Him. And Allah knows best.

Page 173
The second issue: Know that the totality of obligations (majami' al-taklif) is confined to two types with no third:
One of them: abandoning what is forbidden, and to it points His saying: (fear Allah).

The second: performing what is commanded, and to it points His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and seek the means to Him﴾. Since abandoning what is forbidden is by essence prior to performing what is commanded, He therefore placed it first in the mention. We say that abandonment (tark) is prior to action (fi'l) because abandonment is the remaining of a thing in its original non-existence, while action is the bringing about and attainment, and there is no doubt that the non-existence of all originated things precedes their existence; so abandonment is necessarily before action.

If it is said: Why was the means restricted to action, when we know that abandoning sins may also be used as a means to Allah, exalted is He?

We reply: Abandonment is the keeping of a thing in its original non-existence, and that continuous non-existence cannot be used as a means to anything at all. Thus it is established that abandonment cannot be a means. Rather, whoever is called by the impulse of desire to a vile act, then leaves it seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, here the means to Allah, exalted is He, is achieved by that restraint; yet that restraint is of the category of actions. For this reason the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) said: abandoning a thing is an expression for performing its opposite.

Having known this, we say: abandonment and action are two matters considered in the outward acts: what must be abandoned is the prohibited, and what must be performed is the obligatory. They are also considered in morals: what must be attained is the virtuous character traits, and what must be abandoned is the blameworthy traits. They are also considered in thought: what must be performed is reflection upon the proofs indicating monotheism, prophethood and the Return, and what must be abandoned is turning toward doubts. They are also considered in the station of manifestation (maqam al-tajalli): action is absorption in Allah, exalted is He, and abandonment is turning toward other than Allah, exalted is He. The practitioners of spiritual discipline (ahl al-riyadah) call action and abandonment by adornment (tahliyah) and emptying (takhliyah), by erasure (mahw) and sobriety (sahw), by negation (nafy) and affirmation (ithbat), by annihilation (fana') and subsistence (baqa'). In all stations negation precedes affirmation, and for this reason our saying "There is no god but Allah" has negation preceding affirmation within it.

The third issue: al-wasilah is on the pattern fa'ilah, from wasala ilayhi, meaning he drew near to Him. The poet Labid said:

I see people not knowing the worth of their affair,
Is not every man of intellect one who seeks the means to Allah?

That is, one who seeks a means (mutawassil), so al-wasilah is that by which one reaches the desired goal. The Ta'limiyyah (Ta'limites) said: the verse indicates that there is no way to Allah, exalted is He, except through a teacher who teaches us His knowledge and a guide who directs us to knowing Him, because He commanded seeking the means to Him in absolute terms, and belief in Him is among the greatest of pursuits and the noblest of aims, so there must be a means to it.

Our reply: He, exalted is He, only commanded seeking the means to Him after belief in Him, and belief in Him is an expression for knowledge of Him. So this was a command to seek the means to Him after belief and after knowing Him. Therefore it is impossible that this is a command to seek the means to Him in knowing Him. Rather, the intended meaning is seeking the means to Him in attaining His pleasure, and that is through acts of worship and obedience.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and strive in His cause that you may be successful.﴾ Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the abandonment of what is not fitting by His saying (fear Allah), and the performance of what is fitting by His saying ﴿and seek the means to Him﴾, and each of them is hard and heavy upon the self and desire, since the self calls only to this world and sensual pleasures, while the intellect calls only to the service and obedience of Allah and turning away from sensible things, and there is opposition and conflict between the two states; for this reason the scholars coined the example in the places where one seeks this world and the next with two co-wives and two opposites, and with East and West, and with night and day. Since this is so, submission to His saying ﴿fear Allah and seek the means to Him﴾ is among the hardest things for the self and the heaviest upon the nature. For this reason He followed that obligation with His saying: ﴿and strive in His cause that you may be successful.﴾ This verse is a noble verse comprising spiritual secrets, and we will point here to one of them: that those who worship Allah, exalted is He, are of two groups: among them are those who worship Allah for no purpose other than Allah, and among them are those who worship Him for another purpose.

The first station is the noble, lofty station, and to it points His saying: ﴿and strive in His cause﴾, meaning in the path of His servitude and the way of sincerity in knowing Him and serving Him.

The second station is below the first, and to it points His saying: ﴿that you may be successful﴾. And success (al-falah) is a comprehensive term for deliverance from what is disliked and winning what is loved.

Know that when He, exalted is He, guided the believers in this verse to the foundations of all goods and the keys to all felicities, He followed it with describing the state of the disbelievers and the end of one who knows no life or happiness except in this abode, and He mentioned from among those dreadful matters two types:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verses 36–37:

The first of them: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾

And in it are issues:

The first issue: The clause containing the particle "law" (if/even if) is the predicate (khabar) of "inna" (indeed). If it is asked: Why did He use the singular pronoun in His saying, ﴿to ransom themselves thereby﴾, although what precedes is an explanation of "all that is on the earth and the like of it"?

We say: The implied meaning is as if it were said: "to ransom themselves with that which was mentioned."

The second issue: His saying, ﴿and they will have a painful punishment﴾ may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it may be a conjunction (atf) upon the predicate.

The third issue: The purpose of this statement is to illustrate the inescapability of the punishment for them, for there is no way for them to be freed from it. And from the Prophet ﷺ: "It will be said to the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection: 'Tell me, if you had the fill of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say, 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for something easier than that, and you refused.'"

[Page 175]

The second type of threat mentioned in this verse:
His saying: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not be coming out of it, and they will have a lasting punishment.﴾ In it are two issues:

The first issue: Their wish to come out may be understood in two ways:

The first: That they intend this and seek a way out of it, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, they are returned into it﴾ (As-Sajdah: 20).

It has been said: When the flame of the Fire lifts them upward, there they wish to come out. And it has been said: They nearly come out of the Fire because of the intensity of the Fire and its pushing of those being punished.

The second: That they wish this in their hearts and desire it, as He, Exalted is He, said in another place: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 107). This interpretation is confirmed by the reading of one who recited: (They wish that they be taken out of the Fire), with a dammah on the yaa'.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'arite scholars) have argued from this verse that He, Exalted is He, will bring out of the Fire whoever says "There is no god but Allah" sincerely. They said: Because He, Exalted is He, made this meaning part of the threats of the disbelievers and of the kinds of severe warning with which He frightened them; and had this meaning not been specific to the disbelievers, there would have been no point in restricting the disbelievers to it. And Allah knows best.

Among what supports what we have said is His saying: ﴿and they will have a lasting punishment﴾, and this conveys restriction, so the meaning is: "they will have a lasting punishment, not others," just as His saying ﴿for you is your religion﴾ means "for you, not for others," and so it is here.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 38–40 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, a punishment from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾

Regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, there are two views:

The first: When He, exalted is He, mandated in the previous verse the cutting off of hands and feet for taking property by way of highway robbery (muharabah), He explained in this verse that taking property by way of theft also necessitates the cutting off of hands and feet.

The second: When He mentioned the magnification of the matter of killing, saying: ﴿Whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption in the land – it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one – it is as if he had saved mankind entirely﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 32), He mentioned after this the crimes that permit killing and maiming: first the cutting off of the road (highway robbery), and second the matter of theft. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: The grammarians differed concerning the nominative case in His saying ﴿wa-s-sariqu wa-s-sariqah﴾ (the thief, male and female), on several views:

The first, which is the view of Sibawayh and al-Akhfash, is that ﴿al-sariqu wa-l-sariqah﴾ are nominative by being the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is omitted, the estimate being: "What is recited to you is: the thief, male or female, their ruling is such-and-such." The same applies to His saying: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress, flog each one of them﴾ (al-Nur: 2), and to His saying: ﴿And the two who commit it among you, harm them﴾ (al-Nisa': 16). ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "al-sāriqa" and "al-sāriqata" in the accusative, and similarly "al-zāniyata wa-l-zāniya."

Sibawayh's preference in this is the accusative. He said: because the saying of the speaker "Zayd, strike him" is better than your saying "Zayd is, strike him." Also, "fa-qta'u" cannot be the predicate of the subject, because the predicate of the subject does not take the particle fa.

The second view, which is the choice of al-Farra': the nominative is preferable to the accusative, because the alif and lam in ﴿al-sariqu wa-l-sariqah﴾ take the place of "alladhi" (the one who), so the estimate becomes: "The one who stole, cut off his hand." On this estimate, it is good to introduce the particle fa upon the predicate, because it has become a conditional response (jaza'). Also, the accusative is only good if you mean a particular male thief or a particular female thief; but if you intend to direct this punishment at everyone who commits this act, then the nominative is preferable. This view was chosen by al-Zajjaj, and it is the one relied upon.

Among what indicates that the intended meaning of the verse is the condition and its response (shart wa-jaza') are several points:

The first: that God, exalted is He, stated this explicitly in His saying: ﴿a recompense for what they have earned﴾. This is evidence that the cutting was legislated as a recompense for the act of theft, so the recompense must be general in line with the generality of the condition.

The second: that theft is a crime and cutting is a punishment, and linking a punishment to a crime is appropriate; and mentioning a ruling immediately after an appropriate descriptor indicates that the descriptor is the cause (ʿillah) of that ruling.

The third: that if we take the verse in this way, the verse is meaningful; but if we take it as referring to a specific thief, it becomes ambiguous and without benefit, so the first is preferable.

As for the view to which Sibawayh went, it is nothing, and the following points show it:

The first: that he has cast doubt upon the Qur'an transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) from the Messenger (ﷺ) and from the whole community, and that is definitively false. If he says: "I do not say that reading in the nominative is impermissible, but I say the reading in the accusative is preferable," we say: this is also poor, because preferring a reading that only ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read over the reading of the Messenger (ﷺ) and of the whole community in the era of the Companions and the Successors is a reprehensible matter and a rejected statement.

The second: if the reading in the accusative were preferable, it would necessarily follow that among the readers there would be one who read ﴿wa-l-lladhayni ya'tiyanaha minkum﴾ in the accusative; and since no reader is found to have read thus, we know the fall of this view.

The third point: if we say ﴿wa-s-sariqu wa-s-sariqah﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is what we omit, namely our saying "in what is recited to you," then this sentence is complete with its subject and predicate, so to what does the fa in His saying ﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾ attach? If he says: the fa attaches to the verb indicated by His saying ﴿wa-s-sariqu wa-s-sariqah﴾, meaning that if he commits theft, cut off his hands, we say: if at the end of the matter you need to say "the thief, male and female" with the estimate "whoever stole," then mention this first so that you do not need the omission you mentioned.

The fourth: if we choose the reading in the accusative, that does not indicate that theft is the cause of the obligation of cutting; but if we choose the reading in the nominative, the verse conveys this meaning, and this meaning is reinforced by His saying ﴿a recompense for what they have earned﴾. Thus it is established that the reading in the nominative is preferable.

The fifth: Sibawayh said: "They put first what is more important, and what they are concerned with is more significant." The reading in the nominative requires mentioning the act of theft before the obligation of cutting, which indicates that the greatest attention is directed to explaining what relates to the state of the thief insofar as he is a thief. As for the reading in the accusative, it requires that attention be focused on explaining the cutting more than on his being a thief, and it is known that this is not the case, since the purpose of this verse is to show the ugliness of theft and to intensify the deterrence from it. Thus it is established that the reading in the nominative is definitively the one required, and God knows best.

* * *

The second issue: Many of the exegete-jurists (al-mufassirun al-usuliyyun) said: this verse is ambiguous (mujmal) in several respects:

The first: the ruling is attached to theft, and theft in its absolute sense does not necessitate cutting; rather, this theft must be theft of a specific quantity of property, and that quantity is not mentioned in the verse, so it is ambiguous.

The second: He, exalted is He, mandated the cutting of hands, and there is no clarification in it that what is required is the cutting of the right hands or the left; and by consensus, both are not to be cut together, so the verse is ambiguous.

The third: the word "yad" (hand) is a name that covers only the fingers. Do you not see that if someone swears not to touch so-and-so with his hand, and he touches him with his fingers, he breaks his oath? So "yad" is a name that applies to the fingers alone, and applies to the fingers with the palm, and applies to the fingers, palm and forearms up to the elbows, and applies to all of that up to the shoulders. Since the word "yad" is capable of all these divisions, and the specification is not mentioned in this verse, the verse is ambiguous.

The fourth: His saying ﴿fa-qta'u﴾ is addressed to a people, so it is possible that this obligation falls upon the whole community, or upon a specific group among them, or upon a particular individual among them, namely the imam of the time, as most scholars hold. Since the specification is not mentioned in the verse, the verse is ambiguous. Thus it is established by these points that this verse is ambiguous in an absolute sense. This is the statement of this position.

Some of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) said: the verse is not ambiguous at all. This is because we have shown that the alif and lam in His saying ﴿wa-s-sariqu wa-s-sariqah﴾ take the place of "alladhi," and the fa in His saying ﴿fa-qta'u﴾ is for the response of the condition, so the estimate is: "the one who stole, cut off his hand." This was confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a recompense for what they have earned﴾, and that earning necessarily refers to what was mentioned before, namely theft. Thus this becomes evidence that the locus and object of the ruling is the reality of theft, and its consequence is that the punishment is general in every case in which this condition is met, except where a separate evidence necessitates the specification of this general rule. As for His saying "the hands" being general, we say: its implication is the cutting of hands, but since there is consensus that both are not to be cut together, nor is one to begin with the left hand, we excluded that from the generality.

As for his saying that the word "yad" falls among several things, we say: we do not concede this. Rather, "yad" is a name for this limb up to the shoulder, and for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows﴾. Had the upper arms not been included in this name, there would have been no need to restrict it with His saying ﴿up to the elbows﴾. The apparent meaning of the verse therefore requires cutting both hands from the shoulders, as is the view of the Kharijites, except that we set this aside because of a separate evidence.

As for his fourth point, that the address may be to each individual or to a single specific person: we say its apparent meaning is that it is an address to everyone; the application of this is abandoned in cases specified by a separate evidence, and it remains acted upon in the rest. The summary is that we say: the verse is general, and it has become specified by separate evidences in some cases, so it remains a valid proof in what lies beyond them. It is known that this view is better than the view of one who says it is ambiguous and therefore yields no benefit at all.

* * *

The third issue: The majority of jurists (jumhur al-fuqaha') said: cutting is not required except under two conditions: the minimum amount (nisab), and that the theft be from a protected place (hirz). Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and al-Hasan al-Basri said: the amount is not a consideration, so cutting is obligatory for the theft of a little or of a lot, and the protected place is also not a consideration. This is the view of Dawud al-Isfahani and the view of the Kharijites. They relied on the generality of the verse in this question, as we have established, for His saying ﴿wa-s-sariqu wa-s-sariqah﴾ covers theft whether it is little or much, and whether it was stolen from a protected place or from an unprotected place.

When this is established, we say: if we were to go with specification (takhsis), it would have to be either by a single-transmission report (khabar al-wahid) or by analogy (qiyas), and specifying the general wording of the Qur'an by a single-transmission report or by analogy is not permissible. The argument of the majority of jurists (jumhur al-fuqaha') is that there is no need for us to say there is specification. Rather, we say: the word sariqah (theft) is an Arabic word, and we know by necessity that the people of the language do not say of one who takes a grain of wheat from another's wheat, or a single straw, or a small piece of bread, that he has stolen his property. So we know that taking another's property, however it occurs, is not called theft. Also, sariqah is derived from musaraqat ayn al-malik (stealing away from the owner's sight), and there is need for musaraqat ayn al-malik only if the stolen item is something that is an object of desire, in a place of stinginess and reluctance, such that the thief desires to take it and the one from whom it is stolen is strained by its being transferred to another. For this reason we have considered that taking property from a guarded place typical for its kind (hirz al-mithl) is a condition for the obligation of amputation, because what is not placed in a guarded place does not require, in taking it, the stealing away from the eyes, and so its taking is not called theft.

Dawud said: We do not obligate amputation for stealing a single grain, nor for stealing a single straw, but for the smallest thing in which stinginess and reluctance operate. The measures of little and much are not fixed; for a great king may disdain thousands in number, while a poor man may consider a tasu j (a small coin) to be a great deal. For this reason al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If someone says "I owe so-and-so a great amount of property" and then explains it as a grain, his statement is accepted, because it is possible that it was great in his estimation due to the extremity of his poverty and the severity of his need for it. Since the measures of little and much are not fixed, it is necessary to base the ruling on the least thing that is called property.

No one should find it strange and say: how is it permissible to cut off the hand for stealing a single tasuja? For the heretics (mulhidah) have made this a criticism of the Shari'ah, saying: since the hand's value is five hundred dinars of gold, how can it be cut off for the sake of a small amount of property? We have answered this objection by saying that the Law cut off his hand only because he took on baseness and lowliness in stealing that small amount; so it is not far-fetched that the Law should punish him, because of that baseness, with this great punishment. And if this answer is accepted by all, then let it also be accepted by us in obligating amputation for the small and the large.

He said: Among what indicates that it is not permissible to specify the generality of the Qur'an here by a single-transmission report is that those who hold the specification of this generality have differed in several ways. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: amputation is obligatory for a quarter of a dinar, and there is narrated in this his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "No amputation except for a quarter of a dinar." Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: amputation is not permissible except for ten dirhams minted, and there is narrated in this his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "No amputation except for the price of a shield (thaman al-mijann)." And the apparent meaning is that the price of a shield is not less than ten dirhams. Malik, Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is fixed at three dirhams or a quarter of a dinar. Ibn Abi Layla said: it is fixed at five dirhams. Each of these mujtahids criticizes the report which the other narrates, and on this assumption these specifications have become contradictory, so it is necessary that none of them be relied upon, and the knowledge of Allah's ruling be sought from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

He said: No one may say that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, unanimously agreed that amputation is obligatory only for a specific quantity. He said: Because al-Hasan al-Basri used to obligate amputation for theft in general, and used to say: "Beware of cutting off your hand for a dirham." And if there had been a established consensus, al-Hasan al-Basri would not have opposed it, despite his closeness to the time of the Companions and his great caution in matters related to religion. This is the presentation of the position of al-Hasan al-Basri and Dawud al-Isfahani.

As for the jurists, they agreed that a quantity is necessary for the obligation of amputation. Then al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: amputation is for a quarter of a dinar and above, which is the nisab of theft, and all other things are valued by it. Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: amputation is not obligatory for less than ten minted dirhams, and other things are valued by them.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams. Ibn Abi Layla said: five dirhams.

The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the apparent meaning of His statement: ﴿And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ requires amputation for the little and the much. However, the jurists agreed among themselves that amputation is not obligatory for less than a quarter of a dinar, so it is necessary that it remain for a quarter of a dinar and above upon the apparent text. Then this was reinforced by what is narrated, that he, peace be upon him, said: "No amputation except for a quarter of a dinar."

As for what Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, relied upon from his, peace be upon him, saying: "No amputation except for the price of a shield," it is weak for two reasons:

The first: that the price of a shield is unknown, so specifying the generality of the Qur'an by a single report that is mujmal (ambiguous) and of unknown meaning is not permissible.

The second: that if the price of a shield is fixed at ten dirhams, the specification resulting from it in the generality of His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ would be greater than the specification resulting in this verse from his, peace be upon him, saying: "No amputation except for a quarter of a dinar." So the preference lies with this side.

* * *

The Fourth Issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If a man steals for the first time, his right hand is cut off; for the second, his left foot; for the third, his left hand; and for the fourth, his right foot. Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: he is not amputated for the third and fourth time.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, argued by this verse in two ways:

The first: that theft is the cause (illah) for the obligation of amputation, and it has occurred in the third time, so amputation is obligatory in the third time as well. We say that theft is the cause for the obligation of amputation based on His statement: ﴿And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾, and we have explained that the meaning is: "The one who stole, cut off his hand." Also, the fa' in His statement ﴿cut off their hands﴾ indicates that amputation was made obligatory as a recompense for that theft. So theft is the cause for the obligation of amputation, and there is no doubt that theft has occurred in the third time, so what is the obligating factor for amputation is present in the third time, and it is necessary that its obligating effect follow it. It is not permissible that its obligating effect be the amputation in the first time, because a ruling does not precede its cause; for amputation was obligated by the first theft, so there remains only that theft in the third time obligates another amputation, which is what was sought.

The second: He, Exalted, said: ﴿cut off their hands﴾, and the word "hands" (al-aydi) is a plural word whose minimum is three. The apparent meaning requires the obligation of cutting off three hands from the male and female thief. It was left unapplied initially, so it remains applicable at the third theft.

If they say: Ibn Mas'ud recited "cut off their right hands" (aymanahuma), so this ruling is specific to the right hand and not to hands in general, and a shadhdh (irregular) recitation operates like a single-transmission report.

We say: An irregular recitation does not nullify the mutawatir (widely transmitted) recitation, so we rely on the mutawatir recitation in establishing our position. Also, the irregular recitation is not a proof according to us, because we are certain that it is not Qur'an; for if it were Qur'an it would have been mutawatir. For if we allowed that nothing of the Qur'an were transmitted to us by way of tawatur, the door would open for the criticism of the Rafidah and the heretics against the Qur'an; perhaps there were verses in the Qur'an explicitly indicating the imamate of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, which were not transmitted to us; and perhaps there were verses in it indicating the abrogation of most of these laws, which were not transmitted to us. Since that is false, because if it were Qur'an it would be mutawatir, and since it is not mutawatir we are certain that it is not Qur'an. Thus it is established that an irregular recitation is absolutely not a proof.

* * *

The Fifth Issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I make the thief pay back what he stole. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Ahmad and Ishaq said: amputation and the payment of the value are not combined; if he pays, there is no amputation, and if he is amputated, there is no payment. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: he is amputated in every case, and as for payment, it is due from him if he is wealthy, and it is not due from him if he is poor.

The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the verse indicates that theft obligates amputation, and His, peace be upon him, saying: "The hand is responsible for what it takes until it returns it" obligates liability; and both matters have combined in this theft, so it is necessary that both amputation and liability be obligatory. If a claimant argued that combining them is impossible, that would be a counter-argument requiring proof. Furthermore, we say: the right of Allah (hadd Allah) does not prevent the right of the servants (haqq al-ibad), as proven by the fact that recompense and value combine in the case of owned game, and by the fact that if the stolen item were still present, its return would be obligatory by consensus. It is also indicated that the stolen item remained in the owner's possession until the time of cutting off the thief's hand, by agreement; so at the moment of amputation, ownership of it either occurs restricted to the time of amputation, or is traced back to the first moment of the theft. The first is not held by the opponent, and the second requires that one say the ownership of it arose from the time of amputation in the time that preceded that time, and this requires the occurrence of the act in past time. And this is impossible.

The proof of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that He, Exalted, ruled that this amputation is a recompense (jaza'), and recompense is what suffices, so this indicates that this amputation suffices for the crime of theft; and if it suffices, it is necessary that payment not be added to it.

The answer: If the matter were as you say, it would be necessary that the return of the stolen item not be required when it is still existing. And Allah knows best what is correct.

* * *

The Sixth Issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the master (sayyid) has the right to carry out the hadd punishment upon his slaves (mamalik). Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: he does not have this right.

The proof of al-Shafi'i is that His statement: ﴿cut off their hands﴾ is general with regard to all; for this address contains nothing indicating that it is specific to some and not others; and since it covers all, the master is also included in it. It was left unapplied with regard to others than the imam and the master, so it is necessary that it remain applicable with regard to the imam and the master.

* * *

The Seventh Issue: The theologians (al-mutakallimun) used this verse as an argument that the community is obligated to appoint for itself a specific imam. The evidence for this is that He, Exalted, by this verse, obligated the carrying out of the hadd punishment upon thieves and adulterers; so there must be a person who is addressed by this address. The community agreed that it is not permissible for individual members of the populace to carry out the hadd punishments upon offenders; rather, they agreed that it is not permissible to carry out the hadd punishments upon free offenders except by the imam. Since this obligation is a decisive obligation, and the discharge of this obligation is not possible except when an imam exists, and what the obligation cannot be fulfilled without, while being within the power of the obligated person, is itself obligatory, then it is certain that the appointment of an imam is obligatory at that time.

* * *

The Eighth Issue: The Mu'tazilah said: His statement: ﴿a punishment from Allah﴾ indicates that this hadd was carried out upon him in a manner of contempt and humiliation. And if this is so, it is necessary to conclude that he deserves contempt, blame and humiliation; and when this is so, it is impossible to say that he remains deserving of praise and honor, since these are opposites and combining them is impossible. And this indicates that the punishment for a grave sin nullifies the reward of acts of obedience.

واعْلَمْ أنا قَدْ ذَكَرْنا الدَّلائِلَ الكَثِيرَةَ في بُطْلانِ القَوْلِ بِالإحْباطِ في سُورَةِ البَقَرَةِ في تَفْسِيرِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: (لا)
[Page 181]
﴿تُبْطِلُوا صَدَقاتِكم بِالمَنِّ والأذى﴾ (al-Baqarah: 264)، فَلا نُعِيدُها هَهُنا.
