The second view: that the verse is general, concerning anyone whose unbelievers come to him. Then they differed. Among them are those who said the ruling is established in all rulings and is not abrogated (*mansukh*, that is, repealed by a later revelation). This is the view of al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, 'Ata', Abu Bakr al-Asamm and Abu Muslim. Among them are those who said: it is abrogated by God's words: ﴿and judge between them by what God has revealed﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:49). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah. The position of al-Shafi'i is that it is obligatory upon the ruler of the Muslims to judge between the people of *dhimmah* (protected non-Muslim subjects) when they bring their dispute to him, because enforcing the ruling of Islam upon them is a humiliation for them. As for the *mu'ahidun* who have a covenant with the Muslims for a fixed term, it is not obligatory upon the ruler to judge between them; rather he has the choice in that. And this choice mentioned in this verse is specific to the *mu'ahidun*.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all﴾. The meaning is that they used not to come to him for judgment except to seek the easiest and lightest ruling, such as flogging instead of stoning. So when he turned away from them and refused to rule for them, it was hard for them that he turned away from them, and they became enemies to him. So God made clear that their enmity towards him cannot harm him.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you do judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, God loves the just﴾.

That is: judge between them with justice and caution, just as you judged by stoning.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And how would they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is Allah's judgment?﴾ On this verse there are two issues:

The first issue: This is Allah's expression of wonder (ta'jib) directed at His Prophet, peace be upon him, concerning the Jews' appointing him as judge, after they knew what the Torah contains regarding the punishment for the adulterer, and then their refusal to accept that judgment. They turned away from what they believed to be a true ruling to what they believed to be false, seeking a concession (rukhsah). Therefore their ignorance and obstinacy in this incident became evident in several respects:

The first: their turning away from the judgment of their own Book.

The second: their turning to the judgment of one whom they believed to be a false party (mubtil).

The third: their turning away from his judgment after they had appointed him as judge. Allah, exalted is He, thereby made clear the state of their ignorance and obstinacy, lest anyone be deceived by them into thinking that they are the People of the Book and among those who guard the command of Allah. Here there are two questions:

The first question: Where does His saying ﴿in which is Allah's judgment﴾ stand grammatically (i'rab)?

The answer: Either it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the Torah, which is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is (with them); or it is in the nominative as a predicate about it, like your saying: "And with them is the Torah, speaking of Allah's judgment, exalted is He"; or it has no place in the sentence, and the intended meaning is that with them is what makes them independent of arbitration, as you say: "With you is Zayd, who advises you and points you to what is right, so what do you do with anyone else?"

The second question: Why is the Torah feminine (annatha)? The answer: the matter here is based on the apparent wording.

The second issue: A group of the Hanafiyyah (Hanafi jurists) used this verse to argue that the ruling of the Torah and the laws of earlier communities bind us as long as they have not been abrogated (nusikha). This argument is weak. If it were so, the ruling of the Torah would be like the ruling of the Qur'an in the obligation to seek judgment from it, but the Law has forbidden looking into it. Rather, the intended matter here is this particular ruling, which is stoning, because they sought a concession by appointing him as judge.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then they turn away after that, and those are not believers.﴾

His saying ﴿Then they turn away﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to His saying ﴿they make you judge﴾.

His saying (after that) refers to the judgment of Allah which is in the Torah, and it is permissible that it refers to the arbitration itself.

His saying ﴿and those are not believers﴾ has several interpretations:

First: that is, they are not believers in the Torah, even though they display belief in it.

Second: ﴿those are not believers﴾ is a report that they will never believe; it is a statement about the future and not about the past.

Third: even though they asked you for judgment, they are not believers in you, nor do they hold the judgment you give to be valid, and this indicates that they have no faith in anything, and that their whole aim is only to obtain the worldly interests.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 44:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted (aslamu) judged for those who were Jews, and the rabbis (rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (ahbar), by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of God, and they were witnesses to it.﴾

Know that this is a reminder from God, exalted is He, to the Jews who denied the obligation of stoning (al-rajm), and an encouragement for them to be like their predecessors among the righteous scholars of their community and the prophets sent to them. In this are several issues:

**The first issue:** Conjunction (al-'atf) requires difference between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. Therefore there must be a distinction between guidance (huda) and light (nur). Guidance refers to the explanation of the rulings, the laws (shara'i') and the obligations (taklif), while light refers to the explanation of monotheism (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwa) and the return (ma'ad).

Al-Zajjaj said: "*In it is guidance*" means the explanation of the ruling about which they came asking the Prophet (ﷺ) for a verdict. "*And light*" means the explanation that the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) is true.

**The second issue:** Those who hold that the law of those before us (shar'u man qablana) is binding on us, unless there is evidence that it has been abrogated (naskh), argue with this verse. Its argument is that He, exalted is He, said: indeed in the Torah there is guidance and light. What is meant is that it is guidance and light in the foundations of the law (usul al-shar') and its branches (furu'). If it were abrogated and its ruling wholly unbinding, it would not contain guidance and light. It is not possible to restrict guidance and light to what relates to the foundations of religion alone, because He mentioned guidance and light separately; and if both were meant to refer to what relates to the foundations of religion, it would lead to repetition. Furthermore, this verse was revealed concerning the matter of stoning, so the legal rulings must be included in the verse. For although we differ over whether something other than the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is included in the verse, we agree that the occasion of revelation must be included in it.

**The third issue:** His words "*by it the prophets who submitted judged for those who were Jews*" mean the prophets who came after Moses. God sent among the Children of Israel thousands of prophets who had no book with them; He sent them only to uphold the Torah, so that they would observe its limits, perform its obligations, make lawful its lawful things, and make unlawful its unlawful things.

If it is said: every prophet must be a Muslim (muslim), so what is the benefit of His words "*the prophets who submitted*"?

We say there are several answers:

The first: What is meant by "*submitted*" is that they yielded to the judgment of the Torah. Among the prophets were some whose law was not the law of the Torah, and those who were submitting to the judgment of the Torah were those who lived between the mission of Moses and the mission of Jesus, peace be upon them both.

The second: Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, 'Ikrima, Qatada and al-Suddi said: it is possible that what is meant by "*the prophets who submitted*" is Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is because he (ﷺ) judged two Jews to be stoned, and this was the judgment of the Torah. He was mentioned with the plural form to honour him, as in His words: ﴿Indeed Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾ [al-Nahl: 120], and His words: ﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ [al-Nisa': 54]. This is because he had gathered in himself the qualities of goodness that were present in most of the prophets.

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: this is a refutation of the Jews and the Christians, because some of them used to say: all the prophets were Jews or Christians. So He said: "*by it the prophets who submitted judged*", meaning that the prophets were not described as Jews or Christians, but were submitting to God and yielding to His obligations.

The fourth: What is meant by His words "*the prophets who submitted*" is those whose purpose in judging by the Torah was faith, submission, the manifestation of God's rulings, and yielding to His obligations. The aim is to draw attention to the ugliness of the method of these later Jews, for their purpose in claiming to judge by the Torah was taking bribes and securing followers among the common people.

**The fourth issue:** His words "*for those who were Jews*" have two possible meanings:

The first: the meaning is that the prophets judged by the Torah only for those who were Jews, that is, for their sake and among themselves.

The second: it is possible that the meaning, by inversion of order, is: Indeed We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light for those who were Jews, by which the prophets who submitted judged.

**The fifth issue:** As for the rabbaniyyun (rabbis), their interpretation has already been given. As for the ahbar (scholars), Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the jurists (fuqaha'). The lexicographers differed over its singular. Al-Farra' said: it is only *hibr* with a kasra on the ha', and it is said of the learned person. It was named with this name because of the ink (hibr) with which one writes, since he is a possessor of books. Abu 'Ubayda used to say: *habr* with a fatha on the ha'. Al-Layth said: it is *hibr* and *habr*, with kasra and with fatha. Al-Asma'i said: I do not know whether it is *al-hibr* or *al-habr*.

As for its derivation, some people said: its root is from *tahbir*, which is embellishment. In a hadith: "A man will come out of the Fire whose *hibr* and *sibr* have gone," meaning his beauty and splendour. One who embellishes something is *muhabbir*. Since knowledge is the most perfect of the categories of virtue, beauty and excellence, the learned person was for this reason named after it.

Others said: its derivation is from the ink (hibr) with which one writes. This is the view of al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda. And God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** The verse indicates that the prophets, the rabbaniyyun and the ahbar all judge by the Torah. This requires that the rabbaniyyun be of a higher status than the ahbar. Thus it is established that the rabbaniyyun are like the mujtahids (those who exercise independent reasoning), and the ahbar are like ordinary scholars.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of God﴾. In this there are two issues:

**[p. 5]**

**The first issue:** The preservation of the Book of God is of two kinds:

The first: that it be preserved so that it is not forgotten.

The second: that it be preserved so that it is not wasted. God made it obligatory upon the scholars to preserve His Book in these two respects:

One of them: that they memorise it in their hearts and recite it with their tongues.

The second: that they not neglect its rulings and not ignore its laws.

**The second issue:** The *ba'* in His words "*by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of God*" has two possible meanings:

The first: that it governs the word "scholars" (ahbar), so that the meaning is: the scholars of what they were entrusted to preserve.

The second: that the meaning is: they judge by what they were entrusted to preserve. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

\* \* \*

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they were witnesses to it﴾. That is, these prophets, rabbaniyyun and ahbar were witnesses that everything in the Torah is true, correct, and from God. Therefore they certainly used to enforce the rulings of the Torah and guard them against distortion and alteration.

\* Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾.

Know that when He established that the prophets, the rabbaniyyun and the ahbar were standing firm in enforcing the rulings of the Torah without concern, He addressed the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and forbade them from distortion and alteration.

Know that the people's undertaking of distortion must arise from either fear and dread, or from greed and desire. Since fear is a stronger influence than greed, He, exalted is He, mentioned it first, saying: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me.﴾ The meaning is: beware of distorting My Book out of fear of the people, the kings and the nobles, so that you remove from them the obligatory punishments (hudud) and devise stratagems to drop God's obligations from them. So do not be fearful of people, but be fearful of Me and of My punishment.

When He mentioned the matter of dread, He followed it with the matter of desire, saying: ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾. That is, just as I forbade you from altering My rulings out of fear and dread, so I forbid you from altering and changing them for the sake of greed for wealth, status and taking bribes. For all the goods of this world are small, and the bribe you take from them is extremely small. And a bribe, being unlawful gain (suht), is of little blessing, permanence and benefit. Likewise, the wealth you earn is a small thing out of a small thing. Then you destroy by means of it the religion, the everlasting reward and the endless felicities.

It is also possible that their undertaking of distortion and alteration was for both reasons together: fear of the leaders and taking bribes from the common people. And since God prevented them from both, given the baseness and degradation in each of them, this constitutes a decisive proof for the prohibition of distortion and alteration.

**[p. 6]**

Then He followed this striking proof with a severe warning, saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has sent down, those are the disbelievers﴾. In this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** The purpose of this statement is to threaten the Jews for their undertaking of distorting God's ruling concerning the punishment of the married adulterer (muhsan). That is, since they denied God's ruling explicitly stated in the Torah and said that it was not obligatory, they are disbelievers absolutely, deserving the name of faith neither with Moses and the Torah nor with Muhammad and the Qur'an.

**The second issue:** The Khawarij said: everyone who disobeys God is a disbeliever. Most of the imams said: the matter is not so. As for the Khawarij, they argued with this verse and said: it is an explicit text that everyone who judges by other than what God has sent down is a disbeliever, and everyone who commits a sin has judged by other than what God has sent down, so he must be a disbeliever.

The theologians (mutakallimun) and the exegetes (mufassirun) gave several answers to this objection:

The first: this verse was revealed concerning the Jews, so it is specific to them. This is weak, because what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion. Some tried to rebut this question, saying: what is meant is that whoever of these people already mentioned does not judge by what God has sent down, those are the disbelievers. This is also weak, because His words "*whoever does not judge by what God has sent down*" is a statement in which the word "whoever" (man) is introduced in the sense of a condition, so it is general. And the statement of whoever says: what is meant is "whoever does not judge by what God has sent down among those already mentioned," is an addition to the text, and that is not permissible.

The second: 'Ata' said: it is a disbelief short of disbelief (kufr duna kufr). Tawus said: it is not a disbelief that removes one from the religion, like one who disbelieves in God and the Last Day. So they understood the verse as referring to ingratitude for blessings (kufr al-ni'ma), not disbelief in the religion. This too is weak, because when the word "disbelief" (kufr) is used without qualification, it refers to disbelief in the religion.

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: it is possible that the meaning is: whoever does not judge by what God has sent down has done an act resembling the acts of disbelievers, and for that reason is likened to the disbelievers. This is also weak, because it is a departure from the apparent meaning.

The fourth: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya al-Kinani said: His words "*by what God has sent down*" is a general expression, so His words "*whoever does not judge by what God has sent down*" mean: whoever acts contrary to God's ruling in everything God has sent down, those are the disbelievers. This is true, because the disbeliever is the one who acts contrary to God's ruling in everything God has sent down. As for the wrongdoer (fasiq), he acts contrary to God's ruling only in a small part, namely in action, whereas in belief and acknowledgment he is in agreement. This too is weak, because if this verse were a threat specific to one who opposes God's ruling in everything God has sent down, this threat would not apply to the Jews for their opposition to God's ruling concerning stoning. Yet the exegetes agreed that this threat applies to the Jews because of their opposition to God's ruling in the incident of stoning. This shows the invalidity of this answer.

The fifth: 'Ikrima said: His words "*whoever does not judge by what God has sent down*" apply only to one who denies in his heart and rejects with his tongue. As for one who recognises in his heart that it is God's ruling, and acknowledges with his tongue that it is God's ruling, but acts contrary to it, he is judging by what God has sent down, yet is one who abandons it, so he does not necessarily fall under this verse. This is the correct answer, and God knows best.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retribution﴾.

The meaning is that He, exalted is He, has made clear in this verse too that He, exalted is He, had made clear in the Torah that a life is for a life. These Jews also altered this ruling, favouring the Banu al-Nadir over the Banu Qurayza, and restricting the obligation of retaliation (qawd) to the Banu Qurayza rather than the Banu al-Nadir. This is the connection (wajh al-nazm) of the verse. There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: al-Kisa'i read: "al-ʿayn wa'l-anf wa'l-udhun wa'l-sinn wa'l-juruh" (the eye, the nose, the ear, the tooth and the wounds), all in the nominative (raf'). In this there are several aspects (wujuh):

One: it is a coordination (ʿatf) upon the position (mahall) of "anna al-nafs" (that the life), because the meaning is: "And We prescribed for them therein, the life for the life," since the meaning of "kataba" (We prescribed) is "qulna" (We said).

Two: writing (kitaba) may fall upon sentences of this kind; one says: "I wrote 'al-hamdu lillah' (praise be to Allah)" and "I recited 'surah anzalnaha' (a surah which We revealed)".

Three: they are in the nominative by way of resumption (istiʾnaf), the implied sense being: "the life is to be killed for the life, and the eye is to be put out for the eye." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He, in this surah: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians﴾.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr read all of them in the accusative (nasb) except "al-juruh", which is in the nominative. So "al-ʿayn, al-anf and al-udhun" are in the accusative by coordination upon "al-nafs"; then "al-juruh" is a subject (mubtada'), and "qisas" (retaliation) is its predicate (khabar).

Nafi', ʿAsim and Hamza read all of them in the accusative, coordinating some of these upon others, and the predicate of the whole is "qisas". Nafi' read "al-udhn" with a sukun on the dhal wherever it occurs, while the rest read it with a damma and a shadda; both are dialectal forms (lughatan).

The second issue: Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means, "And We ordained for them in the Torah that the life is for the life," meaning that whoever kills a soul without retaliation is subjected to qawd, and Allah did not make for him a blood-money (diyah) for a soul or for a wound; rather it is either pardon or retaliation. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: they used not to kill a man for a woman, so this verse was revealed. As for the limbs, every two persons between whom retaliation applies for a life, retaliation applies between them for all the limbs, provided they are equal in soundness; and if retaliation is impossible for the life, it is likewise impossible for the limbs. When Allah mentioned some of the organs, He generalised the ruling to all of them, saying, ﴿and for wounds is retribution﴾, which is whatever can be subjected to retaliation, such as the two lips, the penis, the two testicles, the nose, the two feet, the two hands and others. As for what retaliation cannot apply to, such as a bruise in flesh, a fracture in bone, or a wound in the belly from which destruction is feared, there is an arsh (fixed compensation) and hukumah (assessed compensation) for it.

Know that this verse indicates that this was a law in the Torah. Whoever says that the law of those before us binds us, unless it has been abrogated by specification, says: this verse is a proof for our law. Whoever denies this says: it is not a proof binding upon us.

The third issue: "al-qisas" here is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e. "and the wounds are subject to mutual retaliation, some with others."

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him﴾. The pronoun in His saying "lahu" (for him) may refer either to the one who pardons or to the one pardoned. As for the first, the sense is that if the injured person or the guardian of the slain pardons, that is an expiation for him, i.e. for the one who pardons; and this is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He, in the verse of retaliation in Surat al-Baqarah (2:178): ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾. Close to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Is one of you unable to be like Abu Damdam? When he left his house he would give his honour away as charity to the people." And ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever gives something of his body in charity, Allah, exalted is He, will expiate for him from his sins to the measure of it." This is the view of most of the exegetes.

The second view: the pronoun in His saying ﴿so it is an expiation for him﴾ refers to the killer and the wounder, meaning that if the one wronged pardons the wrongdoer, that pardon becomes an expiation for the wrongdoer, i.e. Allah will not take him to account after that pardon. As for the wronged person who pardons, his reward is with Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then those are the wrongdoers﴾. There is a question here: He, exalted is He, first said: ﴿then they are the disbelievers﴾, and secondly: ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾; and disbelief is greater than wrongdoing. Since He mentioned the greater threat first, what is the benefit of mentioning the lesser after it?
The answer: disbelief, insofar as it is a denial of the blessing of the Master and a repudiation of it, is disbelief; and insofar as it entails keeping the soul in severe eternal punishment, it is wrongdoing against the soul. So in the first verse He mentioned what concerns his shortcoming in regard to the right of the Creator, glorified is He, and in this verse He mentioned what concerns his shortcoming in regard to his own soul.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 46:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah. And We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light, and confirming what was before it of the Torah, as guidance and instruction for the God-fearing.﴾

Qaffaytu (qaffā) is like ʿaqibtu (ʿaqqaba), when you follow someone; then it is said ʿaqqabtuhu bi-fulan and qaffaytuhu bihi, so that it transitively reaches the second object with the addition of the particle bi (bi).

If it is said: where is the first object in the verse?

We say: it is omitted, and the adverbial phrase, which is His saying ﴿upon their footsteps﴾, stands in its place, because when he is made to follow upon their footsteps, he has indeed been made to follow them with him. The pronoun in (ātharihim) refers to the prophets in His saying ﴿by which the prophets who submitted judge for those who were Jews﴾. Here there are questions:

The First Question: He, exalted is He, described Jesus, son of Mary, as confirming what was before him of the Torah, and that is only the case if his action was according to the law of the Torah, and it is known that he was not so, for the law of Jesus, peace be upon him, was different from the law of Moses, peace be upon him. Therefore He said at the end of this verse ﴿Let the people of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed in it﴾. So how is the way to reconcile these two matters?

The answer: the meaning of Jesus being a confirmer of the Torah is that he acknowledged that it is a book sent down from God, and that it was a truth whose action was obligatory before the abrogation (naskh) came.

The Second Question: Why did He repeat His saying ﴿confirming what was before him﴾?

The answer: there is no repetition in it, because in the first: the Messiah confirms the Torah, and in the second: the Gospel confirms the Torah.

The Third Question: He, exalted is He, described the Gospel with five attributes, saying ﴿in it was guidance and light, and confirming what was before it of the Torah, and guidance and instruction for the God-fearing﴾, and there are three discussions in it:

One of them: what is the difference between these five attributes?

The second: why did He mention guidance twice?

The third: why did He specify it as instruction for the God-fearing?

The answer to the first: the Gospel is guidance in the sense that it contains the proofs indicating monotheism (tawhid) and transcendence (tanzih), and God's exemption from consort, offspring, likeness and opposite, and on prophethood and on the return (ma'ad). This is what is meant by its being guidance. As for its being light, what is meant by it is that it is an explanation of the legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyya) and the details of obligations. As for its confirming what was before it, it is possible to take it as its being a giver of good news of the coming and advent of Muhammad (ﷺ). As for its being guidance a second time, that is because its containing the good news of the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a cause for people to be guided to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). And since the most intense aspect of dispute between the Muslims and the Jews and Christians was on this matter, God, exalted is He, certainly repeated it once more, as an alert that the Gospel indicates with clear indication the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). So it was guidance in this matter, which is the most in need of explanation and affirmation. As for its being instruction, it is because the Gospel contains advice, admonitions and eloquent, emphatic reprimands. He specified them as the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from them, as in His saying ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

The Fourth Question: His saying concerning the attribute of the Gospel ﴿and confirming what was before it﴾ is conjoined to what?

The answer: it is conjoined to the position (mahall) of (fihi huda), and its position is the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the estimate is: And We gave him the Gospel while it was guidance and light and confirming what was before it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein.﴾ Ḥamzah recited (liyaḥkuma) with a kasra on the lām and a fatḥa on the mīm. He made the lām dependent on His words ﴿And We gave him the Gospel﴾, because giving the Gospel means sending it down to him, so the meaning is: "We gave him the Gospel that he might judge." As for the rest of the reciters, they read the lām and the mīm with a jazm (sukūn) in the form of a command (amr). In this reading there are two possibilities:

The first: the sense is "And We said: let the people of the Gospel judge." This would be a report of what was obligated upon them at that time regarding judging by what the Gospel contained. Then the word "said" (qawl) was omitted, because what precedes it, His words "And We ordained" (wa-kataba-nā) and "And We sent them following" (wa-qaffaynā), indicates it. Omitting "said" is common, as in His exalted words: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23], meaning: they will say, "Peace be upon you."

The second: His words "let them judge" (wa-l-yaḥkum) are the beginning of a command to the Christians to judge by what is in the Gospel.

If it is asked: how is it permissible that they be commanded to judge by what is in the Gospel after the Qur'an was revealed?

We answer: the reply to this is from several aspects:

The first: the intended meaning is "let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein of the proofs indicating the prophethood of Muḥammad (ﷺ)." This is the view of al-Aṣamm.

The second: "And let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein, of what has not become abrogated (mansūkh) by the Qur'an."

The third: the intended meaning of His words ﴿And let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾ is to restrain them from distorting and altering what is in the Gospel, as the Jews did by concealing the rulings of the Torah. So the meaning of "let them judge" is: let the people of the Gospel acknowledge what Allah has revealed therein in the manner in which Allah revealed it, without distortion or alteration.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fāsiqūn).﴾ The exegetes differed. Some of them made these three, I mean His words "the disbelievers (al-kāfirūn), the wrongdoers (al-ẓālimūn), the defiantly disobedient (al-fāsiqūn)," attributes of one single subject.

Al-Qaffāl said: there is no harm to the meaning in mentioning each of these three separately with a word, rather it is like saying: whoever obeys Allah is the believer, whoever obeys Allah is the righteous, whoever obeys Allah is the God-fearing (al-muttaqī); for all of these are different attributes belonging to one single subject.

Others said: the first applies to the one who denies (al-jāḥid), and the second and third apply to the one who acknowledges but abandons (al-muqirr al-tārik). Al-Aṣamm said: the first and second apply to the Jews, and the third applies to the Christians.

[Page 11]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book﴾. This is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). His words ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ mean: every Book that descended from the heaven, other than the Qur'an.

His words ﴿and as a guardian over it﴾ involve several issues.

**The first issue: concerning *muhaymin* (guardian, watcher).** There are two views.

The first: al-Khalil (Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Abu ʿUbayda said: it is said, "*hayman al-rajul yuhaymin*," when a man is a watcher over a thing, a witness to it, and a protector of it. Hassan (ibn Thabit) said:

*Indeed the Book is a guardian over our Prophet,*
*and the truth is known to those of understanding.*

The second: they said: the original form of our saying *āmana yu'minu* ("he believes") is that the active participle is *mu'min*, and the original form of *aʾmana yuʾaminu* is *muʾaminun*, with two hamzas. Then the first was changed into a *hāʾ*, as in *haraqtu* and *araqtu*, and *hiyyāka* and *iyyāka*. The second was changed into a *yāʾ*, so it became *muhaymin*. For this reason the commentators said: ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ means a trustworthy one over the Books that came before it.

**The second issue:** The Qur'an was a guardian over the Books because it is the Book that will never be abrogated at all, and alteration and distortion cannot reach it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr 15:9]. Since this is so, the Qur'an's testimony that the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms are true and right remains forever, and so the reality of these Books remains known forever.

**The third issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: it was recited as *(wa-muhaymanan ʿalayhi)* with a *fatha* on the *mīm*, because it is witnessed over by Allah, exalted is He, that He preserves it from distortion and alteration, according to what we have established from the verses, and according to His words ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat 41:42]. The one who guards over it is Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has sent down﴾, meaning: judge between the Jews by the Qur'an and the revelation which Allah, exalted is He, has sent down to you.

﴿And do not follow their desires, turning away from the truth that has come to you﴾. On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** ﴿do not follow﴾ means "do not deviate." Therefore it is followed by *ʿan* (from). As if it were said: "Do not deviate from the truth that has come to you, following their desires."

**The second issue:** It is narrated that a group of Jews said: "Come, let us go to Muhammad (ﷺ), perhaps we can tempt him away from his religion." Then they entered upon him and said: "O Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis and the nobles of the Jews, and if we follow you, all the Jews will follow you. Between us and our adversaries there is a dispute, and we will bring them to you for judgment. Rule for us, and we will believe in you." So Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse.

**The third issue:** Those who criticize the infallibility of the Prophets have held onto this verse and said: "If it were not permissible for them to commit disobedience, He would not have said ﴿do not follow their desires, turning away from the truth that has come to you﴾."

The answer: that is within his capacity, but he does not do it because of the prohibition. It was also said: the address is to him, but the intended meaning is others.

* * *

[Page 12]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a path﴾. On this there are issues:

**The first issue: concerning the word *shir'a* (law).** Regarding its derivation there are two views.

The first: the meaning of *shara'a* is "to explain and clarify."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: the word *shar'* is a verbal noun from "*sharaʿtu al-ihāb*," when you split and skinned the hide.

The second: *shara'a* is derived from *shurūʿ* (beginning) in a matter, which is entering into it. In the language of the Arabs, *al-shariʿa* is the watering place which people approach so that they drink from it. Thus *al-shariʿa* is of the pattern *faʿīla* in the sense of *mafʿūla* (the thing approached), and it refers to the matters which Allah, exalted is He, has obligated upon the responsible persons to begin upon. As for *al-minhāj*, it is the clear path. It is said: "*nahajtu laka al-ṭarīq*" and "*anhajtu*," and both are dialect forms.

**The second issue:** Most scholars have used this verse to argue that the law of those before us does not bind us, because His words ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a path﴾ indicate that every Messenger must necessarily be independent with a particular law, and this negates that the community of one Messenger is obligated by the law of another Messenger.

**The third issue:** There are verses indicating there is no divergence in the way of the Prophets and Messengers, and verses indicating that divergence does occur in it.

As for the first type: His words ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura 42:13], up to His words ﴿that you establish the religion and do not be divided therein﴾ [al-Shura 42:13]. And He said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:90].

As for the second type: it is this verse. The way to reconcile them is to say: the first type of verses is directed to what relates to the foundations of the religion, and the second type is directed to what relates to the branches of the religion.

**The fourth issue:** The address in His words ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a path﴾ is addressed to the three communities: the community of Moses, the community of Jesus, and the community of Muhammad, peace be upon them. The evidence is that these three have been mentioned earlier in His words ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾, then He said ﴿and We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, son of Mary﴾, then He said ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a path﴾, meaning different laws: for the Torah there is a law, for the Gospel there is a law, and for the Qur'an there is a law.

**The fifth issue:** Some said: *al-shirʿa* and *al-minhāj* are two expressions for one meaning, and the repetition is for emphasis, and what is meant by both is the religion. Others said: there is a difference between them. *Al-shirʿa* is an expression for the general *sharīʿa*, and *al-ṭarīqa* (the way) is an expression for the noble qualities of the *sharīʿa*, and this is what is meant by *al-minhāj*. So the *sharīʿa* is the beginning, and the *ṭarīqa* is the end. Al-Mubarrad said: the *sharīʿa* is the beginning of the *ṭarīqa*, and the *ṭarīqa* is the *minhāj* that continues. This is an affirmation of what we have said, and Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

* Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, that is: a group agreed upon one law, or possessors of one community, meaning one religion without disagreement regarding it. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: this indicates that everything occurs by the will of Allah, exalted is He. The Muʿtazila interpreted it as the will of compulsion.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But to test you in what He has given you﴾, namely the different laws, whether you act upon them, submitting to Allah and humbling yourselves to the obligations of Allah, or whether you follow doubts and fall short in action.

* *
﴿So race to good deeds﴾, that is, hasten toward them and compete toward them.
﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾: a resumed statement in the sense of a reason for racing toward good deeds.

﴿Then He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾: He will inform you with what leaves no doubt of the decisive recompense that distinguishes between your righteous and your wrongdoers, and between those who fulfill their work and those who fall short in it. The meaning is that the matter will end in what removes doubts and produces certainty, and that occurs when the good-doer is repaid for his good and the evildoer for his evil.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has sent down, and do not follow their desires﴾. On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** If it is said: His words ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ are as if it were said: "And We sent down to you that judge," and *an* is connected to the imperative, because it is a verb like other verbs. It is also possible that it is coordinated with His words "in truth," meaning: We sent it down in truth and [We sent down] "that judge." His words ﴿and do not follow their desires﴾: we have mentioned that the Jews gathered and intended to bring him into altering his religion, but Allah, exalted is He, protected him from that.

**The second issue:** They said: this verse abrogates the option in His words ﴿So judge between them, or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:42].

**The third issue:** The command to judge is repeated after its mention in the first verse, either for emphasis, or because they are two rulings about which he was commanded together, since they brought the matter before him regarding the adultery of a married person, then they brought the matter before him regarding a killing that had occurred among them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means that they turn you back to their desires, for whoever is turned from the truth to falsehood has been tempted. From this is His words ﴿And they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ [al-Isra 17:73]. The *fitna* here, in their speech, is that which inclines one away from the truth and casts into falsehood. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "I seek refuge in You from the trial of life" [*fitnat al-maḥyā*]. He said: it is that one deviates from the path. The people of knowledge said: this verse indicates that error and forgetfulness are permissible for the Messenger, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾, and deliberate intent in such a matter is not permissible for the Messenger, so nothing remains except error and forgetfulness.

Then He, exalted is He, said: (*fa-in tawallaw*), meaning: if they do not accept your judgment, ﴿then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾. On this there are two issues:

[Page 14]

**The first issue:** The meaning is that He will test them by punishing them in this world for some of their sins, which is that He will give you power over them and punish them in this world with killing and exile. Allah, exalted is He, specified "some" of the sins only because the people were punished in this world for some of their sins, and their punishment for some was sufficient for their destruction and annihilation. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The verse indicates that everything is by the will of Allah, exalted is He, because He does not intend to afflict them for some of their sins without having also willed their sins. This indicates that He, exalted is He, wills both good and evil.

So the *sharīʿa* is the beginning, and the *ṭarīqa* is the end. Al-Mubarrad said: the *sharīʿa* is the beginning of the *ṭarīqa*, and the *ṭarīqa* is the *minhāj* that continues. This is an affirmation of what we have said, and Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

* Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, that is: a group agreed upon one law, or possessors of one community, meaning one religion without disagreement regarding it. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: this indicates that everything occurs by the will of Allah, exalted is He. The Muʿtazila interpreted it as the will of compulsion.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But to test you in what He has given you﴾, namely the different laws, whether you act upon them, submitting to Allah and humbling yourselves to the obligations of Allah, or whether you follow doubts and fall short in action.

* *
﴿So race to good deeds﴾, that is, hasten toward them and compete toward them.
﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾: a resumed statement in the sense of a reason for racing toward good deeds.

﴿Then He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾: He will inform you with what leaves no doubt of the decisive recompense that distinguishes between your righteous and your wrongdoers, and between those who fulfill their work and those who fall short in it. The meaning is that the matter will end in what removes doubts and produces certainty, and that occurs when the good-doer is repaid for his good and the evildoer for his evil.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has sent down, and do not follow their desires﴾. On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** If it is said: His words ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ are as if it were said: "And We sent down to you that judge," and *an* is connected to the imperative, because it is a verb like other verbs. It is also possible that it is coordinated with His words "in truth," meaning: We sent it down in truth and [We sent down] "that judge." His words ﴿and do not follow their desires﴾: we have mentioned that the Jews gathered and intended to bring him into altering his religion, but Allah, exalted is He, protected him from that.

**The second issue:** They said: this verse abrogates the option in His words ﴿So judge between them, or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:42].

**The third issue:** The command to judge is repeated after its mention in the first verse, either for emphasis, or because they are two rulings about which he was commanded together, since they brought the matter before him regarding the adultery of a married person, then they brought the matter before him regarding a killing that had occurred among them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means that they turn you back to their desires, for whoever is turned from the truth to falsehood has been tempted. From this is His words ﴿And they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ [al-Isra 17:73]. The *fitna* here, in their speech, is that which inclines one away from the truth and casts into falsehood. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "I seek refuge in You from the trial of life" [*fitnat al-maḥyā*]. He said: it is that one deviates from the path. The people of knowledge said: this verse indicates that error and forgetfulness are permissible for the Messenger, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾, and deliberate intent in such a matter is not permissible for the Messenger, so nothing remains except error and forgetfulness.

Then He, exalted is He, said: (*fa-in tawallaw*), meaning: if they do not accept your judgment, ﴿then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾. On this there are two issues:

[Page 14]

**The first issue:** The meaning is that He will test them by punishing them in this world for some of their sins, which is that He will give you power over them and punish them in this world with killing and exile. Allah, exalted is He, specified "some" of the sins only because the people were punished in this world for some of their sins, and their punishment for some was sufficient for their destruction and annihilation. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The verse indicates that everything is by the will of Allah, exalted is He, because He does not intend to afflict them for some of their sins without having also willed their sins. This indicates that He, exalted is He, wills both good and evil.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning they are rebellious in disbelief and transgressors therein. He means that turning away from the judgment of Allah, exalted is He, is a great rebellion and transgression in disbelief.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Age of Ignorance?﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Amir read ﴿تَبْغُونَ﴾ (*tabghūna*, "they seek") with a *tā'* (second person, addressing them), while the rest of the readers used a *yā'* (*yabghūna*, third person). Al-Sulami read ﴿أفَحُكْمُ الجاهِلِيَّةِ﴾ (*afa-ḥukmu al-jāhiliyyah*) with *ḥukmu* in the nominative as the *mubtada'* (grammatical inception, i.e., the subject of a nominal sentence), and ﴿يَبْغُونَ﴾ as the *khabar* (predicate), with the returning pronoun (*ḍamīr rājiʿ*, the pronoun linking the predicate back to the subject) omitted because it is clear. Qatada read ﴿أبِحُكْمِ الجاهِلِيَّةِ﴾ (*abi-ḥukmi al-jāhiliyyah*). The meaning is that this judgment which they seek is only the judgment that the judges of the Age of Ignorance pass. By their desires, they wished that Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, would be a judge like those judges.

**The second issue:** The verse has two interpretations.

*The first:* Muqatil said: "There had been bloodshed between Qurayzah and Nadir before Allah sent Muhammad, peace be upon him. When he was sent, they came to him for judgment. The Banu Qurayzah said: 'The Banu Nadir are our brothers; our father is one, our religion is one, and our Book is one. If the Banu Nadir kill one of us, they give us seventy wasq of dates, and if we kill one of them, they take from us one hundred and forty wasq of dates, and the blood-money for our wounds is half of theirs. So judge between us and them.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'I judge that the blood of the Qurazi is equal to the blood of the Nadiri, and the blood of the Nadiri is equal to the blood of the Qurazi. Neither of them has any superiority over the other in blood, in blood-money, or in wounds.' The Banu Nadir became angry and said: 'We will not accept your judgment, for you are our enemy.' So Allah, exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Age of Ignorance?﴾, meaning their first judgment."

It has also been said: whenever a ruling became due against their weak members, they enforced it upon them, but whenever it became due against their powerful members, they did not enforce it upon them. Allah, exalted, forbade them from this through this verse.

*The second:* The purpose of this verse is to reproach the Jews, that they are People of the Book and knowledge, yet they seek the judgment of the Age of Ignorance, which is pure ignorance and plain desire.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ The *lām* (the *lām* of clarification, *lām al-bayān*, which specifies the person or group to whom a statement is addressed) in His words ﴿لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾ (*li-qawmin yūqinūn*, "for a people who are certain") is like the *lām* in ﴿هَيْتَ لَكَ﴾ (*hayta laka*, "come, for you"). That is, this address and this question are for a people who are certain, for they are the ones who know that there is no one more just than Allah in judgment, and no one better than Him in clarification.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 51:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another.﴾

Know that the speech is complete at His saying "allies" (awliya'), and then He begins, saying ﴿They are allies of one another.﴾ It is narrated that ʿUbada ibn al-Samit came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disavowed, in his presence, the alliance with the Jews. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy said: "But I do not disavow them, for I fear the turns of fortune." So this verse was revealed. The meaning of "do not take them as allies" is: do not rely on seeking their help, and do not seek their friendship.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means that he is as if he were like them. This is a severe warning from Allah and an emphasis on the obligation of avoiding those who oppose the religion. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And whoever does not taste it, then he is not of me﴾ (al-Baqarah: 249).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ It is narrated from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that he said: I said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have a Christian scribe." He said: "What is wrong with you? May Allah fight you! Why did you not take a man of faith (ḥanif)? Have you not heard the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾?" I said: "His religion is for him, and his writing is for me." He said: "I will not honour them when Allah has humiliated them, nor will I exalt them when Allah has debased them, nor will I bring them close when Allah has distanced them." I said: "The affair of Basra cannot be completed without him." He said: "The Christian has died, and peace." He meant: suppose he has died, then what will you do after him? Whatever you would do after his death, do it now, and be independent of him by means of another.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us."﴾

Know that what is meant by His words ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ is the hypocrites, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. His words ﴿hastening toward them﴾ mean that they hasten to show affection to the Jews and the Christians of Najran, because they were people of wealth, and they used to help them with their affairs and lend to them. The hypocrites would say: "We only associate with them because we fear that a misfortune may befall us."

Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The "dāʾira" (calamity) is one of the turns of time, like a change of dynasty (dawla). It is what turns from one people to another. The "dāʾira" is what is feared, such as defeat and frightening events. So the "dawāʾir" (calamities) revolve, and the "dawāʾil" (reversals) alternate.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, "We fear that the matter will not be completed for Muhammad (ﷺ), so that the affair will revert to what it was before that."

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a command from Him, so they will become regretful over what they harboured within themselves.﴾
[Page 16]
The exegetes said: "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah is binding, because when the Generous One gives hope of good, He does it. It is equivalent to a promise, because the soul is attached to it and hopes for it. The meaning is: Perhaps Allah will bring a conquest for the Messenger of Allah over his enemies and the victory of the Muslims over their enemies, or a command from Him that will cut off the root of the Jews or expel them from their lands, so that the hypocrites will become regretful over what they had been saying to themselves. That is because they used to doubt the matter of the Messenger and say: "We do not think that his affair will be completed for him." The more evident outcome is that dominion and victory will pass to his enemies. It was also said: "Or a command from Him" means that the Prophet (ﷺ) would be commanded to expose the secrets of the hypocrites and kill them, so they would regret their deeds.

If it is said: The condition for the validity of a division (taqsim) is that it be between two mutually exclusive parts, and His words ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a command from Him﴾ are not like that, because bringing a conquest is included within His words ﴿or a command from Him﴾.

We say: His words ﴿or a command from Him﴾ mean: or a command from Him in which people have absolutely no action, such as [the case of] the Banu al-Nadir, whom Allah cast terror into their hearts, so they were given [their property] into their hands without fighting or an army.

Then Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you? Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers."﴾

Among the issues here:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn Amir recite (yaqulu) without the waw, and so it is in the copies of the people of the Hijaz and Syria. The rest recite it with the waw, and so it is in the copies of the people of Iraq.

Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Omitting the waw here is like including it, because the clause joined by the conjunction contains a mention of what it is joined to. The ones described by His words ﴿they hasten toward them﴾ are those about whom the believers said ﴿Are these the ones who swore by Allah﴾. So when each of the two clauses contains a mention of the other, it is fine to join them with the waw and without the waw. A parallel is His words, the Exalted: ﴿They will say, "They are three, the fourth of them is their dog," and they will say, "They are five, the sixth of them is their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. When each of the two clauses contained a mention of what preceded, that made the mention of the waw unnecessary. Then He said: ﴿And they will say, "They are seven, and the eighth of them is their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and He added the waw. This shows that omitting the waw and including it are both permissible.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: The omission of the waw is on the assumption that it is an answer to a questioner who asks, "What then do the believers say at that time?" So it is said: ﴿those who believe say, "Are these the ones who swore..."﴾.

They differed over the recitation of this verse in another respect. Abu 'Amr recited (wa-yaqula alladhina amanu) in the accusative, in the sense of: "and perhaps those who believe will say." As for the one who reads in the nominative, he made the waw a conjunction joining one clause to another. The recitation of the one who omits the waw supports the nominative reading.

The second issue: The benefit of the believers making this statement is that they are astonished at the state of the hypocrites when they showed inclination toward allying with the Jews and Christians, and they said: they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they are with us and among our helpers. So now, how have they become allies of our enemies, loving to mix with them and to rely on them?

The third issue: His words ﴿their deeds have become worthless﴾ may be from the speech of the believers, and may be from the speech of Allah the Exalted. The meaning is: whatever faith they had displayed has gone, and every good deed they had done is void, because they have now displayed allegiance to the Jews and Christians. Thus they have become losers in this world and the Hereafter. For when their deeds became void, they were left with the hardship of performing those deeds, and none of their fruits or benefits were attained by them; rather, they deserved the curse in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 54 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills. And Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.﴾

Among its issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿĀmir and Nafiʿ read (yartadid) with two dals, while the rest read it with a single, doubled dal. The first (reading) is to make the doubling apparent, and the second is for idgham (assimilation of the two dals).

al-Zajjaj said: Making both dals apparent is the original form, because when the second of a doubled consonant is vocalized with sukun, the doubling becomes apparent, as in His saying: ﴿If a wound touches you﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 140]. In the language it is also permissible to say: in yamassakum (with the doubled form).

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf narrated that the apostates were eleven groups: three in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

The Banu Mudlij, whose leader was Dhu al-Himar, namely al-Aswad al-ʿAnsi. He was a soothsayer who claimed prophethood in Yemen and seized control of its lands, and he expelled the governors of the Messenger of Allah. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote to Muʿadh ibn Jabal and the chiefs of Yemen, and Allah destroyed him at the hand of Fayruz al-Daylami, who attacked him by night and killed him. The Messenger of Allah informed of his killing on the night he was killed, and the Muslims rejoiced. The Messenger of Allah passed away the following day, and news of it reached (Medina) at the end of the month of Rabiʿ al-Awwal.

The Banu Hanifah, the people of Musaylimah, who claimed prophethood and wrote to the Messenger of Allah: "From Musaylimah, the Messenger of Allah, to Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah. To proceed: the earth is half mine and half yours." The Messenger replied: "From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Musaylimah the liar. To proceed: the earth belongs to Allah; He bequeaths it to whomever He wills of His servants, and the good end is for the God-fearing." Abu Bakr fought him with the armies of the Muslims, and he was killed
Page 18
at the hands of Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah. He used to say: "I killed the best of people in the Jahiliyyah and the worst of people in Islam," meaning in my Jahiliyyah and in my Islam.

The Banu Asad, the people of Tulayhah ibn Khuwaylid, who claimed prophethood. The Messenger of Allah sent Khalid against him, and he fled after the fighting to al-Sham, then embraced Islam and his Islam became good.

And seven in the time of Abu Bakr: Fazarah, the people of ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn; Ghatafan, the people of Qurrah ibn Salamah al-Qushayri; Banu Sulaym, the people of al-Fujaʾah ibn ʿAbd Yalil; Banu Yarbuʿ, the people of Malik ibn Nuwayrah; some of the Banu Tamim, the people of Sajah bint al-Mundhir, who claimed prophethood and married herself to Musaylimah the liar; Kindah, the people of al-Ashʿath ibn Qays; and Banu Bakr ibn Wail in Bahrayn, the people of al-Hatm ibn Zayd. Allah sufficed them through the hand of Abu Bakr. And one group in the time of ʿUmar: Ghassan, the people of Jabalah ibn al-Ayham. That was because Jabalah embraced Islam at the hand of ʿUmar, and one day he was circumambulating (the Kaʿbah) with his robe trailing, and a man stepped on the edge of his robe, so he became angry and slapped him. The man complained to ʿUmar, who ruled that retaliation was due against him, unless he pardoned him. He said: "I will buy it for a thousand," but the man refused. He kept raising the ransom until it reached ten thousand, but the man refused anything except retaliation. (Jabalah) asked ʿUmar for a delay, and ʿUmar granted him one. So he fled to the Romans and apostatized.

The third issue: The meaning of the verse: "O you who have believed, whoever among you turns to the disbelievers and reverts from his religion, let him know that Allah, exalted is He, will bring forth other people who will support this religion in the most eloquent manner."

al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Allah knew that some people would turn back from Islam after the death of their Prophet, so He informed them that He would bring a people whom He loves and who love Him. According to this interpretation, this verse is a report of the unseen, and what was reported came to pass accordingly, so it is a miracle.

The fourth issue: They differed about who those people are. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj said: They are Abu Bakr and his companions, because they are the ones who fought the people of apostasy.

ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, the Arabs apostatized, hypocrisy became prevalent, and there befell my father a calamity which, had it befallen the towering mountains, would have crushed them.

al-Suddi said: The verse was revealed concerning the Ansar, because they are the ones who supported the Messenger and helped him in making the religion manifest.

Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning the people of Yemen. It is related with a marfuʿ report that "when this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ pointed to Abu Musa al-Ashʿari and said: 'They are the people of this man.'" Others said: They are the Persians, because it is related that "when the Prophet ﷺ was asked about this verse, he struck his hand on the shoulder of Salman and said: 'This one and his people. Had the religion been suspended at the Pleiades, men from the sons of Persia would have attained it.'"

Some said: It was revealed concerning ʿAli, peace be upon him, and two aspects indicate this:

The first: "When the Messenger ﷺ handed the banner to ʿAli, peace be upon him, on the day of Khaybar, he said: 'Tomorrow I will surely give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love.'" And this is the attribute mentioned in the verse.

The second aspect: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned after this verse His saying: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and the believers who establish prayer and give zakah while bowing﴾, and this verse concerns ʿAli. So it was more fitting to make what precedes it also concern him. This is the sum of the opinions on this verse.

* * *

For us regarding this verse there are several standpoints:

The first standpoint: This verse is among the strongest proofs against the doctrine of the Imamiyyah among the Rafidah. Their doctrine is established as follows: all those who acknowledged the caliphate and imamate of Abu Bakr became disbelievers and apostates, because they denied the explicit text (nass) on the imamate of ʿAli, peace and blessings be upon him. We say: If that were so, Allah, exalted is He, would have brought a people who would fight them, subdue them and return them to the true religion, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Whoever among you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people﴾ to the end of the verse. The word "man" (whoever), in the context of a conditional, is general, so it indicates that everyone who becomes an apostate from the religion of Islam, Allah will bring a people who subdue them, return them and nullify their might. So if those who appointed Abu Bakr to the caliphate were like that, the verse would necessarily require that Allah bring a people who would subdue them and nullify their doctrine. But this did not happen; rather the opposite occurred, for the Rafidah have been the ones subdued and prevented from openly displaying their false claims ever since they existed, and we know the corruption of their claim and doctrine. This is a clear argument for whoever is fair.

The second standpoint: We claim that this verse must be said to concern Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and the evidence for this consists of two aspects:

The first: This verse is specific to fighting the apostates, and Abu Bakr is the one who undertook the fighting of the apostates, as we have explained. It is not possible that the intended person be the Messenger, peace be upon him, because he never fought the apostates, and because He said: ﴿then Allah will bring﴾, and this is for the future, not the present, so these people must not have existed at the time this address was revealed.

If it is said: This is binding on you, because Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, existed at that time.

We say: The answer is in two parts:

The first: The people with whom Abu Bakr fought the people of apostasy did not exist at present.

The second: The meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, said: "then Allah will bring a people able and empowered to wage this war." Although Abu Bakr existed at that time, he was not independent at that time in matters of war, command and prohibition. So the objection is removed. Thus it is established that the intended person cannot be the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, nor can it be ʿAli, peace be upon him, because ʿAli never fought against the people of apostasy, so how could this verse be applied to him?

If they say: Rather, his fighting was with the people of apostasy, because everyone who disputed with him over the imamate was an apostate.

We say: This is false for two reasons:

The first: The name "apostate" applies only to one who has abandoned the Islamic laws, and those who disputed with ʿAli were not like that outwardly, and no one said that he fought them because they had left Islam. ʿAli, peace be upon him, never called them apostates at all. So what these Rafidah, may Allah curse them, say is a slander against all the Muslims and against ʿAli as well.

The second: If everyone who disputed with him over the imamate were an apostate, it would follow that Abu Bakr and his people were apostates. And if that were so, it would necessarily follow from the apparent meaning of the verse that Allah bring a people who would subdue them and return them to the correct religion. But since this never occurred at all, we know that disputing with ʿAli over the imamate is not apostasy. And if it is not apostasy, the verse cannot be applied to ʿAli, because it was revealed concerning those who fight the apostates. Nor can it be said that it was revealed concerning the people of Yemen or the people of Persia, because they never fought against apostates. And even supposing they did fight that battle, they were a flock, followers and tails, and the leader obeyed and commanding in that event was Abu Bakr. It is well known that applying the verse to the one who was the origin of this worship and the obeyed leader in it is more fitting than applying it to the flock, followers and tails. Thus it has become evident, by the clear proof we have mentioned, that this verse is specific to Abu Bakr.

The second aspect in showing that this verse is specific to Abu Bakr: We say: Suppose ʿAli had fought
Page 20
the apostates. Still, Abu Bakr's fighting against the apostates was of higher standing and greater effect in Islam than ʿAli's fighting against those who opposed him over the imamate. This is because it is known by mass transmission (tawatur) that when the Prophet ﷺ died, the Bedouins were agitated and rebelled, and that Abu Bakr is the one who subdued Musaylimah and Tulayhah, and he is the one who fought the seven apostate groups, and he is the one who fought those who withheld zakah. When he did that, Islam became stable, its power grew, and its state expanded. As for when the matter reached ʿAli, peace be upon him, Islam had already spread through East and West, the kings of the world had become subdued, and Islam had come to prevail over all religions and creeds. Thus it is established that Abu Bakr's fighting, may Allah be pleased with him, had a greater effect in supporting and strengthening Islam than ʿAli's fighting, peace be upon him. And it is known that the purpose of this verse is to honor a people who strive to strengthen the religion and support Islam, and since Abu Bakr was the one who undertook that, he must be the one intended by the verse.

The third standpoint regarding this verse: We claim that this verse indicates the validity of Abu Bakr's imamate. For since it has been established by what we have mentioned that this verse is specific to him, we say: Allah, exalted is He, described those whom He intended by this verse with attributes:

The first of them: that He loves them and they love Him.

Since it has been established that the one intended by this verse is Abu Bakr, it follows that His saying: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ is a description of Abu Bakr. And whoever Allah, exalted is He, describes with this cannot be an oppressor, and this indicates that he was rightful in his imamate.

Secondly: His saying, ﴿humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾. This too is a description of Abu Bakr, for the reason we have mentioned, and it is confirmed by what is related in the widely transmitted report that he (ﷺ) said: "The most merciful of my community towards my community is Abu Bakr." Thus he was described as merciful and compassionate towards the believers, and as firm with the disbelievers. Do you not see that at the beginning, when the Messenger (ﷺ) was in Makkah and was in the utmost weakness, how he used to defend the Messenger (ﷺ), and how he used to keep close to him and serve him, and did not care for any of the tyrannical disbelievers and their devils? And at the end of the matter, meaning at the time of his caliphate, how he did not turn to anyone's word, and insisted that fighting the apostates who withheld zakat was necessary, until the matter reached the point where he went out to fight that people alone, until the great Companions came, entreated him and forbade him from going. Then, when the army was sent against them, they were routed, and God, exalted is He, made that the beginning of the dominion of Islam. So His saying, ﴿humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ befits none but him.

Thirdly: His saying, ﴿they strive in the way of God and do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾. This is shared between Abu Bakr and Ali, except that Abu Bakr's share in it is more complete and perfect. That is because Abu Bakr's striving against the disbelievers took place at the beginning of the mission, when Islam was at the utmost weakness and disbelief was at the utmost strength, and he strove against the disbelievers to the extent of his ability and defended the Messenger of God with his utmost effort. As for Ali (peace be upon him), he only began striving on the day of Badr and Uhud, and at that time Islam was strong and the armies were gathered. Thus it is established that Abu Bakr's striving was more perfect than Ali's in two respects:

The first: he preceded him in time, so he was more excellent, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the victory﴾ [al-Hadid: 10].

The second: Abu Bakr's striving took place at a time when the Messenger (ﷺ) was weak, while Ali's striving took place at a time of strength.

Fourthly: His saying, ﴿That is the bounty of God; He gives it to whom He wills﴾. This is fitting for Abu Bakr, because it is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let not those of bounty and ampleness among you swear off﴾ [al-Nur: 22], and we have shown that this verse was about Abu Bakr. And what indicates that all these qualities belong to Abu Bakr is that we have shown by evidence that this verse must be about Abu Bakr, and when that is so, these qualities must necessarily be for Abu Bakr. And when this is established, it becomes necessary to affirm with certainty the validity of his imamate, for if his imamate were invalid, these qualities would not be fitting for him.

If it is said: Why could it not be said that he was described with these qualities during the lifetime of the Messenger (ﷺ), and then after his death, when he undertook the imamate, these qualities ceased and became void?

We say: This is absolutely false, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him﴾. He thus affirmed that they would be described by this quality at the time God brings them in the future, and this indicates God's testimony that he was described with these qualities at the time of his fighting against the people of apostasy, and that was the time of his imamate. Thus it is established from what we have mentioned that this verse indicates the validity of his imamate. As for the claim of the Rafidah, may God curse them, that this verse is about Ali, may God be pleased with him, on the ground that he (ﷺ) said on the day of Khaybar: "I will surely give the banner tomorrow to a man who loves God and His Messenger, and whom God and His Messenger love," and that this was Ali (peace be upon him): we say, this report is of the category of solitary reports (ahad), and according to them it is not permissible to rely on it in practice, so how is it permissible to rely on it in matters of knowledge? Also, establishing this quality for Ali does not necessitate its negation from Abu Bakr; and even if it indicated that, it would not indicate the negation of that whole collection from Abu Bakr. Among those qualities is his being a returner to the charge and not a fleer, and when that is negated from Abu Bakr, the whole collection of those qualities is not realised in him, and this suffices in action by way of the argument from the wording (dalil al-khitab). But the negation of all those qualities is not indicated by the wording. He, exalted is He, only affirmed this quality mentioned in this verse at the time of his later fighting against the apostates. Suppose that this quality was not present at that time; that does not prevent its presence in the future. Moreover, what we have mentioned is a clinging to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, while what they have mentioned is a clinging to the aforementioned report transmitted by solitary chains; and moreover it is opposed by the hadiths indicating that Abu Bakr loved God and His Messenger, and that God loved him and was pleased with him. He, exalted is He, said concerning Abu Bakr: ﴿And you will surely be given so that you are pleased﴾ [al-Layl: 21]. And he (peace be upon him) said: "God manifests Himself to people generally, and manifests Himself to Abu Bakr specifically," and he said: "God never poured anything into my chest except that He poured it into the chest of Abu Bakr." All of this indicates that he loved God and His Messenger, and that God and His Messenger loved him.

As for the second aspect, which is their saying: the verse after this verse indicates the imamate of Ali, so this verse must have been revealed concerning Ali. Our answer: We do not concede that the verse after this verse indicates the imamate of Ali, and we will mention the discussion of it, God willing. This is what is to be said in this place of the discussion, and God knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾, the detailed discussion of love has been mentioned by us in Surat al-Baqarah in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], so there is no benefit in repeating it. There is in it a subtle point: that He, exalted is He, placed His love for them before their love for Him, and this is true, because were it not that God loved them, He would not have granted them success until they became lovers of Him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾. It is like His saying: ﴿harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "adhillah" is the plural of "dhalil", whereas "dhalul" has the plural "dhulul". The meaning of their being "humble" is not that they are abased, but rather the intent is to emphasise their description with gentleness and lowering of the side.
