For whoever is humble before a person does not at all display any arrogance or haughtiness, rather he displays only gentleness and softness; so likewise here. Then His saying: ﴿mighty against the disbelievers﴾ means they display sternness and haughtiness towards the disbelievers. It is also said: "yu'azzunahum", meaning they overpower them, from the saying "'azzahu yu'izzuhu" when he overcame him, as if they are severe upon them with subjugation and domination.

If it is said: Why was it not said "humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers" [with lam for the believers]?

We say: In this there are two aspects:

One: that the word "dhull" is made to include the meaning of mercy and compassion, as if it were said: showing mercy towards them and compassion for them, in the manner of humbleness and modesty.

The second: that He, exalted is He, mentioned the particle "'ala" so as to indicate the loftiness of their station, their merit and their nobility, so that it conveys that their being humble is not because they are inherently abased, but that this humbling was for the sake of their wishing to join to the loftiness of their station the virtue of humility. It was also read as "adhillatan wa a'izzatan" in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (hal).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿they strive in the way of God﴾, meaning for the victory of God's religion, ﴿and do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾. In this there are two aspects:

The first: that this "wa" be for the circumstantial state, for the hypocrites used to watch the disbelievers and fear their blame. So God, exalted is He, makes clear in this verse that whoever is strong in religion does not fear, in supporting God's religion with his hand and tongue, the blame of any blamer.

The second: that this "wa" be for conjunction, and the meaning is that it is their nature to strive in the way of God and for no other purpose, and it is their nature that they are firm in supporting the religion and do not care for the blame of the blamers. The "lawmah" is a single instance of blame, and the indefiniteness of it and of "la'il" is for emphasis, as if it were said: they never at all fear the blame of any one of the blamers.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the bounty of God; He gives it to whom He wills﴾. The word "dhalika" points back to what was previously mentioned of the description of the people with love, humbleness, might, striving, and the absence of fear of even a single blame. So God, exalted is He, makes clear that all of that is by His bounty and kindness, and this is explicit that the obedience of servants is created by God, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah carry the wording to mean the doing of favours (al-alṭaf), and this is far-fetched, for the doing of favours is general with respect to all, so specification requires an additional benefit.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. "Al-Wasi'" points to completeness of power, and "al-'Alim" points to completeness of knowledge. And since God, exalted is He, informed that He would bring forth peoples of this character and description, He reinforced that by stating that He is complete in power, so He is not incapable of this promised matter, and complete in knowledge, so the occurrence of contradiction in His reports and promises is impossible.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 55 (part 1 of 2)**

[Page 23]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe, who establish prayer and give zakah while bowing [in prayer]﴾.

The connection (wajh al-nazm) of the verse is that when He, may He be exalted, had forbidden, in the preceding verses, taking disbelievers as allies (muwalah), He commanded in this verse the allegiance due to those whose allegiance is obligatory. He said: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe﴾, meaning the believers who possess the attributes mentioned. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning His saying ﴿and those who believe﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: the intended meaning is all believers in general. This is because when Ubadah ibn al-Samit disassociated himself from the Jews and said, "I am free before Allah from the alliance of Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and I take Allah and His Messenger as my allies," this verse was revealed in accordance with his statement. It is also narrated that "Abdullah ibn Salam said: O Messenger of Allah, our people have shunned us and sworn that they will not sit with us, and we cannot sit with your companions because of the distance of the dwellings. Then this verse was revealed, and he said:

[Page 23 continued]

"We are content with Allah and His Messenger and with the believers as allies." Accordingly, the verse is general concerning all believers, so every believer is an ally of all believers. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]. On this view, His saying ﴿who establish prayer and give zakah﴾ is a description applying to all believers. The purpose of mentioning these attributes is to distinguish the believers from the hypocrites, for they used to claim faith, but they were not persistent in the prayers and the zakah. Allah, may He be exalted, said concerning the manner of their prayer: ﴿And they do not come to prayer except while lazy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], and He said: ﴿They show off to the people and do not remember Allah except a little﴾ [al-Nisa': 142], and He said concerning their zakah: ﴿stingy toward good﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19]. As for His saying ﴿while bowing﴾, there are, on this view, several aspects:

The first: Abu Muslim said: the intended meaning of ruku' (bowing) is humility (khushu'), that is, they pray and give zakah while being submissive and obedient to all of Allah's commands and prohibitions.

The second: that the intended meaning is: it is their habit to establish prayer, and bowing is singled out for mention as an honour for it, as in His saying: ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43].

The third: some have said that when this verse was revealed, His companions differed concerning these attributes: some had completed the prayer, some had given money to the poor, and some were still in prayer and were bowing. Since they differed concerning these attributes, Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned all of these attributes without exception.

The second opinion: the intended meaning of this verse is a specific individual. On this view there are several statements:

The first: Ikrimah narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: Ata' narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him. It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Salam said: When this verse was revealed I said: O Messenger of Allah, I saw Ali give his ring in charity to a needy person while he was bowing, so we take him as an ally. It is also narrated "from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: One day I prayed the noon prayer with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). A beggar asked in the mosque, but no one gave him anything. The beggar raised his hand to the sky and said: O Allah, bear witness that I asked in the mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ) and no one gave me anything. Ali, peace be upon him, was bowing, so he gestured to him with the little finger of his right hand, on which there was a ring. The beggar came and took the ring in the sight of the Prophet (ﷺ). Then [the Prophet (ﷺ)] said: O Allah, my brother Musa asked You, and said: ﴿My Lord, expand my breast for me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 25] to His saying: ﴿and make him a partner in my affair﴾ [Ta-Ha: 32], and You revealed a speaking Qur'an: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother and give you both authority﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. O Allah, I am Muhammad, Your Prophet and Your chosen one, so expand my breast for me, ease my affair for me, and make for me a minister from my family, Ali, through whom strengthen my back." Abu Dharr said: By Allah, the Messenger of Allah had not finished this statement before Jibril descended and said: "O Muhammad, recite: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾ to the end of it." This is the entirety of what pertains to the narrations on this issue.

* * *

The second issue: The Shi'ah said: this verse indicates that the Imam after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is Ali ibn Abi Talib. Its formulation is that we say: this verse indicates that the intended referent of this verse is an imam, and whenever this is the case, that imam must be Ali ibn Abi Talib.

Explanation of the first stage: the word wali (guardian) in the lexicon has come with the meaning of helper and lover, as in His saying: ﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]. It has also come with the meaning of one who disposes of affairs (mutasarrif), as in his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "Any woman who marries without the permission of her wali (guardian)." We say: here there are two aspects:

The first: the word wali has come with these two meanings, and Allah did not specify which of them is intended. There is no contradiction between the two meanings, so it is necessary to take it as both, and therefore the verse indicates that the believers mentioned in the

[Page 24]

verse have authority over the Ummah.

The second: we say: wali in this verse cannot be in the sense of helper, so it must be in the sense of one who disposes of affairs. We say it cannot be in the sense of helper because the guardianship (wilayah) mentioned in this verse is not general to all believers, on the evidence that He, may He be exalted, mentioned it with the word ﴿innama﴾ ("only"), and ﴿innama﴾ is for restriction (hasr), like His saying: ﴿Allah is only one God﴾ [al-Nisa': 171]. The guardianship mentioned in this verse is not in the sense of support, and when it is not in the sense of support, it is in the sense of disposing of affairs, since wali has no meaning other than these two. Thus the sense of the verse becomes: "The one who disposes of affairs over you, O believers, is only Allah and His Messenger and the believers described by such-and-such attribute." This requires that the believers described by the attributes mentioned in this verse dispose of affairs over the entire Ummah, and there is no meaning of imam except a person who disposes of affairs over the entire Ummah. Thus, by what we have mentioned, it is established that this verse indicates that the person mentioned in it must be the imam of the Ummah.

As for the explanation of the second stage: once what we have mentioned is established, it is necessary that this person be Ali ibn Abi Talib. Its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: whoever establishes the imamate of a particular person by this verse says that person is Ali, and it has been established by what we previously presented that this verse indicates the imamate of a specific person; therefore that person must be Ali, since there is no one who makes a distinction.

The second: the narrations have converged that this verse was revealed concerning Ali. It is not possible to adopt the view of one who says it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, because if it had been revealed concerning him it would have indicated his imamate, and the Ummah has agreed that this verse does not indicate his imamate. Therefore this view is invalid.

The third: His saying ﴿and they are bowing﴾ cannot be taken as coordinated (ma'tuf, 'atf) with what precedes it, because prayer has already been mentioned, and prayer includes bowing, so repeating the mention of bowing would be repetition (tikrar). Therefore it must be taken as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "they give zakah while they are bowing." They agreed that giving zakah while bowing was not done except by Ali, so the verse is specific to him and indicates his imamate by the aspect we have explained. This is the essence of the Shi'ah's argument from this verse for the imamate of Ali, peace be upon him.

The answer: as for taking the word wali in the sense of helper and in the sense of one who disposes of affairs together, this is not permissible, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that it is not permissible to apply a homonymous word (lafz mushtarak) to both of its meanings at once.

As for the second aspect: we say, why is it not permissible that the intended meaning of the word wali in this verse be helper and lover? We will establish the proof that taking the word wali in this sense is preferable to taking it in the sense of one who disposes of affairs. Then we will answer what they have said. We say: what indicates that taking it as helper is preferable are several aspects:

The first: what is appropriate to what precedes this verse and what follows it is nothing other than this meaning. As for what precedes this verse, He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾, and the intention is not "do not take the Jews and Christians as imams who dispose of your souls and your wealth," since the falsity of this is known by necessity. Rather, the intention is "do not take the Jews and Christians as beloved friends and helpers, do not mix with them, and do not support them." Then, having emphasized the prohibition of this, He said: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and the believers﴾, described as such. The apparent meaning is that the guardianship commanded here is the same as the guardianship forbidden earlier. Since the guardianship forbidden earlier is guardianship in the sense of support, the guardianship commanded is guardianship in the sense of support. As for what follows this verse, it is His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not take those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game, from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies. And fear Allah, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 57].

[Page 25]

He repeated the prohibition against taking the Jews, the Christians, and the disbelievers as allies. There is no doubt that the guardianship forbidden is guardianship in the sense of support, so likewise the guardianship in His saying ﴿Your guardian is only Allah﴾ must be in the sense of support. Whoever is fair, sets aside partisanship, and reflects on the beginning and the end of the verse will be certain that the wali in His saying ﴿Your guardian is only Allah﴾ is nothing other than the sense of helper and lover, and it cannot mean imam, because that would be introducing an alien statement between two statements directed toward a single purpose, and that would be in extreme incoherence and weakness, and the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, must be exalted above that.

The second argument: if we took guardianship in the sense of disposing of affairs and imamate, the believers mentioned in the verse would not be described as possessing guardianship at the time of the revelation of the verse, because Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, did not have executive authority during the lifetime of the Messenger. Yet the verse requires that these believers be described as possessing guardianship at present. But if we take guardianship in the sense of love and support, guardianship would be present at the time. Thus it is established that taking guardianship in the sense of love is preferable to taking it in the sense of disposing of affairs. What confirms what we have said is that He, may He be exalted, forbade the believers from taking the Jews and the Christians as allies, then commanded them to ally with these believers. Therefore the allegiance to these believers must be present at the time, so that negation and affirmation apply to one and the same thing. Since guardianship in the sense of disposing of affairs was not present at the time, it is impossible to interpret the verse in that sense.

The third argument: He, may He be exalted, mentioned the believers described in this verse in the plural form in seven places, namely His saying: ﴿those who believe, who establish prayer and give zakah while bowing﴾. Although applying plural expressions to a single person is permissible as a form of honour, it is a metaphor (majaz), not a literal meaning (haqiqah), and the default is to interpret speech according to its literal meaning.

The fourth argument: we have demonstrated by clear proof that the preceding verse, namely His saying: ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾ to the end of the verse, is among the strongest indications of the validity of the imamate of Abu Bakr. Therefore, if this verse indicated the validity of the imamate of Ali after the Messenger, a contradiction would arise between the two verses, and that is false. Therefore it must be affirmed with certainty that this verse does not indicate that Ali is the imam after the Messenger.

The Fifth Argument: Ali ibn Abi Talib knew the interpretation of the Qur'an better than these Rafidis (the Rafida, a term for extreme Shi'a). If this verse indicated his imamate, he would have cited it in one of the assemblies. The people cannot say that he left it out because of taqiyya (dissimulation), because they transmit from him that on the day of the Shura (the council after Umar's death) he invoked the report of Ghadir (Ghadir Khumm), the report of the mubahala (the mutual imprecation with the Christians of Najran), and all his other virtues and merits, and he did not at all invoke this verse to establish his imamate. This necessarily establishes the falsity of the claim of these Rafidis, may Allah curse them.

The Sixth Argument: Suppose that it indicates the imamate of Ali. We agree that, when it was revealed, it did not indicate that the imamate was actual at that moment, because Ali did not have executive authority over the Community during the lifetime of the Messenger (peace be upon him). So there remains only that the verse must be taken to indicate that Ali would become imam after that. If they say this, we say what it implies and understand it as his imamate after Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman, since there is nothing in the verse that determines the time. If they say: the scholars regarding this verse are of two opinions. Some of them said that it does not indicate the imamate of Ali, and some said that it indicates his imamate, and everyone who said this said that it indicates his imamate after the Messenger without any interval. Then the claim that the verse indicates the imamate of Ali in this way is a third claim, and it is false. We respond to it by saying: Who informed you that no one in the Community said this statement? It is possible, indeed it is apparent, that since a proponent argued with this verse for the imamate of Ali, a questioner would raise this question against that argument. So the mention of this possibility and this question is coupled with the mention of this argument.

The Seventh Argument: His saying ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾ is undoubtedly addressed to the Community, and they were certain that the one who had authority over them was Allah and His Messenger. Allah Most High only stated this speech to comfort the believers and to inform them that they have no need to take friends and helpers from among the disbelievers. This is because whoever has Allah and His Messenger as his supporter and helper, what need does he have to seek support and love from the Jews and Christians? If that is so, then the meaning of His saying ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾ is the guardianship in the sense of support and love. There is no doubt that the word walī (guardian) is mentioned only once, so when it is intended here in the sense of support, it is impossible for it to be intended in the sense of executive authority, since it has been established that it is not permissible to use a homonymous word in both of its meanings at once.

The Eighth Argument: Allah Most High praised the believers in the preceding verse by His saying ﴿He loves them and they love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers﴾. When we take His saying ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾ to mean love and support, His saying ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾ conveys the same benefit as His saying ﴿He loves them and they love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers﴾, and His saying ﴿striving in the way of Allah﴾ conveys the same benefit as His saying ﴿establish the prayer and give zakat while bowing﴾. Therefore this verse is consistent with what precedes it, confirming its meaning, and that is more appropriate. By these considerations it is established that the guardianship mentioned in this verse must be in the sense of support, not in the sense of executive authority.

As for the argument on which they relied, namely that the guardianship mentioned in the verse is not general while guardianship in the sense of support is general, its answer comes from two aspects:

The first: We do not concede that the guardianship mentioned in the verse is not general, and we do not concede that the particle ʾinnamā (only) is restrictive. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is only like water We sent down from the sky﴾ (Yunus 10:24). There is no doubt that the life of this world has other likenesses besides this likeness. And He said ﴿The life of this world is only play and amusement﴾ (Muhammad 47:36). There is no doubt that play and amusement may occur in other things as well.

The second: We do not concede that guardianship in the sense of support is general to all the believers. Its explanation is that Allah Most High divided the believers into two groups:

One of them: those whom He made to have authority over them, and they are the ones addressed by His saying ﴿Your guardian is only Allah﴾.

The second: the guardians (awliyā'), and they are the believers who ﴿establish the prayer and give zakat while bowing﴾. When we interpret guardianship here in the sense of support, the meaning is that He made one of the two groups supporters of the second group. The support of the second group is not realized for all the believers, and if it were so, it would follow that within the group who are the supported, they would be supporters of themselves, and that is impossible. So it is established that the support of one of the two groups of the Community is not established for the whole Community, but is specific to the second group of the Community. Therefore it does not follow, from the guardianship mentioned in this verse being specific, that it cannot be in the sense of support. This is a good, subtle answer, which requires reflection.

As for their argument that this verse was revealed concerning Ali, it is disputed. We have explained that most of the exegetes assert that it was revealed concerning the Community as a whole, and the meaning is that Allah Most High commanded the Muslim not to take a beloved and a helper except from among the Muslims. Some of them say that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr.

As for their argument that the verse is specific to the one who gave zakat while bowing, and that this was Ali ibn Abi Talib, we say that this too is weak in several respects:

The first: zakat is a term for the obligatory, not for the recommended, as proven by the saying of Allah Most High ﴿and give zakat﴾. So if he gave obligatory zakat while in the state of bowing, he would have delayed the payment of obligatory zakat beyond the first time of its obligation, and according to most scholars this is disobedience, and it is not permissible to attribute it to Ali (peace be upon him). And interpreting zakat as voluntary charity is contrary to the basic principle, because we have explained that His saying ﴿and give zakat﴾ apparently indicates that everything called zakat is obligatory.

The second: It is fitting for Ali (peace be upon him) to have his heart absorbed in the remembrance of Allah while he is in prayer, and it is apparent that whoever is like this does not free himself to listen to and understand the speech of others. For this reason Allah Most High said ﴿those who remember Allah standing, sitting and on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:191). And how can one whose heart is absorbed in thought free himself to listen to the speech of others?

The third: giving a ring to a poor man during prayer is a great deal of action, and what is fitting for the state of Ali (peace be upon him) is that he would not do that.

The fourth: It is well known that he (peace be upon him) was poor and had no property on which zakat is due. For this reason they say that when he gave three loaves, Surat Hal Ata (Surah 76) was revealed concerning him, and that is not possible unless he was poor. As for one who has property on which zakat is due, it is impossible that he would deserve the great praise mentioned in that surah for giving three loaves. And if he had no property on which zakat is due, it is impossible to take His saying ﴿and they give zakat while bowing﴾ as referring to him.

The Fifth Aspect: Suppose that the intended meaning of this verse is Ali ibn Abi Talib. Still, the argument from the verse is not complete unless it is established that the intended meaning of walī is the one with executive authority, not the helper and lover. This has already been discussed.

* * *

The Third Issue: Know that those who say that the meaning of His saying ﴿and they give zakat while bowing﴾ is that they give zakat while in the state of bowing, have argued from the verse that a small action does not invalidate the prayer, since he gave zakat to the beggar while he was in prayer. There is no doubt that he intended to give zakat while in prayer, so this indicates that such actions do not invalidate the prayer. Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The First Question: What is mentioned in the verse is Allah Most High, His Messenger and the believers, so why did it not say: "Your guardians are..."?

The answer: The original statement is "Your guardian is only Allah," so guardianship was attributed to Allah in the way of primacy. Then, in the same arrangement of establishing it for Him, guardianship was established for the Messenger of Allah and the believers by way of following. If it had been said, "Your guardians are only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe," there would be no primary and secondary element in the speech. In the recitation of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "Your master is only Allah."

The Second Question: What is the grammatical position of ﴿those who establish﴾?

The answer: It is in the nominative case as an apposition (badal) to "those who believe," or one may say the implied sense is "They are those who establish." Or it is in the accusative case as a praise (madh). The purpose of mentioning it is to distinguish the sincere believer from the one who claims faith while being a hypocrite, because that sincerity is recognized only by being constant in prayer while bowing, that is, in the state of humility, submissiveness and lowliness before Allah Most High.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever takes God and His Messenger and those who believe as allies — indeed, the party of God, they are the victorious﴾

There are two issues here.

The first issue: Ḥizb (ḥizb, a group or party) linguistically means a man's companions who are with him in his opinion, and they are the people who gather for the affair of their party. The exegetes have various expressions about it. Al-Ḥasan said: "the soldiers of God." Abū Rawq said: "the allies of God." Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: "the followers (shīʿah) of God." Some said: "the helpers of God." Al-Akhfash said: "the party of God are those who adopt His religion and obey Him, so He gives them victory."

The second issue: His saying ﴿indeed, the party of God, they are the victorious﴾ is a clause occupying the place of the predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtadaʾ), and the returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) is not mentioned because it is known. The estimated sense is: "so he is victorious, because he is among the soldiers of God and His helpers."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not take those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies; and fear Allah, if you are believers.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, in the preceding verse forbade taking the Jews and the Christians as allies, and He pursued the discourse in establishing this. Then here He mentioned the general prohibition against allying with all the disbelievers, and this is this verse. In it are several issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i (al-Kufjar) read ﴿al-kuffari﴾ in the genitive, as a conjunction with His saying ﴿from among those who were given the Scripture﴾, meaning "and from among the disbelievers." The rest read it in the accusative, as a conjunction with His saying ﴿those who have taken﴾, with the implied meaning: "nor the disbelievers."

The second issue: It has been said that Rifa'ah ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith displayed faith and then became hypocrites, and some of the Muslims were friendly with them, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse concerning them.

The third issue: This verse requires a distinction between the People of the Book and the disbelievers, because conjunction requires difference. His saying ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book were not [going to desist]﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1] is explicit that they are disbelievers. The way of reconciling the two is that the disbelief of the polytheists is greater and more severe, so for this reason we specify them with the name of disbelief, and Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: The meaning of their playing with the religion and mocking it is their displaying that with the tongue while persisting in disbelief in the heart. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we are only mocking."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14]. The meaning is that since these people have taken your religion as a mockery and ridicule, do not take them as allies, helpers, or friends, for that is like a matter outside of reason and manliness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you call to the prayer, they take it in mockery and play. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾

When He related in the first verse about them that they had taken the religion of the Muslims in mockery and play, He mentioned here some of what they take from this religion in mockery and play, so He said: ﴿And when you call to the prayer, they take it in mockery and play.﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Does the pronoun in His saying "they take it" (ittakhadhuhā) refer to the prayer (al-salah) or to the calling (al-munadah)?

It is said: There was a man from the Christians in Medina who, whenever he heard the muezzin in Medina say, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," would say, "May the liar be burned." One night his servant-girl came in with fire, and a spark flew from it into the house, so the house caught fire and he and his family were burned.

And it is said: The caller of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would call to the prayer and the Muslims would rise to it, and the Jews said, "Rise, may you not rise; pray, may you not pray," in a manner of mockery, and so the verse was revealed.

And it is said: They said, "O Muhammad, you have innovated something that was not heard of in the past. If you are a prophet, then in what you have introduced you have opposed all the prophets. So from where do you get a cry like the cry of the donkey?" So God sent down this verse.

The second issue: They said: The verse indicates that the adhan is established by the explicit text of the Book, not by dream alone.

The third issue: His saying "in mockery and play" comprises two matters, because when they establish the prayer they say: these actions that we perform are mockery of the Muslims and derision of them, for they think that we are upon their religion, although we are not like that. And since they believed that there is no benefit or profit in it for religion or worldly life, they said that it is play.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾ That is: if they had complete intellect, they would have known that the glorification of the Creator, the Benefactor, and serving Him, combined with the utmost glorification, is not mockery and play; rather it is the best of the deeds of the servants and the most noble of their actions. For this reason some of the wise said: The most noble of movements is the prayer, and the most beneficial of stillnesses is fasting.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 59:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, do you disapprove of us only because we believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us, and in what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?﴾

Know that the connection (*wajh al-nazm*) of this verse is that when God related that they had taken the religion of Islam as a mockery and a game, He said to them: What is it that you disapprove of in this religion? And what do you find in it that would necessitate taking it as a mockery and a game? In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Al-Hasan recited *hal taqmūnā* (تَنْقَمُونَ) with a fatha on the qaf, whereas the eloquent form is with a kasra. It is said: *naqimtu al-shay'a* and *naqamtuhu*, with kasra and fatha of the qaf, meaning you disapproved of the thing when you denied it. The commentators have various expressions for it: *hal taqimūna minnā* means: do you find fault with us? Do you deny? Do you dislike? Some said: punishment is called *niqmah* (نِقْمَة, retribution) because it is inflicted upon what is disapproved of in the action. Others said: the dislike that is followed by anger from the one who dislikes is called *niqmah*, because it is followed by *al-niqmah*, which is punishment. So according to the first view, the word *niqmah* is originally applied to what is disliked, and then punishment is called *niqmah* because it is disliked. According to the second view, the word *niqmah* is originally applied to punishment, and then what is disapproved of and disliked is called *niqmah* because punishment follows it.

**The second issue:** The meaning of the verse is that He says to the People of the Book: Why have you taken this religion as a mockery and a game? Then He said, in the manner of wonder: Do you find in this religion anything except belief in God, and belief in what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), and belief in all the prophets who were before Muhammad? That is to say, this is not something that deserves disapproval. As for belief in God, it is the head of all acts of obedience. As for belief in Muhammad and in all the prophets, it is truth and sincerity, because if the means of confirming the prophethood and messengership of some prophets is the miracle (*al-mu'jiz*), and we have seen that the miracle occurred at the hand of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, then it is obligatory to acknowledge that he is a messenger. As for acknowledging some and denying others, that is self-contradictory speech and a false doctrine. Thus it is established that what we follow is the true religion and the straight path, so why do you disapprove of it in us?

Ibn ʿAbbas said: A group of Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and asked him about which of the messengers he believed in. He said: "We believe in God, and in what was revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Abraham and Ishmael…" up to His saying "and to Him we are submitting." When he mentioned Jesus, they denied his prophethood and said: "By God, we do not know of any people with less share in this world and the Hereafter than you, nor any religion worse than your religion." So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse and what follows it.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, the common reading is *anna* (أنَّ) with a fatha on the alif. Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read *inna* (إنَّ) with a kasra. In the verse there are questions:

**The first question:** How do the Jews disapprove of the Muslims when most of the Jews are defiantly disobedient?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: His saying ﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾ singles them out for disobedience, and it therefore indicates, by way of allusion, that they did not follow them in their disobedience. The meaning is: "You disapprove of us only because we believed, and we have not been disobedient like you."

The second: When He mentioned what the Jews disapprove of in them, namely belief in all the messengers, which is not something that deserves disapproval, He mentioned in its counterpart their disobedience, which does deserve disapproval. Such a construction is good for parallelism. A speaker may say: "Do you find fault with me only because I am chaste and you are immoral, and because I am rich and you are poor?" This is fine for completing the meaning by way of contrast.

The third: The *wāw* may be in the sense of *ma'a* (مَعَ, "together with"), that is: "And you disapprove of us only for believing in God, together with the fact that most of you are disobedient." When one of two opponents is described by blameworthy attributes, and the other acquires many praiseworthy attributes, his acquisition of praiseworthy attributes, together with his opponent's acquisition of blameworthy ones, has a stronger effect in producing hatred and envy in the heart of the opponent.

The fourth: It may be on the assumption that a word has been omitted, the *muḍāf* (مُضاف, a governed noun), that is: "and the belief that you are disobedient."

The fifth: The sense may be: "And you disapprove of us only because we believed in God and because most of you are disobedient," meaning: because of your disobedience you have come to disapprove of faith in us.

The sixth: It is possible that it is a causal clause coordinated with a deleted causal clause, as if it were said: "And you disapprove of us only for the belief, because of your lack of fairness, and because most of you are disobedient."

**The second question:** All the Jews are disobedient and disbelievers, so why did He single out most of them with the attribute of disobedience?

The answer is in two aspects:

The first: It means that most of you say what you say and do what you do only seeking leadership, status, taking bribes, and drawing near to kings. You are, in your religion, disobedient and not upright. For the disbeliever and the innovator may be upright in his own religion, and he may be disobedient in his own religion. It is known that all of them were not like that, so this ruling was specified for most of them.

The second: Mention was made of "most of them" so that it would not be thought that whoever among them believed is included in that.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry, and whom He made into apes and swine, and who worshipped the Taghut. Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way.﴾

And in it are several issues:

The first issue: His saying "min dhalika" (than that) refers to the requital, and the omitted noun must be supplied, and its estimate is: "with something worse than the people of that", because He said: ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾. It is not said that the cursed one is worse than that religion, but rather it is said that he is worse than the one who holds that religion.

If it is said: this requires that those characterized by that religion be judged as evil, and it is known that this is not so.

We say: the speech came according to their own view and belief, for they judged that adherence to that religion is evil, so it was said to them: suppose the matter is as you say, yet the curse of Allah, His anger, and the transformation of forms is worse than that.

The second issue: ﴿mathubah﴾ (requital) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Its pattern is maf'ulah, as in your saying maqulah and majuzah, and it has the meaning of a verbal noun. Verbal nouns have also come in the pattern maf'ul, such as ma'qul and maysur.

If it is said: "mathubah" is specific to goodness, so how does it come in the context of evil?

We say: this is in the manner of His saying: ﴿so give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 21], and the words of the poet:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

The third issue: "man" in His saying ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾ may have two possibilities:

The first: it is in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject. When He said: ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse than that﴾, it is as if someone said: "Who is that?" So it was said: "It is the one whom Allah has cursed." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that, the Fire?﴾ [al-Hajj: 72], as if He said: "It is the Fire."

The second: it may be in the genitive position as a substitute (badal) for "sharr" (evil), and the meaning is: "I will inform you of those whom Allah has cursed."

The fourth issue: Know that He, the Exalted, mentioned several of their attributes:

The first of them: that Allah cursed them.

The second: that He became angry with them.

The third: that He made of them apes and swine, and worshippers of the Taghut. The people of tafsir said: by the apes are meant the people of the Sabbath, and by the swine the disbelievers of the table of 'Isa. It is also narrated that both transformations were among the people of the Sabbath, for their youths were transformed into apes and their elders into swine.

The fifth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf mentioned, regarding His saying ﴿and worshipped the Taghut﴾, several kinds of readings:

One of them: Ubayy read: "wa 'abadu al-taghut" (and they worshipped the Taghut).

Second: Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa man 'abadu" (and whoever worshipped).

Third: "wa 'abida al-taghut" (and the worshipper of the Taghut), in coordination with "al-qiradah" (the apes).

Fourth: "wa 'abidi".

Fifth: "wa 'abbad".

Sixth: "wa 'abda".

Seventh: "wa 'abbada", on the pattern of hattama.

Eighth: "wa 'abid".

Ninth: "wa 'uburu" with two dammas, the plural of 'abid.

Tenth: "wa 'abadah", on the pattern of kafarah.

Eleventh: "wa 'abad", whose origin is 'abadah, the ta' being dropped for the idafah (construct), or it is like khadam, the plural of khadim.

Twelfth: "'abada".

Thirteenth: "'ibad".

Fourteenth: "wa u'bud".

Fifteenth: "wa 'Ubida al-taghut", in the passive form, with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: "and the Taghut was worshipped among them or between them."

Sixteenth: "wa 'abada al-taghut", meaning the Taghut became an object of worship besides Allah the Exalted, as in your saying: amara, when he became a commander (amir).

Seventeenth: Hamzah read: "'abuda al-taghuti" with a fatha on the 'ayn, a damma on the ba', a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the taghut. People criticized this reading against Hamzah, called it a grammatical error, and attributed to him what is not permissible to mention. Some people said it is neither a grammatical error nor a mistake, and they mentioned for it several explanations:

The first: that 'abd is the same as 'abud, except that they put a damma on the ba' for emphasis, as in their saying: rajul hadhir and fatin, meaning one who is extremely cautious and shrewd. So the interpretation of "'abuda al-taghut" is that he reached the utmost limit in obeying Satan, and this is the best of the explanations.

The second: that 'abd and 'abud are two dialectal forms, like sab' and sabu'.

The third: that the plural of 'abud is 'ibad, and the plural of 'ibad is 'ubud, like thimar and thumur. Then they found two consecutive dammas burdensome, so the first was replaced by a fatha.

The fourth: it is possible that he intended "a'bud al-taghut", so it would be like falas and aflas, then the hamzah was dropped and its vowel transferred to the 'ayn.

The fifth: it is possible that he intended "wa 'abadat al-taghut", as it was read, then he dropped the ha' and put a damma on the ba' so it would not be confused with the verb.

The sixth issue: His saying ﴿and worshipped the Taghut﴾. Al-Farra' said: its interpretation is "and made among them the apes and those who worshipped the Taghut." According to this, the relative pronoun is omitted.

The seventh issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) cited this verse as evidence that disbelief occurs by the decree of Allah. They said: the estimate of the verse is "and Allah made among them those who worshipped the Taghut." The meaning of this making can only be understood if He is the One who placed that worship in them, for if the making of that worship were from them, then Allah the Exalted would not have made them worshippers of the Taghut, but rather they themselves would have made themselves so, and that is contrary to the verse. The Mu'tazilah said: its meaning is that He, the Exalted, judged them by that and described them with it, like His saying: ﴿and they made the angels, who are servants of the Merciful, into females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. The discussion of this has preceded many times.

The eighth issue: It has been said: the Taghut is the calf; it has been said: the Taghut is the rabbis; and whoever obeys anyone in disobedience to Allah has worshipped him.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those are worse in position﴾, meaning: those cursed and transformed ones are worse in position than the believers. Regarding the word "makan" (position) there are two views:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: because their position is Saqar, and there is no position worse than it.

The second: the evil is attributed in wording to the position, while in reality it belongs to its people, and this is of the category of metonymy (kinayah), like their saying: so-and-so has long sword-straps and much ashes, and its outcome returns to indicating a thing by mentioning its necessary concomitants and consequences.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and further astray from the right way﴾, meaning: further from the intended path and the true religion. The exegetes said: when this verse was revealed, the Muslims reproached the People of the Book and said: "O brothers of the apes and swine!" So they were disgraced and hung their heads.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," but they had entered with disbelief and they had left with it.﴾

Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: They said: this verse was revealed concerning some of the Jews who used to enter upon the Messenger (ﷺ) and display belief to him out of hypocrisy. So Allah, mighty and majestic, informed him of their state, that they leave your assembly just as they entered, with nothing of your proofs, your affirmations, your advice, and your reminders having taken hold of their hearts.

The second issue: The bā' in His saying, ﴿they had entered with disbelief and they had left with it﴾, indicates that disbelief remained with them in both states, entering and leaving, without any diminution or change in it whatsoever. It is like when you say: Zayd entered with his garment and left with it, meaning his garment remained during the leaving just as it was during the entering.

The third issue: At the entering He mentioned the word "qad" (قد), saying ﴿and they had entered with disbelief﴾, and at the leaving He mentioned the word "hum" (هم), saying ﴿and they had left with it﴾. They said: the benefit of mentioning "qad" is bringing the past close to the present, and the benefit of mentioning "hum" is emphasis in attributing disbelief to them, and negating that it was an act of the Prophet (ﷺ) in that regard. That is, they did not hear from you, O Muhammad, while sitting with you, anything that would necessitate disbelief, so that you would be the one who cast them into disbelief; rather, they are the ones who left with disbelief by their own choice.

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazilah said: He, exalted, attributed disbelief to them in both states, entering and leaving, by way of censure, and He emphasized that attribution with His saying, ﴿and they had left with it﴾. This indicates that it is from the servant and not from Allah.

The answer: the counter-argument from His knowledge and His motive (al-mu'aradah bi'l-'ilm wa'l-da'i).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah knows best what they were concealing﴾, and the purpose of it is to intensify emphasis upon what was in their hearts of earnestness and striving in plotting against the Muslims, scheming against them, and hatred and enmity toward them.

Then Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin and aggression and their consumption of unlawful gain (suḥt). Wretched is what they used to do.﴾

Al-musāraʿah (hastening) in something means beginning it quickly. It has been said: al-ithm (sin) is lying, and al-ʿudwān (aggression) is injustice. It has also been said: al-ithm is what pertains to them specifically, and al-ʿudwān is what goes beyond them to others. As for akl al-suḥt (consuming unlawful gain), it is taking bribery (rishwah). The full discussion has already been given in the explanation of al-suḥt.

Page 34

There are several benefits in this verse:

The first benefit: He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And you see many of them﴾. The reason is that not all of them were doing this; rather, some of them felt shame and refrained.

The second benefit: The word musāraʿah is used for the most part in reference to good, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they hasten to good deeds﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 114], and He said: ﴿We hasten for them in good things﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 56]. So the fitting word in this context would have been ʿajalah (haste). However, Allah the Exalted mentioned the word musāraʿah for a purpose, which is that they would rush into these prohibited acts as though they were in the right regarding them.

The third benefit: The word ithm encompasses all sins and prohibited acts. When Allah the Exalted mentioned after it ʿudwān and the consumption of unlawful gain, this indicates that these two types are the greatest kinds of disobedience and sin.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their saying of sin and their consumption of unlawful gain? Wretched is what they used to produce.﴾

The meaning of (lawlā) here is restriction and reproach, and it carries the sense of (halla) ("why not"). The discussion about the rabbis (rabbāniyyūn) and the scholars (aḥbār) has already been given. Al-Ḥasan said: the rabbāniyyūn are the scholars of the people of the Gospel, and the aḥbār are the scholars of the people of the Torah. Others said: all of it refers to the Jews, since it is connected to their mention. The meaning is that Allah the Exalted considered it remarkable that the scholars of the People of the Book did not forbid their lowly and common folk from acts of disobedience. This indicates that one who abandons forbidding evil is in the same position as one who commits it, because He, the Exalted, censured both groups in this verse with one expression. Indeed, we say that the censure of one who abandons forbidding evil is stronger, because He, the Exalted, said regarding those who commit sin, aggression and consumption of unlawful gain: ﴿Wretched is what they used to do﴾, and He said regarding the scholars who abandon forbidding evil: ﴿Wretched is what they used to produce﴾. Ṣunʿ (production) is stronger than ʿamal (doing), because ʿamal is only called ṣināʿah (craft) when it becomes established, firm and well-rooted. So He made the offence of the doers a non-firm sin, and the sin of those who abandon forbidding evil a firm sin. In reality the matter is indeed like this, because disobedience is a sickness of the soul, and its cure is knowledge of Allah, His attributes and His rulings. When this knowledge is attained and disobedience still persists, it is like a sickness for which the sufferer has taken the medicine yet it has not gone away. Just as there one comes to know that the sickness is severe and strong and hardly ever goes away, so too when a scholar commits disobedience, it shows that the sickness of the heart is at the utmost of strength and intensity. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the most severe verse in the Qur'an. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: there is no verse in the Qur'an more frightening to me than this one, and Allah knows best.

The meaning of (lawlā) here is restriction and reproach, and it carries the sense of (halla) ("why not"). The discussion about the rabbis (rabbāniyyūn) and the scholars (aḥbār) has already been given. Al-Ḥasan said: the rabbāniyyūn are the scholars of the people of the Gospel, and the aḥbār are the scholars of the people of the Torah. Others said: all of it refers to the Jews, since it is connected to their mention. The meaning is that Allah the Exalted considered it remarkable that the scholars of the People of the Book did not forbid their lowly and common folk from acts of disobedience. This indicates that one who abandons forbidding evil is in the same position as one who commits it, because He, the Exalted, censured both groups in this verse with one expression. Indeed, we say that the censure of one who abandons forbidding evil is stronger, because He, the Exalted, said regarding those who commit sin, aggression and consumption of unlawful gain: ﴿Wretched is what they used to do﴾, and He said regarding the scholars who abandon forbidding evil: ﴿Wretched is what they used to produce﴾. Ṣunʿ (production) is stronger than ʿamal (doing), because ʿamal is only called ṣināʿah (craft) when it becomes established, firm and well-rooted. So He made the offence of the doers a non-firm sin, and the sin of those who abandon forbidding evil a firm sin. In reality the matter is indeed like this, because disobedience is a sickness of the soul, and its cure is knowledge of Allah, His attributes and His rulings. When this knowledge is attained and disobedience still persists, it is like a sickness for which the sufferer has taken the medicine yet it has not gone away. Just as there one comes to know that the sickness is severe and strong and hardly ever goes away, so too when a scholar commits disobedience, it shows that the sickness of the heart is at the utmost of strength and intensity. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the most severe verse in the Qur'an. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: there is no verse in the Qur'an more frightening to me than this one, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 64–65 (part 1 of 2):

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained up. Chained up are their own hands, and they are cursed for what they said."﴾

Know that there are several issues (masa'il) in this verse.

The first issue: There is a difficulty at this point. Allah the Exalted related of the Jews that they said this, and there is no doubt that Allah the Exalted is truthful in all that He reports. Yet we see the Jews unanimously and in agreement that we do not say this and do not believe it at all. Moreover, any doctrine attributed to rational people must necessarily be known to be false by necessity of reason, and the claim that "the hand of Allah is chained" is a false claim by the immediate judgment of reason. For our saying "Allah" is the name of a Being who is eternal, able to create the world, bring it into existence and form it, and this Being cannot have a chained hand or a restricted and deficient power; otherwise, how could He, with deficient power, preserve and govern the world?

Having established this, we say: a severe difficulty arises regarding how to validate this report and this narration. We say: there are several answers to it:

The first: Perhaps the people said this by way of argument (ilzam). When they heard His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], they said: "If He needed a loan, He would be poor and powerless." Then, when they judged that the God who borrows something from His servants is poor with chained hands, Allah related this statement of theirs.

The second: Perhaps when the people saw the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) in extreme hardship, poverty and need, they said by way of mockery and derision: "The God of Muhammad is poor with a chained hand." When they said that, Allah related this statement of theirs.

The third: The exegetes said: The Jews were among the people with the most wealth and property. When Allah sent Muhammad and they denied him, Allah restricted their livelihood. At that point the Jews said: "The hand of Allah is chained," meaning withheld from giving, by way of describing Him with miserliness. The ignorant person, when he falls into trial, hardship and affliction, says words like these.

The fourth: Perhaps among them were those who followed the doctrine of the philosophers, that He is necessitating by His essence, that the occurrence of events from Him can only be in one manner and one course, and that He is not able to bring about events in other than the ways in which they occur. So they expressed the lack of capacity for change and alteration by "the chaining of the hand."

The fifth: Some said: The intended meaning is the statement of the Jews: "Allah will not punish us except for the number of days in which we worshipped the calf." But they expressed His not punishing them except for this span of time with this corrupt expression, and they deserved the curse because of the corruption of the expression and the failure to observe proper manners. This is the view of al-Hasan. Thus it is established that this report is sound under all these interpretations, and Allah knows best.

The second issue: The chaining and spreading of the hand is a well-known metaphor (majaz) for miserliness and generosity. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor spread it out completely﴾. They said: The reason for this is that the hand is the instrument of most actions, especially for giving property and spending it, so they named the cause by the effect (ism al-sabab 'ala al-musabbab) and attributed generosity and miserliness to the hand, the palm, the fingers and the fingertips. Thus it is said of the generous: "one whose palm overflows, whose hand is spread out," and "open of fingertips, flowing of fingers." And it is said of the miserly: "tight of fingers, closed of palm, tightly clenched of fingertips."

If it is said: Since His saying "the hand of Allah is chained" means miserliness, it must be that His saying "Chained up are their hands" also means miserliness, so that the correspondence holds. And miserliness is one of the blameworthy attributes which Allah the Exalted forbade, so how is it permissible for Him to invoke this against them?

We say: His saying "the hand of Allah is chained" is an expression for lack of ability to give and bestow. Then, the lack of ability to give sometimes arises from miserliness, sometimes from poverty, and sometimes from incapacity. Likewise, His saying "Chained up are their hands" is an invocation against them for lack of power and ability, whether that comes about through incapacity, poverty or miserliness. On this interpretation the difficulty disappears.

The third issue: His saying "Chained up are their hands, and they are cursed for what they said" has two aspects:

The first: It is an invocation against them. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, teaches us to invoke this against them, just as He taught us the exception in His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and just as He taught us to invoke against the hypocrites in His saying: ﴿So Allah increased them in disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], and against Abu Lahab in His saying: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1].

The second: It is a report. Al-Hasan said: "Their hands were chained in the Fire of Hell in actuality," meaning they were tied to their necks as recompense for them for this statement.

If it is said: If this chaining is decreed for them as recompense for this statement, then it should have been said: "so their hands were chained."

We say: The conjunction was omitted, although it is implied, but it was omitted for a purpose: when it was omitted, His saying "Chained up are their hands" became like a sentence begun afresh, and the beginning of a sentence with a thing gives it added strength and firmness, because beginning with something indicates intense concern with it and strong attention to establishing it. A parallel to this place in omitting the particle of consequence is His saying: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in mockery?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67], and He did not say "so they said." As for His saying "and they are cursed for what they said," al-Hasan said: "They were punished in this world with the jizyah, and in the Hereafter with the Fire."

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, both His hands are spread out.﴾

Know that the discussion of this verse is of great importance, for many verses of the Qur'an speak of the affirmation of the hand. Sometimes the word mentioned is "hand" without specifying the number, as He said: ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. Sometimes it affirms two hands for Allah the Exalted: among them is this verse, and among them is His saying to Iblis the accursed: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad: 75]. And sometimes it affirms "hands" in plural, as He said: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, livestock?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71].

Having understood this, we say: The community has differed in interpreting the hand of Allah the Exalted. The Mujassimah (anthropomorphists) said: It is a bodily organ as it is with regard to every person, and they argued for this with His saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk, or do they have hands with which they strike, or do they have eyes with which they see, or do they have ears with which they hear? Say, "Call your partners, then plot against me"﴾ [al-A'raf: 195].

The way of inference: He, the Exalted, disputed the divinity of the idols on the ground that they have none of these limbs. So if these limbs were not found in Allah, it would follow that there is a defect in His being God. And since that is false, it is necessary to affirm these limbs for Him. They said: Also, the name "hand" is laid down for this organ, so applying it to something else is abandoning the language, and that is not permissible.

Know that the refutation of this view rests on the fact that He, the Exalted, is not a body. The proof of this is that a body cannot be free of motion and rest, and both are created things; and whatever cannot be free of a created thing is itself created. Also, every body is limited in magnitude, and whatever is limited in magnitude is created. Also, every body is composed of parts, and whatever is such is capable of composition and dissolution, and whatever is such needs something to compose and assemble it, and whatever is such is created. Thus it is established by these considerations that it is impossible for Him, the Exalted, to be a body, and therefore it is impossible for His hand to be a bodily organ.

As for the majority of the Monotheists (muwahhidun), they have two views regarding the word "hand":

The first: the view of those who say: The Qur'an, since it indicates the affirmation of the hand for Allah the Exalted, we believe in it; and reason, since it indicates that the hand of Allah cannot be an expression for a particular body and a compound organ made of parts and components, we believe in that too. As for what the hand is and what its reality is, we have entrusted knowledge of it to Allah the Exalted. This is the path of the Salaf.

As for the theologians (mutakallimun), they said: "Hand" is used in the language in several senses:

One: the limb, which is known.

Two: a favour (ni'mah); one says: "So-and-so has a hand upon me, for which I thank him."

Three: power (quwwah). He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Possessors of hands and vision﴾ [Sad: 45], which they interpreted as possessors of powers and intellects. Sibawayh relates that they said: "You have no hand in this," meaning the negation of complete power.

Four: ownership (milk). One says: "This estate is in the hand of so-and-so," meaning in his ownership. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He in whose hand is the knot of marriage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], meaning he owns it.

Five: intense care and special attention. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿What I created with My hands﴾ [Sad: 75], and the intended meaning is the singling out of Adam, peace be upon him, with this honour, for He, the Exalted, is the Creator of all created beings. And one says: "My hand is a pledge for you to fulfil," when he guarantees something to him.

Having understood this, we say: With regard to Allah, "hand" cannot mean the limb, but all the other meanings are applicable. There is also another view: Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, may Allah have mercy on him, held in some of his statements that the hand is an attribute subsisting in the Essence of Allah the Exalted, an attribute other than power, whose function is creation by way of distinction (istifa'). He said: What indicates this is that He, the Exalted, made the occurrence of the creation of Adam by His two hands a cause for Adam's honour and selection. So if "hand" meant power, it could not be a cause of selection, because that is found in all created things. Therefore there must be affirmed another attribute beyond power, by which creation and bringing into being occur by way of distinction. Most scholars, however, held that the hand with regard to Allah the Exalted is an expression for power and for favour.

If it is said: If you interpret the hand of Allah the Exalted as power, then this is problematic, for the power of Allah the Exalted is one, while the text of the Qur'an speaks of affirming two hands at one time and of affirming "hands" at another. And if you interpret it as favour, then the text of the Qur'an speaks of affirming two hands, and the favours of Allah are not limited, as He said: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

The answer: If we choose to interpret the hand as power, the answer to the stated difficulty is that the people made their saying "the hand of Allah is chained" an allusion to miserliness, so they were answered in accordance with their own statement, and it was said: "Rather, both His hands are spread out," meaning: the matter is not as you describe Him as miserly; rather He is generous in perfection, for whoever gives with his hand gives in the most complete manner. And if we choose to interpret the hand as favour, the answer to the stated difficulty is in two respects:

The first: that it is a relation according to genus; then under each of the two genera fall types without end. So it is said: His two favours are the favour of religion and the favour of worldly life, or the favour of the outward and the favour of the inward, or the favour of benefit and the favour of averting harm, or the favour of hardship and the favour of ease.

The second: that the intended meaning of the dual is the intensification in describing the favour. Do you not see that their saying "labbayka" means: standing in obedience to You after standing (in obedience), and likewise "sa'dayka" means: assistance after assistance, and it does not mean two obediences or two assistances? Likewise in the verse: the meaning is that the favour is abundant and continuous, not as it is claimed, that it is withheld and restrained.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿He spends as He wills.﴾ That is, He provides and creates as He wills; if He wills, He restricts, and if He wills, He expands. And He said: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would rebel in the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27], and He said: ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verses 64–65 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He does what He wills and decides﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], and He said: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and take it away from whom You will; You exalt whom You will and abase whom You will; in Your hand is the good﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26], up to His words.

Know that this verse is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), because they said: it is obligatory upon God Most High to give reward to the obedient; it is obligatory upon Him not to punish him; it is obligatory upon Him not to admit the disobedient to Paradise; and, according to some of them, it is obligatory upon Him to punish him. This prohibition, restriction and constraint functions as a shackle, so in reality they are sayers that the hand of God is chained. As for the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), they are the ones who say that the sovereignty is His, and no one has any claim upon Him, nor does anyone have any objection to Him, as He said: ﴿Say: Who could prevent God at all if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth together?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17]. So His statement, glorified is He: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills﴾ does not hold true except according to this doctrine and this position. And praise be to God for the upright religion and the straight path.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And surely many of them will increase in rebellion and disbelief through what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: By "many" are meant the scholars of the Jews. That is, they increased, upon the descent of what was sent down to you from your Lord, of the Qur'an and the proofs, in severity of disbelief and extremism in denial, as one says: "My admonition has only increased you in evil." It has also been said: their persistence in disbelief is an increase on their part in disbelief.

The second issue: Our companions said: the verse indicates that God Most High does not take into account the interests of religion and of the world. For since God Most High knew that they would increase in disbelief and misguidance upon the sending down of those verses, had His actions been caused by considering the interests of His servants, it would have been impossible for Him to send down those verses. Since He sent them down, we know that God Most High does not take into account the interests of His servants. A parallel to this is His statement: ﴿so it added defilement to their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

If they say: God knew from their state that they would commit that increase in disbelief whether He sent the verses down or not, and therefore it was good of Him to send them down.

We say: Then according to this assumption, that increase did not occur because of the sending down of those verses, and this requires that attributing the increase in disbelief to the sending down of those verses be false, and that is a denial of the explicit text of the Qur'an.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And We cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾.

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is that God Most High explained that they deny his prophethood only after the proofs of its truth had become manifest, out of envy, and out of love of status, following, wealth and leadership.

Then He, may He be exalted, explained that since they preferred this world over the Hereafter, God, as He deprived them of the happiness of religion, likewise deprived them of the happiness of this world. For each group among them remained persistent in its own doctrine and position, exaggerating in supporting it and disparaging everything else of the other doctrines and positions, to glorify itself and to promote its own doctrine. This became a cause of intense hostility arising between their sects and communities, and the matter reached the point that some of them declared others to be unbelievers, and some of them waged war against others.

Regarding His statement: ﴿And We cast among them enmity and hatred﴾ there are two views:

The first: What is meant is the enmity between the Jews and the Christians, since their mention came in His statement: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians [as allies]﴾. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: That what is meant is the occurrence of enmity
[p. 39]
among the sects of the Jews, for some of them are Jabriyyah (fatalists), some of them are Qadariyyah (proponents of free will), some of them are Muwahhidah (unitarians), and some of them are Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists). Likewise among the sects of the Christians: such as the Malkaniyyah (Melkites), the Nestorians and the Jacobites (Ya'qubiyyah).

If it is said: this meaning is fully present among the sects of the Muslims as well, so how can it be made a fault of the Jews and Christians?

We say: these innovations only arose after the era of the Companions and the Successors (al-Tabi'un). As for that time, none of that existed, and so it was indeed proper for the Messenger and his Companions to make that a fault of the Jews and Christians.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾.

This explains another type of trials upon the Jews, namely that whenever they resolve upon some matter, they return defeated, losing, subdued and cursed, as God Most High said: ﴿Humiliation has been stamped upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112]. Qatadah said: You will not meet a Jew in any town without finding him among the most humiliated of people.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾. That is, there does not arise in their affair any strength of might and protection, except that they strive in the land to cause corruption, by deceiving the weak and devising some kind of cunning and scheming secretly.

It has been said: when they opposed the judgment of the Torah, He set Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) over them; then, when they caused corruption again, He set Butrus al-Rumi over them; then, when they caused corruption again, He set the Magians over them; then, when they caused corruption again, He set the Muslims over them.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And God does not love the corrupters﴾, and this indicates that one who strives in the land with corruption is abhorred by God Most High.
