One: the limb, which is known.

Two: a favour (ni'mah); one says: "So-and-so has a hand upon me, for which I thank him."

Three: power (quwwah). He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Possessors of hands and vision﴾ [Sad: 45], which they interpreted as possessors of powers and intellects. Sibawayh relates that they said: "You have no hand in this," meaning the negation of complete power.

Four: ownership (milk). One says: "This estate is in the hand of so-and-so," meaning in his ownership. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He in whose hand is the knot of marriage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], meaning he owns it.

Five: intense care and special attention. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿What I created with My hands﴾ [Sad: 75], and the intended meaning is the singling out of Adam, peace be upon him, with this honour, for He, the Exalted, is the Creator of all created beings. And one says: "My hand is a pledge for you to fulfil," when he guarantees something to him.

Having understood this, we say: With regard to Allah, "hand" cannot mean the limb, but all the other meanings are applicable. There is also another view: Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, may Allah have mercy on him, held in some of his statements that the hand is an attribute subsisting in the Essence of Allah the Exalted, an attribute other than power, whose function is creation by way of distinction (istifa'). He said: What indicates this is that He, the Exalted, made the occurrence of the creation of Adam by His two hands a cause for Adam's honour and selection. So if "hand" meant power, it could not be a cause of selection, because that is found in all created things. Therefore there must be affirmed another attribute beyond power, by which creation and bringing into being occur by way of distinction. Most scholars, however, held that the hand with regard to Allah the Exalted is an expression for power and for favour.

If it is said: If you interpret the hand of Allah the Exalted as power, then this is problematic, for the power of Allah the Exalted is one, while the text of the Qur'an speaks of affirming two hands at one time and of affirming "hands" at another. And if you interpret it as favour, then the text of the Qur'an speaks of affirming two hands, and the favours of Allah are not limited, as He said: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

The answer: If we choose to interpret the hand as power, the answer to the stated difficulty is that the people made their saying "the hand of Allah is chained" an allusion to miserliness, so they were answered in accordance with their own statement, and it was said: "Rather, both His hands are spread out," meaning: the matter is not as you describe Him as miserly; rather He is generous in perfection, for whoever gives with his hand gives in the most complete manner. And if we choose to interpret the hand as favour, the answer to the stated difficulty is in two respects:

The first: that it is a relation according to genus; then under each of the two genera fall types without end. So it is said: His two favours are the favour of religion and the favour of worldly life, or the favour of the outward and the favour of the inward, or the favour of benefit and the favour of averting harm, or the favour of hardship and the favour of ease.

The second: that the intended meaning of the dual is the intensification in describing the favour. Do you not see that their saying "labbayka" means: standing in obedience to You after standing (in obedience), and likewise "sa'dayka" means: assistance after assistance, and it does not mean two obediences or two assistances? Likewise in the verse: the meaning is that the favour is abundant and continuous, not as it is claimed, that it is withheld and restrained.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿He spends as He wills.﴾ That is, He provides and creates as He wills; if He wills, He restricts, and if He wills, He expands. And He said: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would rebel in the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27], and He said: ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verses 64–65 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He does what He wills and decides﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], and He said: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and take it away from whom You will; You exalt whom You will and abase whom You will; in Your hand is the good﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26], up to His words.

Know that this verse is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), because they said: it is obligatory upon God Most High to give reward to the obedient; it is obligatory upon Him not to punish him; it is obligatory upon Him not to admit the disobedient to Paradise; and, according to some of them, it is obligatory upon Him to punish him. This prohibition, restriction and constraint functions as a shackle, so in reality they are sayers that the hand of God is chained. As for the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), they are the ones who say that the sovereignty is His, and no one has any claim upon Him, nor does anyone have any objection to Him, as He said: ﴿Say: Who could prevent God at all if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth together?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17]. So His statement, glorified is He: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills﴾ does not hold true except according to this doctrine and this position. And praise be to God for the upright religion and the straight path.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And surely many of them will increase in rebellion and disbelief through what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: By "many" are meant the scholars of the Jews. That is, they increased, upon the descent of what was sent down to you from your Lord, of the Qur'an and the proofs, in severity of disbelief and extremism in denial, as one says: "My admonition has only increased you in evil." It has also been said: their persistence in disbelief is an increase on their part in disbelief.

The second issue: Our companions said: the verse indicates that God Most High does not take into account the interests of religion and of the world. For since God Most High knew that they would increase in disbelief and misguidance upon the sending down of those verses, had His actions been caused by considering the interests of His servants, it would have been impossible for Him to send down those verses. Since He sent them down, we know that God Most High does not take into account the interests of His servants. A parallel to this is His statement: ﴿so it added defilement to their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

If they say: God knew from their state that they would commit that increase in disbelief whether He sent the verses down or not, and therefore it was good of Him to send them down.

We say: Then according to this assumption, that increase did not occur because of the sending down of those verses, and this requires that attributing the increase in disbelief to the sending down of those verses be false, and that is a denial of the explicit text of the Qur'an.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And We cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾.

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is that God Most High explained that they deny his prophethood only after the proofs of its truth had become manifest, out of envy, and out of love of status, following, wealth and leadership.

Then He, may He be exalted, explained that since they preferred this world over the Hereafter, God, as He deprived them of the happiness of religion, likewise deprived them of the happiness of this world. For each group among them remained persistent in its own doctrine and position, exaggerating in supporting it and disparaging everything else of the other doctrines and positions, to glorify itself and to promote its own doctrine. This became a cause of intense hostility arising between their sects and communities, and the matter reached the point that some of them declared others to be unbelievers, and some of them waged war against others.

Regarding His statement: ﴿And We cast among them enmity and hatred﴾ there are two views:

The first: What is meant is the enmity between the Jews and the Christians, since their mention came in His statement: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians [as allies]﴾. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: That what is meant is the occurrence of enmity
[p. 39]
among the sects of the Jews, for some of them are Jabriyyah (fatalists), some of them are Qadariyyah (proponents of free will), some of them are Muwahhidah (unitarians), and some of them are Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists). Likewise among the sects of the Christians: such as the Malkaniyyah (Melkites), the Nestorians and the Jacobites (Ya'qubiyyah).

If it is said: this meaning is fully present among the sects of the Muslims as well, so how can it be made a fault of the Jews and Christians?

We say: these innovations only arose after the era of the Companions and the Successors (al-Tabi'un). As for that time, none of that existed, and so it was indeed proper for the Messenger and his Companions to make that a fault of the Jews and Christians.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾.

This explains another type of trials upon the Jews, namely that whenever they resolve upon some matter, they return defeated, losing, subdued and cursed, as God Most High said: ﴿Humiliation has been stamped upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112]. Qatadah said: You will not meet a Jew in any town without finding him among the most humiliated of people.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾. That is, there does not arise in their affair any strength of might and protection, except that they strive in the land to cause corruption, by deceiving the weak and devising some kind of cunning and scheming secretly.

It has been said: when they opposed the judgment of the Torah, He set Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) over them; then, when they caused corruption again, He set Butrus al-Rumi over them; then, when they caused corruption again, He set the Magians over them; then, when they caused corruption again, He set the Muslims over them.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And God does not love the corrupters﴾, and this indicates that one who strives in the land with corruption is abhorred by God Most High.

﴿Then He said, Exalted is He:﴾ ﴿Had the People of the Book believed and been mindful of God, We would have removed their misdeeds from them and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss.﴾

Know that when He, Exalted is He, had emphasized their blame and the ugliness of their way, He made clear that if they believed and were mindful of God, they would attain the felicities of the Hereafter and of this world. The felicities of the Hereafter are confined to two kinds. The first is the lifting of punishment. The second is the bestowal of reward. The lifting of punishment is what is meant by His words, ﴿We would have removed their misdeeds from them﴾, and the bestowal of reward is what is meant by His words, ﴿and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss﴾.

If it is said: belief alone is an independent cause sufficient to bring about the expiation of misdeeds and the granting of good deeds. Why then did He add the condition of mindfulness of God to it?

We say: what is meant is that one brings faith for the purpose of God-consciousness and obedience, and not for some other immediate aim, such as what the hypocrites do.

* * *

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet.﴾

Know that when He, Exalted is He, had made clear in the first verse that if they believed they would win the felicities of the Hereafter, He also made clear in this verse that if they believed they would win the felicities of this world, finding its good things and its bounties. There are three aspects to "upholding" the Torah and the Gospel:

The first: that they act according to what they contain, including fulfilling the covenants of God contained in them, and acknowledging that they include the proofs indicating the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second: upholding the Torah means upholding its rulings and its limits, as one says "he upheld the prayer" when he fulfilled its rights. One does not say of someone who did not fulfill its conditions that he upheld it.

The third: they kept it before their eyes so that they would not slip in any of its limits. All these aspects are good, but the first is the best.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and what was revealed to them﴾, there are two views:

The first: it is the Qur'an.

The second: it is the books of the other prophets, such as the book of Sha'ya (Isaiah), the book of Habaqquq (Habakkuk), and the book of Daniyal (Daniel), for these books are full of good news of the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ), upon him be blessings and peace.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾, know that when the Jews persisted in denying Muhammad (ﷺ), upon him be blessings and peace, drought and hardship befell them, and they reached the point of saying, ﴿The hand of God is chained up﴾. So God, Exalted is He, made clear that if they abandoned that disbelief, the situation would be reversed and abundance and plenty would come. In His words, ﴿they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ there are several aspects:

The first: what is meant is exaggeration in describing plenty and abundance, not that there is literally an above and a below. The meaning is that they would eat continuously and abundantly, as you say, "So-and-so is in goodness from his crown to his feet," meaning that goodness is dense and abundant with him.

The second: eating from above refers to the descent of rain, and from beneath the feet refers to the emergence of vegetation, as God, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96].

The third: eating from above is the abundance of fruit-bearing trees, and from beneath the feet are productive crops.

The fourth: what is meant is that He would provide them with gardens of ripe fruit, so they would pick what hangs down from the tops of trees and gather what has fallen to the ground beneath their feet.

The fifth: it seems that this is an allusion to what befell the Jews of the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir, namely the cutting of their palm trees, the ruining of their crops, and their expulsion from their homelands.

* * *

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾. The meaning of iqtisad (moderation, the middle way) in the lexicon is balance in action, without excess or deficiency. Its root is qasd (aiming straight). This is because whoever knows his goal aims at it on the straight path without deviation or agitation. As for one who does not know the place of his aim, he is bewildered, going at one time to the right and at another to the left. For this reason, iqtisad was used to describe the action that leads to the goal. Then, regarding this moderate community, there are two views:

The first: that what is meant by them are those among the People of the Book who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam from the Jews and al-Najashi from the Christians. They were moderate in their religion and upon its straight course, and did not incline to either extreme of excess or neglect.

The second: what is meant by them are the disbelievers among the People of the Book who are upright in their religion, in whom there is no severe obstinacy or complete harshness, as He said: ﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75].

* * *

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿But many of them—evil is what they do.﴾ Within it is the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "And many of them—how evil is their deed!" What is meant by "them" are the rude, blameworthy, hated people, on whom proof has no effect and to whom speech brings no benefit.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 67:

﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. God commanded the Messenger not to look at the small number of those who act with moderation and the large number of the wicked, and not to fear their harm. So He said: (convey), meaning: be patient in conveying what I have sent down to you, including exposing their secrets and the scandals of their deeds. God will protect you from their plotting and safeguard you from their schemes.

Al-Hasan narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God sent me with His message, and I was distressed by it. I knew that people would deny me, and that the Jews, the Christians and the Quraysh would threaten me. When God sent down this verse, the fear was entirely removed." It is also reported that the Prophet (ﷺ), during his residence in Mecca, would openly recite part of the Qur'an and conceal part of it, out of concern for his own safety from the hasty aggression of the polytheists towards him and his companions. When God strengthened Islam and supported it with the believers, He said to him: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, meaning: do not be concerned about anyone, and do not leave out anything of what has been sent down to you out of fear that some harm may befall you.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' read (risalatahu) in this verse and in al-An'am (﴿where He places His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]) in the plural form (risalatihi/risalatahu as plural, risalatihi), and in al-A'raf (﴿with My message﴾ [al-A'raf: 144]) in the singular. Hafs, from 'Asim, read the opposite: in al-Ma'idah and al-An'am in the singular, and in al-A'raf in the plural. Ibn Kathir read all of them in the singular. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read all of them in the plural.

The argument of those who read the plural is that the messengers are sent with various kinds of messages and with differing rulings in the Shari'ah, and every verse that God sent down to His Messenger (ﷺ) is a message; therefore the plural form is appropriate. As for those who read the singular, they say: the whole Qur'an is one message. Furthermore, the singular form may also indicate plurality even without being pluralized, as in His saying: ﴿and call out for destruction, many destructions﴾ [al-Furqan: 14], where a singular noun is used for a plural. Likewise here, the word "risalah" (message), though singular, is intended in the plural sense.

The second issue: One may ask: the meaning of His saying ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ is: "If you do not convey His message, then you have not conveyed His message." What is the benefit of this statement?

The majority of the exegetes answered that what is intended is: if you fail to convey even one of them, you are like one who has conveyed none of them. This answer, in my view, is weak, because one who conveys part and leaves out part, if it were said that he had left out the whole, would be speaking falsely; and if it were said that the degree of sin in leaving out a part is equal to the degree of sin in leaving out the whole, that too is impossible and inadmissible. Thus this answer falls away.

The more correct view, in my opinion, is that this was stated according to the pattern of the line:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is (my) poetry,"

meaning that my poetry has reached such perfection and eloquence that, whenever it is said of it that it is "my poetry," its praise has reached an extreme beyond which nothing can be added. Thus this statement conveys complete exaggeration from this aspect. Similarly here: "If you do not convey His message, then you have not conveyed His message" means that the failure to convey cannot be described with a threat greater than this: that you have failed to convey. This therefore serves as an alert to the utmost degree of threat and warning. And God knows best.

The third issue: The exegetes mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse:

The first: it was revealed concerning the matter of stoning and retaliation, as previously mentioned in the story of the Jews.

The second: it was revealed concerning the Jews' mockery of the religion and their defamation of it, while the Prophet remained silent about them, and then this verse was revealed.

The third: when the verse of choice was revealed, namely His saying: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 28], he did not present it to them out of fear that they would choose this world; then this verse was revealed.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning the matter of Zayd and Zaynab bint Jahsh. 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "Whoever claims that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concealed anything of the revelation has committed a grave slander against God, and God says: ﴿O Messenger, convey﴾. Had the Messenger of God concealed any part of the revelation, he would have concealed His saying: ﴿and you were concealing within yourself what God was to disclose﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]."

The fifth: it was revealed concerning jihad, for the hypocrites disliked it, and so he would sometimes refrain from urging them to jihad.

The sixth: when God's saying was revealed: ﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge﴾ [al-An'am: 108], the Messenger remained silent about the defamation of their gods, and then this verse was revealed, saying: (convey), meaning the faults of their gods, and do not hide them from them; and God will protect you from them.

The seventh: it was revealed concerning the rights of the Muslims. This is because he said during the Farewell Pilgrimage, after explaining the laws and the rites: "Have I conveyed (the message)?" They said: "Yes." He, peace be upon him, said: "O God, bear witness."

The eighth: It is reported that he (ﷺ) once rested under a tree during one of his journeys and hung his sword upon it. A bedouin came to him while he was asleep, took his sword, drew it, and said: "O Muhammad, who will protect you from me?" He said: "God." The bedouin's hand trembled, the sword fell from his hand, and he struck his head against the tree until his brain was scattered. Then God revealed this verse and made clear that He would protect him from people.

The ninth: he used to be in awe of the Quraysh, the Jews and the Christians, and God removed that awe from his heart through this verse.

The tenth: the verse was revealed concerning the virtue of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him). When this verse was revealed, he took his hand and said: "Whoever I am his master (mawla), then 'Ali is his master. O God, befriend whoever befriends him, and be the enemy of whoever is his enemy." 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) met him and said: "Congratulations to you, O son of Abu Talib! You have become my master and the master of every believing man and woman." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali.

Know that although these reports are numerous, the more appropriate interpretation is that God assured him of protection from the plotting of the Jews and the Christians, and commanded him to openly convey the message without concern for them. This is because what comes before this verse by a great deal and what comes after it by a great deal were speech addressed to the Jews and the Christians; it was therefore impermissible to place this single verse in between in a manner that would make it unrelated to what precedes and what follows it.

The fourth issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾, there is a question: how can this be reconciled with what is reported, that the Prophet (peace be upon him) had his face wounded on the day of Uhud and his front tooth was broken?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: what is meant is that He protects him from being killed, and this includes an alert that he is obliged to endure every kind of affliction short of death. How severe is the burden placed upon the prophets, peace be upon them!

The second: this verse was revealed after the day of Uhud.

Know that what is meant by "the people" here is the disbelievers, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Indeed God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. Its meaning is that He does not enable them to achieve what they want. It is reported from Anas (may God be pleased with him): "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was guarded by Sa'd and Hudhayfah until this verse was revealed. Then he put his head out from a leather tent and said: 'Disperse, O people, for God has protected me from people.'"

[p. 42]

[p. 43]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, you do not stand on anything until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded him to convey (al-tabligh), whether it was pleasing to the listener or burdensome to him, He commanded him to say this speech to the People of the Book, even though it was very hard for them. So He said: ﴿O People of the Book﴾, from among the Jews and the Christians, ﴿you do not stand on anything﴾ of the religion, and there is nothing in your hands of the truth and the correct path, just as you say: "This is nothing" when you want to belittle it and diminish its importance.

And His saying: ﴿until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾

This has been mentioned before, and the repetition is for emphasis.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾, and in it there are two aspects:

The first: Do not grieve over them because of the increase of their transgression and disbelief, for the harm of that returns to them, not to you or to the believers.

The second: Do not grieve because of the descent of the curse and punishment upon them, for they are among the disbelievers who deserve that. Ibn ʿAbbas narrated that "a group of Jews came and said: O Muhammad, do you not acknowledge that the Torah is true from Allah, exalted is He? He said: Yes. They said: Then we believe in it and we do not believe in anything other than it," and this verse was revealed.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 5, verse 69**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

The interpretation of this verse has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah, but some issues remain here:

[Page 44]

**The first issue:** The apparent grammar (i'rab) requires that it be said *wa-al-Sabi'in* (والصابئين, in the accusative). This is how Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Kathir read it. The grammarians have several explanations for the well-known reading (*wa-al-Sabi'un*, in the nominative):

The first, which is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is that *al-Sabi'un* is in the nominative by way of the inceptive (*ibtida'*, the nominative of the subject), with the intention of postponement. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve, and so are the Sabians," and the predicate of it is omitted. The benefit of not coordinating them with those before them is that the Sabians are the most astray of the groups mentioned in this verse. It is as if it were said: All these groups, if they believe and do righteous deeds, God accepts their repentance and removes their sin, and even the Sabians, for if they believe they too will be like this.

The second is the view of al-Farra', that the word *inna* (إنّ) is weak in governing here. Its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: *inna* only governs because it resembles the verb, and it is well known that the resemblance between a verb and a particle is weak.

The second: even though it governs, it governs only the noun (اسم), but the predicate remains nominative by virtue of being the predicate of the subject, and this particle has no effect on raising the predicate. This is the view of the Kufans, and we have demonstrated it with evidence in Surat al-Baqarah in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6].

The third: its effect appears only in some nouns. As for nouns whose condition does not change when the governing words differ, the effect of this particle does not appear in them, and the matter here is like that, because the noun here is His saying *alladhina* (الذين), and this word shows no effect of nominative, accusative or genitive.

Having established this, we say: when the noun of *inna* is such that no effect of case appears in it, the noun coordinated with it permits the accusative by the governing of this particle, and the nominative by the cancellation of its governing. So it is not permissible to say *inna Zaydan wa-'Amrun qa'imani* (إنّ زيدًا وعمرٌو قائمان), because *Zaydan* shows the effect of case. But it is permissible to say *inna ha'ula'i wa-ikhwatuka yukrimunana* (إنّ هؤلاء وإخوتك يُكرموننا), *inna hadha nafsuhu shuja'un* (إنّ هذا نفسُه شجاعٌ), and *inna Qata'ma wa-Hindun 'indana* (إنّ قطامِ وهندٌ عندنا). The reason for the permissibility of this is that *inna* was originally weak in governing; when it becomes such that no effect appears in its noun, it becomes extremely weak. So the nominative is permitted by virtue of the ruling established before this particle entered upon it, namely its being an inceptive subject. This is the explanation of al-Farra's view, and it is a good view and better than the view of the Basrans, because what they said implies that the speech of God, in the order in which it came, is not correct, and correctness is only achieved by dismantling this arrangement. But according to al-Farra's view there is no need for this, so it is preferable.

**The second issue:** Some grammarians said: There is no doubt that the particle *inna* is among the governing words that enter upon the inceptive subject and predicate. That the subject is an inceptive subject and the predicate a predicate is a real attribute, established both when this particle enters and before it, and being an inceptive subject requires the nominative.

Having established this, we say: the word coordinated with the noun of *inna* may be in the accusative, based on the governing of this particle, and it may also be in the nominative, because it is in reality an inceptive subject about which something is said and which is itself a predicate.

The author of al-Kashshaf criticised this, and said: It is only permissible to make it nominative by coordinating it with the position of *inna* and its noun after the predicate has been mentioned. You say: *inna Zaydan munṭaliqun wa-'Amran* (إنّ زيدًا منطلقٌ وعمرًا), with the accusative according to the wording, and *wa-'Amrun* (وعمرٌو) with the nominative according to the position of *inna* and its noun, because the predicate has already come first. But before that predicate it is not permissible, because if we made it nominative according to the position of *inna* and its noun, the governing of their predicate would be the subject, and if that were so, the governing of their predicate would be the inceptive, because the inceptive is the one that affects both the subject and the predicate together. In that case the later predicate would have to be nominative by the particle *inna* and by the meaning of the inceptive, and so one nominative word would have two different governing agents, and that is impossible.

Know that this speech is weak, and its weakness is shown in several aspects:

The first: these things which the grammarians call "raising" and "governing" do not mean that they are so by their essences or by their own selves, for no intelligent person would say this. Rather the meaning is that they are indicators, by convention and terminology, of these vowel-markings. The gathering of many indicators upon one thing is not impossible. Do you not see that all parts of created things are indicators of the existence of God, exalted is He?

The second weakness of this answer is that he built it upon the premise that the particle *inna* affects the accusative of the noun and the nominative of the predicate, whereas the Kufans deny this and say: this particle has no effect at all on raising the predicate. We have settled this question in Surat al-Baqarah.

The third: when many things are coordinated, with some following others, a single predicate is not a predicate about all of them, because the predicate about a thing is an expression of defining its condition and explaining its attribute. It is impossible that the condition and attribute of one thing should be identical with the condition and attribute of another, because one attribute cannot subsist in different essences.

Having established this, it becomes clear that the predicate, although it is one in wording, is multiple in estimation, and this multiplicity necessarily exists according to estimation and intention. When multiplicity exists in reality, it is not impossible that some should be raised by the particle and some by the inceptive. By this estimation, there is no necessity of two governing agents gathering upon one nominative. What confirms this is that he himself conceded that after mentioning the noun and its predicate, the nominative and accusative are permitted for the coordinated word. There is no doubt that this coordinated word is permitted this only because we supply a predicate for it, and we rule that this supplied predicate is nominative by the inceptive.

Having established this, we say: if the mention of a predicate is accepted when we coordinate a noun with a noun, then sound reason rules that one must judge by estimating a predicate, and that is achieved only by supplying many predicates. By this estimate, the objection of the necessity [that he mentioned] falls away. And God knows best.

* * *

**The third issue:** When God, exalted is He, had made clear that the People of the Book are not upon anything until they believe, He made clear that this ruling is general for all, and that no one obtains excellence or distinction except by believing in God and the Last Day and doing righteous deeds. This is because a human being has two powers: the theoretical power and the practical power. The perfection of the theoretical power is only by knowing the Truth, and the perfection of the practical power is only by doing good. The most excellent of knowledge is knowledge of the most noble of existent things, which is God, glorified and exalted is He. The perfection of knowing Him is achieved only by His being able to gather and resurrect, so the best of knowledge is undoubtedly belief in God and the Last Day. The best of good deeds are two things: persevering in deeds which show the glorifying of the One worshipped, and striving to bring benefit to creation, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Reverence for the command of God and compassion for the creatures of God." Then God, exalted is He, made clear that whoever comes with this belief and this deed will come to the Resurrection without fear or grief. The benefit of mentioning both is that fear relates to the future, and grief to the past. So He said: ﴿no fear shall be upon them﴾, because of what they witness of the terrors of the Resurrection; ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾, because of what they missed of the good things of this world, since they found matters greater, more noble and better than what they had obtained in this world. Whoever is like this does not grieve over the good things of this world.

[Page 46]

If it is said: How is it possible for a responsible person who is not protected from it to be free of the terrors of the Resurrection?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: God, exalted is He, made this conditional on righteous deeds, and one does not bring righteous deeds unless one has abandoned all sins.

The second: if fear occurs, it is a minor passing matter which is not counted.

**The fourth issue:** The Mu'tazila said: God, exalted is He, made the absence of fear and the absence of grief conditional upon belief and righteous deeds. Something conditional upon another thing is non-existent when the condition is absent. It follows that whoever does not come with righteous deeds along with belief will experience fear and grief, and that prevents forgiveness of the one who committed a major sin.

The answer: the one who committed a major sin does not definitively know that God will forgive him inevitably, so fear and grief are present before the forgiveness is made manifest.

**The fifth issue:** God, exalted is He, said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, and then said at the end of the verse: ﴿whoever believes in God﴾. In this repetition there are two benefits:

The first: the hypocrites used to claim that they were believers, so the benefit of this repetition is to exclude them from the promise of the absence of fear and the absence of grief.

The second benefit: God, exalted is He, stated the word "belief" without restriction, and belief includes divisions, and the most noble of them is belief in God and the Last Day. So the benefit of the repetition is to draw attention to the fact that these two divisions are the most noble divisions of belief. We have mentioned many aspects regarding His saying: ﴿That is because those who disbelieved﴾, and all of them are suitable for this place.

**The sixth issue:** The pronoun referring back to the noun of *inna* is omitted, and the estimate is: *man amana minhum* (من آمن منهم), "whoever of them believes." The omission is permissible because it is known. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Whenever a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group they denied and a group they killed.﴾

Know that the purpose is to explain the arrogance of the Children of Israel and the severity of their rebellion against fulfilling the covenant of God. This is connected to what God opened the surah with, namely His saying: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾. So He said: ﴿Certainly We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, meaning: We created the proofs and created the intellect (al-'aql) that guides to the manner of reasoning (al-istidlal), and We sent to them messengers to make known the laws (al-shara'i') and rulings (al-ahkam). And His saying: ﴿Whenever a messenger came to them with what﴾

Page 47
﴿their souls did not desire﴾ is a conditional clause (jumla shartiyya) that stands as a qualifier (sifa) of His saying "messengers" (rusulan), and the returning pronoun (al-raji') is omitted. The estimate is: "Whenever a messenger from among them came to them with what their souls did not desire," that is, with what opposes their desires and contradicts their appetites of the hardships of obligation.

Here there are questions:

The first: Where is the answer of the condition (jawab al-shart)? For His saying: ﴿a group they denied and a group they killed﴾ cannot be the answer of this condition, because one messenger cannot be two groups.

The answer: The answer of the condition is omitted, and its omission is permissible because the mentioned statement is evidence for it. The estimate is: "Whenever a messenger came to them, they opposed him." Then it is said: How did they oppose him? It is said: "a group they denied and a group they killed." As for his saying, "one messenger cannot be two groups," we say: His saying "whenever a messenger came to them" indicates the multiplicity of messengers, so necessarily He made them two groups.

The second question: Why was one of the two verbs mentioned in the past tense and the other in the present tense?

The answer: He, exalted is He, explained how they used to deny Jesus and Moses in every situation, and how they used to rebel against His commands and obligations, and that he (peace be upon him) died in the wilderness (al-tih), according to some of them, due to the ill-omen of their rebellion against accepting his word concerning fighting the tyrants (al-jabbarin).

As for killing, it is what happened to them concerning Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both, and they had also intended to kill Jesus, although God prevented them from their aim, while they claim that they killed him. So the mention of denial in the past tense here is an indication of their dealings with Moses, peace be upon him, because many periods have passed since that time. And the mention of killing in the present tense is an indication of their dealings with Zakariyya, Yahya and Jesus, peace be upon them all, because that time was near, so it was like the present.

The third question: What is the benefit of fronting the object in His saying: ﴿a group they denied and a group they killed﴾?

The answer: You have known that fronting only occurs for the sake of great concern, so denial and killing, although both are reprehensible, yet denying the prophets and killing them, peace and blessings be upon them, is more vile. So the fronting was for this benefit.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they thought that there would be no trial﴾. In this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu 'Amr recited (أن لا تكونُ فتنةٌ) with the ـُ on the nun of "takūnu" (raf', nominative), while the rest recited it with the fatha (nasb, accusative). Al-Wahidi gave a good explanation for this, saying: Verbs are of three types. The first type indicates the firmness and stability of a thing, like: knowing (al-'ilm), certainty (al-tayaqqun), and clarification (al-tabayyun). What is like this is followed by the light "an" (an-nasiba li-l-fi'l, the "an" that governs the verb), because the heavy "anna" indicates the firmness and stability of a thing. When knowing indicates stability and firmness, and the heavy "anna" conveys this meaning, there is a correspondence and affinity between them. An example from the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿And they know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾ [al-Nur: 25]; ﴿Do they not know that Allah accepts repentance from His servants?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104]; ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14], where the "bi" is superfluous.

The second type: a verb that indicates the opposite of firmness and stability, like: atma'u (I hope/desire), akhafu (I fear), and arju (I hope). For this type only the light "an" that governs the verb is used. Allah says: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive me my sin﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82]; ﴿You fear that the people will snatch you away﴾ [al-Anfal: 26]; ﴿So We feared that he would burden them﴾ [al-Kahf: 80].

The third type: a verb that sometimes takes this course and sometimes that course, like: hasiba (to reckon/think) and its sisters. Sometimes it is used in the sense of atma'u and arju concerning what is not firm and stable, and sometimes in the sense of knowing concerning what is firm and stable.

Having understood this, we say: it is possible to construe hasban here so that it conveys firmness and stability, because those people were certain that they would not fall into trial and punishment through that denial and killing. It is also possible to construe it so that this firmness is not conveyed, in that they were denying and killing to preserve status and following, while in their hearts they knew that this was an error and a sin. Since the wording admits each of these two meanings, the validity of each of these two readings becomes apparent. Whoever read (أن لا تكونُ) with the raf' meant: that it would not occur. The heavy "anna" was then lightened and "la" was made a substitute for the omitted pronoun. If you said "'alimtu an yaqūlu" with the raf', it would not be good unless you brought in something that serves as a substitute for the omitted pronoun, such as sin, sawfa, or qad, as in His saying: ﴿He knew that there would be among you those who are ill﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. The reading with the nasb is clear.

Then al-Wahidi said: Both readings have come in the Qur'an. Like the reading of one who used the nasb and placed the light "an" after it is His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 4]; ﴿Or do those who perpetrate evil deeds think that We will make them﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21]; ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think that they will be left﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1–2]. Like the reading of one who used the raf' is: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 80]; ﴿Do they think that what We supply them with is﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55]. These are lightened from the heavy form, because the verb-governing "an" is not followed by "lan". Parallel to these two views in opinion is His saying: ﴿You think that it will be done to you﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25]; ﴿If they both think that they can maintain the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. And from the raf' is His saying: ﴿And we thought that no human or jinn would ever speak a lie against Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 5]; ﴿And they thought, as you thought, that Allah would not send anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 7]. Here the "an" is the light form of the heavy one, like His saying: ﴿He knew that there would be among you those who are ill﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], because the verb-governing "an" does not combine with "lan", since "lan" conveys emphasis, while the verb-governing "an" conveys non-firmness, as we have established.

The second issue: the verb hasiba is among the verbs that must have two objects. However, His saying ﴿And they thought that there would be no trial﴾ is a clause that took the place of the two objects of hasiba, because its meaning is: they thought the trial was not descending upon them.

The third issue: the commentators gave several interpretations of "al-fitnah" (the trial). It is confined to the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. The punishment of this world has types: among them drought, among them plague, among them killing, among them enmity, among them hatred among themselves, and among them misfortune and ill omen. All of these had befallen them, and each of the commentators took the trial to mean one of these aspects.

Know that their thinking that no trial would occur admits two meanings:

The first: they believed that abrogation (naskh) was impossible under the law of Musa (peace be upon him), and they believed that what was obligatory upon them, regarding every messenger who came with a different law, was to deny him and kill him.

The second: although they believed in themselves that they were mistaken in that denial and killing, they used to say: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved," and they believed that the prophethood of their forefathers and fathers would ward off from them the punishment they deserved because of that killing and denial.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then they became blind and deaf; then Allah turned to them; then many of them became blind and deaf again. And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾.

In it are issues.

The first issue: the verse indicates that their blindness and deafness to guidance to the truth occurred twice.

The commentators differed about what is meant by these two occurrences, in several views:

The first: what is meant is that they became blind and deaf in the time of Zakariyya, Yahya, and 'Isa (peace be upon them). Then Allah turned to some of them, in that some of them were granted success to believe in Him. Then many of them became blind and deaf again in the time of Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), by denying his prophethood and message. He said ﴿many of them﴾ because although most of the Jews persisted in disbelief in Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), a group of them believed in him, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions.

The second: they became blind and deaf when they worshipped the calf; then they repented of it, so Allah turned to them; then many of them became blind and deaf again through excessive demands (al-ta'annut), namely their asking to see Allah openly and for the angels to descend.

The third: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in Surat Bani Isra'il what may be an explanation of this verse, saying: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you would surely cause corruption in the land twice, and you would surely become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the dwellings, and it was a promise fulfilled﴾ ﴿Then We gave back to you the return over them and supplied you with wealth and sons and made you greater in numbers﴾ [al-Isra': 4–6]. This is in the sense of ﴿they became blind and deaf﴾. Then He said: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to disfigure your faces and to enter the masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra': 7]. This is in the sense of His saying ﴿then many of them became blind and deaf﴾.

The fourth: His saying ﴿they became blind and deaf﴾ was only with respect to a messenger sent to them, such as Dawud, Sulayman, and others, and they believed in him, so Allah turned to them. Then a period of interruption (fatrah) occurred, and they became blind and deaf a second time.

The second issue: it was recited ("'Umu" and "Summu") with a damma, on the reading that Allah blinded them and deafened them (ʿamahumu Allah wa-ṣammahumu Allah), meaning He struck them and smote them with blindness and deafness, just as one says "nazaktuhu" when one strikes him with the nazk, which is a short spear, and "rakibtuhu" when one strikes him with one's knee (rukbah).

The third issue: concerning His saying ﴿then many of them became blind and deaf﴾ there are several views:

The first: according to the view of those Arabs who say: "The fleas ate me" (akalūnī al-baraghīth).

The second: that ﴿many of them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in His saying ﴿they became blind and deaf﴾. Substitution is common in the Qur'an. Allah said: ﴿He who perfected everything He created﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7], and He said: ﴿And for Allah, of the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. This substitution is most fitting here, because if He had said "they became blind and deaf," that would have suggested that all of them became so; but when He said ﴿many of them﴾, it indicates that this applies to the majority, not to all.

The third: that His saying ﴿many of them﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimate is: they are many of them.

The fourth issue: there is no doubt that what is meant by this blindness and deafness is ignorance and disbelief. We say: the doer of this ignorance is either Allah, exalted is He, or the servant. The first nullifies the view of the Mu'tazilah, and the second is false, because a person never chooses for himself to acquire ignorance and disbelief.

If they say: they only chose it because they thought it was knowledge.

We reply: the sum of this is that they chose this ignorance only because of a prior ignorance. However, ignorances do not go on in an infinite chain; rather they must end at the first ignorance. It is not permissible for its doer to be the servant, for the reason we have mentioned. Therefore it must be that its doer is Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾, that is, of the killing of the prophets and the denial of the messengers. The purpose of this is intimidation (tahdid).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verses 72–73:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had thoroughly addressed the Jews, He began here to address the Christians. He related that a group among them said, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." This is the doctrine of the Ya'qubiyya (Jacobites), for they say that Mary gave birth to a god. The likely meaning of this doctrine is that they say: Allah, exalted is He, indwelt the essence of Jesus and became united with the essence of Jesus. Then He, exalted is He, related of the Messiah that he said: ﴿O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.﴾ This is an alert to the decisive proof against the corruption of the Christian doctrine, because he, upon him be peace, did not distinguish between himself and others in that the signs of createdness (hudith) are manifest upon him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ Its meaning is clear. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued that the punishment of sinners is not everlasting. They said: This is because He, exalted is He, made the greatest kind of threat and warning concerning the polytheists to be that Allah has forbidden them Paradise, made their abode the Fire, and that they have no helper who will support them nor intercessor who will intercede for them. So if the condition of the sinful among the believers were like that, the warning against the polytheists regarding their polytheism by this threat would have no benefit left.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: ﴿thalathatin﴾ ("three") is put in the genitive by the construct (idafa), and it is not permissible to put it in the accusative, because its meaning is "one of three." But when you say "rabi' thalatha" ("fourth of three"), here both the genitive and the accusative are permissible, because its meaning is that which made the three into four by being among them.

The second issue: Regarding the interpretation of the saying of the Christians, "the third of three," there are two approaches:

The first: the saying of some exegetes, which is that they intended by this that Allah, Mary and Jesus are three gods. What confirms this is His saying, exalted is He, to the Messiah: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116]. So His saying "the third of three" means "one of three gods," or "one of three gods." The proof that this is what is meant is His saying, exalted is He, in refuting them: ﴿And there is no god except one God.﴾ And according to this interpretation, there is an implied ellipsis in the verse, except that the mention of "gods" has been omitted, because that is known from their doctrines. Al-Wahidi said: One who says "Indeed, Allah is the third of three" does not become a disbeliever if he does not intend by it "the third of three gods," for there are no two things except that Allah is the third of them by knowledge, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7].

The second approach: the theologians (mutakallimun) related from the Christians that they say: one essence (jawhar wahid), three aqanim (hypostases): Father, Son, and the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus). These three are one god, just as "the sun" is a name that encompasses the disc, the ray, and the heat. By "the Father" they mean the essence, by "the Son" the Word (kalima), and by "the Spirit" life (hayat). They affirmed the essence, the Word, and the life, and they said: The Word, which is the speech of Allah, mixed with the body of Jesus like the mixing of water with wine, and like the mixing of water with milk. They claimed that the Father is god, the Son is god, the Spirit is god, and all of them are one god.

Know that this is evidently false by the immediate judgment of reason, for three cannot be one, and one cannot be three. Nowhere in this world is there a doctrine more corrupt or more manifestly false than the doctrine of the Christians.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there is no god except one God.﴾ Regarding "min" (in ﴿min ilah﴾) there are two opinions:

One of them: it is a superfluous (za'ida) particle, and the construction is: "wa ma ilahun illa ilahun wahid."

The second: it conveys the meaning of comprehensiveness (istighraq), and the construction is: "wa ma fi al-wujud min hadhihi al-haqiqa illa fardun wahid" (there is in existence, of this reality, nothing but one single individual).

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict those who disbelieve among them a painful punishment.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is: "those who persisted upon this religion will surely be afflicted," because many of them repented from Christianity.

They affirmed the essence, the Word, and the life, and they said: The Word, which is the speech of Allah, mixed with the body of Jesus like the mixing of water with wine, and like the mixing of water with milk. They claimed that the Father is god, the Son is god, the Spirit is god, and all of them are one god.

Know that this is evidently false by the immediate judgment of reason, for three cannot be one, and one cannot be three. Nowhere in this world is there a doctrine more corrupt or more manifestly false than the doctrine of the Christians.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there is no god except one God.﴾ Regarding "min" (in ﴿min ilah﴾) there are two opinions:

One of them: it is a superfluous (za'ida) particle, and the construction is: "wa ma ilahun illa ilahun wahid."

The second: it conveys the meaning of comprehensiveness (istighraq), and the construction is: "wa ma fi al-wujud min hadhihi al-haqiqa illa fardun wahid" (there is in existence, of this reality, nothing but one single individual).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict those who disbelieve among them a painful punishment.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is: "those who persisted upon this religion will surely be afflicted," because many of them repented from Christianity.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 74–76:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

Al-Farra' said: This is a command in the form of a question, like His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91] in the verse on the prohibition of wine.

* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him, and his mother was a truthful woman﴾. That is: he is no more than a messenger from among the messengers who passed away before him, who came with signs from Allah just as they came with their like. If Allah healed the blind and the leper and raised the dead through his hand, then He had already brought the staff to life and made it a moving serpent, and split the sea through the hand of Moses. And if He created him without a male, then He created Adam without a male or a female. ﴿And his mother was a truthful woman﴾. There are several explanations of this:

The first: she affirmed the signs of her Lord and everything her son reported from Him. Allah the Exalted said in describing her: ﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12].

The second: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit, and it appeared to her as a man in every respect﴾ [Maryam: 17]. When Gabriel spoke to her and she affirmed him, the name "truthful woman" applied to her.

The third: the meaning of her being a truthful woman is her utmost distance from sins and the intensity of her diligence and striving in upholding the rites of worship. The one who is perfect in this quality is called a siddiq. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are with the ones whom Allah has blessed of the prophets and the truthful ones﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They both used to eat food﴾.
Know that the purpose of this is to argue against the falsity of the Christians' claim, and its explanation is in several respects:

The first: everyone who has a mother came into being after he was not, and everyone of that kind is a created being, not a god.

The second: they were both in need, for they both had an extreme need for food, whereas God is the one who is free of need from all things. How, then, can it be conceived that he is a god?

The third: some have said that His saying ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ is a metaphor for having come into being, because whoever eats food must inevitably come into being. But this, in my view, is weak in several respects:

The first: not everyone who eats has come into being, for the people of Paradise eat and do not come into being.

The second: eating is an expression of need for food, and this need is among the strongest proofs that he is not a god. So what need do we have to take it as a metaphor for something else?

The third: the god is the one able to create and bring into being. If he were a god, he would be able to repel the pain of hunger from himself without food and drink. Since he could not repel harm from himself, how can it be conceived that he is the god of the worlds? In sum, the falsity of the Christians' claim is too evident to require proof.

* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them, then look how they are turned away﴾. It is said: "Afakahu yafikuhu ifkan" when he turned him away. Falsehood (ifk) is lying, because it is a turning away from the truth. Everything turned away from something is "ma'fuk" from it. And "afakat al-ardu" means the land was turned away from rain. The meaning of His saying ﴿how are they turned away﴾ is: how are they turned away from the truth? Our companions said: the verse shows that they are turned away from reflecting on the truth. A person cannot turn himself away from truth and sincerity toward falsehood, ignorance and lying, because a rational person does not choose that for himself. So we know that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the One who turned them away from that.

* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, what possesses for you neither harm nor benefit?﴾
This is another proof against the falsity of the Christians' claim, and it admits of several kinds of argument:

The first: the Jews were hostile to him and intended him harm, yet he could not harm them; and his helpers and companions loved him, yet he could not bring them any worldly benefit. How can it be conceived that one who is unable to harm or benefit is a god?

The second: the Christian doctrine is that the Jews crucified him, broke his ribs, and when he became thirsty and asked them for water, they poured vinegar into his nostrils. How can it be conceived that one who is so weak is a god?

The third: the god of the world must be free of need from everything other than himself, and everything other than him must be in need of him. If Jesus were like that, it would be impossible for him to be occupied with worshipping Allah the Exalted, for a god does not worship anything; rather, it is the servant who worships the god. Since it is known through consistent transmission that he was constant in obedience and worship, we know that he only did so because he was in need of others in obtaining benefits and repelling harms. Whoever is like that, how could he be able to bring benefits to the servants and repel harms from them? And if that is so, he is a servant like the other servants. This is precisely the argument Allah the Exalted related from Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said to his father: ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, and does not avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42].
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. What is meant by this is a warning, that is: He hears their disbelief and knows their inner thoughts.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the right way.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, first spoke about the falsehoods of the Jews, and then spoke secondly about the falsehoods of the Christians and established the overpowering proof against their invalidity and corruption, He then addressed the whole of both groups with this address, saying: ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth.﴾ Ghuluww (excess, exaggeration) is the opposite of taqsir (negligence, falling short), and its meaning is going beyond the limit. This is because the truth lies between the two extremes of excess and deficiency, and the religion of God lies between excess and negligence. His saying ﴿beyond the truth﴾ is an adjective of the verbal noun, meaning: do not commit excess in your religion an excess that is other than the truth, that is, a false excess. This is because excess in religion is of two kinds: excess of truth, which is to go to great lengths in establishing and affirming it, and excess of falsehood, which is to labour at establishing doubts and concealing proofs. That excess is what the Jews, may God curse them, did when they attributed to him (ﷺ) fornication and that he was a liar, and the Christians claimed divinity for him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the right way.﴾ On this there are two issues:

The first issue: Ahwa' (desires) here means the doctrines to which desire calls without proof. Al-Sha'bi said: God did not mention the word hawa (desire) in the Qur'an except to condemn it. He said: ﴿And do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of God﴾ [Sad: 26], ﴿and he followed his desire, so he perished﴾ [Ta-Ha: 16], ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3], ﴿Have you seen one who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. Abu 'Ubaydah said: We have not found hawa used except in a context of evil; one does not say "so-and-so yahwa good," rather one says "he wants good and loves it." Some of them said: Desire is a god worshipped besides God. It was said: hawa was named hawa because it plunges (yahwi) its companion into the Fire. And he recited in condemnation of desire:

Indeed desire is humiliation itself,
so when you desire, you have met with humiliation.

A man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Praise be to God who made my desire to be in accordance with your desire." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Every desire is misguidance."

The second issue: He, exalted is He, described them with three degrees of misguidance. He made clear that they were astray before, then He mentioned that they were leading others astray, then He mentioned that they persisted in that state until they are now astray as they were. There is no state closer to the servant to God's displeasure and nearer to God's punishment than this state, from which we seek God's refuge. It is possible that the meaning is that they went astray and led others astray, then they went astray because of their belief that this leading astray was guidance to the truth. It is also possible that the meaning of the first misguidance is straying from the religion, and of the second misguidance, straying from the path to Paradise.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 5, verses 78–81:

Know that when He, exalted is He, addressed the People of the Book with this address, He described their predecessors, so He said, exalted is He:

[Page 54]

﴿Those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud (David) and Isa (Jesus) son of Maryam (Mary). That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾ ﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed. Evil was what they used to do.﴾ ﴿You see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieve. Evil is what their souls have sent forward for them, that Allah became angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿If they had believed in Allah, and the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies. But many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

﴿Those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud and Isa son of Maryam.﴾

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, i.e. Qur'anic exegesis) said: it means the People of the Sabbath and the People of the Table. As for the People of the Sabbath, the folk of Dawud, who were the people of Ayla, when they transgressed on the Sabbath by taking the fish, as Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this story in Surat al-A'raf, Dawud said: "O Allah, curse them and make them a sign," and they were transformed into apes. As for the People of the Table, when they ate from the Table and did not believe, Isa said: "O Allah, curse them as You cursed the People of the Sabbath," and they became swine. They were five thousand men, among whom there was no woman or child. Some scholars said: the Jews used to boast that "we are the descendants of the Prophets," so Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this verse to show that they were cursed upon the tongues of the Prophets. It was also said: Dawud and Isa, peace be upon them both, gave good news of Muhammad (ﷺ) and cursed whoever would deny him. This is the view of al-Asamm.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾ The meaning is that the curse was on account of their disobedience and their excessiveness in that disobedience.

Then He, exalted is He, explained the disobedience and transgression with His saying:

﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed.﴾ Regarding the word "tanahaw" (mutual forbidding, from the root n-h-y) here, there are two meanings:

The first, which is the view of the majority, is that it is a reciprocal form (tafa'ul) from "nahy" (prohibition), meaning: they did not forbid one another. Ibn Mas'ud related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever approves the deeds of a people is one of them, and whoever increases the numbers of a people is one of them."

The second meaning of "tanahi" is that it is from "intiha'" (desisting), as one says: "intaha 'an al-amr" and "tanahaa 'anhu" when he refrained from it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Evil is what they used to do.﴾ The lam in "labi'sa" is the lam of oath, as if He said: "I swear, evil is what they used to do," and that is committing sins and transgression, and abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil.

If it is said: desisting from something after it has already occurred is not possible, so why did He blame them for it?

We answer: the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: that what is meant is that they did not desist from repeating a wrong they had committed.

The second: they did not desist from a wrong which they intended to commit and had prepared its instruments and tools.

The third: they did not desist from persisting in a wrong they had committed.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieve.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, described their predecessors with what has preceded, He described those present among them as taking as allies the disbelievers and the worshippers of idols. What is meant by them is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, when they incited the polytheists against the Messenger (ﷺ). We have discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided in the way than those who believe"﴾ [al-Nisa': 51].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Evil is what their souls have sent forward for them﴾, meaning: evil is what they sent forward of deeds for their return in the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that Allah became angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide forever﴾: the place of "an" (that) is in the nominative case. You say: "bi'sa rajulan Zayd" (what an evil man Zayd is), and its nominative case is like the nominative case of "Zayd." Regarding "Zayd" there are two possibilities:

The first: that it is a subject (mubtada'), and "bi'sa" together with what it governs is its predicate.

The second: that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, as if when he said "bi'sa rajulan," it was said: "What is he?" and he replied: "Zayd," meaning: he is Zayd.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If they had believed in Allah, and the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies. But many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ The meaning is: if they had believed in Allah, and in the Prophet, who is Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, and in what was revealed to him of the Torah, as they claim, they would not have taken the polytheists as allies, because the prohibition of that is emphasized in the Torah and in the law of Musa, peace be upon him. When they did that, it became clear that their aim was not to uphold the religion of Musa, peace be upon him, but rather their aim was leadership and status, so they strive to attain it by whatever means they are able to. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, described them as defiantly disobedient, saying: ﴿But many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ There is another view on this, mentioned by al-Qaffal, which is that the meaning is: even if these polytheists who take allies believed in Allah and Muhammad (ﷺ), these Jews would not have taken them as allies. This view is good, and there is nothing in the speech that rejects it.
