As for the People of the Table, when they ate from the Table and did not believe, Isa said: "O Allah, curse them as You cursed the People of the Sabbath," and they became swine. They were five thousand men, among whom there was no woman or child. Some scholars said: the Jews used to boast that "we are the descendants of the Prophets," so Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this verse to show that they were cursed upon the tongues of the Prophets. It was also said: Dawud and Isa, peace be upon them both, gave good news of Muhammad (ﷺ) and cursed whoever would deny him. This is the view of al-Asamm.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾ The meaning is that the curse was on account of their disobedience and their excessiveness in that disobedience.

Then He, exalted is He, explained the disobedience and transgression with His saying:

﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed.﴾ Regarding the word "tanahaw" (mutual forbidding, from the root n-h-y) here, there are two meanings:

The first, which is the view of the majority, is that it is a reciprocal form (tafa'ul) from "nahy" (prohibition), meaning: they did not forbid one another. Ibn Mas'ud related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever approves the deeds of a people is one of them, and whoever increases the numbers of a people is one of them."

The second meaning of "tanahi" is that it is from "intiha'" (desisting), as one says: "intaha 'an al-amr" and "tanahaa 'anhu" when he refrained from it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Evil is what they used to do.﴾ The lam in "labi'sa" is the lam of oath, as if He said: "I swear, evil is what they used to do," and that is committing sins and transgression, and abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil.

If it is said: desisting from something after it has already occurred is not possible, so why did He blame them for it?

We answer: the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: that what is meant is that they did not desist from repeating a wrong they had committed.

The second: they did not desist from a wrong which they intended to commit and had prepared its instruments and tools.

The third: they did not desist from persisting in a wrong they had committed.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieve.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, described their predecessors with what has preceded, He described those present among them as taking as allies the disbelievers and the worshippers of idols. What is meant by them is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, when they incited the polytheists against the Messenger (ﷺ). We have discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided in the way than those who believe"﴾ [al-Nisa': 51].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Evil is what their souls have sent forward for them﴾, meaning: evil is what they sent forward of deeds for their return in the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that Allah became angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide forever﴾: the place of "an" (that) is in the nominative case. You say: "bi'sa rajulan Zayd" (what an evil man Zayd is), and its nominative case is like the nominative case of "Zayd." Regarding "Zayd" there are two possibilities:

The first: that it is a subject (mubtada'), and "bi'sa" together with what it governs is its predicate.

The second: that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, as if when he said "bi'sa rajulan," it was said: "What is he?" and he replied: "Zayd," meaning: he is Zayd.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If they had believed in Allah, and the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies. But many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ The meaning is: if they had believed in Allah, and in the Prophet, who is Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, and in what was revealed to him of the Torah, as they claim, they would not have taken the polytheists as allies, because the prohibition of that is emphasized in the Torah and in the law of Musa, peace be upon him. When they did that, it became clear that their aim was not to uphold the religion of Musa, peace be upon him, but rather their aim was leadership and status, so they strive to attain it by whatever means they are able to. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, described them as defiantly disobedient, saying: ﴿But many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ There is another view on this, mentioned by al-Qaffal, which is that the meaning is: even if these polytheists who take allies believed in Allah and Muhammad (ﷺ), these Jews would not have taken them as allies. This view is good, and there is nothing in the speech that rejects it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 82:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God; and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward the believers those who say, "We are Christians."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned some of the conditions of the People of the Book, both Jews and Christians, He mentioned in this verse that the Jews are at the extreme of hostility toward the Muslims. For this reason He made them companions of the polytheists in intensity of hostility. Indeed, He drew attention to the fact that they are more hostile than the polytheists, in that He mentioned them before the polytheists. By my life, they are indeed so. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No two Jews are alone with a Muslim without intending to kill him." God, exalted is He, also mentioned that the Christians are gentler in disposition than the Jews and closer to the Muslims than they are.

Page 56
Here there are two issues:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata' and al-Suddi said: what is meant is al-Najashi and his people, who came from Abyssinia to the Messenger (ﷺ) and believed in him. It does not refer to all Christians, given the evident hostility of the Christians toward the Muslims. Others said: it is the doctrine of the Jews that it is obligatory for them to inflict harm upon whoever opposes them in religion by any means whatsoever. If they are able to kill, well and good; otherwise, by seizing property, by theft, or by some kind of deception, scheming and trickery. As for the Christians, their doctrine is not that, rather harming them in their religion is forbidden. This is the aspect of the difference.

The second issue: The purpose of explaining this difference is to lighten the matter of the Jews for the Messenger (ﷺ). The lam in His saying "you will surely find" (la-tajidanna) is the lam of oath, and the implied meaning is: "By oath, you will surely find the Jews and the polytheists to be the most intense of people in hostility toward the believers." I have already explained to you that this rebelliousness and disobedience is an ancient habit of theirs, so empty your mind of them and do not concern yourself with their scheming and their plotting.

Then God, exalted is He, mentioned the cause of this difference, saying: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.﴾

In the verse there are two issues:

The first: The cause of this difference is that the Jews are particularly characterized by intense greed for this world. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will surely find them the greediest of people for life, even more than those who associate partners [with God]﴾ (al-Baqarah: 96). Here He paired them in greed with the polytheists who deny the Hereafter. Greed is the source of blameworthy character traits, because whoever is greedy for this world casts his religion aside in pursuit of worldly things and commits every forbidden and reprehensible act for the sake of worldly gain. Therefore his hostility is necessarily intensified toward everyone who obtains wealth or status. As for the Christians, they are for the most part turned away from this world, devoted to worship, and abandoning the pursuit of leadership, pride and haughtiness. Whoever is like this does not envy people, does not harm them, and does not quarrel with them; rather he is gentle in disposition in seeking the truth and easy to be led by it. This is the distinction between these two groups in this matter, and it is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.﴾

Here is a subtle and beneficial point in seeking religion: the disbelief of the Christians is more grievous than the disbelief of the Jews, because the Christians dispute over matters of divinity and prophethood, whereas the Jews dispute only over prophethood. There is no doubt that the former is more grievous. Then, although the Christians, despite the grossness of their disbelief, were not intensely greedy for the pursuit of this world, but rather there was in their hearts some inclination toward the Hereafter, God honored them by His saying: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward the believers those who say, "We are Christians."﴾ As for the Jews, although their disbelief is lighter in comparison with the disbelief of the Christians, God expelled them and singled them out for additional curse. This was due to nothing other than their greed for this world, and this alerts you to the soundness of his saying (ﷺ): "Love of this world is the root of every sin."

The second issue: "Qiss" and "qissis" are a title for the head of the Christians, and the plural is qissisun. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: the Christians fabricated the Gospel and introduced into it what is not part of it, and one of their scholars remained upon the truth and the religion; his name was Qissis, and whoever follows his guidance and religion is a qissis. Qutrub said: qass and qissis mean a scholar of the Byzantine (Rum) language, and this is among the matters in which the two languages agree. As for "ruhban," it is the plural of rahib, like rukban (plural of rakib) and furban (plural of faris). Some said: ruhban is singular, and its plural is rahabin, like qurban and qarabin, and its origin is from al-rahbah, in the sense of fear.

Page 57
If it is said: how does God praise them for this, when He says: ﴿But monasticism, they invented it﴾ (al-Hadid: 27), and when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "There is no monasticism in Islam"?
We reply: That [quality] became praiseworthy in contrast to the Jews' way of harshness and severity, and this measure does not necessitate that it is praiseworthy absolutely.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾. The pronoun in His saying "they heard" (sami'u) refers to the priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban) among them who believed. "What has been sent down" means the Qur'an, and "to the Messenger" means Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means al-Najashi (the Negus) and his companions. That is because Ja'far al-Tayyar (may Allah be pleased with him) recited to them Surat Maryam, and al-Najashi took a straw from the ground and said: "By Allah, what you recited adds nothing beyond what Allah said in the Gospel, not even this much." And they continued weeping until Ja'far finished the recitation.

As for His saying ﴿you see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: the meaning is that their eyes are filled with tears until they overflow, because "fayd" (overflowing) is when a vessel or other thing is filled until what is in it spills out from its sides.

The second: the meaning is an emphasis in describing them with weeping, so their eyes are made as though they overflow of themselves.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿from what they have recognized of the Truth﴾, that is: from what was sent down to Muhammad, and it is the Truth.

If it is said: what is the difference between "min" (from) and "min" (from) in His saying ﴿from what they have recognized of the Truth﴾?

We say: the first (min) indicates the starting point of the action, and the implied meaning is that the overflowing of tears began from recognizing the Truth, and it was because of it and by its cause. The second (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning that they recognized part of the Truth, which is the Qur'an, and so Allah made them weep; how much more so if they recognized all of it.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿they say: Our Lord, we have believed﴾, that is, in what we heard and testified, that it is true, ﴿so write us down among the witnesses﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

The first: he means the community of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, who bear witness to the Truth. This is derived from His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾.

The second: that is, with every one of Your prophets and the believers among Your servants who testified that You have no god but You.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿And what is [the reason] for us not to believe in Allah and what has come to us of the Truth, while we aspire that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people﴾

Here there are two issues:

The first: the author of al-Kashshaf said: the position (mahall) of "la nu'minu" (we do not believe) is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), in the sense of "not believing," like your saying "standing." The waw in His saying "wa natma'u" (and we aspire) is the waw of circumstance.

If it is asked: what is the governing element (al-'amil) of the first and second circumstantial clauses?

We say: the governing element of the first is the meaning of the verb contained in the lam, as if it were said: "What has happened to us while we are not believing?" In the second, the meaning of this verb is present, but restricted by the first circumstance; for if you removed the first and said "And what is [the reason] for us and we aspire," it would not be a complete statement. It is also permissible that "wa natma'u" be a circumstantial clause of "la nu'minu," on the basis that they rebuked themselves for not monotheizing Allah while nevertheless aspiring to accompany the righteous. And it is permissible that it be conjoined to His saying "la nu'minu," in the sense: "What is [the reason] for us that we combine trinitarianism with aspiring to the company of the righteous?"

The second issue: the estimated sense of the verse is: "and our Lord admit us along with the righteous people into His Paradise and the abode of His good pleasure." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance that they will be pleased with﴾ [al-Hajj: 59]. Except that the omission is good because it is known.

* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally; and that is the reward of the doers of good﴾. ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of Hellfire﴾.

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that they deserved that reward merely by the saying, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾, and that is not possible, since mere saying does not bring reward.

The second issue: the verse indicates that the believing sinner does not remain eternally in the Fire, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that is the reward of the doers of good﴾, and this good-doing must be the one previously mentioned of knowledge, which is His saying ﴿from what they have recognized of the Truth﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83], and of affirming it, which is His saying ﴿so Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾. If this is so, then this verse indicates that this knowledge and this affirmation necessitate that he receive this reward. The person who commits a grave sin also possesses this knowledge and this affirmation, so it is necessary that he receive this reward. As for his being moved from Paradise to the Fire, that is invalid by consensus; or it is said: he is punished for his sin and then moved to Paradise, and that is what was to be proven.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of Hellfire﴾. His saying ﴿those are the companions of Hellfire﴾ implies restriction, meaning: those are the companions of Hellfire and no others; and "the companion of a thing" is the one who is constantly attached to it and never separates from it. This requires restricting this perpetuity to the disbelievers. Thus this verse, from these two aspects, is among the strongest proofs that eternal abiding in the Fire does not apply to the believing sinner.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 87:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾

Know that when Allah, may He be exalted, had thoroughly argued with the Jews and the Christians, He returned after that to the explanation of the rulings and mentioned a portion of them.

The first category: what relates to the lawfulness of foods, drinks and pleasures. He said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾. And in this there are several issues.

The first issue: al-tayyibat (the good things) are the delightful things that souls desire and hearts incline toward. Regarding the verse there are two views. The first: it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) described the Day of Resurrection to his companions in the house of Uthman ibn Maz'un (رضي الله عنه), and he exaggerated and extended his speech in warning and admonition. So they resolved to renounce the world, to forbid themselves the good foods and delicious drinks, to fast by day and stand in prayer by night, not to sleep on beds, to castrate themselves, to wear coarse woolen garments, and to wander in the land. The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of this, so he said to them: "Indeed I was not commanded with that. Your selves have a right over you. So fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep. For I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, I eat meat and fat, and I approach women. Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me."

With this statement the connection (nazm) between this verse and what precedes it becomes clear. Allah praised the Christians, saying that among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban), and their practice is to abstain from the good things of this world and its pleasures. When He praised them, that praise could give the impression of encouraging the Muslims to follow the same path. So He mentioned, after this verse, that (meaning) to remove that misconception, so that it would be clear to the Muslims that they are not commanded to do that.

If it is said: what is the wisdom in this prohibition? It is known that love of this world dominates natures and hearts. When a person expands in pleasures and good things, his inclination toward them grows strong and his desire for them becomes great. The more those blessings are abundant and lasting, the stronger and greater that inclination becomes. And the more the inclination grows in strength and desire, the more his greed in seeking the world increases and his absorption in acquiring it deepens. That prevents him from being absorbed in knowing Allah and obeying Him, and prevents him from seeking the happiness of the Hereafter. As for when he turns away from the pleasures of this world and its good things, then the more complete and lasting that turning away is, the weaker that inclination becomes and the less the desire. At that point the soul is free to seek knowledge of Allah, may He be exalted, and to be absorbed in serving Him. If the matter is so, what is the wisdom in Allah, may He be exalted, forbidding monasticism (al-rahbaniyyah)?

The answer to this comes from several aspects:

The first: excessive monasticism and complete abstention from good things and pleasures cause weakness in the principal organs, which are the heart and the brain. When weakness falls upon them, thought becomes disordered and the intellect becomes confused. There is no doubt that the most perfect of happinesses and the greatest of closenesses to Allah is knowledge of Allah, may He be exalted. So when extreme monasticism causes disruption in that through the way we have explained, there is no doubt that its prohibition took place.

The second: the sum of what you have mentioned is that the soul's preoccupation with seeking sensory pleasures prevents it from perfecting itself with intellectual happinesses. This is accepted, but only regarding weak souls. As for lofty and perfect souls, their use in sensory activities does not prevent them from perfecting themselves with intellectual happinesses. For we observe that souls may be so weak that when they occupy themselves with one important matter, it becomes impossible for them to occupy themselves with another important matter. And the stronger the soul is, the more perfect this state becomes. If it is so, then pure monasticism is an indication of a kind of weakness and deficiency, while perfection lies in fulfilling both aspects and perfecting oneself among people.

The third: whoever enjoys sensory pleasures has as his purpose to be helped by them in attaining intellectual pleasures. His discipline and striving are more complete than the discipline of one who turns away from sensory pleasures, because directing a portion of the soul toward obedience is more difficult and harder than turning away from the soul's portion entirely. So perfection in this is more complete.

The fourth: complete monasticism necessitates the ruin of the world and the cessation of tillage and procreation. As for abandoning monasticism while persisting in knowledge, love and acts of obedience, this brings about the flourishing of both this world and the Hereafter. So this state is more perfect. This is the sum of the discussion on this aspect.

The second view on the interpretation of this verse: what al-Qaffal mentioned, which is that Allah, may He be exalted, said at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. He thus made clear that just as it is not permissible to make lawful what is forbidden, likewise it is not permissible to forbid what is lawful. The Arabs used to forbid some good things that Allah, may He be exalted, had not forbidden, namely the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. Allah, may He be exalted, has related this in this surah and in surah al-An'am. They used to make lawful carrion, blood and other things. So Allah, may He be exalted, commanded that they should not forbid what Allah has made lawful, nor make lawful what Allah has forbidden, so that they would fall under His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts﴾.

The second issue: His saying ﴿do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ may bear several meanings:

The first: do not believe in the forbidding of what Allah, may He be exalted, has made lawful for you.

The second: do not declare with the tongue the forbidding of what Allah has made lawful for you.

The third: do not avoid them with an avoidance resembling the avoidance of forbidden things. These three aspects pertain to belief, speech and action.

The fourth: do not forbid them to others through a fatwa.

The fifth: do not bind yourselves to forbidding them through a vow or an oath. A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1].

The sixth: that one mixes what is usurped with what is owned in a mixture such that distinction is not possible for him. At that point the whole becomes forbidden. That mixing is a cause for forbidding what was previously lawful for him. Likewise the ruling applies when what is impure is mixed with what is pure. The verse is capable of all these aspects, and it is not far-fetched to apply it to all of them. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying ﴿and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ has several aspects:

The first: Allah, may He be exalted, made the forbidding of good things a transgression and injustice, so He forbade transgression in order that the prohibition of forbidding them would fall within it.

The second: since He made the good things lawful, He forbade excess in them by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not transgress﴾. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾ [al-A'raf: 31].

The third: meaning, since Allah has made the good things lawful for you, be content with these lawful things and do not go beyond them to what He has forbidden to you.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good. And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾

Page 61

Concerning this there are several issues:

First issue: His saying, "And eat" (wakulu), is in the form of a command, and its apparent meaning is obligation, but what is intended here is permissibility and allowance. The companions of al-Shafi'i (Shafi'i scholars) used it as evidence that voluntary acts do not become obligatory by commencing them. They said: the apparent meaning of this verse requires the permissibility of eating absolutely, so it includes what comes after one has begun fasting. Its ultimate point is that it was specified in some cases, but a general (ʿāmm) text is valid as evidence outside the place of specification.

Second issue: His saying, ﴿lawful and good﴾ (ḥalālan ṭayyiban), may be connected to the eating, or it may be connected to the thing eaten. On the first reading the sense is: "Eat, lawful and good, of what Allah has provided for you." On the second reading the sense is: "Eat of the provision which is lawful and good." As for the first reading, it is a proof for the Mu'tazilah that provision is only ever lawful, because the verse on this reading indicates permission to eat everything Allah has provided, and Allah only permits the eating of what is lawful, so it follows that whatever is provision is lawful. As for the second reading, it is a proof for our companions (the Ash'arites) that provision may be unlawful, because He specified the permission to eat as applying to provision which is lawful and good; were it not that provision may not be lawful, this specification and restriction would serve no purpose.

Third issue: He did not say, "Eat whatever He has provided you," but said, ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided you﴾, and the word "min" (of) indicates partiality. It is as if He said: "Limit your eating to a part, and devote the remainder to charities and good works," because this is guidance to abandoning extravagance, as He said: ﴿And do not be wasteful﴾ [al-A'raf: 31].

Fourth issue: ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided﴾ indicates that He has undertaken the provision of every person, for if He had not undertaken to provide for him, He would not have said, ﴿eat of what Allah has provided you﴾. And when Allah has undertaken to provide for him, it is necessary that he not exaggerate in seeking, and that he rely upon the promise of Allah the Exalted and His benevolence, for He is too generous to break His promise. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware, fear Allah and seek with moderation." As for His saying, ﴿And fear Allah﴾, it is an emphasis on the enjoining of what He commanded; He reinforced it with His saying, ﴿in whom you are believers﴾, because belief in Him necessitates piety in adhering to what He commanded and in refraining from what He forbade.

[Page 62]

The second type of rulings mentioned in this passage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the slips in your oaths﴾.

We have mentioned that He, exalted is He, has clarified in this passage several kinds of laws and rulings. It remains to ask: what is the connection between this ruling and what precedes it, such that it is fitting to mention it after it? We say: We have mentioned that the cause of the revelation of the first verse was that some of the Companions made the foods and clothing unlawful for themselves, chose monasticism, and swore to that. When Allah, exalted is He, forbade them from it, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, then how should we act regarding our oaths?" So Allah revealed this verse.

[Page 62, continued]

Know that the discussion of what the oath of *laghw* (idle oath) is has already been covered thoroughly in Surat al-Baqarah, in the explanation of His saying: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the slips in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾. So there is no point in repeating it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But He will hold you accountable for the oaths you have bound﴾, and in this there are several issues.

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read (عَقَّدْتُمُ) with a doubled *qaf* and without an *alif*. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read (عَقَدْتُمْ) with a single *qaf* and without an *alif*. Ibn 'Amir read (عاقَدْتُمْ) with an *alif* and a single *qaf*. Al-Wahidi said: It is said: "'Aqada fulan al-yamin, al-'ahd, and al-habl 'aqdan" (meaning he bound/knotted the oath, the covenant, and the rope) when he confirmed and firmly established it. Similarly, *'aqqada*, with the doubling, means to confirm, and likewise *'aqada*, with the *alif*.

Having understood this, we say: As for the one who reads with the single *qaf*, it applies to both the few and the many. One says: "Zayd bound his oath," and "They bound their oaths." As for the one who reads with the doubling, know that Abu 'Ubaydah rejected this reading and said: The doubling indicates repetition, one time after another, so the reading with doubling would entail that the expiation is dropped for a single oath, because it was not repeated.

Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, answered him in two ways:

The first: Some have said that (*'aqada*) with the single and the doubled *qaf* has the same meaning.

The second: Grant that it indicates repetition, as in His saying: ﴿and she locked the doors﴾ [Yusuf: 23]. Yet this repetition is achieved by binding it with the heart and the tongue together. Whenever one combines the heart and the tongue, repetition has occurred. But if one binds the oath with only one of them without the other, he has not truly bound it. As for the one who reads with the *alif*, it is of the form of *mufa'alah* that is specific to one party, like *'afahu Allah* (Allah pardoned him), *tara'qtu al-na'l* (I repaired the sandal), and *'aqabtu al-lissa* (I punished the thief). So this reading is like the reading of the one who reads with the single *qaf*.

The second issue: The (*ma*) with the verb functions as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the meaning is: "But He will hold you accountable for your binding, or for your binding of oaths, or for your mutual binding of oaths."

The third issue: There is an ellipsis in the verse. The meaning is: "But He will hold you accountable for what you have bound, when you break them," so the time of the accountability is omitted because it was known to them; or "for the breaking of what you have bound," so the thing modified is omitted. As for how al-Shafi'i used this verse to argue that the *ghamus* oath (the false oath sworn to deceive) requires expiation, we have already mentioned it in Surat al-Baqarah.

* *
* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Its expiation is feeding ten needy people, from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave﴾.

[Page 63]

Know that the verse indicates that the obligation in the expiation of an oath is one of three matters, by way of choice. If one is unable to do all of them, then the obligation is something else, which is fasting.

In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The meaning of an optional obligation (*wajib mukhayyar*) is that he is not required to perform each of these three, nor is it permissible for him to leave them all. Whenever he performs whichever one of these three he wishes, he is free of the obligation. When these three conditions are combined, that is the optional obligation. Some jurists said: It is one, not specified. This statement may have two meanings:

The first: It is said that the obligation upon him is to bring into existence one of these three, without specifying which. This is impossible by reason, because a thing that is not specified in itself is impossible to exist in itself, and whatever is like that is not something for which obligation can be meaningfully imposed.

The second: It is said that the obligation upon him is one specified in itself and in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, but its specific identity is unknown to the one who performs it. This too is impossible, because for that thing to be obligatory in particular in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, means that it is not permissible to abandon it under any circumstances, while the community (*ummah*) has agreed that it is permissible for him to abandon it on the condition that he performs another. Combining these two statements is combining affirmation and negation, which is impossible. The full discussion of this is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*).

The second issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The share of each needy person is one *mudd*, which is two-thirds of a *mann*. This is also the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan and al-Qasim. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The obligation is half a *sa'* of wheat, or a *sa'* of other than wheat.

The argument of al-Shafi'i is that He, exalted is He, mentioned in the feeding only His saying: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾. This "average" either means what is average by custom, or what is average by the Law (*shar'*). If what is meant is what is average by custom, then two-thirds of a *mann* of wheat, when ground into flour or made into bread, becomes close to a *mann*, and that is sufficient for one day's food, apparently. If what is meant is what is average in the Law, then no quantity is mentioned for it in the Law except in one place, which is what has been related in the report about the one who broke his fast in the daytime during Ramadan, that the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to feed sixty needy people without mention of a quantity. The man said: "I cannot find [it]." Then a basket (*'araq*) containing fifteen *sa'* was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Feed this." That indicates that the amount of food for a needy person is a quarter of a *sa'*, which is a *mudd*. This is not binding for the expiation of an oath, because that was legislated with the word "charity" in an unrestricted sense, without a quantity being specified for feeding the family. So its amount is determined by reference to the charity of fitr (*sadaqat al-fitr*), and it has been established by the text that its amount is a *sa'*, not a *mudd*.

The argument of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾, and the "average" (*awsat*) is the most just (*a'dal*). What al-Shafi'i mentioned is the least that suffices, whereas the most just is with condiment (*idam*). Likewise it was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah have mercy on them both: a *mudd* with its condiment, and the condiment usually costs as much as another *mudd* or more.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, answered that His saying: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾ may mean the average in quantity, for a person may be very light in eating, so one loaf suffices him, and he may be a heavy eater, so two *mann* do not suffice him; but the average, typical person needs of bread about what approaches a *mann*. It may also mean the average in value, neither expensive like sugar, nor cheap of low price like bran and maize; the average is wheat, dates, raisins and bread. It may also mean the average in goodness and pleasure. Since the wording allows each of these two meanings, we say: the wording must be taken to mean what we have mentioned, for two reasons.

The first: The condiment is not obligatory by consensus, so there remains only the interpretation of the wording as the average in the quantity of food.

The second: This quantity is obligatory with certainty, and the remainder is doubtful, because the wording has no indication of it. So we make the certain obligatory and set aside the doubtful. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The obligation is the transfer of ownership (*tamlik*) of the food. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If one provides lunch or dinner to ten needy people, it is valid.

The argument of al-Shafi'i: The obligation in this expiation is one of three matters: either feeding, or clothing, or manumission. Then we agree that the obligation in clothing is transfer of ownership, so it must be that the obligation in feeding is also transfer of ownership.

The argument of Abu Hanifah: The verse indicates that the obligation is feeding, and providing lunch or dinner is feeding, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿and they give food, despite their love for it﴾ [al-Insan: 8], and His saying: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾, and feeding one's family is by enabling them, not by transfer of ownership. It is said in custom: "So-and-so feeds the poor," when he sets food before them and enables them to eat it. And when it is established that He commanded feeding, it must be sufficient.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, answered: The obligation is either a *mudd* or more, and lunch and dinner may be less than that, so one is not free of the obligation except by certainty. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Only the food of ten people suffices him. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If he feeds one needy person for ten days, it is valid.

The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him: The foundation of this matter is devotional worship (*ta'abbud*) whose meaning is not rationally understood, and whatever is like that requires reliance upon the source of the text.

The fifth issue: Clothing (*kiswah*) in language means garment, which is anything one is clothed with. As for what suffices in expiation, it is the least that falls under the name of clothing: a wrapper, a cloak, a shirt, trousers, a turban, or a veil, one garment for each needy person. This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid, and it is the school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

The sixth issue: The meaning of "neck" (*raqabah*) is the whole person (a slave). It was said that the origin of this figurative usage is that among the Arabs a captive would have his hands tied to his neck with a rope, so when he was released, that rope was untied, and the release from the neck was called "unbinding the neck," and then this was applied to manumission. The position of the Zahiri scholars is that any slave at all suffices. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The slave that suffices in expiation is any slave free of a defect that prevents work, whether young or old, male or female, provided that she or he is a believer. It is not permissible to free a disbeliever in any of the expiations, nor a *mukatab* (a slave under a contract of self-purchase), nor to buy a close relative in order to free him. These matters we have already mentioned in the verse on *zihar*.

The seventh issue: One might ask: What is the benefit of putting feeding before manumission, when manumission is undoubtedly better?

We say: There are several answers:

The first: The purpose is to alert that this expiation is obligatory by choice, not in sequence. For if it were obligatory in sequence, it would be required to begin with the most severe.

The second: Feeding is mentioned first because it is easier, since food is more widely available, and the purpose is to alert that He, exalted is He, takes into account lightness and ease in the obligations.

The third: Feeding is better, because a free poor person may not find food, and there may be no one to give him food, so he falls into hardship. As for the slave, it is obligatory upon his master to feed him and clothe him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So whoever does not find [the means], then fasting three days﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If he has his sustenance and that of his dependants for a day and a night, and some surplus that would feed ten needy people, the expiation by feeding is obligatory for him. If he does not have this much, it is permissible for him to fast. According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, it is permissible for him to fast if he has wealth that does not require zakat, so that one who owes no zakat is considered to be without means.

[Page 66]

The argument of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that He, exalted is He, made the permissibility of fasting conditional upon not finding these three things. Something conditional on a condition is absent when the condition is absent. So when these three things are found, it must not be permissible to fast. We have set aside this ruling when one finds the sustenance of oneself and one's dependants for a day and a night, because that is like a matter of necessity. We have also seen in the Shari'ah that whenever there is a conflict between the right of the self and the right of another, giving priority to the right of the self is obligatory. Therefore the verse must remain in force in cases other than this one.

The second issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the more correct of his two opinions that one may fast three days, either consecutively or separately, as one wishes.

Abu Hanifa said: consecutiveness is obligatory.

The argument of al-Shafi'i is that He, exalted is He, required the fasting of three days. Whoever fasts three days separately has fasted three days, so he is released from the obligation.

The argument of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is what is reported in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud: "So a fast of three consecutive days." Their reading does not differ from their narration.

The answer is that an irregular reading (qira'ah shadhdhah, a reading not transmitted with the full chain of mass transmission) is rejected. For if it were Qur'an, it would have been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur, reports so numerous that their agreement on falsehood is impossible). For if we allowed that something of the Qur'an need not be transmitted by tawatur, it would open the way for the attacks of the Rafidah and the atheists (malahidah) on the Qur'an, and that is false. So we know that an irregular reading is rejected and cannot serve as evidence.

Also, it is reported in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he read: "Then a number of other days, consecutive." Yet consecutiveness was not a condition there. They answered this by saying that it has been reported from the Prophet ﷺ that a man said to him: "I owe days of Ramadan; should I make them up separately?" He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Tell me, if you had a debt and you paid the dirham, then the dirham, would it not suffice you?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then Allah is more worthy to pardon and to overlook."

We say: although this hadith was an answer to this question about fasting in Ramadan, its wording is general and its reasoning is general across all fasts. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the consideration is for the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause (sabab). Therefore this is among the strongest proofs for the permissibility of separating the days here too.

The third issue: whoever fasts six days for two oaths is released, whether or not he specifies one of the three days for one of the two oaths. The evidence is that He, exalted is He, required the fasting of three days upon him, and he has performed them, so he is released from the obligation.

[Page 66 marker as above]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the expiation of your oaths when you swear﴾. His saying "that" refers to what was mentioned before: the food, the clothing, and the freeing of a slave. That is, that which was mentioned is the expiation of your oaths when you swear and break them, because expiation is not obligatory merely by swearing. However, He omitted mention of the breaking because it is understood, as He said: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:184], meaning: then he breaks the fast.

Al-Shafi'i used this verse to show that expiation before breaking the oath is permissible. He said: The verse indicates that each of the three things is an expiation for the oath when the swearing occurs. So if he performs it after swearing and before breaking, he has performed the expiation for that oath, and if that is so, he is released from the obligation. He said: His saying ﴿when you swear﴾ contains a subtle point, which is an indication that expiation before the oath is not permissible. As for after the oath and before breaking it, that is permissible.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And guard your oaths﴾. In this there are two views.

The first: what is meant is "Reduce your oaths and do not multiply them." Kuthayyir said:

Few are his oaths; he guards his oath,
and if an oath slips from him, he is still righteous.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 5, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous sacrifices, and divining arrows are but defilement [rijs] from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾

Know that this is the third category of the rulings mentioned in this context. Its connection with what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, said earlier: ﴿Do not prohibit the good things which Allah has made lawful for you﴾, up to His saying: ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾. Then, since intoxicants and gambling are among the matters that are considered good, He, exalted is He, clarified that they are not included among the lawful things, but among the prohibited ones.

Know that we have discussed the meaning of intoxicants (khamr) and gambling (maysir) in Surat al-Baqarah, and we discussed the meaning of idolatrous sacrifices (anṣab) and divining arrows (azlam) at the beginning of this surah, at His saying: ﴿and what is sacrificed on the stone altars, and [that you seek decision] by divining arrows﴾. Whoever wants a thorough treatment should refer to these passages.

Regarding the derivation (ishtiqaq) of the word khamr there are two views:

The first: intoxicant was called khamr because it "covers" (khamarat) the intellect, meaning it mixes with it and conceals it.

The second: Ibn al-A'rabi said: it was left to stand and then fermented (ikhtamarat), meaning its smell changed.

Maysir is their gambling over the slaughtered camel. Anṣab are the idols they set up and worshipped. Azlam are arrows on which was written "good" and "bad."

Know that He, exalted is He, described these four categories with two attributes. The first is His saying: "rijs." In the language, rijs is anything regarded as detestable from an action. It is said: "the man committed rijs" (rajusa al-rajulu rijsan) and (rajisa yarjasu), when he performs an ugly action. Its root is from ar-rajs with a fatha on the ra', which is the intensity of a sound. It is said: "a rajjas cloud," when it has an intense sound of thunder. So rijs is an action that is strong in degree and complete in rank in ugliness.

The second attribute is His saying: ﴿from the work of Satan﴾. This also completes its being rijs, because Satan is impure and wicked, since he is a disbeliever, and a disbeliever is impure, according to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ [At-Tawbah: 28]. And the wicked calls only to the wicked, according to His saying: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men﴾ [An-Nur: 26]. Also, whatever is attributed to Satan, the purpose of that attribution is to emphasize the completeness of its ugliness. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Moses struck him and killed him. He said, "This is from the work of Satan"﴾ [Al-Qasas: 15].

Then, when He, exalted is He, had described these four with these two attributes, He said: ﴿so avoid it﴾, meaning, keep away from it. To what does the pronoun "it" (hu) refer? There are two views:

The first: it refers to rijs, and rijs applies to the four mentioned, so the command to avoid it encompasses all of them.

The second: it refers to the omitted noun that was annexed, as if it were said: "indeed, the matter of intoxicants and gambling, or engaging in them, or what is similar to that," and for this reason He said: ﴿is defilement from the work of Satan﴾.

And know that when He, exalted is He, commanded that these things be avoided, He mentioned in them two kinds of harm. The first is what relates to this world, and it is His saying:

﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾

﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling﴾.

And know that we will explain the aspect of enmity and hatred first in wine and then in gambling.

As for wine, know that the apparent situation of one who drinks wine is that he drinks it with a group, and his purpose in that drinking is to feel at ease with his companions and to rejoice in conversing and speaking with them. So his purpose in that gathering was to strengthen friendship and love. However, in most cases that turns into its opposite, because wine removes the intellect. When the intellect is removed, desire and anger take control without the intellect resisting them. When they take control, a dispute arises among those companions. That dispute may lead to beating, killing, and abusive speech, and that produces the most severe enmity and hatred. Satan thus makes it appear that gathering for drinking necessitates strengthening friendship and love, but in the end the matter reverses and the utmost enmity and hatred results.

As for gambling, in it, in exchange for the benefit of helping the needy, there is the ruin of the owners of wealth. For whoever is defeated in gambling once is driven by that to persist in it, hoping that he may perhaps become the winner. It may happen that he never attains that, until no wealth remains for him, and until he gambles away his beard, his family, and his children. Without doubt, after that he remains poor and destitute, and becomes the greatest of enemies to those who had defeated him. Thus it becomes clear from this aspect that wine and gambling are two great causes of stirring up enmity and hatred among people. And without doubt, the intensity of enmity and hatred leads to blameworthy conditions of chaos, confusion, and strife, and all of that is contrary to the interests of the world.

[Page 68]

If it is asked: why did He combine wine and gambling with idols and divining arrows, and then single out those two at the end of the verse?

We say: because this verse is an address to the believers, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine and gambling﴾. The intent is to forbid them from wine and gambling, and to show that these four are close in ugliness and harm. Since the intent of this verse is the prohibition of wine and gambling, and He joined idols and divining arrows to wine and gambling only to emphasize the ugliness of wine and gambling, therefore He singled those two out with mention at the end of the verse.

As for the second kind of harms found in wine and gambling: the harms related to religion. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer﴾. We say: as for wine preventing the remembrance of Allah, it is clear, because drinking wine produces pleasure and bodily delight, and when the soul is absorbed in bodily pleasures, it becomes heedless of the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. As for gambling preventing the remembrance of Allah and prayer, it is similar, because if one is winning, his absorption in the pleasure of victory prevents anything else from occurring to his mind. Without doubt, this state is among the things that turn one away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer.

If it is said: the verse is explicit that the ʿillah (effective cause) for the prohibition of wine is these meanings. Yet these meanings were already present before wine was prohibited, while the prohibition had not yet been established. This casts doubt on the soundness of this reasoning.

We say: this is one of the proofs that the non-existence of a ruling in the presence of an explicitly stated ʿillah does not invalidate its being an ʿillah.

And when He, exalted is He, made clear that drinking wine and playing with gambling involve these great harms in religion, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ It is narrated that when His saying, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [Surah an-Nisa', 4:43], ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient explanation regarding wine." Then when this verse was revealed, ʿUmar said: "We have desisted, O Lord."

And know that although this is apparently an interrogative, its real meaning is a prohibition. This figurative usage is appropriate because He, exalted is He, condemned these actions and made their ugliness evident to the addressee. Then, when He asked him about abandoning them, the addressee could only acknowledge abandoning them. It is as if it were said to him: "Will you do it after its ugliness has become as clear as it has?" Thus His saying ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ functions as the explicit statement by Allah, exalted is He, of the obligation to desist, coupled with the accountable person's acknowledgment of that obligation.

And know that this verse indicates the prohibition of drinking wine in several respects:

First: the opening of the sentence with innama (only), because this word is for restriction. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: there is no abomination and no part of Satan's work except these four.

Second: He, exalted is He, linked wine and gambling with the worship of idols. From this is His saying, ﷺ: "The drinker of wine is like the worshipper of an idol."

Third: He, exalted is He, commanded avoidance, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation.

Fourth: He said: ﴿so that you may prosper﴾. He made avoidance a part of success, and if avoidance is success, then committing it is failure.

Fifth: He explained the types of harm that arise from them in this world and in religion, namely the occurrence of hostility and hatred among creatures, and the occurrence of turning away from the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and from prayer.

Sixth: His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ This is among the most effective means of being restrained. It is as if it were said: the harms and ugly qualities contained in these have been recited to you; so will you desist despite these deterrents? Or will you remain in the state you were in when you had not been admonished with these admonitions?

[Page 69]

Seventh: after that, He, may He be exalted, said:

﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance.﴾

Its apparent meaning is that what is intended by "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger" is obedience to them concerning what was mentioned before, namely their command to avoid wine (khamr) and gambling (maysir). His words "and beware" mean: beware of opposing them in these obligations.

Eighth: His words, ﴿But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance.﴾ This is a great threat and a severe warning against whoever opposes this obligation and turns away from it, rejecting Allah's ruling and His clarification. The meaning is: if you turn away, the proof has already been established against you, and the Messenger has fulfilled his duty of conveying, giving notice, and warning. As for the punishment of whoever opposes this obligation and turns away from it beyond that, it is up to Allah, exalted is He. There is no doubt that this is a severe threat. Thus each of these eight aspects is an overwhelming proof and a manifest argument for the prohibition of wine.

Know that whoever is fair and abandons arbitrariness will recognize that this verse is an explicit text that every intoxicant is forbidden. This is because, when He, may He be exalted, mentioned His words, ﴿Satan only desires to cause enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer.﴾ He followed it with, ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ Thus He made the prohibition of drinking wine dependent on wine containing those corruptions. It is known by self-evident reason that those corruptions arise only from wine's effect in causing intoxication. This establishes with certainty that the reason for His words, ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ is that wine has the effect of intoxicating. When this is established, it becomes certain that every intoxicant is forbidden. Whoever understands this reasoning and yet remains insistent on his position has no cure for his obstinacy. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 93:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good. And Allah loves the good-doers.﴾

Concerning the verse, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** It is narrated that when the verse prohibiting wine was revealed, the Companions said: "Our brothers drank wine on the day of Uhud and then were killed; so what is their condition?" Then this verse was revealed. The meaning is: there is no sin upon them for that, because they drank it at a time when it was permitted. This verse is similar to His saying, the Exalted, concerning the abrogation (naskh) of the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning: when you faced Bayt al-Maqdis, you faced it by My command, so I will not waste that. As He said: ﴿So their Lord answered them: Indeed I will not waste the work of any worker among you, male or female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195].

[p. 70]

**The second issue:** In common usage in the language, *ta'am* (food) is generally the opposite of *sharab* (drink). Therefore *ta'm* (eating/tasting) should also be the opposite of *shurb* (drinking). However, the word *ta'am* may also be applied to drinks, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever does not taste it, then he is of me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249]. Accordingly, His saying ﴿for what they have eaten﴾ may mean "for what they have drunk of wine." It is also possible that the meaning of *ta'm* refers to enjoyment of what is eaten and drunk. The Arabs say: *tata'amma tat'am*, meaning "taste, so that you desire." When the meaning of the word refers to tasting, it suits both what is eaten and what is drunk.

**The third issue:** Some ignorant people claimed that when Allah, the Exalted, explained concerning wine that it is forbidden when it causes enmity and hatred and prevents one from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, He explained in this verse that there is no blame upon one who has consumed it if none of those corruptions result from it, but rather various benefits result from it, such as obedience, piety and goodness to creation. They said: It is not possible to interpret it as referring to the condition of one who drank wine before the verse of prohibition was revealed, because if that were the intention, He would have said: "There was no blame upon those who ate," as He mentioned something similar in the verse on the change of the qiblah, when He said: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. But He did not say that; rather He said: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ up to His saying: ﴿if they fear Allah and believe﴾. And there is no doubt that *idha* (when/if) refers to the future, not the past.

Know that this view is rejected by the consensus of the entire Ummah. As for their claim that *idha* refers to the future and not the past, its answer is what Abu Bakr al-Asamm narrated: when the prohibition of wine was revealed, Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, what about our brothers who died after drinking wine and gambling? And what about those absent from us in the lands who do not know that Allah has forbidden wine, and who are consuming it?" So Allah revealed these verses. According to this interpretation, the permissibility was established for the future from the time this verse was revealed, but with respect to the absent ones to whom this text had not reached.

**The fourth issue:** Allah, the Exalted, made the condition for the removal of blame the attainment of piety and faith twice, and in the third instance the attainment of piety and goodness. The scholars differed in interpreting these three levels in several ways:

The first: Most of them said: it is the practice of *ittiqa'* (being mindful and guarding oneself).

The second: its continuation and steadfastness in it. The third: guarding oneself against wronging people, together with adding goodness toward them.

The second view: the first is guarding oneself against all sins before the revelation of this verse. The second is guarding oneself against wine and gambling and what is in this verse. The third is guarding oneself against what will be prohibited after this verse; this is the view of al-Asamm. The third view: guarding oneself against disbelief, then against major sins, then against minor sins. The fourth view: what al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned. He said: The first piety is an expression of guarding oneself against undermining the validity of abrogation (naskh), because the Jews would say: abrogation indicates *bada'* (a change of mind in God, which is impossible). So when the believers heard the prohibition of wine after it had been permitted, He obligated them to guard themselves against this corrupt doubt. The second piety is acting in accordance with this verse, which is abstaining from drinking wine. The third piety is an expression of persistence in the piety mentioned in the first and second, and then goodness to creation is added to this piety.

The fifth view: the purpose of this repetition is emphasis and intensification in urging faith and piety. If it is said: Why did He make the lifting of blame concerning the consumption of food conditional upon faith and piety, when it is known that whoever does not believe and does not fear Allah, and then consumes some of the permissible things, there is no blame upon him for that consumption; rather, he is blameworthy for abandoning faith and abandoning piety; but that has no connection to the consumption of that permissible thing, so mentioning this condition in this context is not permissible?

We say: this is not for making it a condition, but rather to explain that those people concerning whom this verse was revealed were characterized by these qualities, as a praise of them and a commendation of their states in faith, piety and goodness. An example of this is that someone says to you: "Is there any blame upon Zayd for what he did, when you know that the matter is permissible?" So you say: "There is no blame upon anyone for what is permissible if he guards himself against the forbidden things and is a believer and a good-doer," meaning that if Zayd remains a believer and a good-doer, then he is not held accountable for what he did.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ The meaning is that when He, the Exalted, made goodness a condition for the removal of blame, He explained that the effect of goodness is not only in removing blame, but also in being loved by Allah. There is no doubt that this rank is the most noble of ranks and the highest of stations, and the explanation of Allah's love for His servants has already been presented.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 94:**

[Allah said:] ﴿O you who believe! Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach.﴾

Know that this is another type of ruling. The connection (wajh al-nazm) is that, just as He said, ﴿Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87], and then excepted from that the wine and gambling, so too He excepted this kind of game from the lawful things and showed that it is included among the forbidden things.

Here there are several issues:

The first issue: The lam in His saying ﴿Allah will surely test you﴾ is the lam of the oath (lam al-qasam, the lam used to introduce an oath), because the lam and the nun may serve as the answer to an oath. When the oath itself is omitted, they are used as an indication of the oath.

The second issue: The waw in His saying "la-yabluwannakum" is fathah (vowelled with a fatha) because two unvowelled letters came together (iltiqa' al-sakinayn).

The third issue: "la-yabluwannakum" means: He will surely test your obedience from your disobedience; that is, He will deal with you as one who tests.

The fourth issue: Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: Allah tested them with game while they were in the state of ihram in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, to the extent that the wild animals and birds would come upon them in their camps, so that they could take them with their hands and hunt them with their spears. They had never seen the like of that, so Allah forbade them from it as a test. Al-Wahidi said: What the hands can reach of the game are the chicks, the eggs and the young of the wild animals, and what the spears reach are the large ones. Some said: This is not permissible, because "sayd" (game) is the name for a wild animal that flees, not for what does not flee.

The fifth issue: The meaning of minimisation and belittling in His saying ﴿with something of the game﴾ is that it is known that this is not one of the great trials in which the obligation is difficult and burdensome, like being tested by giving up lives and wealth. Rather, it is an easy test. Allah tested the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) with the game of the land, just as He tested the Children of Israel with the game of the sea, which is fish.

[Page 72]

The sixth issue: The "min" (from/of) in His saying ﴿of the game﴾ is partitive (li-l-tab'id) in two respects:
One: the intended game is that of the land, not of the sea.
Two: the game of the state of ihram, not the game of the state of non-ihram (ihlal).
Al-Zajjaj said: It may be explanatory (li-l-tabyin), as in His saying ﴿so shun the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30].

The seventh issue: By "sayd" (game) is meant the object hunted (al-maf'ul), as evidenced by His saying ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾. When "sayd" is in the sense of the verbal noun, it is an action (hadath), and what is described as being reached by the hand and the spears is only a concrete thing (ayn).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿That Allah may know who fears Him unseen﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: This is figurative (majaz), because He is Knowing, has always been and will always be Knowing. They differed about its meaning. It was said: We will deal with you as one who seeks to know. It was said: So that the known thing may become manifest, which is the fear of the one who fears. It was said: This is by omission of the mudaf (an omitted governed noun, i.e., a construction that omits a word), and the estimate is: That the friends of Allah may know who fears Him unseen.

The second issue: His saying "bil-ghayb" (unseen) has two aspects:
The first: who fears Him while in a state of faith in the unseen, as He mentioned at the beginning of His Book: ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾.
The second: who fears in the unseen, that is, fears Him with sincerity and reality, and the situation does not differ due to the presence or absence of anyone, as is the case with the hypocrites, who, when they meet those who believe, say "We believe," and when they are alone with their devils they say "We are with you."

The third issue: The "ba'" (with) in His saying "bil-ghayb" is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (bi-l-hal), and the meaning is: who fears Him while being absent from His sight. Similar to this is His saying ﴿whoever fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾ [Qaf: 33], and ﴿they fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18]. As for the meaning of "al-ghayb" (the unseen), we have mentioned it in His saying ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment﴾. What is meant is the punishment of the Hereafter, and the discipline (ta'zir) in this world. Ibn Abbas said: This punishment is that his belly and back are beaten with a painful beating and his clothes are stripped off. Al-Qaffal said: This is permissible, because the name "punishment" (adhab) may fall upon beating, as He called the flogging of the two fornicators a punishment, saying ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2], and He said ﴿upon them is half of the punishment imposed on the chaste women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and He said, relating from Sulayman about the hoopoe: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 95 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾. And concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: As for the meaning of "game" (al-sayd), there are two opinions. The first is that it is that which is wild, whether or not it is edible. On this view, if the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) kills a predatory beast whose meat is not eaten, he is liable, but the compensation is not to exceed the value of a sheep. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. Zufar said: it is obligatory, whatever amount it reaches.

The second opinion is that game is that whose meat is eaten. On this view, no compensation at all is obligatory for killing a predatory beast. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, conceded that no compensation is obligatory for killing the five vermin (al-fawasiq al-khams) or for killing a wolf.

The evidence of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an: that which is unlawful to eat is not game, so it must not be compensated. We said it is not game because game is that which is lawful to eat, due to His saying, exalted is He, after this verse: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers; but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾. This implies the complete lawfulness of the game of the sea and the lawfulness of the game of the land outside the time of ihram. So it is established that game is that whose flesh is lawful, and the predatory beast is not lawful to eat, so it must not be game. And when it is established that it is not game, it must not be compensated, because the default is no compensation. We abandoned this default regarding compensation for game by the ruling of this verse, so it remains in what is not game in accordance with the default.

As for the report, it is the well-known hadith, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Five vermin: there is no blame upon the muhrim for killing them, whether in the sacred area or outside it: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the rat, and the rabid dog." In another narration: "and the ravaging beast." The argument from it is in several respects:

The first: his saying "and the ravaging beast" is an explicit text on the matter.

The second: he (peace be upon him) described them as "vermin" (fawasiq) and then ruled that killing them is permitted. A ruling mentioned after a suitable description indicates that the ruling is caused by that description. This shows that being vermin is the cause for the permissibility of killing them. There is no meaning to their being vermin except that they are harmful, and the quality of harm is stronger in predatory beasts, so it is necessary that killing them be permitted.

The third: the Lawgiver singled them out for permission to kill, and he singled them out for this ruling because of their particular abundance of harm, and the quality of harm is more complete in predatory beasts. So it is necessary to say that killing them is permitted. And when the permissibility of killing them is established, they must not be subject to compensation, for the reason we explained in the first proof.

The argument of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him: the predatory beast is game, so it falls under His saying: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾. We said it is game because of the verse of the poet:
"A lion that was raised in its den and hunted"
And because of the saying of Ali, peace be upon him:
"The game of kings is hares and foxes, *** and when I ride, my game is the heroes."

The answer: We have already shown by the indication of the verse that what is unlawful to eat is not game, and an anonymous line of poetry does not contradict that. As for the verse of Ali, peace be upon him, it is not relevant, because according to us the fox is lawful.

The second issue: "ihram" (ḥurum) is the plural of ḥarām, and concerning it there are three opinions. The first: it is said that ḥurum means "those who are in the state of ihram for Hajj." It is said: "and you have entered the sacred area (al-Haram)." It is said: both are intended by the verse. And does the one in ihram for 'Umrah enter into it? There is a difference of opinion on this.

The third issue: His saying ﴿do not kill﴾ conveys prohibition of killing directly and prohibition of it indirectly by causing it. So it is not permitted for him to approach game as long as he is in the state of ihram, neither with weapons nor with trained animals such as dogs and birds, whether the game is game of the lawful area or game of the sacred area. As for the one who is not in ihram, he may hunt in the lawful area, but he may not hunt in the sacred area. And when we say ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾, it encompasses both matters, meaning the one who is in ihram and the one who is within the sacred area. The verse thus indicates all these rulings.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever among you kills it intentionally, the compensation is the like of what he killed from the livestock﴾. And concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: ʿĀsim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read (fa-jazāʾun) with tanwīn and (mithlu) in the nominative. The meaning is: then there is upon him a compensation equivalent to the slain game. So "mithlu" is nominative because it is an attribute of the word "jazāʾun." He said: it is not appropriate to make jazāʾ an idafah to mithl. Do you not see that there is not upon him "a compensation like what he killed" in reality? Rather, upon him is the compensation of the slain, not a compensation like the slain which he did not kill. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from the livestock﴾ may be an attribute of the indefinite noun which is "jazāʾun"; the meaning is: a compensation from the livestock equivalent to what he killed. As for the rest of the reciters, they read (fa-jazāʾu mithli) with the idafah of the compensation to the mithl, and they said: although what is obligatory upon him is the compensation of the slain and not a compensation like it, yet they say: "I honor your like," meaning "I honor you." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿There is nothing like His likeness﴾ [al-Shura: 11], the implied meaning being: "There is nothing like Him." And He said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose likeness is in darknesses﴾ [al-An'am: 122], the implied meaning being: "like one who is in darknesses." There is another interpretation: the meaning is "the compensation of the like of what he killed from the livestock," like your saying "a ring of silver," meaning "a ring made of silver."

The second issue: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: if the muhrim kills game by mistake, nothing is obligatory upon him. This is also the view of Dawud. The majority of jurists said: compensation is obligatory upon him whether he killed intentionally or by mistake. The argument of Dawud is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whoever among you kills it intentionally﴾ is mentioned in the context of a condition, and when the condition is absent the conditioned thing is absent, so compensation is not obligatory when intention is absent. He said: What confirms this is that He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾, and retribution occurs only in intentional acts, not in mistakes. And His saying ﴿whoever returns﴾ means: whoever returns to what was previously mentioned. This indicates that what was previously mentioned of killing which requires compensation is intentional killing, not mistaken killing. The argument of the majority is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾. Since that is forbidden by the state of ihram, his act becomes prohibited by ihram, so its ruling is not dropped by error or ignorance, as in shaving the head and as in the liability for the property of a Muslim. For when the prohibition was established for the right of the owner, it was not changed by its being a mistake or intentional, so likewise here. They also argue with His saying, peace be upon him: "For the hyena, a ram is due if the muhrim kills it," and with the saying of the Companions: "For the gazelle, a sheep is due," and there is no mention of intention in it.

Dawud answered that the explicit text of the Qur'an takes precedence over the report of a single narrator, the saying of a Companion, and analogy.

* * *

The third issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the compensation for game must be like the slain. However, they differed regarding "the like." Al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: game is of two kinds: there is that which has a like, and there is that which has no like.
