That which has a like is compensated by its like from the livestock, and that which has no like is compensated by its value. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: the obligatory "like" is the value.

The evidence of al-Shafi'i: the Qur'an, the report, consensus, and analogy. As for the Qur'an, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever among you kills it intentionally, the compensation is the like of what he killed from the livestock﴾. The argument from it is in four respects:

The first: a group of reciters read (fa-jazāʾun) with tanwīn, and its meaning is: then a compensation from the livestock equivalent to what he killed. Whoever says it is "like it in value" has contradicted the explicit text.

The second: another group read (fa-jazāʾu mithli mā qatala) with idafah, and the implied meaning is: "the compensation of what he killed from the livestock," meaning the compensation equal to what he killed must be from the livestock. Whoever does not make it obligatory has contradicted the explicit text.

The third: the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (fa-jazāʾuhu mithlu mā qatala mina al-naʿam), and this is explicit in what we have said.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Two men of justice among you shall judge it, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ is explicit that this compensation which two just men among them judge must be an offering reaching the Ka'bah.

If it is said: he buys an offering with that value.

We say: the text is explicit that the thing which two just men judge must be an offering. You say the obligatory thing is the value, and then he has the choice: if he wishes, he buys with it an offering to be sent to the Ka'bah, and if he wishes, he does not do so. So that is contrary to the text.

As for the report: what Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah narrated, that "he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the hyena: is it game? He said: Yes, and for it is a ram, if the muhrim takes it." This is an explicit text.

As for consensus: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the reports have come in succession from 'Ali, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, in different lands and at different times, that they judged the compensation for game as the like from the livestock: for the ostrich they judged a camel, for the wild ass a cow, for the hyena a ram, for the gazelle a she-goat, for the deer a sheep, for the hare a jafra (a female kid weaned from its mother), and in one narration an 'anaq (a female young goat); for the lizard (ḍabb) a sukhlah (a young kid), and for the jerboa a jafra. This indicates that they looked to the thing nearest in resemblance to the game from the livestock, not to its value, for had they judged by value it would have varied with the variation of prices. The ẓabyu is the large male gazelle, and the ghazal is the female. The yarbu' is the large mouse that lives in the desert. The jafra is the female young of goats once it has separated from its mother; the male is jafr. The 'anaq is the female young of goats once it has grown strong before completing a year.

As for analogy: the purpose of the compensation is the recompense of the one destroyed, and there is no doubt that the more complete the likeness, the more complete the recompense, so the obligation of the like is more fitting.

The argument of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, Exalted: There is no dispute that when the slain game has no like, it is compensated by its value. So the meaning of "like" in His saying ﴿the compensation is the like of what he killed from the livestock﴾ is the value in this case, and so it must be in all other cases, because a single word cannot be understood to carry more than one meaning.

The answer: the reality of likeness is a known matter, and the Lawgiver obligated observing likeness, so it is obligatory to observe it to the utmost possibility. If it is possible to observe it in the form itself, it is obligatory to do so; and if it cannot be observed except through value, it is sufficient to rely on value out of necessity.

* * *

Issue 4: A group of people in a state of ihram kill a game animal. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: only one compensation (jaza') is obligatory upon them; this is also the view of Ahmad and Ishaq. Abu Hanifah, Malik and al-Thawri, may Allah have mercy on them all, said: a full compensation is obligatory upon each one of them. The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the verse indicates the obligation of an equivalent (mithl), and the equivalent of one is one. This is reinforced by what is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said in accordance with our view. The proof of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, is that each one of them is a killer, so it is obligatory that a full compensation be obligatory upon each one of them. The explanation of the first: if a group each swore that he would not kill a game animal, and they then killed one game animal, each one of them would be bound by an expiation (kaffarah). Likewise, retaliation (qisas) connected with killing is obligatory upon a group who kill one person. Since it is established that each one of them is a killer, it follows that a full compensation is obligatory upon each one of them, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally, then the compensation is an equivalent of what he has killed of the livestock﴾. His saying ﴿whoever among you kills it intentionally﴾ is a general form, so it encompasses all the killers. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, answered that killing is one act, so it is impossible for it to be completed by more than one agent. When they combine, one killing is produced by the sum of their actions. If that is so, it is impossible that each one of them be a killer in reality. And if it is established that each one of them is not a killer, he does not fall under this verse. As for the killing of a group for one person, that is established by way of ta'abbud (unexplained divine command), and likewise the statement regarding the obligation of multiple expiations.

* * *

Issue 5: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: if a muhrim indicates a game animal to another, and the one indicated kills it, the one who indicated does not bear the compensation. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: he bears it. The proof of al-Shafi'i is that the obligation of compensation is tied to killing in this verse, and indication is not killing, so it is necessary that liability not be obligatory. Also, it is a replacement for something destroyed, so it is not obligatory through indication, like the expiation for killing and the blood-money (diyah), and like indicating the property of a Muslim. The proof of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, is that 'Umar was asked about this issue, so he consulted 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and the two of them agreed that the compensation is obligatory upon him. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he made the compensation obligatory upon the one who indicated. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, answered that the explicit text of the Qur'an is better than the report of some of the Companions.

* * *

Issue 6: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: if one wounds a gazelle and its value is reduced by a tenth, then he must pay a tenth of the value of a sheep. Dawud said: he bears no liability at all except for killing. Al-Muzani said: he must pay a sheep. The proof of Dawud is that the verse indicates that the condition for the obligation of compensation is killing, so if killing is not found, it is necessary that compensation not be obligatory at all. Its answer: what is tied to killing is the obligation of an equivalent of the one killed, and according to us this is not obligatory when there is no killing, so his statement falls.

* * *

Issue 7: If one shoots from within the sacred area (hill) while the game is within the sacred area (haram), and the arrow passes over part of the Haram, al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it becomes unlawful and he bears the compensation. Abu Hanifah said: it does not become unlawful. The proof of al-Shafi'i is that the cause of slaughter is composed of parts, some of which are permissible and some of which are forbidden, namely passing through the Haram. Whenever the forbidden and the permissible combine, the forbidden prevails over the permissible, especially in slaughter, where the original rule is prohibition. The proof of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, is that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ is a prohibition on hunting while he is in the Haram. Since neither of these two conditions is found, the prohibition must not arise.

* * *

Issue 8: If a person in the state of non-ihram (halal) hunts a game animal and brings it into the Haram, he must release it; and if he slaughters it, it becomes unlawful and he bears the compensation. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is lawful and there is no liability upon him. The proof of al-Shafi'i is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you, not permitting game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. The proof of Abu Hanifah is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾; He forbade killing game while being in the state of ihram, and this covers game he hunted in the non-sacred area and game he hunted in the Haram.

* * *

Issue 9: If a muhrim kills a game animal and pays a compensation, then kills another game animal, he must pay another compensation. Dawud said: it is not obligatory. The proof of the majority: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally, then the compensation is an equivalent of what he has killed of the livestock﴾ apparently indicates that the cause of the obligation of compensation is killing, so it is necessary that the ruling be repeated when the cause is repeated.

If it is said: when a man says to his wives, "Whichever of you enters the house is divorced," and one of them enters twice, only one divorce takes effect.

We say: the difference is that killing is the cause of the obligation of compensation, so the ruling must be repeated when the cause is repeated. But here, entering the house is a condition for the occurrence of divorce, so the ruling is not required to repeat when the condition is repeated.

The proof of Dawud: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾; He made the requital for one who returns to be retribution, not expiation.

Issue 10: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: if one hits a game animal that is one-eyed, or whose foot or leg is broken, he ransoms it with its equivalent, and the healthy is more beloved to me. On this basis, the large is better than the small. The male is ransomed with a male and the female with a female. The better course is that it not be altered, because the text of the Qur'an requires an equivalent. Although the female is more excellent than the male in that she bears young, the male is more excellent than the female because its flesh is more tasty and its form more beautiful.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿judged by two just men among you﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

Issue 1: Ibn 'Abbas said: he means: two righteous, just men judge concerning the compensation for the game, ﴿among you﴾, that is, from among the people of your religion and faith, two just jurists; they examine what is most similar to it among the livestock, and they judge accordingly. Whoever supported the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, in obligating the value, used this as evidence, saying: estimation is what requires examination and effort (ijtihad), whereas creation and form are evident and observable, requiring no ijtihad.

The answer: the aspects of resemblance between livestock and game are diverse and numerous, so ijtihad is necessary to distinguish the stronger from the weaker. What confirms the correctness of what we have mentioned is that Maymun ibn Mihran said: a Bedouin came to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "I have hit such-and-such game." Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and the Bedouin said: "I came to you to ask you, and you ask someone else?" Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What do you find objectionable in that? Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿judged by two just men among you﴾. I consulted my companion, and when we agree upon something, we command you accordingly." And it is reported from Qabisah ibn Jabir that when he was in the state of ihram he struck a gazelle and it died; he asked 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf was beside him. 'Umar said to 'Abd al-Rahman: "What do you think?" He said: "It is obligatory upon him to give a sheep." 'Umar said: "I too think so," and said: "Go and give a sheep." Qabisah said: "I went out to my companion and said to him: 'The Commander of the Faithful did not know what to say until he asked someone else.'" He said: "'Umar came upon me, struck me with the whip, and said: 'Do you kill in the Haram and belittle the ruling?' Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿judged by two just men among you﴾; I am 'Umar, and this is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf."

Issue 2: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: that which has an equivalent is of two kinds. What the Companions have judged with a ruling is not to be departed from in favour of anything else, because they witnessed the revelation and attended the interpretation. And what the Companions did not judge concerning is referred to the ijtihad of two just men, who examine the three categories of livestock, and whatever is closest in resemblance to it, they both require it. Malik said: arbitration is required both in what the Companions judged and in what they did not judge. The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him: the verse indicates that it is necessary that two just men judge it; when two of the Companions judged it, it has entered under the verse, and moreover that is preferable, for the reason we mentioned, that they witnessed the revelation and attended the interpretation.

Issue 3: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is permissible for the killer to be one of the two just men if he erred in it; but if he did so intentionally, it is not permissible, because by it he becomes a transgressor (fasiq). Malik said: it is not permissible, as in the valuation of destroyed property. The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that He, exalted is He, obligated that two just men judge it; and when the killing proceeds from him by mistake, he is just, so when he and another judge it, two just men have judged it. Also, it is reported that one of the Companions trampled a gazelle with his horse, and he asked 'Umar about it. 'Umar said: "Judge." He said: "You are just, O Commander of the Faithful, so judge." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I only commanded you to judge, and I did not command you to vouch for me." He said: "I see in it a young goat that has gathered water and trees." 'Umar said: "Do what you see fit." On this basis, our companions said: it is permissible that both of them be killers.

* * *

Issue 4: If two just men judge with one equivalent, and two other just men judge with another equivalent, there are two views:
One: he chooses.
The second: he takes the stricter.

Issue 5: Some of those who affirm analogy (qiyas) said: the verse indicates that acting upon analogy and ijtihad is permissible, because He, exalted is He, delegated the determination of the equivalent to the ijtihad and conjectures of people. This is weak, because there is no doubt that the Lawgiver has commanded us to act upon conjecture in many cases. Among them: ijtihad in the direction of the qiblah; among them: acting upon the testimony of two witnesses; among them: acting upon the valuation of appraisers regarding the values of destroyed property and the arsh (compensation) for injuries; among them: acting upon the arbitration of judges in determining the equivalent of the game killed, as in this verse; among them: the layman's acting upon a fatwa; among them: acting upon conjecture in worldly interests. However, we say: if you claim that likening one legal case to another legal case in a legal ruling is the very same as these issues we have enumerated, that is false by the immediate judgment of reason; and if you concede that they are different, it does not follow that conjecture being a proof in those cases makes it a proof in the question of analogy, unless we analogize this question to those issues, and that requires establishing analogy by analogy, which is invalid.

Moreover, the difference between the two categories is evident: in all the cases mentioned, the ruling applied to one specific person, at one time, in one incident; whereas a ruling established by analogy is a general law binding upon all the responsible persons, remaining for all time. Specifying the rulings of individual particular persons is impossible, whereas specifying the general rulings and universal laws that remain until the end of time is not impossible. Thus the difference is clear, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

Issue 1: In the verse there are two views:
The first: the meaning is that they judge it as an offering (hady) that is driven to the Ka'bah and slaughtered there. This confirms the view of those who obligate the equivalent by way of physical form, because He, exalted is He, did not say "they judge it as something with which an offering is bought," but said "they judge it as an offering," which is explicit that they judge by the offering alone and nothing else.
The second: that the meaning is that they judge it as something with which that which is an offering is bought. This is remote from the apparent wording, and the correct view is the first. The word "hady" (offering) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in His saying "bihi" (by it). The sense is: they judge by that equivalent a sheep, or a cow, or a camel; so the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the equivalent, and "hady" is a circumstantial qualifier of it. Upon recognizing these two considerations, who would doubt that what is obligatory is the equivalent by way of physical form? And Allah knows best.

**The second issue: the phrase ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ is an attribute (ṣifah) of the word ﴿hadyan﴾ (an offering), because its idafah (genitive construction) is not a true idafah. Its underlying form is *bālighan al-Ka'bata* (reaching the Ka'bah), but the tanwin (nunation) has been dropped for lightness (istikhfāf). A similar case is the verse ﴿a cloud that brings us rain﴾ (ʿāriḍun mumṭirunā).**

**The third issue: the Ka'bah was named the Ka'bah because of its height and its squareness (tarbuʿ). The Arabs call every square-built house a ka'bah. What is meant by "the Ka'bah" here is the whole sacred precinct (al-Ḥaram), because slaughtering and sacrificing do not take place within the Ka'bah itself, nor beside it adjacent to it. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ (al-Ḥajj 22:33).**

**The fourth issue: The meaning of ﴿reaching the Ka'bah﴾ is that the animal is slaughtered in the Ḥaram. If one gives the equivalent of the game killed to the poor alive, it is not permitted; rather, he is obliged to slaughter it in the Ḥaram. If he slaughters it in the Ḥaram, al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him) said: he is obliged to give it in charity within the Ḥaram too. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) said: he may give it in charity wherever he wishes. Al-Shāfiʿī conceded that he may fast wherever he wishes, because there is no benefit in it for the poor of the Ḥaram.**

**[Page 79]**

The argument of al-Shāfiʿī: the act of slaughtering itself is an inflicting of pain, so it cannot be an act of worship (qurbah). Rather, the act of worship is delivering the meat to the poor. So His saying ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ requires that this offering be delivered to the people of the Ḥaram and the Ka'bah.

The argument of Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him): once it has reached the Ka'bah, it has become an offering that has reached the Ka'bah, so he must be discharged of the obligation.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Or an expiation: feeding needy people, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾. In this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿aw kaffāratu ṭaʿām﴾ (or the expiation of feeding), with the expiation in the genitive of the food. The rest read ﴿aw kaffāratun﴾ with the nominative and tanwin, and ﴿ṭaʿāmu﴾ in the nominative without tanwin. As for the justification of the first reading: when He gave the responsible person a choice among three things — the offering, fasting and feeding — the idafah was fitting, as if it were said: the expiation of food, not the expiation of an offering nor the expiation of fasting, so the idafah is sound because the expiation is one of these things. As for the justification of the reading with tanwin, it is that He made it a conjunction (ʿaṭf) to His saying ﴿then a recompense﴾ and ﴿feeding needy people﴾ as an explanatory appositive (ʿaṭf bayān), because the food is the expiation itself, and the expiation was not made an idafah to the food, because the expiation is not for the food; rather, the expiation is for killing the game.

**The second issue:** Al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on them) said: the word ﴿aw﴾ (or) in this verse is for choice (takhyīr). Aḥmad and Zufar said: it is for sequence (tartīb).

The argument of the first group: the word ﴿aw﴾ in its basic linguistic usage is for choice, and saying it is for sequence abandons the apparent meaning.

The argument of the others: the word ﴿aw﴾ may come for choice, as in His saying: ﴿Their recompense is only that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides﴾ (al-Māʾidah 5:33). The intention there is to assign each of these rulings to a specific case, so it is established that this word admits of sequence. We say: the evidence shows that the intended meaning is sequence, because the obligation here was legislated as a severe measure, by the proof of His saying: ﴿that he may taste the harm of his deed. God has pardoned what is past; but whoever returns, God will take retribution from him﴾ (al-Māʾidah 5:95). And choice contradicts severity.

The answer: removing the like is not a greater punishment than removing the food, so choice does not detract from the degree of punishment achieved in obligating the equivalent.

**The third issue:** If one kills game that has an equivalent, al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him) said: he is given a choice among three things. If he wishes, he brings out the equivalent; if he wishes, he assesses the equivalent in dirhams, buys food with those dirhams and gives it in charity; and if he wishes, he fasts. As for game that has no equivalent, he has a choice between two things: that he assess the game in dirhams, buy food with those dirhams and give it in charity; or that he fast. Based on what we have mentioned, the game that has an equivalent is for buying food only at the value of its equivalent. Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik (may God have mercy on them) said: he buys food only at its value.

The argument of al-Shāfiʿī: the equivalent from the livestock (naʿam) is the recompense, and the food is built upon it, so it is substituted by it, just as one substitutes food for fasting. Also, assessing the equivalent of the game is more precise in measurement than assessing the game itself.

The argument of Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him): when the equivalent of a destroyed thing becomes obligatory, it is to be measured by the destroyed thing and not by anything else where possible, and the food became obligatory only as an equivalent of the destroyed thing, so it must be estimated by it.

**The fourth issue:** They differed about the place of assessment. Most jurists said: it is assessed in the place where the game was killed. Al-Shaʿbī said: it is assessed in Mecca at the price of Mecca, because the expiation is made with it.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Al-Farrāʾ said: *al-ʿadl* is what equals a thing from a different kind, and *al-ʿidl* is the like. You say: "I have the *ʿidl* of your boy or your sheep" when you have a boy equal to a boy or a sheep equal to a sheep. But if you want its value from a different kind, you put a fatḥah on the ʿayn and say *ʿadl*. Abū al-Haytham said: *al-ʿadl* is the like, and *al-ʿidl* is the value; *al-ʿadl* is the name of a load equated with another load that is made equal to it, and *al-ʿidl* is your assessing of one thing by another thing of a different kind. Al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-ʿadl* and *al-ʿidl* are the same.

His saying ﴿ṣiyāman﴾ (in fasting) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), as you say: "I have two raṭls of honey" and "a house full of books." The basic principle in it is the introduction of the particle *min* (of) before it; if it is not mentioned, you put it in the accusative. You say: "two raṭls of honey" (min al-ʿasal) and "the equivalent of that of fasting" (min al-ṣiyām).

**The sixth issue:** The position of al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) is that he fasts one day for each *mudd*; this is also the view of ʿAṭāʾ. The position of Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) is that he fasts one day for each half a ṣāʿ. The basis of this question is that both agree that fasting is measured by the food of one day, except that the food of a day, according to al-Shāfiʿī, is measured by the *mudd*, and according to Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) it is measured by half a ṣāʿ, as we mentioned concerning the expiation of oaths.

**The seventh issue:** Most jurists claimed that the choice in determining one of these three belongs to the one who killed the game. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan (may God have mercy on him) said: it belongs to the two arbiters. The argument of the majority: He, exalted, obligated on the one who killed the game one of these three things by way of choice, so the one who killed the game must be given the choice among whichever of them he wishes. The argument of Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him): He, exalted, placed the choice in the hands of the two arbiters, saying: ﴿two just men among you shall judge it as an offering﴾, meaning such-and-such.

Our answer: the interpretation of the verse is: "then a recompense equal to what he killed of the livestock, or an expiation of feeding the needy, or the equivalent of that in fasting." As for what "two just men judge" by it, it is the specification of the equivalent, either in value or in the form (khilqah) of the animal.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿that he may taste the harm of his deed﴾. In this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** *al-wabāl* in the language is an expression for what is in it of heaviness and disagreeableness. It is said: "a *marʿan wabīl*" (a pasture that is harmful) when there is in it unhealthiness; and "*māʾun wabīl*" (water that is unwholesome) when it is not digested well; and "*ṭaʿāmun wabīl*" (heavy food) is that which weighs on the stomach so that it is not digested. He, exalted, said: ﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizing﴾ (al-Muzzammil 73:16), meaning heavy.

**The second issue:** God, exalted, named that *wabāl* only because He gave him a choice among three things: two of them necessitate a reduction of wealth, which is heavy on the disposition — namely the recompense by the equivalent and the feeding — and the third necessitates the inflicting of pain on the body, which is fasting, and that too is heavy on the disposition. The meaning is that He, exalted, obligated on the one who killed the game one of these things, each of which is heavy on the disposition, so that he would refrain from killing game within the Ḥaram and while in the state of iḥrām.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿God has pardoned what is past; but whoever returns, God will take retribution from him. And God is Mighty, Possessor of retribution﴾. In this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** In the verse there are two views:

The first: God has pardoned what passed in the Jāhiliyyah and what preceded the prohibition in Islam.

The second view, which is the view of those who require the recompense only for the first offence: as for the second offence, they do not require recompense for it, and they say: it is too great for the charity of recompense to expiate it. According to this, the meaning is: God pardoned what passed the first time by means of paying the recompense; and whoever returns to it a second time, there is no expiation for his offence, but God will take retribution from him. The argument of this view is that the ﴿fa-﴾ (then) in His saying ﴿then God will take retribution from him﴾ is the fāʾ of the apodosis (fāʾ al-jazāʾ), and the recompense is what suffices; so this indicates that this retribution suffices for this sin, and its sufficiency prevents the obligation of anything else, and that requires that the recompense not be obligatory upon him.

**The second issue:** Sībawayh said, regarding His saying ﴿and whoever returns, God will take retribution from him﴾, and His saying ﴿and whoever disbelieves, I shall let him enjoy for a little while﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:126), and His saying ﴿so whoever believes in his Lord, he shall not fear﴾ (al-Jinn 72:13), that in these verses there is an implied elided element (iḍmār), and the estimate is: "and whoever returns, *he* — God will take retribution from him"; "and whoever disbelieves, then *I* will let him enjoy"; "and whoever believes in his Lord, *he* does not fear." In sum, there must be an implied subject (mubtadaʾ) of which that verb becomes the predicate. The proof of this is that the verb becomes itself a conditional apodosis, so there is no need to introduce the particle of apodosis upon it; and introducing the *fāʾ* upon the verb would then be superfluous. But when we posit an implied subject, we need to introduce the *fāʾ* upon it so that it is linked to the condition, and then the *fāʾ* is not superfluous. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 96:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers.﴾ On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The meaning of *al-ṣayd* (game) is *al-maṣīd* (that which is caught). Everything caught from the sea comes in three kinds: fish, all of whose species are lawful, and frogs, all of whose species are unlawful, and scholars differ about what lies beyond these two. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said that it is unlawful. Ibn Abi Layla and most scholars said that it is lawful, and they relied on the generality of this verse. The meaning of "the sea" here includes all waters and rivers.

**The second issue:** He, Exalted is He, joined the food of the sea to its game with a conjunction, and conjunction implies difference. The scholars mentioned several explanations:

The first, and the best, is what Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned: that *al-ṣayd* is what is caught by cunning while it is alive, and *al-ṭaʿām* (food) is what is found of what the sea has cast up or from which the water has receded, without any effort in taking it. This is the most sound of what has been said on this point.

The second explanation: *ṣayd al-baḥr* is the fresh (*ṭarī*) catch, while *ṭaʿām al-baḥr* is that which has been salted. When it becomes old, the name "game" no longer applies to it. This is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Muqatil and al-Nakha'i. It is weak, because what has become salted was fresh and game at the beginning, so this would lead to repetition.

The third: hunting may be for eating and may be for other purposes, such as hunting shellfish for pearls, or hunting some sea creatures for their bones and teeth. So there is a difference between hunting from the sea and eating from the food of the sea. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: a fish floating on the surface of the sea is lawful. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is unlawful. Al-Shafi'i's proof is the Qur'an and a report. As for the Qur'an, it is possible to eat it, so it is food, and therefore it must be lawful, based on His saying: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food.﴾ As for the report, it is his saying, peace be upon him, about the sea: "Its water is pure, and its dead (creatures) are lawful." (ﷺ)

[p. 82]

**The fourth issue:** His saying, *"and for the travelers"* means: lawful for you is the game of the sea, for the resident and for the traveler. The fresh catch is for the resident, and the salted is for the traveler.

**The fifth issue:** Concerning the case of His saying ﴿as a provision for you﴾, there are two views:

The first: Al-Zajjaj said it is in the accusative because it is an emphatic infinitive (*maṣdar muʾakkad*). However, when He said ﴿Lawful for you﴾, it was an indication that it is a favour granted to them, just as when He said ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] it was an indication that He had prescribed this for them, so He said: "Allah has prescribed for you."

The second: The author of *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary) said it is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), meaning: lawful for you as a means of giving you enjoyment.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you remain in the state of ihram.﴾

On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** He, Exalted is He, mentioned the prohibition of game for the one in the state of ihram in three places in this surah: from His saying ﴿not hunting game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ up to His saying ﴿But when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾; and from His saying ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ up to His saying ﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you remain in the state of ihram.﴾

**The second issue:** The game of the sea is that which cannot live except in water. As for that which cannot live except on land, and that which can live sometimes on land and sometimes in the sea, all of that is game of the land. On this basis, the tortoise, the crab, the frog and waterfowl are all game of the land, and whoever kills them must pay compensation (*al-jazāʾ*).

**The third issue:** The Muslims agreed that game is forbidden to the one in ihram. They differed about game that is caught by a non-muhrim (one not in ihram): is it lawful for the one in ihram? On this there are four views.

The first, which is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Tawus, and which al-Thawri and Ishaq also mentioned, is that it is unlawful for him in every case. They relied on His saying ﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you remain in the state of ihram.﴾ This is because the game of the land includes what the one in ihram hunts and what the non-muhrim hunts, and all of that is game of the land. Abu Dawud related in his *Sunan*, from Humayd al-Tawil, from Ishaq ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, from his father, who said: "Al-Harith, the deputy of Uthman over al-Ta'if, prepared food for Uthman, and in it he put partridges, sand grouse and wild animal meat. He sent to Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and the messenger came to him, and he came. They said to him: Eat. Ali said: Feed us with lawful provision, for we are in the state of ihram. Then Ali, peace be upon him, said: I adjure Allah, whoever is here from the Ashja', do you know that a man presented the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a wild ass while he was in the state of ihram, and he refused to eat it? They said: Yes."

The second view, which is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the meat of game is permissible for the one in ihram on condition that he did not hunt it and it was not hunted for him. The proof for it is what Abu Dawud related in his *Sunan* from Jabir, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The game of the land is lawful for you as long as you do not hunt it or it is not hunted for you.'"

The third view, which is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that if it is hunted for the one in ihram without his assistance or his gesture, it becomes lawful for him. It was related "from Abu Qatada that he hunted a wild ass while he was not in ihram, among companions who were in ihram. They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'Did you gesture, did you assist?' They said: No. He said: 'Is there any of its meat left?'" He made it permissible in the absence of gesture and assistance, without detail.

[p. 83]

Know that these two views are based on specifying the generality of the Qur'an by a solitary report (*khabar al-wāḥid*). The second view is extremely weak.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ The purpose of this is a warning, so that a person will be constant in obedience and cautious against disobedience.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for the people, and the sacred month, and the offerings, and the garlands﴾.

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is that God, exalted is He, in the previous verse prohibited hunting for the one in ihram. So He made clear that just as the Haram is a cause of safety for wild animals and birds, so too it is a cause of safety for people from calamities and fears, and a cause of attaining goodness and happiness in this world and the Hereafter. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Amir read (qayyiman) without an alif, and its meaning is an intensification of its being the one that establishes the important affairs of the people, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a upright religion﴾ [al-An'am: 161]. The rest read it with an alif. We have thoroughly examined this in the surah of al-Nisa'.

The second issue: (ja'ala) here has two opinions. The first: that it means He made clear and decreed. The second: that it means He made (it) into something, so the first is by command and definition, and the second by creating the motives in the hearts of the people to glorify it and draw near to Him.

The third issue: the Ka'bah was named Ka'bah because of its height. It is said of a girl when her breasts protrude and emerge: ka'ibun and ka'ab. The ankle of a person is called ka'b because of its protrusion from the shin. So when the mention of the Ka'bah rose in this world and its matter became famous throughout the world, it was named by this name. For this reason they say of one whose matter is great: "So-and-so's ka'b has risen high."

The fourth issue: His saying, ﴿qiyaman lil-nas﴾, its root is (qiwam), because it derives from qama yaqumu, and it is that by which an affair is kept upright and set right. Then they mentioned here, regarding the Ka'bah being a cause of the establishment of the people's interests, several aspects:

The first: that the people of Makkah needed the presence of the people of the regions with them, so that they could buy from them what they needed throughout the year, for Makkah is a narrow town with no pasture and no crops, and what they need is rarely found there. So God made the Ka'bah honored in hearts until the people of the world became eager to visit it, so they travel to it from every deep mountain pass for the sake of trade and bring all the desired and sought-after goods. Thus that became a cause of abundant blessings for the people of Makkah.

The second: the Arabs used to fight and raid one another except in the Haram, so the people of the Haram were safe for their lives and their wealth, to the extent that if a man met the killer of his father or his son in the Haram, he would not be touched. And if a man committed the greatest crimes and then sought refuge in the Haram, he would not be touched. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that We have made a safe sanctuary while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67].

The third: the people of Makkah, because of the Ka'bah, became the people of God and His special ones and the masters of creation until the Day of Resurrection, and everyone draws near to them and honors them.

The fourth: God made the Ka'bah a means of establishment for the people in their religion, because of the great rites and noble acts of worship He placed in it, and made those rites a cause of erasing sins, raising ranks, and multiplying honors.

Know that it is not far-fetched to take the verse as including all these aspects, because the establishment of livelihood is either by abundance of benefits, which is the first aspect we mentioned; or by warding off harms, which is the second aspect; or by attaining standing and leadership, which is the third aspect; or by attaining religion, which is the fourth aspect. Since the Ka'bah was a cause of attaining these four categories, and it is established that the establishment of livelihood consists only of these four, it is established that the Ka'bah is a cause of the establishment of the people.

The fifth issue: what is meant by His saying, ﴿qiyaman lil-nas﴾ is: for some of the people, namely the Arabs. This metaphor is apt because when the people of any region say "the people did such-and-such and made such-and-such," they mean only the people of their own town. For this reason they were addressed in this address according to their custom.

The sixth issue: know that the verse indicates that God, exalted is He, made four things a cause of the standing and establishment of the people. The first: the Ka'bah, and we have already explained the meaning of its being a cause of the people's standing. As for the second: it is the Sacred Month, and the meaning of its being a cause of the people's standing is that the Arabs used to kill one another in the other months and raid one another; but when the Sacred Month came, fear disappeared, they were able to travel and trade, and they were safe for their lives and their wealth. They would gather in the Sacred Month provisions sufficient for them throughout the year. Had it not been for the sanctity of the Sacred Month, they would have perished and been destroyed by hunger and hardship. So the Sacred Month was a cause of the establishment of their livelihood in this world as well, and it is a cause of gaining great reward through performing the rites of Hajj.

Know that God, exalted is He, intended by the Sacred Month the four sacred months, but He expressed them with the singular term, because He treated it in the manner of a genus.

As for the third: it is the offering (hady), and it was a cause of the people's standing only because the hady is what is brought as a gift to the House and slaughtered there, and its meat is distributed among the poor, so that becomes a rite for the one who offers it and a means of sustenance for the poor.

As for the fourth: it is the garlands, and the aspect of their being a standing for the people is that whoever intends the House in the Sacred Month is not touched by anyone; and whoever intends it outside the Sacred Month while having an offering, having garlanded it and garlanded himself with bark from the trees of the Haram, is not touched by anyone. So much so that a man of the Arabs would meet a garlanded offering and die of hunger, yet he would never touch it at all, and its owner would not touch it either. All of this was only because God, exalted is He, placed in their hearts the glorification of the Sacred House; so everyone who intends it or draws near to it becomes safe from all calamities and fears. When God, exalted is He, mentioned that He made the Ka'bah the Sacred House a standing for the people, He mentioned after it these three: the Sacred Month, the offering, and the garlands. This is because these three became a cause of the establishment of livelihood only through their connection to the Sacred House, and so this was evidence of the greatness of this House and the extent of its nobility.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is so that you may know that God knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and that God is Knowing of all things﴾.

The meaning is: when God, exalted is He, knew from eternity that the inclination of the Arabs' nature was intense eagerness for killing and raiding, and knew that if this state persisted among them they would be unable to obtain what they needed of the benefits of livelihood, and that would lead to their annihilation and complete extinction, He arranged in that a subtle arrangement: He placed in their hearts a strong conviction in the glorification of the Sacred House and the glorification of its rites. So this became a cause of attaining security in the Sacred Land and in the Sacred Month. When security was attained in this place and in this time, they were able to obtain what they needed in this time and this place, and the interests of their livelihood were set right. It is known that such an arrangement is possible only if He, exalted is He, was from eternity

صفحة ٨٥
knowing of all knowables, both universals and particulars, so that He knows that evil predominates over their nature, that this leads them to destruction and the cutting off of offspring, and that this cannot be averted except by this subtle means, namely placing the glorification of the Ka'bah in their hearts, so that this becomes a cause of attaining safety in some places and at some times. Then the interests of their livelihood are set right in that place and at that time. This is precisely the proof on which the theologians relied for His being Knowing, for they say: His acts are firm, perfected, and conforming to interests, and whoever is so is knowing. It is known that placing the glorification of the Ka'bah in the hearts of the Arabs so that this becomes a cause of attaining safety in some places and at some times, so that it becomes a cause of their ability to obtain the interests of livelihood, is an act of the utmost perfection and firmness. So that is a compelling proof and a dazzling demonstration that the Maker of the world, glory be to Him and exalted is He, knows all knowables. Therefore He said: ﴿That is so that you may know﴾, meaning: that arrangement of subtle wisdom is so that you may reflect on it, and thus know that it is a subtle arrangement and a firm, perfected act; so that you may know ﴿that God knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾. Then, once you know that, you know that His knowledge, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is an eternal, pre-eternal attribute, necessarily existent; and whatever is so cannot be restricted to some things rather than others, so it must be that it relates to all knowables. And if that is so, God, glory be to Him, is knowing of all knowables. Therefore He said: ﴿and that God is Knowing of all things﴾. How excellent this order is in this reckoning! Praise be to God who guided us to this, and we would not have been guided had God not guided us.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 98:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the kinds of His mercy towards His servants, He mentioned after it that He is severe in punishment, because faith is not complete except with hope (raja') and fear (khawf). As the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "If the fear of the believer and his hope were weighed, they would be balanced." Then, immediately after this, He mentioned what indicates mercy, which is His being Forgiving and Merciful. This indicates that the side of mercy is predominant, because He, exalted is He, mentioned earlier the kinds of His mercy and generosity, then mentioned that He is severe in punishment, then mentioned immediately after it two attributes from the attributes of mercy, which is His being Forgiving and Merciful. This is an alert to a subtle point, which is that the beginning of creation and bringing into existence was for the sake of mercy, and the apparent meaning is that the concluding (of the verse) is only upon mercy.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey; and Allah knows what you disclose and what you conceal.﴾ Know that when He, exalted is He, preceded the warning and the encouragement with His words ﴿that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, He followed it with the imposition of obligation through His words ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey﴾. That is, he was charged with conveying (the message), so when he conveyed it, he was discharged of the obligation, and the matter remains on your side. And I am aware of what you disclose

صفحة ٨٦
and what you conceal. So if you oppose, know that Allah is severe in punishment, and if you obey, know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: not equal are the evil and the good.﴾
Know that when He, exalted is He, restrained from disobedience and encouraged obedience with His words ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, then He followed it with the imposition of obligation through His words ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey﴾, then He followed it with encouragement to obedience and deterrence from disobedience through His words ﴿and Allah knows what you disclose and what you conceal﴾, He followed it with another kind of encouragement to obedience and deterrence from disobedience, saying: ﴿Say: not equal are the evil and the good.﴾ This is because "the evil" (al-khabith) and "the good" (al-tayyib) are of two kinds. One of them is the corporeal (jismani), which is evident to everyone.

The second is the spiritual (ruhani). The worst of the spiritual evils is ignorance and disobedience, and the best of the spiritual goods is knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and obedience to Allah, exalted is He. This is because a body to which some impurity clings becomes loathsome in the sight of those with sound natures, so likewise souls characterized by ignorance of Allah and turning away from obedience to Allah, exalted is He, become loathsome in the sight of perfected, sanctified souls.

As for souls that know Allah, exalted is He, and are constant in serving Allah, exalted is He, they become radiant with the lights of divine knowledge, delighted by nearness to the pure, sanctified souls. Just as the evil and the good are not equal in the world of corporeal things, so likewise they are not equal in the world of spiritual things. Rather, the separation between them in the world of spiritual things is greater, because the harm of the corporeal evil's impurity is a small thing, and its benefit is good but brief. But the impurity of the spiritual evil has a great, lasting, everlasting harm, and the goodness of the spiritual good has a great, lasting, everlasting benefit, namely nearness to the neighborhood of the Lord of the worlds, joining the company of the angels brought near, and companionship with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. So this is among the greatest aspects of encouragement to obedience and deterrence from disobedience.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And even if the abundance of the evil pleases you﴾. That is, what is evil in the world of spiritual things may be good in the world of corporeal things, and may be abundant in quantity and great in pleasure. Yet, despite its abundance, the pleasure of its enjoyment and the ease of its attainment, it is a cause of deprivation from the everlasting, eternal, perpetual felicities, to which He alludes with His words ﴿But the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]. Since the matter is so, the evil, even if its abundance pleases you, cannot be equal to the good, which is knowledge, love, obedience, and delight in spiritual felicities and divine honors.
When He, exalted is He, mentioned these many encouragements to obedience and warnings against disobedience, He followed them with another aspect that confirms them, saying: ﴿So be mindful of Allah, O people of understanding, that you may succeed﴾. That is: be mindful of Allah after these clear explanations and strong definitions, and do not proceed to oppose Him, that you may become successful in worldly and religious goals, both immediate and deferred.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey; and Allah knows what you disclose and what you conceal.﴾ Know that when He, exalted is He, preceded the warning and the encouragement with His words ﴿that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, He followed it with the imposition of obligation through His words ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey﴾. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 101–102 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾.

The first issue: concerning the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are several aspects.

The first: when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿The duty of the Messenger is only to convey [the message]﴾, the implied meaning becomes as if He had said: What the Messenger has conveyed to you, take it and be submissive to it; and what the Messenger has not conveyed to you, do not ask about it or delve into it, for if you delve into what carries no obligation upon you, perhaps there will come to you, as a result of that corrupt delving, obligations that are burdensome and hard upon you.

The second: when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿The duty of the Messenger is only to convey [the message]﴾, this is a claim by him to prophethood. Then the unbelievers would demand of him, after the manifestation of the miracles, other miracles out of obstinacy, as He, exalted is He, related about them: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra: 90], up to His saying: ﴿Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Was I but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra: 93]. The meaning is: I am a messenger commanded to convey the message, the laws and the rulings to you, and God, exalted is He, has established the proof of the truth of my claim to prophethood by manifesting many kinds of miracles. After that, demanding more is an arbitrary imposition, and that is not within my power. Perhaps their manifestation would bring about what would distress you, such as that if they were to appear, everyone who opposed afterward would deserve punishment in this world. Then, when the Muslims heard the unbelievers demanding these miracles of the Messenger ﷺ, an inclination toward their manifestation arose in their hearts, so this verse made them aware that they should not seek that, for perhaps its manifestation would bring about what would distress them.

The third aspect: this is connected to His saying: ﴿And God knows what you disclose and what you conceal﴾. So leave matters as they appear, and do not ask about frightening circumstances, for if they were disclosed to you, they would distress you.

The second issue: (ashya') is the plural of (shay'), and it is not declinable (ghayr munsarifa). The grammarians have several views on the reason for its prohibition of declension:

The first: al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: our word shay', its original plural is shay'a' (shay'a'), on the pattern of fa'la' (fa‘lā’), so they found the conjunction of the two hamzas at its end heavy, and they moved the first hamza, which is the lam of the root, to the beginning of the word, so it became la'fa' (la‘fā’). This necessitates the prohibition of declension for three reasons, one of which is mentioned, and two of which occurred to me:

As for the first, which is the one mentioned: since the word was originally on the pattern of fa'la' like ḥamrā' (red, feminine), therefore ḥamrā' is not declined. 50 The second: since it was originally (shaya'a') and then became (ashya'a'), this was an assimilation to the form of the diptote (ma'dūl), as in ʿĀmir and ʿUmar, and Zāfir and Zufar, and ʿadl (deviation of form) is one of the causes of the prohibition of declension.

The third: when we cut the last letter from it and made it the first, and the word, insofar as its last letter has been cut from it, became like half of a word, and half a word does not accept inflection; and insofar as that letter which we cut from it we did not delete entirely, but attached it to its beginning, the word became as if it remained whole in its entirety, so we therefore prohibited it from some forms of inflection but not others, as an indication of this state. This is what came to mind on this occasion.

The second view on the cause of the prohibition of declension: what al-Akhfash and al-Farra' mentioned, namely that (ashya') is of the pattern af'ilā', like their saying aṣdiqā' and aṣfiyā', then they found the conjunction of the yā' and the two hamzas heavy, so they put forward the hamza. Since (ashya') was originally (ashyiyā') on the pattern of aṣdiqā' and af'ilā', and that is among what does not admit declension, so likewise here.

The third view: what al-Kisā'ī mentioned, namely that (ashya') is on the pattern of af'āl, except that they did not decline it because it resembles outwardly ḥamrā' and ṣafrā'. Al-Zajjāj imposed upon him that asmā' and abnā' should also be non-declinable. In my view, al-Zajjāj's objection is worthless, because al-Kisā'ī could say: analogy requires that for abnā' and asmā' as well, but its application was abandoned due to the textual evidence, since the text is stronger than analogy, and no textual evidence was found in the word ashya', so it was necessary to proceed with it according to analogy. Also, the verifying grammarians agreed that grammatical causes do not necessitate universal consistency. Do you not see that if we say: the agentive quality necessitates the nominative case, we would be obliged to judge that nominative inflection occurs in all positions, as when we say jā'anī hā'ulā'i and ḍaraba'nī hadhā; rather we say: that is the analogy, so it is acted upon, unless a text opposes it. Likewise the case regarding what al-Zajjāj objected to al-Kisā'ī.

The third issue: "It was narrated from Anas that they asked the Prophet ﷺ and pressed him with questions, so he stood upon the pulpit and said: Ask me, for by God, you will not ask me about anything while I am in this place except that I will inform you of it. Then ʿAbdullāh ibn Ḥudhāfa al-Sahmī stood up, and he was being slandered regarding his lineage, and said: O Prophet of God, who is my father? He said: Your father is Ḥudhāfa ibn Qays. And Surāqa ibn Mālik said — and it is narrated ʿUkkāsha ibn Miḥṣan — O Messenger of God, is the Hajj obligatory upon us every year? The Messenger of God ﷺ turned away from him until he repeated it two or three times. Then he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Woe to you! What makes you certain that I would not say yes? By God, if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it became obligatory you would have abandoned it, and if you had abandoned it you would have disbelieved. So leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed only through the abundance of their questions. So when I command you with something, do from it what you are able, and when I forbid you from something, avoid it." Another man stood up and said: O Messenger of God, where is my father? He said: "In the Fire." When the anger of the Messenger ﷺ intensified, ʿUmar stood up and said: We are content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Prophet. Then God, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

Know that asking about things may lead to the disclosure of hidden matters whose disclosure is disliked, and may entail difficult and arduous obligations. Therefore it is best for the intelligent person to remain silent about what carries no obligation upon him. Do you not see that the one who asked about his father did not feel secure that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, might attribute him to someone other than his father and so he would be disgraced? As for the one who asked about the Hajj, he nearly became one of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed the greatest of the Muslims in crime among the Muslims is one who was the cause of the prohibition of something lawful," since it was not secure that he might say the Hajj is obligatory every year. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr used to say: God has made lawful and unlawful; so what He made lawful, make lawful, and what He made unlawful, avoid; and He left between these matters things that He neither made lawful nor made unlawful, and that is a pardon from God, exalted is He, and then he would recite this verse. Abu Thaʿlaba al-Khushani said: God has ordained obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; and He has pardoned things out of no forgetfulness, so do not search after them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾, and in it are several aspects:

The first: by the first verse He explained that those things about which they asked, if they were disclosed to them, would distress them; then by this verse He explained that if they asked about them, they would be disclosed to them. So the sum of the statement is that if they asked about them, they would be disclosed to them, and if they were disclosed to them, they would distress them. It follows from the combination of the two premises that if they asked about them, there would appear to them what would distress them and not gladden them.

The second aspect in interpreting the verse: that the question is of two kinds. One is asking about something that was not permissible to mention in the Book and the Sunnah in any way; this question is forbidden by His saying: ﴿Do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾.

The second kind of question: asking about something that the Qur'an has revealed, but the listener did not understand it as he should; here the question is obligatory, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾. The benefit of mentioning this category is that when He forbade asking in the first verse, it might have given the impression that all kinds of questioning are forbidden, so He mentioned this to distinguish this category from that one.

If it is said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿And if you ask about them﴾ refers to the things mentioned in His saying ﴿Do not ask about things﴾; so how can it be conceived that asking about those very things is both forbidden and permitted at the same time?

We say: the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: it is permissible that asking about them was forbidden before the Qur'an was revealed concerning them, and was commanded after the Qur'an was revealed concerning them.

The second: although they are two different kinds, in that each of them concerns one and the same thing being asked about, therefore for this reason the unity of the pronoun is acceptable, even though in reality they are two different kinds.

The third aspect in interpreting the verse: that His saying ﴿Do not ask about things﴾ indicates their questions about those things; so His saying ﴿And if you ask about them﴾, meaning, if you ask about those questions when the Qur'an is being revealed, it will be made clear to you whether those questions are permissible or not. The sum is that the intended meaning of this verse is that asking first is obligatory, so that it may be known whether it is permissible to ask about such and such or not.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God has pardoned it﴾, and in it are several aspects:

The first: God has pardoned what passed of your questions and of your angering the Messenger because of them, so do not return to the like of them.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned that those things which they asked about, if they were disclosed to them, would distress them; so He said: ﴿God has pardoned it﴾, meaning, pardoned what appears at those questions of what would distress you, weigh upon you, and be hard for you in the obligations.

The third: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, and the sense is: Do not ask about things which God has pardoned in the verse, ﴿if they were disclosed to you, they would distress you﴾. This is weak, because if the statement is sound without changing the arrangement, it is not permissible to resort to inversion. On this aspect, His saying ﴿God has pardoned it﴾ means: He withheld from it, refrained from mentioning it, and did not impose any obligation regarding it. This is like His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I have pardoned you regarding the charity of horses and slaves," meaning, I have lightened it for you by dropping it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾. This verse indicates that what is meant by His saying ﴿God has pardoned it﴾ is what we mentioned in the first aspect.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿A people before you asked about them, then they became disbelievers because of them﴾. The exegetes said: this refers to the people of Ṣāliḥ, who asked for the she-camel and then slaughtered her; and the people of Mūsā said: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, and that became a calamity upon them; and the Children of Israel ﴿said to a prophet of theirs: Raise up for us a king that we may fight in the way of God﴾, and He said: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them﴾, and ﴿They said: How can he have kingship over us when we are more worthy of kingship than him?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247]; so they asked for it and then disbelieved in it. And the people of ʿIsā asked for the table and then disbelieved in it. So it is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: Those people asked, and when they were given their request, that distressed them; so do not ask about things, lest if you are given your request, that distress you. If it is said: He, exalted is He, first said ﴿Do not ask about things﴾, and then here said ﴿A people before you asked about them﴾, and it would have been better to say: ﴿A people asked about them﴾; so what is the reason for this?

We say: the answer is from two aspects:

The first point: asking about a thing is an expression for asking about a state of it or an attribute of it, whereas asking for the thing itself means requesting that thing in its own right. One says "sa'altuhu dirhaman" (I asked him for a dirham), meaning I requested the dirham from him, and one says "sa'altuhu 'ani'l-dirham" (I asked him about the dirham), meaning I asked him about the description and characteristics of the dirham. Thus the earlier peoples asked God to bring forth the she-camel from the rock and to send down the table (al-ma'idah) from heaven; they were asking for the thing itself. As for the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), they did not ask for that; rather, they asked about the states and attributes of things. Since the two kinds of question differ in type, the expression also differs. Nevertheless, both kinds share one common quality: they are immersion in superfluities (fudul) and the undertaking of what is not needed, and in them lies the risk of harm (mafsadah). Something that is not needed and carries the risk of harm must be avoided by any sensible person. God, exalted is He, thereby made clear that the people of Muhammad (peace be upon him), in asking about the states of things, resemble those earlier peoples in asking for those things, in that each of these is superfluous and an immersion in what has no benefit.

The second point in the answer: the pronoun in His words ﴿قَدْ سَأَلَهَا﴾ (Indeed a people before you asked them) does not refer back to the things they asked about, but rather to their questions about those things. The meaning is: a people before you asked those corrupt questions that you have mentioned, and when they were answered, they became disbelievers because of them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 101–102 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾.

The first issue: concerning the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are several aspects.

The first: when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿The duty of the Messenger is only to convey [the message]﴾, the implied meaning becomes as if He had said: What the Messenger has conveyed to you, take it and be submissive to it; and what the Messenger has not conveyed to you, do not ask about it or delve into it, for if you delve into what carries no obligation upon you, perhaps there will come to you, as a result of that corrupt delving, obligations that are burdensome and hard upon you.

The second: when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿The duty of the Messenger is only to convey [the message]﴾, this is a claim by him to prophethood. Then the unbelievers would demand of him, after the manifestation of the miracles, other miracles out of obstinacy, as He, exalted is He, related about them: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra: 90], up to His saying: ﴿Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Was I but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra: 93]. The meaning is: I am a messenger commanded to convey the message, the laws and the rulings to you, and God, exalted is He, has established the proof of the truth of my claim to prophethood by manifesting many kinds of miracles. After that, demanding more is an arbitrary imposition, and that is not within my power. Perhaps their manifestation would bring about what would distress you, such as that if they were to appear, everyone who opposed afterward would deserve punishment in this world. Then, when the Muslims heard the unbelievers demanding these miracles of the Messenger ﷺ, an inclination toward their manifestation arose in their hearts, so this verse made them aware that they should not seek that, for perhaps its manifestation would bring about what would distress them.

The third aspect: this is connected to His saying: ﴿And God knows what you disclose and what you conceal﴾. So leave matters as they appear, and do not ask about frightening circumstances, for if they were disclosed to you, they would distress you.

The second issue: (ashya') is the plural of (shay'), and it is not declinable (ghayr munsarifa). The grammarians have several views on the reason for its prohibition of declension:

The first: al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: our word shay', its original plural is shay'a' (shay'a'), on the pattern of fa'la' (fa‘lā’), so they found the conjunction of the two hamzas at its end heavy, and they moved the first hamza, which is the lam of the root, to the beginning of the word, so it became la'fa' (la‘fā’). This necessitates the prohibition of declension for three reasons, one of which is mentioned, and two of which occurred to me:

As for the first, which is the one mentioned: since the word was originally on the pattern of fa'la' like ḥamrā' (red, feminine), therefore ḥamrā' is not declined. 50 The second: since it was originally (shaya'a') and then became (ashya'a'), this was an assimilation to the form of the diptote (ma'dūl), as in ʿĀmir and ʿUmar, and Zāfir and Zufar, and ʿadl (deviation of form) is one of the causes of the prohibition of declension.

The third: when we cut the last letter from it and made it the first, and the word, insofar as its last letter has been cut from it, became like half of a word, and half a word does not accept inflection; and insofar as that letter which we cut from it we did not delete entirely, but attached it to its beginning, the word became as if it remained whole in its entirety, so we therefore prohibited it from some forms of inflection but not others, as an indication of this state. This is what came to mind on this occasion.

The second view on the cause of the prohibition of declension: what al-Akhfash and al-Farra' mentioned, namely that (ashya') is of the pattern af'ilā', like their saying aṣdiqā' and aṣfiyā', then they found the conjunction of the yā' and the two hamzas heavy, so they put forward the hamza. Since (ashya') was originally (ashyiyā') on the pattern of aṣdiqā' and af'ilā', and that is among what does not admit declension, so likewise here.

The third view: what al-Kisā'ī mentioned, namely that (ashya') is on the pattern of af'āl, except that they did not decline it because it resembles outwardly ḥamrā' and ṣafrā'. Al-Zajjāj imposed upon him that asmā' and abnā' should also be non-declinable. In my view, al-Zajjāj's objection is worthless, because al-Kisā'ī could say: analogy requires that for abnā' and asmā' as well, but its application was abandoned due to the textual evidence, since the text is stronger than analogy, and no textual evidence was found in the word ashya', so it was necessary to proceed with it according to analogy. Also, the verifying grammarians agreed that grammatical causes do not necessitate universal consistency. Do you not see that if we say: the agentive quality necessitates the nominative case, we would be obliged to judge that nominative inflection occurs in all positions, as when we say jā'anī hā'ulā'i and ḍaraba'nī hadhā; rather we say: that is the analogy, so it is acted upon, unless a text opposes it. Likewise the case regarding what al-Zajjāj objected to al-Kisā'ī.

The third issue: "It was narrated from Anas that they asked the Prophet ﷺ and pressed him with questions, so he stood upon the pulpit and said: Ask me, for by God, you will not ask me about anything while I am in this place except that I will inform you of it. Then ʿAbdullāh ibn Ḥudhāfa al-Sahmī stood up, and he was being slandered regarding his lineage, and said: O Prophet of God, who is my father? He said: Your father is Ḥudhāfa ibn Qays. And Surāqa ibn Mālik said — and it is narrated ʿUkkāsha ibn Miḥṣan — O Messenger of God, is the Hajj obligatory upon us every year? The Messenger of God ﷺ turned away from him until he repeated it two or three times. Then he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Woe to you! What makes you certain that I would not say yes? By God, if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it became obligatory you would have abandoned it, and if you had abandoned it you would have disbelieved. So leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed only through the abundance of their questions. So when I command you with something, do from it what you are able, and when I forbid you from something, avoid it." Another man stood up and said: O Messenger of God, where is my father? He said: "In the Fire." When the anger of the Messenger ﷺ intensified, ʿUmar stood up and said: We are content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Prophet. Then God, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

Know that asking about things may lead to the disclosure of hidden matters whose disclosure is disliked, and may entail difficult and arduous obligations. Therefore it is best for the intelligent person to remain silent about what carries no obligation upon him. Do you not see that the one who asked about his father did not feel secure that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, might attribute him to someone other than his father and so he would be disgraced? As for the one who asked about the Hajj, he nearly became one of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed the greatest of the Muslims in crime among the Muslims is one who was the cause of the prohibition of something lawful," since it was not secure that he might say the Hajj is obligatory every year. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr used to say: God has made lawful and unlawful; so what He made lawful, make lawful, and what He made unlawful, avoid; and He left between these matters things that He neither made lawful nor made unlawful, and that is a pardon from God, exalted is He, and then he would recite this verse. Abu Thaʿlaba al-Khushani said: God has ordained obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; and He has pardoned things out of no forgetfulness, so do not search after them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾, and in it are several aspects:

The first: by the first verse He explained that those things about which they asked, if they were disclosed to them, would distress them; then by this verse He explained that if they asked about them, they would be disclosed to them. So the sum of the statement is that if they asked about them, they would be disclosed to them, and if they were disclosed to them, they would distress them. It follows from the combination of the two premises that if they asked about them, there would appear to them what would distress them and not gladden them.

The second aspect in interpreting the verse: that the question is of two kinds. One is asking about something that was not permissible to mention in the Book and the Sunnah in any way; this question is forbidden by His saying: ﴿Do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾.

The second kind of question: asking about something that the Qur'an has revealed, but the listener did not understand it as he should; here the question is obligatory, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾. The benefit of mentioning this category is that when He forbade asking in the first verse, it might have given the impression that all kinds of questioning are forbidden, so He mentioned this to distinguish this category from that one.

If it is said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿And if you ask about them﴾ refers to the things mentioned in His saying ﴿Do not ask about things﴾; so how can it be conceived that asking about those very things is both forbidden and permitted at the same time?

We say: the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: it is permissible that asking about them was forbidden before the Qur'an was revealed concerning them, and was commanded after the Qur'an was revealed concerning them.

The second: although they are two different kinds, in that each of them concerns one and the same thing being asked about, therefore for this reason the unity of the pronoun is acceptable, even though in reality they are two different kinds.
