The third aspect in interpreting the verse: that His saying ﴿Do not ask about things﴾ indicates their questions about those things; so His saying ﴿And if you ask about them﴾, meaning, if you ask about those questions when the Qur'an is being revealed, it will be made clear to you whether those questions are permissible or not. The sum is that the intended meaning of this verse is that asking first is obligatory, so that it may be known whether it is permissible to ask about such and such or not.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God has pardoned it﴾, and in it are several aspects:

The first: God has pardoned what passed of your questions and of your angering the Messenger because of them, so do not return to the like of them.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned that those things which they asked about, if they were disclosed to them, would distress them; so He said: ﴿God has pardoned it﴾, meaning, pardoned what appears at those questions of what would distress you, weigh upon you, and be hard for you in the obligations.

The third: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, and the sense is: Do not ask about things which God has pardoned in the verse, ﴿if they were disclosed to you, they would distress you﴾. This is weak, because if the statement is sound without changing the arrangement, it is not permissible to resort to inversion. On this aspect, His saying ﴿God has pardoned it﴾ means: He withheld from it, refrained from mentioning it, and did not impose any obligation regarding it. This is like His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I have pardoned you regarding the charity of horses and slaves," meaning, I have lightened it for you by dropping it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾. This verse indicates that what is meant by His saying ﴿God has pardoned it﴾ is what we mentioned in the first aspect.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿A people before you asked about them, then they became disbelievers because of them﴾. The exegetes said: this refers to the people of Ṣāliḥ, who asked for the she-camel and then slaughtered her; and the people of Mūsā said: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, and that became a calamity upon them; and the Children of Israel ﴿said to a prophet of theirs: Raise up for us a king that we may fight in the way of God﴾, and He said: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them﴾, and ﴿They said: How can he have kingship over us when we are more worthy of kingship than him?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247]; so they asked for it and then disbelieved in it. And the people of ʿIsā asked for the table and then disbelieved in it. So it is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: Those people asked, and when they were given their request, that distressed them; so do not ask about things, lest if you are given your request, that distress you. If it is said: He, exalted is He, first said ﴿Do not ask about things﴾, and then here said ﴿A people before you asked about them﴾, and it would have been better to say: ﴿A people asked about them﴾; so what is the reason for this?

We say: the answer is from two aspects:

The first point: asking about a thing is an expression for asking about a state of it or an attribute of it, whereas asking for the thing itself means requesting that thing in its own right. One says "sa'altuhu dirhaman" (I asked him for a dirham), meaning I requested the dirham from him, and one says "sa'altuhu 'ani'l-dirham" (I asked him about the dirham), meaning I asked him about the description and characteristics of the dirham. Thus the earlier peoples asked God to bring forth the she-camel from the rock and to send down the table (al-ma'idah) from heaven; they were asking for the thing itself. As for the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), they did not ask for that; rather, they asked about the states and attributes of things. Since the two kinds of question differ in type, the expression also differs. Nevertheless, both kinds share one common quality: they are immersion in superfluities (fudul) and the undertaking of what is not needed, and in them lies the risk of harm (mafsadah). Something that is not needed and carries the risk of harm must be avoided by any sensible person. God, exalted is He, thereby made clear that the people of Muhammad (peace be upon him), in asking about the states of things, resemble those earlier peoples in asking for those things, in that each of these is superfluous and an immersion in what has no benefit.

The second point in the answer: the pronoun in His words ﴿قَدْ سَأَلَهَا﴾ (Indeed a people before you asked them) does not refer back to the things they asked about, but rather to their questions about those things. The meaning is: a people before you asked those corrupt questions that you have mentioned, and when they were answered, they became disbelievers because of them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 5, Verse 103**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿God has not instituted any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham﴾. There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** Know that when Almighty God forbade people from investigating matters they were not obligated to investigate, He likewise forbade them from binding themselves to matters they were not obligated to bind themselves to. Since the unbelievers used to forbid themselves the benefit of these animals even though they were in dire need of benefiting from them, God, exalted is He, explained that this was false, saying: ﴿God has not instituted any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham﴾.

**The second issue:** Know that it is said: fa'ala (did), 'amila (worked), taffa (began to), ja'ala (made), anshaa (created), and aqbala (turned toward). Some of these are more general than others, and the most general of them is fa'ala, because it applies to the actions of the limbs and the actions of the hearts. As for its applying to the actions of the limbs, this is evident. As for its applying to the actions of the hearts, the evidence for this is the statement of God, exalted is He: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him, neither we nor our fathers﴾, up to His statement: ﴿Thus did those before them act﴾ [an-Nahl: 33]. As for 'amila, it is more specific than fa'ala, because it applies only to the actions of the limbs, and it does not apply to resolve, determination, or intention. The evidence for this is the statement of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The intention of the believer is better than his deed." He made the intention better than the deed. So if the intention were a deed, it would follow that the intention is better than itself. As for ja'ala, it has several meanings:

First: judgment, as in His statement: ﴿They have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, into females﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 19].

Second: creation, as in His statement: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

Third: in the sense of making something become, as in His statement: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 3].

(Inna) [page break artifact in the source text]

Having understood this, we say: His statement ﴿God has not made﴾ means: God has not judged with that, nor legislated it, nor commanded it.

**The third issue:** God, exalted is He, mentioned four things here:

The first is the **bahira**. It is a form (fa'ila) from *bahr*, which means splitting. It is said: "He split (bahara) her camel," meaning he slit her ear. It has the meaning of the passive participle (maf'ul). Abu 'Ubayda and az-Zajjaj said: When a she-camel gave birth to five offspring and the last of them was a male, they would split the ear of the she-camel, refrain from riding her and slaughtering her, and let her loose for their idols. Her wool was not shorn, she was not loaded, she was not driven away from water, she was not prevented from pasture, and no benefit was taken from her. If an exhausted person encountered her, he would not ride her out of reluctance.

As for the **sa'iba**, it is an active participle (fa'ila) from *saba*, meaning to move across the surface of the earth. It is said: "The water flowed (saba)" and "the snake slithered (sabat)." So the sa'iba is the one left alone until she roams wherever she wishes. She is also the *musayyaba*, like 'ishatin radiya, in the sense of marḍiyya (pleasing). They mentioned several meanings for it:

First: what Abu 'Ubayda mentioned, namely that when a man fell ill, or returned from a journey, or made a vow, or gave thanks for a blessing, he would let a camel loose. It had the same status as the bahira in all the rulings they applied to it.

Second: al-Farra' said: When a she-camel gave birth to ten offspring, all of them female, she was let loose. She was not ridden, not milked, her wool was not shorn, and no one drank her milk except a child or a guest.

Third: Ibn 'Abbas said: The sa'iba is the one let loose for the idols, that is, freed for them. A man would let loose whatever he wished of his property, bring it to the *sadana* (the attendants, who were the servants of their gods), and they would feed the wayfarers from its milk.

Fourth: The sa'iba is the slave who is freed on the condition that he has no patronage (wala'), no blood-money obligation ('aql), and no inheritance.

As for the **wasila**, the exegetes said: If a ewe gave birth to a female, it was for them; if she gave birth to a male, it was for their gods; and if she gave birth to a male and a female, they said: she has joined (wasalat) her brother.

As for the **ham**, it is said: *hamahu yahmihi*, meaning he protected it, when he guarded it. There are several meanings for it:

First: the stallion camel, when the offspring of his offspring had been ridden, was said to have had his back protected (hama dhahrahu), that is, he was guarded from being ridden. He was not ridden, not loaded, and not prevented from water or pasture until he died, at which point men and women would eat him.

Second: when a she-camel had produced ten offspring, they said: she has protected her back (hamat dhahraha). Abu Muslim related this.

Third: the ham is the stallion who mates with camels for ten years and is then let go free. This is among the livestock whose backs were forbidden. This is the view of as-Suddi.

If it is said: If it is permissible to free slaves, male and female, then why is it not permissible to free these beasts from slaughter, from exhaustion, and from pain?

We say: Man was created to serve God, exalted is He, and to worship Him. So when he rebels against the obedience of God, exalted is He, he is punished by being placed under bondage. When bondage is removed from him, he is free to worship God, exalted is He, and this is a praiseworthy act of worship. As for these animals, they were created for the benefit of those who are obligated (the mukallafun). Therefore, leaving them and neglecting them entails the loss of a benefit to their owner, without anything in return. Thus the difference is evident. Furthermore, when a human who was a slave is freed, he becomes able to secure his own interests. But when a beast is freed and left alone, it cannot take care of its own interests, and so it falls into kinds of trouble more severe and harder than those it was in while it was owned. Thus the difference is evident.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God, and most of them do not reason﴾.

[p. 92]

The exegetes said: 'Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i had ruled Mecca, and he was the first to alter the religion of Isma'il. He took up idols, set up images, and instituted the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila, and the ham.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I saw him in the Fire, harming the people of the Fire with the stench of his intestines." The *qusub* is the intestine, and its plural is *aqsab*. It is also related as "dragging his intestines in the Fire."

Ibn 'Abbas said: His statement ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God﴾ refers to 'Amr ibn Luhayy and his companions, who attributed these falsehoods and fabrications to God in their prohibition of these livestock. The meaning is that the leaders invent lies against God, while as for the followers and the common people, most of them do not reason. Therefore, they inevitably invent these falsehoods against God by following those leaders.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾

The meaning is well known. It is a refutation of the people of taqlid (blind imitation), and we have fully explored the discussion of it in many places.

Know that the wāw in His saying ﴿أوَلَوْ كانَ آباؤُهُمْ﴾ (awa-law kāna ābā'uhum, "even though their fathers...") is the wāw of ḥāl (the circumstantial wāw), upon which the interrogative hamza of denunciation (hamzat al-inkār) has entered. Its implied sense is: "Do I reckon them to be thus, even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?"

Know that following (al-iqtidā') is only permissible with a scholar who is guided (al-ʿālim al-muhtadī). A person becomes a scholar who is guided only when he bases his speech upon proof and evidence. If he is not like that, he is not a guided scholar, and therefore it is obligatory that following him is not permissible.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 105:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, take care of yourselves. Those who go astray cannot harm you if you are guided.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

**The first issue:** When Allah had explained the various kinds of obligations, laws and rulings, and then said: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey, and Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾, up to His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "What we found our fathers doing is enough for us"﴾, it is as if He, exalted is He, said: these ignorant people, despite all the forms of emphasis that preceded in warning, admonition, encouragement and intimidation, have not benefited from any of it. Rather, they remained persistent in their ignorance, diligent in their ignorance and misguidance. So, O believers, do not be concerned with their ignorance and misguidance. Rather, be submissive to Allah's obligations, obedient to His commands and prohibitions, so their misguidance and ignorance will not harm you. Therefore He said: ﴿O you who believe, take care of yourselves. Those who go astray cannot harm you if you are guided.﴾

[p. 93]

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿عَلَيْكم أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ (ʿalaykum anfusakum), meaning: guard yourselves against involvement in sins and persistence in wrongdoing. The grammarians (al-nahwiyyun) said: ʿalayka, ʿindaka and dūnaka are among the ism al-fiʿl (verb-like nouns, words functioning as verbs). The Arabs say ʿalayka, ʿindaka and dūnaka, and they make them govern an object, placing them in the position of a verb, and they put the object in the accusative after them. It is said: ʿalayka Zaydan, as if it were said: "Take Zayd, for he has come upon you" (ʿalāka, i.e., he has approached you); ʿindaka Zaydan, i.e., he is present with you, so take him; and dūnaka, i.e., he is near you, so take him. There is no disagreement among the grammarians about permitting the accusative after these three particles. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf) reported the reading ﴿عَلَيْكم أنْفُسُكم﴾ with the nominative (rafʿ) from Nafiʿ.

**The third issue:** They mentioned several explanations for the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul):

The first: what al-Kalbi reported from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that: "When the Prophet ﷺ accepted the jizya (poll tax, a tax levied on non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule) from the People of the Book, and did not accept anything from the Arabs except Islam or the sword, the hypocrites reproached the believers for accepting the jizya from some disbelievers but not from others. So this verse was revealed: ﴿does not harm you﴾, i.e., the blame of those who blame, when you are upon guidance."

The second: that the believers were distressed by the continuation of the disbelievers in their disbelief and misguidance, so it was said to them: ﴿take care of yourselves﴾, and of what you are charged with of reforming them and walking them on the path of guidance. ﴿The misguidance of the misguided will not harm you﴾, nor the ignorance of the ignorant.

The third: that they used to grieve over their kinsmen when they died in disbelief, so they were forbidden from that. However, the closest view to me is that when He related about some of them that when it was said to them: ﴿Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "What we found our fathers doing is enough for us﴾, He mentioned this verse. Its purpose is to make clear that the believers should not imitate them in this corrupt way, but rather should remain firm in their religion, and know that the ignorance of those ignorant people will not harm them as long as they are firmly rooted in their religion and steadfast in it.

**The fourth issue:** If it is said: The apparent meaning of this verse suggests that enjoining good and forbidding evil is not obligatory.

We say: the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first, which is the view of most people: the verse does not indicate that. Rather, it establishes that the one who obeys his Lord will not be held accountable for the sins of the disobedient. As for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil, it is established by evidences. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, gave a sermon and said: "You recite this verse, ﴿O you who believe, take care of yourselves﴾, and you place it in other than its proper place. I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: ‘When people see wrongdoing and do not change it, it is near that Allah will encompass them all with punishment.’"

The second aspect concerning the interpretation of the verse: what is reported from Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿUmar, that they both said: His saying ﴿take care of yourselves﴾ refers to the end of time. Ibn Masʿud said when this verse was recited to him: "This is not its time. As long as your hearts are united, and you have not been clothed with factions, and some of you have not tasted the violence of others, then enjoin good and forbid evil. But when hearts and desires differ, and you are clothed with factions, and each person is left to himself, then the interpretation of this verse comes." This view, in my opinion, is weak, because His saying ﴿O you who believe﴾ is a general address, and it is also an address to those present. So how can one exclude the present and specify the absent?

The third aspect concerning the interpretation of the verse: what ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak held, when he said: "This is the most emphatic verse concerning the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. For He said: ﴿take care of yourselves﴾, meaning: take care of your co-religionists, and ﴿the misguidance of the misguided disbelievers will not harm you﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], meaning: your co-religionists. So His saying ﴿take care of yourselves﴾ means that some of you should admonish one another, encourage one another to good deeds, and deter one another from vices and evil deeds." What confirms this is what we explained: that His saying ﴿take care of yourselves﴾ means guard yourselves. So this is a command to guard ourselves, and if that guarding is not achieved except by enjoining good and forbidding evil, then it is obligatory.

The fourth aspect: the verse is specific to disbelievers whom it is known that admonition will not benefit, and who will not abandon disbelief because of enjoining good. In such a case, it is not obligatory for a person to command them to good. What confirms this view is what we mentioned concerning the occasion of revelation: that the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, when they reproached the Muslims for taking the jizya from the People of the Book but not from the polytheists.

The fifth aspect: the verse is specific to the case where a person, when enjoining good and forbidding evil, fears for himself, his honour or his property. In that case, his own self is safe, and the misguidance of one who goes astray and the ignorance of one who is ignorant does not harm him. Ibn Shubruma used to say: "Whoever flees from two has fled, and whoever flees from three has not fled."

The sixth aspect: "It will not harm you, when you are guided, that you enjoin good and forbid evil, the misguidance of one who goes astray and does not accept that."

The seventh aspect: ﴿take care of yourselves﴾ refers to performing the obligations, among which is enjoining good when able. If they do not accept that, then you should not feel estranged by it, for you have discharged your obligation, so the misguidance of others will not harm you.

The eighth aspect: He, exalted is He, said to His Messenger: ﴿So fight in the cause of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾ [al-Nisa’: 84]. That does not indicate that the command to enjoin good is lifted from the Messenger. So likewise here.

**The fifth issue:** It was read ﴿لا يَضُرَّكُمْ﴾ (lā yaḍurrakum) with a fatha on the raʾ, in the jussive mood, as an answer to His saying ﴿take care of yourselves﴾. It was also read with a damma on the raʾ, and in that there are two possibilities:

One: as a statement of fact, i.e., "the one who goes astray does not harm you."

The second: that its original form is the fatha as a response, but the raʾ was given a damma to match the damma of the ḍād.

[p. 94]

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾, meaning: your destination and the destination of those who opposed you, ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, i.e., He will recompense you for your deeds.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 106 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest⟩.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded the preservation of the self in His saying ﴿upon you is [the care of] yourselves⟩, He commanded the preservation of wealth in His saying ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you⟩. In this verse there are two issues.

The first issue: they agreed that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that Tamim al-Dari and his brother 'Adi were Christians who went out to Syria, and with them was Badil, the freedman of 'Amr ibn al-'As, who was a Muslim emigrant. They went out for trade. When they arrived in Syria, Badil fell ill, and he wrote a document containing a copy of everything he had, and placed it among the cloth, and did not inform his companions of this. Then he made them his executors and commanded them to deliver his property to his family when they returned. Badil died, and they took from his property a silver vessel inlaid with gold, worth three hundred mithqals, and they delivered the rest of the property to his family when they came back. The family searched and found the document, and in it was mention of the vessel. They said to Tamim and 'Adi: "Where is the vessel?" They said: "We do not know. Whatever was handed to us, we handed to you." So they brought the matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

The second issue: His saying ﴿testimony among you﴾ means the testimony of what is among you, and "what is among you" is a metaphor for dispute and contention. He attributed the testimony to the dispute because witnesses are only needed when a dispute arises. The omission of "what" (ma) from ﴿testimony among you﴾ is permissible since it is evident, and its parallel is His saying ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78], meaning "what is between me and you", and His saying ﴿there has been cut off between you﴾ [al-An'am: 94] according to the reading of the one who put it in the accusative. His saying ﴿when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest﴾ means the testimony needed at the approach of death. ﴿At the time of bequest⟩ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿when death approaches one of you⟩, because the time of the approach of death is the time of the bequest, so that time is identified by these two events occurring in it, as one says: "Come to me when the sun declines, at the time of the noon prayer." By the approach of death is meant its imminence and the appearance of its signs, as in His saying ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, that he make bequest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. They said: His saying ﴿when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest﴾ is evidence for the obligation of bequest, because He, exalted is He, made the time of the approach of death other than the time of bequest, and this would only be the case if they were mutually related, and this relation arises when bequest is obligatory.

﴿Two just men from among you, or two others from outside your own [community], if you are travelling in the land and the calamity of death befalls you. You shall detain them after the prayer, and they will swear by Allah, if you doubt, "We will not sell it for any price, even if it be to a near relative, nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed we would then be among the sinners."⟩

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Two just men from among you﴾, and in it there are two issues:

The first issue: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the meaning is that two just men from among you should bear witness. The estimated sense of the verse is: the testimony of what is among you at the stated time of death is that two just men from among you bear witness. This ellipsis is acceptable because it is known.

The second issue: the commentators differed concerning His saying "from among you" (minkum) on two views:

The first, which is the view of the majority of commentators: the meaning is "two just men from among you, O assembly of believers", that is, from the people of your religion and community. His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own [community], if you are travelling in the land﴾ means: or the testimony of two others from outside the people of your religion and community, when you are on a journey. So two just Muslims are acceptable as witnesses both at home and while travelling. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Shurayh, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin and Ibn Juraij. They said: if a person is in a foreign land and does not find a Muslim to call as a witness to his bequest, it is permissible for him to call a Jew, a Christian, a Magian, a worshipper of idols, or any disbeliever, and their testimony is accepted; and the testimony of disbelievers against Muslims is not permitted except in this case. Al-Sha'bi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: a man from among the Muslims fell ill in a foreign land, and he did not find any Muslim to call as a witness to his bequest, so he called two men from the People of the Book. They came to Kufa and went to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who was its governor, and they informed him of the event and presented his estate and his bequest. Abu Musa said: "This is a matter that did not occur after what happened in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him." Then he made them swear in the mosque of Kufa after the afternoon prayer, by Allah, that they had neither lied nor altered, and he accepted their testimony. Then, among those who held this view, some said: this ruling remains firm, and some said: it has been abrogated.

The second view, which is the view of al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and the majority of jurists, is that His saying ﴿just men from among you﴾ means from among your relatives, and His saying ﴿or two others from outside your [community]﴾ means from among strangers, ﴿if you are travelling in the land﴾, that is, if death is anticipated during a journey and there is no one with you from among your relatives, then call two strangers as witnesses to the bequest. They placed relatives first because they are more knowledgeable about the condition of the deceased, more affectionate toward him, and more merciful and compassionate toward his heirs. Those who went to the first view argued for the soundness of their position with several arguments:

The first argument: He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, thereby generalizing this address to all believers. So when He said after it ﴿or two others from outside your [community]﴾, the meaning is necessarily "or two others from outside all believers".

The second argument: He, exalted is He, said ﴿or two others from outside your [community], if you are travelling in the land﴾. This indicates that the permissibility of calling these two others as witnesses is conditional upon the one calling them being on a journey. Had these two witnesses been Muslims, the permissibility of calling them would not have been conditioned upon travel, since calling a Muslim as a witness is permitted both while travelling and at home.

The third argument: the verse indicates the obligation of taking an oath upon these two witnesses after the prayer, and the Muslims agree that a Muslim witness is not obliged to take an oath. So we know that these two witnesses are not Muslims.

The fourth argument: the occasion of revelation of this verse is what we have mentioned, the testimony of the two Christians concerning Badil, who was a Muslim.

The fifth argument: what we have related, that Abu Musa al-Ash'ari judged by the testimony of the two Jews after he had made them swear, and no one among the Companions objected to him, so that was a consensus.

The sixth argument: we only permit calling disbelievers as witnesses when we do not find anyone from among the Muslims, and necessities permit what is forbidden. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, permitted tayammum, shortening of the prayer, breaking the fast in Ramadan, and eating carrion in a state of necessity? And necessity is present in this matter, because when a Muslim's end draws near in a foreign land and he does not find a Muslim to call as a witness to himself, and the testimony of disbelievers is not accepted, he will lose most of his important affairs, for perhaps zakat and expiations were due upon him and he did not pay them, and perhaps he had deposits or debts that were in his liability. Just as the testimony of women is accepted regarding matters that pertain to women's affairs, such as menstruation, pregnancy, childbirth and the cry of a newborn, because men cannot be present at these conditions, we are content in these matters with the testimony of women out of necessity, so likewise here. As for the one who says that this ruling has been abrogated, it is far-fetched, because most of the Ummah agrees that Surat al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, and there is no abrogated ruling in it.

Those who held the second view argued with His saying: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], and a disbeliever is not just.

The first responded to this: why is it not permissible that by "just" is meant one who is just in refraining from lying, not one who is just in religion and belief? The proof of this is that we have agreed on the acceptance of the testimony of people of desires and innovations, even though they are not just in their doctrines; but since they were just in refraining from lying, we accepted their testimony, so likewise here. Even if we grant that a disbeliever is not just, His saying ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ is general, whereas His saying in this verse ﴿two just men from among you or two others from outside your [community], if you are travelling in the land﴾ is specific, for it required the testimony of a just man from among us when at home, and sufficed with the testimony of one who is not from among us when travelling. So this verse is specific, and the verse you cited is general, and the specific takes precedence over the general, especially when the specific is later in revelation, and there is no doubt that Surat al-Ma'idah is late. So giving precedence to this specific verse over the general verse you cited is obligatory by consensus, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿or two others from outside your [community], if you are travelling in the land and the calamity of death befalls you﴾.

In it there are two issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿or two others﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿two﴾, and the estimated sense is: the testimony of your [community] is that two from among you bear witness, or two others from outside your [community].

The second issue: His saying ﴿if you are travelling in the land and the calamity of death befalls you﴾ is intended to clarify that the permissibility of calling two others from outside is conditional upon the one calling them being a traveller journeying in the land, and the signs of the approach of death having appeared upon him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You shall detain them after the prayer﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: ﴿tahbisunahuma⟩ (you shall detain them), that is, you shall stop them, as a man says: "So-and-so passed by me on a horse and halted his mount over me," that is, stopped it; and "I detained the man on the road to speak with him," that is, I stopped him.

If it is asked: what is the grammatical position of ﴿you shall detain them﴾?

We say: it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if it were said: "How shall we act if doubt arises concerning them?" And it was said: "You shall detain them."

The second issue: His saying ﴿after the prayer﴾ has several views. The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: after the prayer of the people of their religion.

The second: the majority of commentators said: after the afternoon prayer (al-'asr).

If it is asked: how was it known that the meaning is the afternoon prayer, given that what is mentioned is the prayer in general?

We say: this specification was known through several considerations:

One: this time was well known among them for taking oaths after it, so restriction by what is known and famous dispensed with restriction by explicit wording.

Second: it was reported that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the afternoon prayer, summoned 'Adi and Tamim, and had them swear at the pulpit, so the Messenger's action became evidence for the restriction.

Third: all the people of the religions venerate this time, mention Allah in it, and guard against false oaths, and the People of the Book pray at sunrise and sunset.

The third view: al-Hasan said: the meaning is after the noon prayer or after the afternoon prayer, because the people of the Hijaz used to sit for judgement after these two.

The fourth view: the meaning is after performing the prayer, whatever prayer it may be, and the purpose of taking the oath after establishing the prayer is that the prayer forbids indecency and evil, so the oath-taker's avoidance of lying at that time is more complete and perfect, and Allah knows best.

The third issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: oaths are made more solemn in cases of blood, divorce, manumission, and property when it reaches two hundred dirhams, according to time and place. So he swears after the afternoon prayer in Mecca between the Corner and the Station, in Medina at the pulpit, in Jerusalem at the Rock, and in the rest of the lands in the noblest of the mosques. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: he swears without the oath being restricted to any time or place, and this is contrary to the verse, and because the purpose of it is to inspire awe and exalt. Without doubt, what al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned is stronger.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They shall swear by God: "If you doubt them, we will not sell it for any price, even if it concerns a relative."﴾ On this there are several issues:

First issue: The fa' in His saying ﴿They shall swear by God﴾ is for the consequence (jaza'), meaning: you detain the two of them, and they then come forward to swear because of that detention.

Second issue: His saying ﴿If you doubt them﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) between the oath and what is sworn to. The meaning is: if you have doubts about the two of them and suspect them, then make them swear. By this, those who say the verse was revealed concerning the testimony of disbelievers argue, because having a Muslim witness swear is not permitted. Whoever says the verse was revealed concerning a Muslim, says it has been abrogated (mansukhah). It is reported from 'Ali, peace be upon him, that he used to have a witness and a narrator swear when there was suspicion.

Third issue: His saying ﴿We will not sell it for any price﴾ means: they swear by God that we will not sell the covenant of God for any worldly thing, saying: "We will not take for it any price." This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who exchange the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77], that is, we will not take and will not substitute. Whoever sells something has in fact bought its price. His saying ﴿even if it concerns a relative﴾ means: we will not sell the covenant of God for anything of this world, even if that thing is a gift to a relative or to oneself. He singled out the relative for mention because the inclination toward them is most complete and the flattery on their account is greatest. This is like His saying: ﴿Be upholders of justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves or parents and close relatives﴾ [An-Nisa': 135].
* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of God﴾. On this there are two issues:

First issue: This is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon His saying ﴿We will not sell it for any price﴾, meaning that they swear while saying: "We will not sell it for any price, nor will we conceal the testimony of God," that is, the testimony which God commanded to be preserved and made known.

Second issue: It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he paused at His saying "testimony" (shahadatan), then began "Allahi" with a prolonged alif (al-madd), by dropping the particle of oath and replacing it with the interrogative particle. It is also reported from him without prolongation, in accordance with what Sibawayh mentioned, that some of them say: "Allahi, certainly it was such-and-such," and the meaning is "tallahi" (by God).
* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinners﴾, meaning: if we conceal it, we would be among the sinners.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verses 107–108:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then if it is discovered that the two had committed a sin﴾. Al-Layth, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "'Athara al-rajulu ya'thuru 'uthuran" means: when a man comes upon a matter that no one else has come upon. "A'thartu fulanan 'ala amri" means: I made so-and-so aware of my affair, i.e., I informed him of it. "'Athara al-rajulu ya'thuru 'athratan" means: when he stumbles upon something. The lexicographers said: the root of 'athara in the sense of "to become aware" derives from the 'athrah (stumble), which is falling. This is because the one who stumbles only stumbles over a thing he did not see. So when he stumbles over it, he becomes aware of it and looks at what it is. Hence it is said of everyone who becomes aware of a matter that was hidden from him: "'athara 'alayhi" (he has discovered it). And "a'thara ghayrahu" means: when he informs him of it. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And thus We made them known to them﴾ [al-Kahf: 21], i.e., We informed them. The meaning of the verse is: if the discovery and the awareness occur that the two had committed a treachery and incurred sin through the false oath.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then two others from among those who have the prior claim, will stand in their place﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the meaning of the verse is: if, after the two executors have sworn, it is discovered that they incurred sin, i.e., that they broke the oath by lying in a statement or by betraying property, then two men from the relatives of the deceased will stand in the oath in their place, and they will swear by Allah: "We have indeed found the two non-Muslims to have betrayed, lied, and altered, and we have not transgressed in this, nor have we lied." It is reported that when the first verse was revealed, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed the afternoon prayer and summoned Tamim and 'Adi, and made them swear by the side of the pulpit, by Allah, besides whom there is no god, that no betrayal had been found in this property among us. When they swore, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) let them go, and they concealed the vessel for a period. Then it came to light, and they differed. It was said: it was found in Makkah. It was also said: when the period lengthened, they brought out the vessel, and this reached the Banu Sahm, who confronted them. They said: 'We had bought it from him.' They (the Banu Sahm) said: 'Did we not tell you: has our companion sold anything, and you said no?' They said: 'We had no evidence, so we disliked being discovered, and so we concealed it.' The matter was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed: ﴿Then if it is discovered﴾ up to the end of the verse. 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Rifa'ah of the Banu Sahm then stood and swore by Allah after the afternoon prayer, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) handed the vessel to them and to the heirs of the deceased."

Tamim al-Dari used to say after he had embraced Islam: "Allah and His Messenger spoke the truth. I took the vessel, and I repent to Allah the Exalted."

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this incident remained hidden until Tamim al-Dari embraced Islam. When he embraced Islam, he informed of it and said: "I swore falsely. My companion and I sold the vessel for a thousand and divided the price." Then he paid five hundred dirhams from his own share, took five hundred from his companion, and paid the thousand to the heirs (mawali) of the deceased.

The second issue: His saying ﴿two others standing in their place﴾ means: in place of the two witnesses who are not of their religion. His saying ﴿from among those who have the prior claim﴾ refers to the heirs (mawali) of the deceased. People have said much about why the heirs of the deceased were described with this description, but the most correct view in my opinion is one aspect only: they were described thus because, when their property was taken, their right to it became established against them. Whoever takes another's property has sought to make his attachment to that property dominate the owner's attachment to it, so it is correct to describe the owner as having a claim over that property.

The third issue: As for His saying ﴿the two with the prior claim﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: that the predicate of the subject is omitted, and the sense is: "they are the two with the prior claim." This is because, when He said ﴿two others standing in their place﴾, it was as if it were said: "And who are they?" So it was said: "the two with the prior claim."

The second: that it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yaqumani," and the sense is: "the two with the prior claim will stand."

The third: al-Akhfash permitted that His saying ﴿al-awlayani﴾ be an attribute (sifah) of His saying ﴿two others﴾. This is because an indefinite noun, when its mention has preceded and then reference is made back to it, becomes definite, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿like a niche in which is a lamp﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. So "misbah" (lamp) is indefinite, then He said "al-misbah" (the lamp), then He said "fi zujajah" (in a glass), then He said "al-zujajah" (the glass). This is like your saying: "I saw a man," then a person says: "Who is the man?" So by returning to its mention it becomes definite.

The fourth: it is permissible that His saying ﴿al-awlayani﴾ be a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿two others﴾, and the substitution of a definite for an indefinite is common.

The fourth issue: He described them as "two with the prior claim" for two reasons:

The first: the meaning of "al-awlayani" is "the two nearest to the deceased."

The second: it is permissible that the meaning is "the two with the prior claim by the oath," and the reason for this is that the two executors had claimed that the deceased had sold the silver vessel, so the oath passed to the heirs of the deceased, because the two executors had claimed that their testator had sold the vessel while they denied that. So the oath became their right. This is like the case where a person acknowledges a debt to another and then claims that he has paid it: it is ruled that the oath is returned to the one who first claimed the debt, because he has become the defendant in asserting that he has fulfilled it.

The fifth issue: The well-known reading of the majority is ﴿istahakka﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', and "al-awlayani" is the dual of "al-uwla." We have mentioned its basis. The reading of Hamzah and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr is "al-awwalin" in the plural, and it is an epithet for all the heirs mentioned in His saying ﴿from among those who have the prior claim (istahakka 'alayhim)﴾. Its sense is: "from among the first ones whose property was taken from them." They were called "the first ones" because they were mentioned first in the wording. Do you not see that ﴿O you who believe, the testimony between you﴾ had preceded, and likewise ﴿two persons of justice among you﴾ was mentioned verbally before His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾. Hafs alone read ﴿al-awlayani﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', in the dual. Its basis is that the two executors whose betrayal became apparent were more entitled than others by reason that the deceased had appointed them for the executorship. And when they betrayed the property of the heirs, it became correct to say that the heirs had the prior claim over them, i.e., the two executors betrayed their property. al-Hasan read "al-awwalani," and its basis is evident from what has preceded.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers."﴾

The meaning is clear: that is, we have not transgressed in pursuing this property, nor in attributing betrayal to them. His saying ﴿indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers﴾ means: indeed, if we swore while certain of the lie, believing in falsehood and vanity, we would then be among the wrongdoers.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is more likely to bring the testimony in its proper form, or they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths.﴾

The meaning: that ruling which We have mentioned and the method which We have legislated is closer to bringing the testimony in its proper form, and that they would not bring the testimony not in its proper form; rather, they fear that they would swear to what they have mentioned, out of fear that oaths would be returned to the heirs after their oaths, so their lie would become apparent and they would be disgraced among the people.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾

The meaning: fear Allah lest you betray in trusts, and listen to the admonitions of Allah, i.e., act upon them and obey Allah in them. ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾: this is a threat and warning to whoever opposes the judgment and commands of Allah. This is the statement on the interpretation of this verse, which the exegetes agreed is of extreme difficulty in grammar, composition and ruling. al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated in "al-Basit" from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "This verse is the most intricate of the rulings in this surah." The ruling we have mentioned in this verse is abrogated according to most jurists, and Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verses 107–108:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then if it is discovered that the two had committed a sin﴾. Al-Layth, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "'Athara al-rajulu ya'thuru 'uthuran" means: when a man comes upon a matter that no one else has come upon. "A'thartu fulanan 'ala amri" means: I made so-and-so aware of my affair, i.e., I informed him of it. "'Athara al-rajulu ya'thuru 'athratan" means: when he stumbles upon something. The lexicographers said: the root of 'athara in the sense of "to become aware" derives from the 'athrah (stumble), which is falling. This is because the one who stumbles only stumbles over a thing he did not see. So when he stumbles over it, he becomes aware of it and looks at what it is. Hence it is said of everyone who becomes aware of a matter that was hidden from him: "'athara 'alayhi" (he has discovered it). And "a'thara ghayrahu" means: when he informs him of it. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And thus We made them known to them﴾ [al-Kahf: 21], i.e., We informed them. The meaning of the verse is: if the discovery and the awareness occur that the two had committed a treachery and incurred sin through the false oath.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then two others from among those who have the prior claim, will stand in their place﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the meaning of the verse is: if, after the two executors have sworn, it is discovered that they incurred sin, i.e., that they broke the oath by lying in a statement or by betraying property, then two men from the relatives of the deceased will stand in the oath in their place, and they will swear by Allah: "We have indeed found the two non-Muslims to have betrayed, lied, and altered, and we have not transgressed in this, nor have we lied." It is reported that when the first verse was revealed, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed the afternoon prayer and summoned Tamim and 'Adi, and made them swear by the side of the pulpit, by Allah, besides whom there is no god, that no betrayal had been found in this property among us. When they swore, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) let them go, and they concealed the vessel for a period. Then it came to light, and they differed. It was said: it was found in Makkah. It was also said: when the period lengthened, they brought out the vessel, and this reached the Banu Sahm, who confronted them. They said: 'We had bought it from him.' They (the Banu Sahm) said: 'Did we not tell you: has our companion sold anything, and you said no?' They said: 'We had no evidence, so we disliked being discovered, and so we concealed it.' The matter was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed: ﴿Then if it is discovered﴾ up to the end of the verse. 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Rifa'ah of the Banu Sahm then stood and swore by Allah after the afternoon prayer, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) handed the vessel to them and to the heirs of the deceased."

Tamim al-Dari used to say after he had embraced Islam: "Allah and His Messenger spoke the truth. I took the vessel, and I repent to Allah the Exalted."

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this incident remained hidden until Tamim al-Dari embraced Islam. When he embraced Islam, he informed of it and said: "I swore falsely. My companion and I sold the vessel for a thousand and divided the price." Then he paid five hundred dirhams from his own share, took five hundred from his companion, and paid the thousand to the heirs (mawali) of the deceased.

The second issue: His saying ﴿two others standing in their place﴾ means: in place of the two witnesses who are not of their religion. His saying ﴿from among those who have the prior claim﴾ refers to the heirs (mawali) of the deceased. People have said much about why the heirs of the deceased were described with this description, but the most correct view in my opinion is one aspect only: they were described thus because, when their property was taken, their right to it became established against them. Whoever takes another's property has sought to make his attachment to that property dominate the owner's attachment to it, so it is correct to describe the owner as having a claim over that property.

The third issue: As for His saying ﴿the two with the prior claim﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: that the predicate of the subject is omitted, and the sense is: "they are the two with the prior claim." This is because, when He said ﴿two others standing in their place﴾, it was as if it were said: "And who are they?" So it was said: "the two with the prior claim."

The second: that it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yaqumani," and the sense is: "the two with the prior claim will stand."

The third: al-Akhfash permitted that His saying ﴿al-awlayani﴾ be an attribute (sifah) of His saying ﴿two others﴾. This is because an indefinite noun, when its mention has preceded and then reference is made back to it, becomes definite, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿like a niche in which is a lamp﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. So "misbah" (lamp) is indefinite, then He said "al-misbah" (the lamp), then He said "fi zujajah" (in a glass), then He said "al-zujajah" (the glass). This is like your saying: "I saw a man," then a person says: "Who is the man?" So by returning to its mention it becomes definite.

The fourth: it is permissible that His saying ﴿al-awlayani﴾ be a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿two others﴾, and the substitution of a definite for an indefinite is common.

The fourth issue: He described them as "two with the prior claim" for two reasons:

The first: the meaning of "al-awlayani" is "the two nearest to the deceased."

The second: it is permissible that the meaning is "the two with the prior claim by the oath," and the reason for this is that the two executors had claimed that the deceased had sold the silver vessel, so the oath passed to the heirs of the deceased, because the two executors had claimed that their testator had sold the vessel while they denied that. So the oath became their right. This is like the case where a person acknowledges a debt to another and then claims that he has paid it: it is ruled that the oath is returned to the one who first claimed the debt, because he has become the defendant in asserting that he has fulfilled it.

The fifth issue: The well-known reading of the majority is ﴿istahakka﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', and "al-awlayani" is the dual of "al-uwla." We have mentioned its basis. The reading of Hamzah and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr is "al-awwalin" in the plural, and it is an epithet for all the heirs mentioned in His saying ﴿from among those who have the prior claim (istahakka 'alayhim)﴾. Its sense is: "from among the first ones whose property was taken from them." They were called "the first ones" because they were mentioned first in the wording. Do you not see that ﴿O you who believe, the testimony between you﴾ had preceded, and likewise ﴿two persons of justice among you﴾ was mentioned verbally before His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾. Hafs alone read ﴿al-awlayani﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', in the dual. Its basis is that the two executors whose betrayal became apparent were more entitled than others by reason that the deceased had appointed them for the executorship. And when they betrayed the property of the heirs, it became correct to say that the heirs had the prior claim over them, i.e., the two executors betrayed their property. al-Hasan read "al-awwalani," and its basis is evident from what has preceded.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers."﴾

The meaning is clear: that is, we have not transgressed in pursuing this property, nor in attributing betrayal to them. His saying ﴿indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers﴾ means: indeed, if we swore while certain of the lie, believing in falsehood and vanity, we would then be among the wrongdoers.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is more likely to bring the testimony in its proper form, or they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths.﴾

The meaning: that ruling which We have mentioned and the method which We have legislated is closer to bringing the testimony in its proper form, and that they would not bring the testimony not in its proper form; rather, they fear that they would swear to what they have mentioned, out of fear that oaths would be returned to the heirs after their oaths, so their lie would become apparent and they would be disgraced among the people.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾

The meaning: fear Allah lest you betray in trusts, and listen to the admonitions of Allah, i.e., act upon them and obey Allah in them. ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾: this is a threat and warning to whoever opposes the judgment and commands of Allah. This is the statement on the interpretation of this verse, which the exegetes agreed is of extreme difficulty in grammar, composition and ruling. al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated in "al-Basit" from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "This verse is the most intricate of the rulings in this surah." The ruling we have mentioned in this verse is abrogated according to most jurists, and Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 109:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers and say, "What was the response you received?"﴾.

Know that it is the custom of Allah, exalted is He, in this Noble Book that whenever He mentions many kinds of laws (shara'i'), obligations (taklif) and rulings (ahkam), He follows them either with matters of divinity (ilahiyyat), or with an explanation of the states of the Prophets, or with an explanation of the states of the Resurrection, so that this serves to reinforce what has been mentioned before of obligations and laws. Therefore, when He had mentioned before many kinds of laws, He followed them first with a description of the states of the Resurrection, and then He mentioned the states of ʿIsa. As for the description of the states of the Resurrection, it is His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: regarding this verse there are two opinions. One of them is that it is connected to what precedes it, and on this assumption there are two views:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: its implied meaning is, "And fear Allah on the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers." It is not permissible for it to be in the accusative of time (zarf) governed by this verb, because they were not commanded to be mindful of Allah on that Day, but it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

The second: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is permissible that the implied meaning be: "And Allah does not guide the wicked people on the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers," that is, He does not guide them to Paradise, as He said: ﴿Nor to guide them to a path, ﴿except the path of Hell﴾ [al-Nisa': 169].

The second opinion: that it is disconnected from what precedes it, and on this assumption there are two views:

The first: that the implied meaning is: "Remember the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers."

The second: that the implied meaning is: "On the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers, such-and-such will be the case."

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying (ma-dha) is in the accusative governed by (ajabtum) as the accusative of its verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "What kind of response were you answered with? A response of denial or a response of affirmation?" Had the answer been intended, it would have been said: "With what were you answered?" If it is asked: What is the benefit of this question? We say: it is a rebuke of their people, just as His saying: ﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked, ﴿for what sin she was killed﴾ [al-Takwir: 8–9], the purpose of it is to rebuke the one who committed that act.

* The third issue: The apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen"﴾ indicates that the Prophets do not bear witness for their nations. The reconciliation of this with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness and We bring you against these as a witness?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41] is problematic. Also, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a just nation that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]; so if our nation bears witness for the rest of mankind, then the Prophets are more worthy of bearing witness for their nations.

The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: a group of the exegetes said: the Resurrection has tremors and terrors, to the extent that hearts depart from their places upon witnessing them. So the Prophets, peace be upon them, at the witnessing of those terrors forget most matters, and therefore they say, "We have no knowledge." Then when their hearts return to them, at that point they bear witness for the nations. This answer, although a great multitude of the eminent scholars held it, is weak in my view; because He, exalted is He, said concerning the people of reward: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103], and He also said: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing﴾ [Abasa: 38–39]. Rather, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteousness—will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62]. So how could the state of the Prophets and Messengers be less than that? It is well known that if they were afraid they would be of lower rank than those about whom Allah, exalted is He, informed that they will absolutely not fear.

The second aspect: that what is meant by it is exaggeration in establishing their disgrace, like someone who says to another: "What do you say about so-and-so?" and he replies: "You know about him better than I do," as if it were said: "There is no need for testimony concerning him, because it is evident." This too is not strong; because the question was asked about the whole nation, and not all the nation were disbelievers, so that the Messengers would intend by the negation a rebuke and disgrace of them.

The third aspect in the answer, and it is the most correct, and it is the one chosen by Ibn ʿAbbas: that they only said, "We have no knowledge," because You know what they manifested and what they concealed, while we know only what they manifested. So Your knowledge of them is more penetrating than our knowledge. For this reason they negated knowledge from themselves, because their knowledge in the sight of Allah is as no knowledge.

The fourth aspect in the answer: that they said, "We have no knowledge," except that we knew their response to us during our lifetime, and we do not know what came from them after our death; and reward and recompense are based on the final outcome, and that is not known to us. For this reason they said, "We have no knowledge." His saying, ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ bears witness to the soundness of these two answers.

The fifth aspect, which occurred to me at the time of writing: it has been established in the science of the principles of jurisprudence (ʿilm al-usul) that knowledge is one thing and conjecture (zann) is another, and what is obtained by anyone regarding the states of others is only conjecture, not knowledge. For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "We judge by the outward, and Allah takes care of the inner secrets," and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, you bring your disputes before me, and perhaps some of you is more eloquent in his argument, so whoever I give a judgment in his favor which is not his right, I have cut for him a piece of the Fire," or words to this effect. So the Prophets said: "We have absolutely no knowledge of their states; what we have obtained of their states is only conjecture, and conjecture was regarded in this world, because the rulings in this world were based on conjecture. As for the Hereafter, there is no regard for conjecture in it, because the rulings in the Hereafter are based on the realities of things and the inner aspects of matters. For this reason they said: ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾, and they did not at all mention the conjecture they had, because conjecture has no weight on the Day of Resurrection.

The sixth aspect: that when they knew that He, glorified and exalted is He, is the All-Knowing who does not ignore, the All-Wise who does not act foolishly, the Just who does not wrong, they knew that their saying would bring no benefit and would ward off no harm; so they saw that good manners lie in silence and in entrusting the matter to the justice of the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting, who never dies.

The fourth issue: It is read (ʿallamu al-ghuyub) with the accusative. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the implied meaning is that the speech is complete with His saying: ﴿Indeed, You are﴾, meaning: You are the One described by Your well-known attributes of knowledge and others. Then (ʿallama al-ghuyub) is in the accusative as an expression of specification (ikhtisas), or as a vocative (nida'), or as a description of the subject of (inna).

The fifth issue: The verse indicates the permissibility of applying the word al-ʿAllam (the All-Knowing) to Him, just as it is permissible to apply the word al-Khallaq (the Creator) to Him. As for al-ʿAllamah (the one who knows abundantly), they have unanimously agreed that it is not permissible to apply it to Him, and perhaps the reason is the feminine form of the word that it contains.

[p. 103]

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 5, verses 110–111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When God said, "O Jesus son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you and upon your mother"﴾. There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** Know that we have explained that the purpose of His saying, may He be exalted, to the Messengers, ﴿What response did you receive?﴾, is to rebuke those among their nations who rebelled. The nation most in need of rebuke and censure is the Christians, who claim to be the followers of Jesus, peace be upon him. This is because the criticism of the other nations was limited to the prophets, whereas the criticism of these accursed people extended to the majesty and grandeur of God, in that they ascribed to Him what no rational person would ascribe to God, namely taking a wife and a son. Therefore God, may He be exalted, mentioned that He would enumerate the kinds of His blessings upon Jesus in the presence of the Messengers, one by one. The intent of this is to rebuke the Christians and reprimand them for the evil of their saying, since each one of those enumerated blessings upon Jesus indicates that he is a servant and not a god. The benefit of this narrative is to alert the Christians who were living at the time this verse was revealed to the ugliness of their saying and the feebleness of their creed and belief.

**The second issue:** The position of ﴿idh﴾ (when) may be in the nominative case as a subject, meaning: "That is when God said," and it may be that the meaning is: "Remember when God said."

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿When God said﴾ is expressed in the past tense rather than the future, and there are several reasons for this:

The first: it indicates the nearness of the Resurrection, so that it is as if it has already arisen and occurred, since everything that is coming is near. It is said: "The army has come" when their arrival is near. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿The command of God has come﴾ (al-Nahl: 1).

The second: it is a narration of a present state (*hikayat al-hal*, the narration of a state as if it were present). A parallel to this is a man saying to his companion: "It is as if you and I have entered such-and-such a town and done such-and-such there, when a crier cried out and you left me and answered him." A parallel to it in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified, with no escape﴾ (Saba': 51); ﴿If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve﴾ (al-Anfal: 50); ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾ (Saba': 31). The reason in all these verses is what we have mentioned, namely that it is expressed by way of narrating the state.

**The fourth issue:** ﴿Jesus son of Mary﴾ — "Jesus" may be in the nominative case, since it is a singular vocative (*munada*) described by an annexed noun. It may also be in the accusative case, since it is intended as an annexation, and then "son" was made an emphasis (*tawkid*). Anything similar to this allows two possibilities, as in *ya Zayd ibn ʿAmr* and *ya Zaydu ibn ʿAmr*. The grammarians have recited:

*O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud*

with the first (noun) in the nominative or the accusative, as we have explained.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿My blessing upon you﴾ intends the plural, like His saying: ﴿If you tried to count God's blessings, you could not number them﴾ (al-Nahl: 18). This is permissible because it is an annexed noun that can refer to a genus.

Know that God, may He be exalted, explained His blessing upon him by several matters, the first of which is His saying: ﴿When I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾. There are two views concerning it:

The first: The Holy Spirit is Gabriel, peace be upon him. "The Spirit" is Gabriel and "the Holy" is God, as if He annexed him to Himself in honour of him.

The second: Souls differ in their essence. Some are pure and luminous, some are wicked and dark, some are radiant, some are turbid, some are good, and some are base. For this reason he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Souls are armies mustered" (a *hadith*). God, may He be exalted, singled out Jesus with the pure, luminous, radiant, sublime, and good spirit. Someone may say: Since this verse indicates that the strengthening of Jesus came from Gabriel or through his particular spirit, this casts doubt on the evidence of miracles for the truthfulness of the Messengers. For before we know the infallibility of Gabriel, we may permit that he helped Jesus in this, in order to lead people astray and mislead them. So, as long as the infallibility of Gabriel is not known, this objection is not removed; and as long as the prophethood of Jesus, peace be upon him, is not known, the infallibility of Gabriel is not known, so a circularity arises. The answer to this is what is established in our principle, that the Creator is none other than God, and by this the objection is removed.

The second of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾. As for Jesus' speech in the cradle, it is his saying: ﴿I am a servant of God; He has given me the Scripture﴾ (Maryam: 30). His saying ﴿You spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*, a clause or phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). The meaning is: he speaks to them as a child and as a grown man, without his speech differing between these two times. This is a noble distinction which he possessed, and which none of the prophets before him or after him attained.

The third of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when I taught you the Book, the Wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel﴾.

Concerning "the Book" there are two views. One is that it means writing, which is script. The other is that it means the genus of books, since a person first learns short and easy books, then ascends from them to the noble books. As for "the Wisdom," it refers to the theoretical sciences and the practical sciences. Then He mentioned after it "the Torah and the Gospel," and concerning this there are two views:

The first: they were singled out for mention after the mention of the books as a mark of honour, like His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ (al-Baqarah: 238), and His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ (al-Ahzab: 7).

The second, which is the stronger: the grasp of the secrets of the divine books is attained only by one who has become proficient in the various kinds of the apparent legal and rational sciences which scholars investigate. Thus His saying "the Torah and the Gospel" refers to the secrets which no one comprehends except the greatest of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace.

* * *

The fourth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you shaped from clay the likeness of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it, and it became a bird by My permission﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Nafi' recited ﴿fa-takūnu ṭā'iran﴾ (it becomes a bird), and the others recited ﴿ṭayran﴾ without an *alif*. *Ṭayr* is the plural of *ṭa'ir*, like *ḍa'n* and *ḍa'in*, and *rakb* and *rakib*.

**The second issue:** Here He mentioned ﴿then you breathed into it﴾ (*fa-tanfukhu fīhā*, with feminine pronoun), while in Al ʿImran He mentioned ﴿then I breathe into it﴾ (*fa-anfukhu fīhi*, with masculine pronoun).

The answer: His saying ﴿the likeness of a bird﴾ means a form like the form of a bird. So His saying ﴿then you breathe into it﴾ has its pronoun referring to the *kāf* (the "like" of the likeness), because it is the description of the form which Jesus would create and breathe into; it does not refer to the form which is annexed to it, because that is not of his creation nor of his breathing in any way.

Having understood this, we say: the *kāf* is made feminine according to meaning, because it indicates the form which is like the form of a bird, and it is made masculine according to its outward form. Since this is so, it is permissible for the pronoun referring to it to occur sometimes in the masculine and sometimes in the feminine.

**The third issue:** He, may He be exalted, stipulated permission in the creation of the clay in the likeness of a bird, and in its becoming that thing a bird. He repeated His saying ﴿by My permission﴾ to emphasise that this occurred by the power of God, may He be exalted, and His creating it, not by the power of Jesus or his bringing it into being.

Fifth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you healed the blind-born and the leper by My permission﴾. The healing of the blind-born (*al-akmah*) and the leper is well known. Al-Khalili said: the *akmah* is one who was born blind, and the *a'ma* is one who was born seeing and then became blind.

Sixth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you brought the dead out by My permission﴾, that is, when you brought the dead out of their graves alive by My permission, i.e., by My doing that at your supplication, and at your saying to the dead: "Come out by God's permission from your grave." The mention of permission in these actions is only in the sense of attributing the real act to God, may He be exalted, like His saying: ﴿No soul can die except by God's permission﴾ (Al ʿImran: 145), meaning: except by God's creating death in it.

Seventh of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear signs﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

[p. 105]

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿when you came to them with the clear signs﴾ may mean these clear signs which were mentioned earlier; in this case the *alif* and *lam* are for previous reference. It may also mean the genus of clear signs.

**The second issue:** It is narrated that when he, peace and blessings be upon him, displayed these wondrous miracles, the Jews intended to kill him, but God, may He be exalted, rescued him from them by raising him to heaven.

* * *

Then God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Those of them who disbelieved said, "This is nothing but clear magic"﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *sahir* (a magician) with an *alif*, and likewise in Yunus, Hud, and al-Saff. Ibn ʿAmir and ʿAsim recited it with an *alif* only in Yunus, and the others recited *sihr* (magic). Whoever recited *sahir* indicates the man, and whoever recited *sihr* indicates by it what he brought. Both are good, because each of them has been mentioned before. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: the preferred reading is *sihr*, because it may be applied to the event and to the person. As for its application to the event, it is obvious. As for its application to the person, you say: "This is magic," meaning: "one who possesses magic," as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But righteousness is in him who believes﴾ (al-Baqarah: 177), meaning: one who has righteousness. The poet said:

*For it is only advance and retreat*

**The second issue:** If it is said: He, may He be exalted, began here to enumerate His blessings upon Jesus, peace be upon him, and the saying of the disbelievers about him, ﴿This is nothing but clear magic﴾, is not one of the blessings, so how did He mention it here?

The answer: Among the well-known proverbs is that every possessor of a blessing is envied. The disbelievers' criticism of Jesus, peace be upon him, with this statement indicates that God's blessings upon him were great. Therefore, its mention is fitting when enumerating the blessings, for the reason we have mentioned.

Eighth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger﴾. The meaning of revelation has already been explained. Whoever says that they were prophets says: that revelation is the revelation given to the prophets. Whoever says that they were not prophets says: what is meant by it is inspiration, intuition, and the casting of something into the heart, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: suckle him﴾ (al-Qasas: 7), and His saying: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ (al-Nahl: 68). He mentioned this in the context of enumerating blessings because becoming a person whose word is accepted by people and who is beloved in their hearts is among the greatest of God's blessings upon a human being. God, may He be exalted, mentioned that when He cast that inspiration into their hearts, they believed and submitted.
