He mentioned belief before submission because belief is a quality of the heart, while submission is an expression of outward compliance and humility; that is, they believed with their hearts and complied with their outward selves.

If it is said: He, may He be exalted, said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿Remember My blessing upon you and upon your mother﴾, and yet all the blessings He mentioned are specific to Jesus, peace be upon him, and his mother has no connection to any of them.

We say: everything that the child attains of noble blessings and lofty ranks is attained by way of inclusion and following the mother. For this reason God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ (al-Muminun: 50), so He made them together one sign because of the strong connection of each of them to the other. It is narrated that when God, may He be exalted, said to Jesus: ﴿Remember My blessing upon you,﴾ he used to wear hair cloth, eat the leaves of trees, store nothing for the morrow, and say: "With each day comes its sustenance. Whoever has no house will be ruined, and whoever has no child will die. Wherever he spends the evening, he sleeps there."

[p. 103]

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 5, verses 110–111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When God said, "O Jesus son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you and upon your mother"﴾. There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** Know that we have explained that the purpose of His saying, may He be exalted, to the Messengers, ﴿What response did you receive?﴾, is to rebuke those among their nations who rebelled. The nation most in need of rebuke and censure is the Christians, who claim to be the followers of Jesus, peace be upon him. This is because the criticism of the other nations was limited to the prophets, whereas the criticism of these accursed people extended to the majesty and grandeur of God, in that they ascribed to Him what no rational person would ascribe to God, namely taking a wife and a son. Therefore God, may He be exalted, mentioned that He would enumerate the kinds of His blessings upon Jesus in the presence of the Messengers, one by one. The intent of this is to rebuke the Christians and reprimand them for the evil of their saying, since each one of those enumerated blessings upon Jesus indicates that he is a servant and not a god. The benefit of this narrative is to alert the Christians who were living at the time this verse was revealed to the ugliness of their saying and the feebleness of their creed and belief.

**The second issue:** The position of ﴿idh﴾ (when) may be in the nominative case as a subject, meaning: "That is when God said," and it may be that the meaning is: "Remember when God said."

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿When God said﴾ is expressed in the past tense rather than the future, and there are several reasons for this:

The first: it indicates the nearness of the Resurrection, so that it is as if it has already arisen and occurred, since everything that is coming is near. It is said: "The army has come" when their arrival is near. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿The command of God has come﴾ (al-Nahl: 1).

The second: it is a narration of a present state (*hikayat al-hal*, the narration of a state as if it were present). A parallel to this is a man saying to his companion: "It is as if you and I have entered such-and-such a town and done such-and-such there, when a crier cried out and you left me and answered him." A parallel to it in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified, with no escape﴾ (Saba': 51); ﴿If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve﴾ (al-Anfal: 50); ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾ (Saba': 31). The reason in all these verses is what we have mentioned, namely that it is expressed by way of narrating the state.

**The fourth issue:** ﴿Jesus son of Mary﴾ — "Jesus" may be in the nominative case, since it is a singular vocative (*munada*) described by an annexed noun. It may also be in the accusative case, since it is intended as an annexation, and then "son" was made an emphasis (*tawkid*). Anything similar to this allows two possibilities, as in *ya Zayd ibn ʿAmr* and *ya Zaydu ibn ʿAmr*. The grammarians have recited:

*O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud*

with the first (noun) in the nominative or the accusative, as we have explained.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿My blessing upon you﴾ intends the plural, like His saying: ﴿If you tried to count God's blessings, you could not number them﴾ (al-Nahl: 18). This is permissible because it is an annexed noun that can refer to a genus.

Know that God, may He be exalted, explained His blessing upon him by several matters, the first of which is His saying: ﴿When I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾. There are two views concerning it:

The first: The Holy Spirit is Gabriel, peace be upon him. "The Spirit" is Gabriel and "the Holy" is God, as if He annexed him to Himself in honour of him.

The second: Souls differ in their essence. Some are pure and luminous, some are wicked and dark, some are radiant, some are turbid, some are good, and some are base. For this reason he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Souls are armies mustered" (a *hadith*). God, may He be exalted, singled out Jesus with the pure, luminous, radiant, sublime, and good spirit. Someone may say: Since this verse indicates that the strengthening of Jesus came from Gabriel or through his particular spirit, this casts doubt on the evidence of miracles for the truthfulness of the Messengers. For before we know the infallibility of Gabriel, we may permit that he helped Jesus in this, in order to lead people astray and mislead them. So, as long as the infallibility of Gabriel is not known, this objection is not removed; and as long as the prophethood of Jesus, peace be upon him, is not known, the infallibility of Gabriel is not known, so a circularity arises. The answer to this is what is established in our principle, that the Creator is none other than God, and by this the objection is removed.

The second of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾. As for Jesus' speech in the cradle, it is his saying: ﴿I am a servant of God; He has given me the Scripture﴾ (Maryam: 30). His saying ﴿You spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*, a clause or phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). The meaning is: he speaks to them as a child and as a grown man, without his speech differing between these two times. This is a noble distinction which he possessed, and which none of the prophets before him or after him attained.

The third of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when I taught you the Book, the Wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel﴾.

Concerning "the Book" there are two views. One is that it means writing, which is script. The other is that it means the genus of books, since a person first learns short and easy books, then ascends from them to the noble books. As for "the Wisdom," it refers to the theoretical sciences and the practical sciences. Then He mentioned after it "the Torah and the Gospel," and concerning this there are two views:

The first: they were singled out for mention after the mention of the books as a mark of honour, like His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ (al-Baqarah: 238), and His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ (al-Ahzab: 7).

The second, which is the stronger: the grasp of the secrets of the divine books is attained only by one who has become proficient in the various kinds of the apparent legal and rational sciences which scholars investigate. Thus His saying "the Torah and the Gospel" refers to the secrets which no one comprehends except the greatest of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace.

* * *

The fourth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you shaped from clay the likeness of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it, and it became a bird by My permission﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Nafi' recited ﴿fa-takūnu ṭā'iran﴾ (it becomes a bird), and the others recited ﴿ṭayran﴾ without an *alif*. *Ṭayr* is the plural of *ṭa'ir*, like *ḍa'n* and *ḍa'in*, and *rakb* and *rakib*.

**The second issue:** Here He mentioned ﴿then you breathed into it﴾ (*fa-tanfukhu fīhā*, with feminine pronoun), while in Al ʿImran He mentioned ﴿then I breathe into it﴾ (*fa-anfukhu fīhi*, with masculine pronoun).

The answer: His saying ﴿the likeness of a bird﴾ means a form like the form of a bird. So His saying ﴿then you breathe into it﴾ has its pronoun referring to the *kāf* (the "like" of the likeness), because it is the description of the form which Jesus would create and breathe into; it does not refer to the form which is annexed to it, because that is not of his creation nor of his breathing in any way.

Having understood this, we say: the *kāf* is made feminine according to meaning, because it indicates the form which is like the form of a bird, and it is made masculine according to its outward form. Since this is so, it is permissible for the pronoun referring to it to occur sometimes in the masculine and sometimes in the feminine.

**The third issue:** He, may He be exalted, stipulated permission in the creation of the clay in the likeness of a bird, and in its becoming that thing a bird. He repeated His saying ﴿by My permission﴾ to emphasise that this occurred by the power of God, may He be exalted, and His creating it, not by the power of Jesus or his bringing it into being.

Fifth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you healed the blind-born and the leper by My permission﴾. The healing of the blind-born (*al-akmah*) and the leper is well known. Al-Khalili said: the *akmah* is one who was born blind, and the *a'ma* is one who was born seeing and then became blind.

Sixth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you brought the dead out by My permission﴾, that is, when you brought the dead out of their graves alive by My permission, i.e., by My doing that at your supplication, and at your saying to the dead: "Come out by God's permission from your grave." The mention of permission in these actions is only in the sense of attributing the real act to God, may He be exalted, like His saying: ﴿No soul can die except by God's permission﴾ (Al ʿImran: 145), meaning: except by God's creating death in it.

Seventh of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear signs﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

[p. 105]

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿when you came to them with the clear signs﴾ may mean these clear signs which were mentioned earlier; in this case the *alif* and *lam* are for previous reference. It may also mean the genus of clear signs.

**The second issue:** It is narrated that when he, peace and blessings be upon him, displayed these wondrous miracles, the Jews intended to kill him, but God, may He be exalted, rescued him from them by raising him to heaven.

* * *

Then God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Those of them who disbelieved said, "This is nothing but clear magic"﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *sahir* (a magician) with an *alif*, and likewise in Yunus, Hud, and al-Saff. Ibn ʿAmir and ʿAsim recited it with an *alif* only in Yunus, and the others recited *sihr* (magic). Whoever recited *sahir* indicates the man, and whoever recited *sihr* indicates by it what he brought. Both are good, because each of them has been mentioned before. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: the preferred reading is *sihr*, because it may be applied to the event and to the person. As for its application to the event, it is obvious. As for its application to the person, you say: "This is magic," meaning: "one who possesses magic," as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But righteousness is in him who believes﴾ (al-Baqarah: 177), meaning: one who has righteousness. The poet said:

*For it is only advance and retreat*

**The second issue:** If it is said: He, may He be exalted, began here to enumerate His blessings upon Jesus, peace be upon him, and the saying of the disbelievers about him, ﴿This is nothing but clear magic﴾, is not one of the blessings, so how did He mention it here?

The answer: Among the well-known proverbs is that every possessor of a blessing is envied. The disbelievers' criticism of Jesus, peace be upon him, with this statement indicates that God's blessings upon him were great. Therefore, its mention is fitting when enumerating the blessings, for the reason we have mentioned.

Eighth of them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger﴾. The meaning of revelation has already been explained. Whoever says that they were prophets says: that revelation is the revelation given to the prophets. Whoever says that they were not prophets says: what is meant by it is inspiration, intuition, and the casting of something into the heart, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: suckle him﴾ (al-Qasas: 7), and His saying: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ (al-Nahl: 68). He mentioned this in the context of enumerating blessings because becoming a person whose word is accepted by people and who is beloved in their hearts is among the greatest of God's blessings upon a human being. God, may He be exalted, mentioned that when He cast that inspiration into their hearts, they believed and submitted. He mentioned belief before submission because belief is a quality of the heart, while submission is an expression of outward compliance and humility; that is, they believed with their hearts and complied with their outward selves.

Whoever has no house will be ruined, and whoever has no child will die. Wherever he spends the evening, he sleeps there."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 112:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?"﴾ In this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** In His saying "(When [the disciples] said)" there are two possibilities:

The first: "I inspired the disciples when the disciples said."

The second: "Remember when the disciples said."

**The second issue:** "﴿Can your Lord﴾": al-Kisa'i read "(Can you [tasta'īu])" with a *ta'* and "(your Lord [rabbaka])" with a *fatha* on the *ba'*, with the *lam* of "hal" assimilated into the *ta'*. The reason for the assimilation is that the *lam* and the *ta'* are close in articulation, since both are among the letters of the tip of the tongue and the roots of the upper front teeth. The closer one letter is to another, the better assimilation becomes. This reading is related from Ali and Ibn Abbas. From Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, it is related that she said: "They were too knowledgeable about Allah to say 'Can He [yastati'u]?' They only said, 'Can you ask your Lord?'" And from "Mu'adh ibn Jabal": "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught me to read '(Can you [tasta'īu])' with a *ta'* and '(your Lord [rabbaka])' with a *fatha*."

The rest of the readers read "(Can He [yastati'u])" with a *ya'* and "(your Lord [rabbuka])" with a *damma* on the *ba'*, with the letters pronounced separately.

As for the first reading, its meaning is: "Can you ask your Lord?" They said: this reading is better than the second, because the second reading implies their doubt about the ability of Jesus, whereas the second implies their doubt about the ability of Allah. There is no doubt that the first is better.

As for the second reading, there is a difficulty in it: He, may He be exalted, related about them that they said: ﴿We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. How, after belief, is it permissible to say that they remained doubtful about the power of Allah, may He be exalted, to do that?

The answer to this is in several respects:

**The first:** He, may He be exalted, did not describe them as believers or Muslims. Rather, He related their claim to these two, and then followed that with His saying, as a report about them: ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ This indicates that they were doubtful and hesitant. Indeed, this statement does not come from one who is perfect in faith. They also said: ﴿and that we may know that you have spoken the truth to us﴾, and this indicates a sickness of the heart. Likewise, the saying of Jesus, peace be upon him, to them: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾ indicates that they were not perfect in faith.

**The second answer:** They were believers, but they asked for this sign so that they might gain greater tranquility, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿but [I ask] that my heart may be satisfied﴾. Witnessing such a sign undoubtedly produces tranquility, and for this reason they said: ﴿and our hearts may be assured﴾.

**The third answer:** The intent of this speech is a question about whether that is permissible in wisdom or not. This is because the acts of Allah, may He be exalted, are conditioned upon the consideration of aspects of wisdom. In a situation where no aspect of wisdom is present, the act is impossible, for what is impossible from the standpoint of wisdom is like what is impossible from the standpoint of power. This answer accords with the view of the Mu'tazila. As for our view, it is to be understood as: has Allah, may He be exalted, decreed that, and has He known its occurrence? For if He had not decreed it and had not known it would occur, it would be impossible and not within the scope of power, because the opposite of what is known is not within the scope of power.

**The fourth answer:** al-Suddi said: "﴿Can your Lord﴾" means: "Would your Lord obey you if you asked Him?" This is a derivation based on the view that *istatā'a* means *ata'a* (to obey), and the *sin* is additional.

**The fifth answer:** Perhaps the intended "Lord" is Gabriel, peace be upon him, because he used to nurture him and single him out with various kinds of help. For this reason He, may He be exalted, said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾, meaning: you claim that he nurtures you and singles you out with various kinds of honor, so can he send down a table from heaven upon you?

**The sixth answer:** The purpose of this question is not that they were doubtful about it. Rather, the purpose is to establish that this matter is extremely evident, like someone who takes the hand of a weak person and says: "Can the sultan feed this one?" His aim in saying this is that the matter is clear and obvious, and no sensible person may doubt it. So it is here as well.

**The third issue:** al-Zajjaj said: "(al-mā'ida [the table])" is a form of the verb *māda yamīdu*, meaning "to move," as if it sways with what is upon it. Ibn al-Anbari said: it was called *mā'ida* because it is a gift, from the Arabic saying: "Fulan *māda* Fulan *yamīduhu* *maydan*," meaning he did good to him. So *mā'ida*, according to this view, is a form of *al-mayd* in the sense of "giving." Abu Ubayda said: "(al-mā'ida)" is a form with the meaning of a passive participle, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾, and its origin is *mūdah*, meaning its owner was given it, i.e., it was given to him and he was favored with it. The Arabs say: "Fulan *mādanī* [favored me]," meaning he did good to him.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿He said, "Fear Allah, if you are believers."﴾ In this there are two possibilities:

The first: Jesus said: "Fear Allah concerning your specifying of the miracle, for it falls under the category of insistence and dictating, and for a servant in the presence of his Lord this is a grave sin. Also, it is a demand for a miracle after many miracles have already come, and this too is a grave sin."

The second: He commanded them to be conscious of Allah so that consciousness would become the means of attaining this request, as He said: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2–3], and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means to Him﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 35]. His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ means: if you are believers in His, may He be glorified and exalted, being capable of sending down the table, then fear Allah, so that your consciousness of Him may become a means to attaining this request.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be assured, and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truly to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾

The meaning is: when they made this request, Jesus said to them, "Indeed, many miracles have already preceded, so fear Allah in seeking this miracle after those overwhelming miracles." They replied and said, "We do not seek this table merely so that it may be a miracle, but for a collection of many matters:"

The first: "We wish to eat from it, for hunger has overcome us and we find no other food."

The second: "Although we know the power of Allah through proof, when we witness the descent of this table, certainty increases and tranquility grows stronger."

The third: "Although we know your truthfulness through all the other miracles, when we witness this miracle, certainty and recognition increase and tranquility is confirmed."

The fourth: "All those miracles you have brought were earthly miracles, whereas this is a heavenly miracle, and it is more wondrous and greater. So when we witness it, we shall be among its witnesses: we will bear witness concerning it to those of the Children of Israel who were not present, and we shall be among its witnesses to Allah for His perfect power, and to you for prophethood."

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said, "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, which will be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers."﴾

In this there are issues:

The first issue: As for the discussion of (Allahumma, "O Allah"), it has been treated thoroughly in the surah of Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Master of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. So His saying "Allahumma" is a vocative, and His saying "Rabbana" is a second vocative. As for His saying ﴿takunu lana﴾ ("be for us"), it is an attribute of the table and not a response to the imperative. In the reading of Abdullah it is (takun), because he made it a response to the imperative. Al-Farra' said: Whenever an indefinite noun is followed by an imperative, the verb after it may be in the jussive or the nominative. An example is His saying: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ ﴿who will inherit from me﴾ [Maryam: 5-6], with both jussive and nominative, and ﴿So send him with me as a helper, confirming me﴾ [al-Qasas: 34], with both jussive and nominative.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾, meaning: we shall take the day on which the table descends as a festival, which we and those who come after us will honor. It descended on a Sunday, and so the Christians took it as a festival. In the language, 'id (festival) is a name for what returns to you at a known time, and its derivation is from 'ada, ya'ud, so its root is return. The festival was named 'id because it returns every year with new joy. His saying ﴿and a sign from You﴾ means a proof of Your oneness and of the validity of the prophethood of Your messenger. ﴿And provide for us﴾ means: provide us with food that we may eat. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾.

The second issue: Reflect on this order. When the disciples asked for the table, they mentioned purposes in their request, placing the eating first, saying ﴿We wish to eat from it﴾, and postponing the spiritual religious purposes. As for Jesus, when he asked for the table and mentioned his purposes in it, he placed the religious purposes first and postponed the purpose of eating, saying ﴿and provide for us﴾. At this point there becomes apparent to you the ranks and degrees of the spirits, in that some are spiritual and some are corporeal. Then, because of the intensity of the purity of his religion and the radiance of his spirit, when Jesus, peace be upon him, mentioned provision with his words ﴿and provide for us﴾, he did not stop at it, but passed from the provision to the Provider, saying ﴿and You are the best of providers﴾. So his saying "Rabbana" is a beginning from him with the mention of the Real, glorified and exalted is He; his saying "send down upon us" is a transition from the Essence to the Attributes; his saying ﴿which will be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ is an indication of the spirit's delight in the blessing not insofar as it is a blessing, but insofar as it proceeds from the Benefactor; his saying ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is an indication that this table is a proof for the people of reflection and inference; and his saying ﴿and provide for us﴾ is an indication of the portion of the soul. All of this is a descent from the presence of majesty. So observe how he began with the most noble, then the more noble, descending to the lower and the lowest. Then he said ﴿and You are the best of providers﴾, which is an ascent once again from creation to the Creator, from other than Allah to Allah, and from the lowest to the most noble. At that point there becomes apparent to you a whiff of the manner of the ascent and descent of the luminous, radiant, divine spirits. O Allah, make us among its people.

The third issue: In the reading of Zayd, "yakunu lana 'idan li-awwalina wa-akhirina" (with the masculine verb), and the feminine form is in accordance with the meaning of "ayah" (sign).

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be assured, and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truly to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾

The meaning is: when they made this request, Jesus said to them, "Indeed, many miracles have already preceded, so fear Allah in seeking this miracle after those overwhelming miracles." They replied and said, "We do not seek this table merely so that it may be a miracle, but for a collection of many matters:"

The first: "We wish to eat from it, for hunger has overcome us and we find no other food."

The second: "Although we know the power of Allah through proof, when we witness the descent of this table, certainty increases and tranquility grows stronger."

The third: "Although we know your truthfulness through all the other miracles, when we witness this miracle, certainty and recognition increase and tranquility is confirmed."

The fourth: "All those miracles you have brought were earthly miracles, whereas this is a heavenly miracle, and it is more wondrous and greater. So when we witness it, we shall be among its witnesses: we will bear witness concerning it to those of the Children of Israel who were not present, and we shall be among its witnesses to Allah for His perfect power, and to you for prophethood."

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said, "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, which will be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers."﴾

As for His saying ﴿a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾, meaning: we shall take the day on which the table descends as a festival, which we and those who come after us will honor. In the language, 'id (festival) is a name for what returns to you at a known time, and its derivation is from 'ada, ya'ud, so its root is return. The festival was named 'id because it returns every year with new joy. His saying ﴿and a sign from You﴾ means a proof of Your oneness and of the validity of the prophethood of Your messenger. ﴿And provide for us﴾ means: provide us with food that we may eat. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾.

The second issue: Reflect on this order. When the disciples asked for the table, they mentioned purposes in their request, placing the eating first, saying ﴿We wish to eat from it﴾, and postponing the spiritual religious purposes. As for Jesus, when he asked for the table and mentioned his purposes in it, he placed the religious purposes first and postponed the purpose of eating, saying ﴿and provide for us﴾. At this point there becomes apparent to you the ranks and degrees of the spirits, in that some are spiritual and some are corporeal. Then, because of the intensity of the purity of his religion and the radiance of his spirit, when Jesus, peace be upon him, mentioned provision with his words ﴿and provide for us﴾, he did not stop at it, but passed from the provision to the Provider, saying ﴿and You are the best of providers﴾. So his saying "Rabbana" is a beginning from him with the mention of the Real, glorified and exalted is He; his saying "send down upon us" is a transition from the Essence to the Attributes; his saying ﴿which will be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ is an indication of the spirit's delight in the blessing not insofar as it is a blessing, but insofar as it proceeds from the Benefactor; his saying ﴿and a sign from You﴾ is an indication that this table is a proof for the people of reflection and inference; and his saying ﴿and provide for us﴾ is an indication of the portion of the soul. All of this is a descent from the presence of majesty. So observe how he began with the most noble, then the more noble, descending to the lower and the lowest. Then he said ﴿and You are the best of providers﴾, which is an ascent once again from creation to the Creator, from other than Allah to Allah, and from the lowest to the most noble. At that point there becomes apparent to you a whiff of the manner of the ascent and descent of the luminous, radiant, divine spirits. O Allah, make us among its people.

The third issue: In the reading of Zayd, "yakunu lana 'idan li-awwalina wa-akhirina" (with the masculine verb), and the feminine form is in accordance with the meaning of "ayah" (sign).

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God said: "Indeed, I will send it down to you. But whoever among you disbelieves afterward, I will surely punish him with a punishment with which I will not punish anyone among the worlds."﴾

Issues:

First issue: Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀsim and Nāfiʿ read ﴿munazziluhā﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdīd), while the rest read it without doubling (takhfīf). Both are two dialects (lughatān) meaning the same (nazala and anzala). It was also said: with tashdīd it means "sending it down again and again," and with takhfīf it means once.

Second issue: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves afterward﴾ means after the sending down of the table (al-māʾidah), ﴿I will punish him with a punishment with which I will not punish anyone among the worlds.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbās said: this means He will transform them into swine. It was also said: into monkeys. It was also said: a kind of punishment with which no one else will be punished. Al-Zajjāj said: it is possible that this punishment is hastened for them in this world, and it is possible that it is deferred to the Hereafter. As for His words ﴿among the worlds﴾, it means the worlds of their own time.

Third issue: It was said that they asked ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) this request when they were in a desert without water or food, and for this reason they said: "We want to eat from it."

Fourth issue: Scholars differed over whether ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) asked for the table for himself or asked it for his people, although he attributed it to himself outwardly. Both are possible, and God knows best.

Fifth issue: Scholars differed over whether the table was in fact sent down. Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid said it was not sent down, and they argued with two points:

The first: when the people heard His words ﴿I will punish him with a punishment with which I will not punish anyone among the worlds﴾, they sought forgiveness and said, "We do not want it."

The second: He described the table as an ʿīd (festival); if it had occurred, that ʿīd would have remained until the Day of Resurrection.

The great majority of exegetes said: it was sent down, [because God said]: ﴿Indeed, I will send it down to you﴾, and this is a definite promise of sending down without being conditioned on any condition, so this descent must have occurred.

The answer to the first point: His words ﴿But whoever among you disbelieves afterward, I will punish him﴾ are a condition and its consequence, having no connection to His words ﴿Indeed, I will send it down to you﴾.

The answer to the second point: the day it was sent down was an ʿīd for them and for those after them who were upon their law (sharʿ).

Sixth issue: It is related that when ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) wished to supplicate, he wore wool, then said: ﴿O God, our Lord, send down upon us﴾, and a red table (sufrah) descended between two clouds, one cloud above it and another below it, while they looked at it until it fell before them. Then he (peace be upon him) wept and said: "O God, make me among the grateful. O God, make it a mercy and do not make it a disfigurement and a punishment." And he said to them:

Page 111

"Let the best of you in deeds stand, uncover it, mention the name of God over it, and eat from it." Shamʿūn, the head of the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn), said: "You are most deserving of that." So ʿĪsā stood, performed ablution, prayed, and wept. Then he uncovered the cloth and said: "In the name of God, the best of providers." Behold, there was a roasted fish without thorns or scales, dripping fat; at its head was salt, at its tail vinegar, and around it were all kinds of herbs except leeks; and behold, there were five loaves of bread, on one of which was olives, on the second honey, on the third butter, on the fourth cheese, and on the fifth dried meat. Shamʿūn said: "O Spirit of God, is this from the food of this world or from the food of the Hereafter?" He said: "It is neither of them, but it is something God created by His exalted power. Eat what you have asked for, and be thankful, and God will increase you and add to you of His bounty." The disciples said: "O Spirit of God, if only you would show us another sign from this sign." He said: "O fish, come back to life by God's permission," and it thrashed. Then he said to it: "Return as you were," and it returned roasted. Then the table flew away. Then they disobeyed after it, and so they were transformed into monkeys and swine.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 5, verse 116:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when God says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God'?"﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** This is connected to His words: ﴿When God said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favor upon you"﴾. According to this view, this speech is addressed to Jesus on the Day of Resurrection. Others have said that God spoke these words to Jesus, peace be upon him, when He raised him up to Himself, and they relied on the apparent meaning of His words, ﴿And when God said﴾. The word (idh) is used for the past. The first view is more correct, because God followed this account with His words: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119], and this refers to the Day of Resurrection. As for relying on the word (idh), the answer to it has already been given.

**The second issue:** Regarding His words, ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"?﴾, there are two questions. The first: how does an interrogative form befit the Knower of the unseen? The second: God knew that Jesus, peace be upon him, had not said this, so why did He address him with it? If you say that the purpose is to rebuke and reprimand the Christians, we say: none of the Christians went so far as to affirm the divinity of Jesus and Mary while denying the divinity of God, so how is it permissible to attribute this statement to them when none of them said it?

The answer to the first question is that it is an interrogative used in the manner of denunciation.

The answer to the second question is that a god (ilah) is the Creator, and the Christians believe that the creator of the miracles that appeared at the hands of Jesus and Mary was Jesus, peace be upon him, and Mary, while God Most High did not create them at all. If that is so, then the Christians have said that the creator of those miracles is Jesus and Mary, and God Most High is not their creator. Thus it is correct that they affirmed, with regard to some things, that Jesus and Mary are two gods besides Him, while God Most High is not a god besides them. By this interpretation, this account and narration are valid.

*     *     *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say"﴾. As for His words, "Glory be to You," we have explained it in His words: ﴿Glory be to You, we have no knowledge﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32].

Know that when God Most High asked Jesus, "Did you say such and such?", Jesus did not say "I said it" or "I did not say it." Rather, he said: "It is not for me to say what I have no right to say," and this is not right. It implies that it is not for me to say this speech. When he had made clear that it was not for him to say this speech, he began to explain whether this statement had come from him or not. He did not say, "I did not say this speech," because that would amount to a claim of purity and freedom from blame, and the setting is one of humility and submission. Nor did he say, "I said it." Rather, he entrusted that matter to His all-encompassing knowledge of everything.

So he said: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾. This is an exaggeration in courtesy and in displaying humility and lowliness in the presence of majesty, and in wholly entrusting matters to the Truth, glorified is He.

*     *     *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself﴾. There are two issues regarding this:

**The first issue:** The commentators have mentioned various expressions for it: "You know what I conceal, and I do not know what You conceal." It has been said: "You know what is with me, and I do not know what is with You." It has been said: "You know what is in my unseen, and I do not know what is in Your unseen." It has been said: "You know what I did in the world, and I do not know what You will do in the Hereafter." It has been said: "You know what I say and do, and I do not know what You say and do."

**The second issue:** The Mujassimah (anthropomorphists) relied on this verse and said: the nafs (self) is the person, and that requires that He, exalted is He, be a body.

The answer to this is in two respects:

First: the nafs is an expression for the essence (dhat). It is said: "the nafs of a thing" and "its dhat" with one meaning.

Second: the intended meaning is "You know what I know, and I do not know what You know." However, He stated this speech in the manner of correspondence and parallelism (mutabaqah and mushakalah), which is a form of eloquent speech.

*     *     *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾. This is an emphasis of the two preceding clauses, namely His words, ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾, and His words, ﴿You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself﴾.

[p. 112]

Then Allah, exalted is He, said, relating the words of ʿIsa: ﴿I did not tell them anything except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ (An) is explanatory (mufassira), and what it explains is the pronoun in (bihi) ("with which"), which refers to the saying that was commanded. The meaning is: "I told them nothing except a saying You commanded me with, and that saying is that I should say to them: Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." Know that the original form would have been: "I did not command them except with what You commanded me," but he placed "saying" in the place of "command," out of regard for good manners, so that he would not make himself and his Lord two commanders together. The original form is indicated by the mention of the explanatory (an).
* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them⁠﴾, meaning: I was a witness over what they did for as long as I remained among them.

﴿Then when You caused me to die⁠﴾, and what is meant is death in the sense of being raised up to heaven, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will cause you to die and raise you to Myself⁠﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 55].

﴿You were the Watcher over them⁠﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the Guardian over them, the one who observes their conditions.

﴿And You are a Witness over all things⁠﴾. That is, You are the Witness regarding me while I was among them, and You are the Witness over them after my separation from them. So "shahid" means "witness," and it is permissible to interpret it as seeing, as knowing, or as speech in the sense of testimony. Thus "al-Shahid" is among the names of the real attributes under all these interpretations.

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise⁠﴾. And in this there are issues:

The first issue: the meaning of the verse is clear, but there is a question: how was it permissible for ʿIsa, peace be upon him, to say: ﴿and if You forgive them⁠﴾, when Allah does not forgive shirk?

The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: when Allah said to ʿIsa, peace be upon him: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?⁠﴾, it became known that a group of Christians related this statement from him, and one who relates this disbelief from another is not a disbeliever but a sinner, since he lied in this report; and forgiveness of sin is permissible. For this reason, he sought forgiveness from Allah, exalted is He.

The second: according to our school, it is permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to admit disbelievers into Paradise and to admit ascetics and worshippers into Hell, because the dominion is His and no one can object to Him. So ʿIsa mentioned this statement, and his purpose in it was to entrust all matters to Allah, and to abandon interference and objection entirely. For this reason he concluded the speech with His saying: ﴿indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise⁠﴾, meaning: You are capable of what You will, and wise in all that You do; no one can object to You. So who am I, and what business do I have delving into the affairs of lordship? As for his saying that Allah does not forgive shirk, we say: His forgiving it is permissible according to us and according to the majority of the Basran Mu'tazilites. They said: because punishment is a right of Allah over the sinner, and waiving it benefits the sinner, while waiving it does not harm Allah; so it must be good. Rather, the revealed textual evidence in our law indicates that it does not occur; perhaps this textual evidence did not exist in the law of ʿIsa, peace be upon him.

The third aspect of the answer: when that people uttered this disbelief, ʿIsa, peace be upon him, considered it possible that some of them had repented from it. So he said: ﴿If You punish them⁠﴾, meaning: I know that those who are punished died upon disbelief, so You may punish them because they are Your servants, and You have decreed punishment upon every one of Your servants who disbelieved; ﴿and if You forgive them⁠﴾, meaning: I know that they repented from disbelief, and You have decreed forgiveness for one who repents from disbelief.

The fourth aspect: we have mentioned that some people said that Allah's saying to ʿIsa: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?⁠﴾ was said at his being raised to heaven, not on the Day of Resurrection. According to this view, the answer is easy, because His saying: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants⁠﴾ means: if You cause them to die upon this disbelief and punish them, then they are Your servants and that is Your right; and if You bring them out by Your grace from the darkness of disbelief to the light of faith and forgive them what has passed of them, that is also Your right. On this interpretation, there is no difficulty.

The second issue: some of our companions used this verse as evidence for the intercession of Muhammad ﷺ on behalf of sinners. They said: ʿIsa's statement ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants⁠﴾ does not concern the people of reward, because punishment is not fitting for them; nor does it concern the disbelievers, because His saying ﴿and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise⁠﴾ is not fitting for them. So it indicates that this applies only to sinful believers. And if the intercession of sinners is established in the case of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, it is established in the case of Muhammad ﷺ a fortiori, since there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The third issue: al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated that in the codex of ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud) it reads: "And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful." I heard my shaykh and my father, may Allah have mercy on him, say: "The Exalted in Might, the Wise" is more fitting here than "the Forgiving, the Merciful," because His being Forgiving and Merciful resembles the state that necessitates forgiveness and mercy for every needy one; whereas might and wisdom do not necessitate forgiveness. For His being Mighty requires that He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, and that no one can object to Him; so when He is Mighty, exalted above all grounds of obligation, and then decrees forgiveness, generosity is more complete here than if His being Forgiving and Merciful were what necessitates forgiveness and mercy. Thus his expression, may Allah have mercy on him, would have been: "He is exalted above all, then He decrees mercy," and that would be more perfect. Other people said: if he had said, "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," this would have suggested that he was interceding for them. When he said, "indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise," this shows that his aim was to entrust the matter entirely to Allah, exalted is He, and to abstain from interfering in this matter in every respect.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿God said, "This is a day when the truthful will profit from their truthfulness."﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: They agreed that the intended meaning of "this day" is the Day of Resurrection, and the meaning is that their truthfulness in the world will benefit them in the Hereafter. The evidence that what we have mentioned is the intended meaning is that the truthfulness of the disbelievers will not benefit them on the Day of Resurrection. Do you not see that Iblis said: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], so this truthfulness did not benefit him. This statement is also a confirmation from God the Exalted of Jesus in his saying: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me to say﴾.

The second issue: The majority of reciters read (yawmu) with a ḍammah (raf', nominative), while Nafi' read it with a fatḥah (naṣb, accusative), and Abu 'Ubayda preferred this reading. As for the one who reads with the ḍammah, al-Zajjaj said: the estimated meaning is: "This day is the day of the benefit of the truthful." As for the naṣb, there are several possibilities:

The first: that it is an adverbial of time (ẓarf) for (qāla, "said"), and the estimated meaning is: "God said this statement to Jesus on the day when [the truthful] benefit."

The second: that the estimated meaning is: "This truthfulness occurs on the day when the truthful benefit from their truthfulness." It is permissible, according to this interpretation, to make time-adverbs predicates of events, as in your saying: "The fighting is on Saturday" and "The pilgrimage is on the Day of 'Arafah," meaning: it occurs on that day.

The third: al-Farra' said: "yawma" was attached to something that is not a noun, so it was built on the fatḥah, as in "yawma'idhin" (on that day). The Basrians said: this is an error, because a time-adverb is only built when it is attached to a built element, as in the poet al-Nabigha's saying:

"At the time when I reproached grey hair for youth"

(ḥīn) is built because it is attached to a built element, which is the past verb. Likewise His saying: ﴿on a day when no soul will possess anything﴾ [al-Infitar: 19] is built because it is attached to (lā), which is built. Here, however, the attachment is to an inflected element, because (yanfa'u, "benefits") is a present/future verb, and the future verb is inflected, so attachment to it does not require building. And God knows best.

* * *
Then God the Exalted said: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph.﴾

Know that when God informed that the truthfulness of the truthful in the world benefits them in the Hereafter, He explained the manner of that benefit, which is reward. The reality of reward is that it is pure, lasting benefit accompanied by honour. So His saying: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ indicates pure benefit free from grief and worry, and His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ indicates permanence. Consider this subtle point: wherever He mentions reward, He says: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, and wherever He mentions the punishment of sinful people among the believers, He mentions the word "khulūd" (abiding) without adding "ta'bīd" (eternity). As for His saying: ﴿God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph﴾, it indicates honour. This is the apparent view of the theologians (mutakallimūn). But according to the people of illuminated spirits, shining with the lights of God's majesty, beneath His saying: ﴿God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ there are wondrous secrets that pens do not permit such as these; may God make us among their people. As for His saying: ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, the majority hold that "that" refers to the whole of what preceded, from His saying: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾. In my view, it is possible that "that" is specific to His saying: ﴿God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾, for it is established among people of understanding that the entirety of Paradise with all that is in it, in relation to the good pleasure of God, is like nonexistence in relation to existence. How could it be otherwise, when Paradise is the object of desire and appetite, while good pleasure is an attribute of the Real? What correspondence is there between them? This statement repels the nature of the literalist speaker, but "each is made easy for that for which he was created."

* * *
Then God the Exalted said: ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾

It was said: this is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "Who gives them that great triumph?" So it was said: "The One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth." In this noble conclusion there are many secrets, and we mention a few of them. The first: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them﴾ and did not say "and whoever is in them," so He gave precedence to non-rational beings over rational ones. The reason for this is to alert that all created beings are subjected under the grip of His power, might, decree and destiny, and in that subjection they are like inanimate objects that have no power and like beasts that have no intellect. Thus the knowledge of all is, in relation to His knowledge, as no knowledge, and the power of all, in relation to His power, as no power. The second: the opening of the surah was with mention of the covenant concluded between lordship and servanthood, when He said: ﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts﴾. The perfect state of the believer is to begin in servanthood and to arrive at complete annihilation of the self. The first is the Sharia and is the beginning; the last is the Haqiqa (reality) and is the end. Thus the opening of the surah is from the Sharia, and its close is with mention of God's greatness, majesty, might, power and exaltedness, and that is the arrival at the station of Reality. How excellent, then, is the correspondence between that opening and this close.

The third: the surah includes many kinds of knowledge. Among them is the explanation of laws, rulings and obligations. Among them is the debate with the Jews over their denial of the Sharia of Muhammad (ﷺ), and among them is the debate with the Christians over their saying of the Trinity. So He closed the surah with this comprehensive point establishing all these matters, for He said: ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them﴾. Its meaning is that everything other than the Real, glorified is He, is possible in its essence and existent through His bringing into existence, exalted is He. Since this is so, He is the owner of all possible and existing things, the originator of all spirits and bodies. Once this is established, there follows the establishment of all the matters mentioned in this surah. As for the rightness of imposing obligations however He wills and desires, this is established, because He, glorified is He, since He is owner of all, may dispose of all by command, prohibition, reward and punishment as He wills and desires; so the claim of imposing obligations in whatever manner the Real, glorified and exalted is He, intends is sound. As for the refutation of the Jews, since He, glorified is He, is owner of the dominion, He has the right by virtue of ownership to abrogate the Sharia of Moses and establish the Sharia of Muhammad, upon both of them be blessings and peace. Thus their being two created servants is established. It is therefore apparent, by the demonstration we have mentioned, that this verse which God made the conclusion of this surah is a decisive proof of the soundness of all the sciences which this surah contains. And God knows best the secrets of His speech.

The commentary on this surah is complete, by the praise and grace of God, and may His blessings be upon the best of His creation, our master Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, and may He grant them abundant peace.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿God said, "This is a day when the truthful will profit from their truthfulness."﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: They agreed that the intended meaning of "this day" is the Day of Resurrection, and the meaning is that their truthfulness in the world will benefit them in the Hereafter. The evidence that what we have mentioned is the intended meaning is that the truthfulness of the disbelievers will not benefit them on the Day of Resurrection. Do you not see that Iblis said: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], so this truthfulness did not benefit him. This statement is also a confirmation from God the Exalted of Jesus in his saying: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me to say﴾.

The second issue: The majority of reciters read (yawmu) with a ḍammah (raf', nominative), while Nafi' read it with a fatḥah (naṣb, accusative), and Abu 'Ubayda preferred this reading. As for the one who reads with the ḍammah, al-Zajjaj said: the estimated meaning is: "This day is the day of the benefit of the truthful." As for the naṣb, there are several possibilities:

The first: that it is an adverbial of time (ẓarf) for (qāla, "said"), and the estimated meaning is: "God said this statement to Jesus on the day when [the truthful] benefit."

The second: that the estimated meaning is: "This truthfulness occurs on the day when the truthful benefit from their truthfulness." It is permissible, according to this interpretation, to make time-adverbs predicates of events, as in your saying: "The fighting is on Saturday" and "The pilgrimage is on the Day of 'Arafah," meaning: it occurs on that day.

The third: al-Farra' said: "yawma" was attached to something that is not a noun, so it was built on the fatḥah, as in "yawma'idhin" (on that day). The Basrians said: this is an error, because a time-adverb is only built when it is attached to a built element, as in the poet al-Nabigha's saying:

"At the time when I reproached grey hair for youth"

(ḥīn) is built because it is attached to a built element, which is the past verb. Likewise His saying: ﴿on a day when no soul will possess anything﴾ [al-Infitar: 19] is built because it is attached to (lā), which is built. Here, however, the attachment is to an inflected element, because (yanfa'u, "benefits") is a present/future verb, and the future verb is inflected, so attachment to it does not require building. And God knows best.

* * *
Then God the Exalted said: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph.﴾

Know that when God informed that the truthfulness of the truthful in the world benefits them in the Hereafter, He explained the manner of that benefit, which is reward. The reality of reward is that it is pure, lasting benefit accompanied by honour. So His saying: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ indicates pure benefit free from grief and worry, and His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ indicates permanence. Consider this subtle point: wherever He mentions reward, He says: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, and wherever He mentions the punishment of sinful people among the believers, He mentions the word "khulūd" (abiding) without adding "ta'bīd" (eternity). As for His saying: ﴿God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph﴾, it indicates honour. This is the apparent view of the theologians (mutakallimūn).
